News.title: Meghan Markle’s dad’s handwriting ‘probably matches’ labels on child abuse DVDs, forensic expert claims
News.content:
Next

HANDWRITING by the Duchess of Sussex’s estranged father appears to match that on DVDs of the most extreme abuse images, it is claimed.

Six discs labelled with marker pen contained the worst kind of illegal content in the giant stash handed to child protection officers in the Philippines.



And the distinctive lettering was found to be a probable match to handwritten notes penned by 82-year-old Thomas Markle Snr.

In what appeared to be a ballpoint pen draft of a letter among his belongings, he railed at daughter Meghan’s refusal to meet him.



He sniped: “There are men sitting in prison who have committed unspeakable crimes and murder and their daughters visit them.”

The letters and other handwritten notes have now been compared with writing on the DVDs.



Eminent forensic document analyst Susan Ord told The Sun: “In my opinion, it is probable the handwritten letters and writing on the gold CDs are written by the same person.

“There are some similarities between some of the handwriting on paper and writing on the CDs.

“Any differences could be due to different writing tools used, writing surfaces, or natural variation.”

The handwriting clue emerged yesterday as cops began analysing Markle Snr’s computers, DVDs, mobile phones, VHS and Hi8 tapes, film negatives, SD data cards, books and pictures.



Horrific abuse content has already been linked to the ex-Hollywood lighting director after searches aided by an IT technician found his CV and phone number on a hard drive.

He is now formally under investigation by the Philippines National Police’s Women and Children Protection Centre in a probe which looks certain to be expanded to the US and Mexico.

News.title: Brexit row erupts as No10 backtracks on Andy Burnham’s EU free movement referendum pledge
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham’s bid to betray Brexit was in chaos last night as No10 backtracked on a promised referendum on free movement.

The PM had suggested earlier in the day that he would not return Britain to the EU’s visa-free arrangement without holding a public vote.



Yet within hours his spokeswoman said the “process” of getting closer to Brussels had not been decided, adding: “We are not talking about a referendum.”

It came after Mr Burnham said signing up to the EU’s freedom of movement could form part of his wider renegotiation with the bloc.



This would allow 450million EU citizens the unfettered right to live and work in the UK.

But it remains a “red line” in Labour’s manifesto, along with rejoining the customs union and single market during this Parliament.



The PM was asked yesterday on ITV’s Good Morning Britain if he would reinstate free movement without a referendum.

He replied: “No. Yesterday, I was asked about how things have changed in the ten years since Brexit, and the truth of the matter is we’ve lost immigration control in the way that we once had.”

When pushed about whether he wanted Britain to rejoin the EU, he replied: “In my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here.”

During this summer’s Makerfield by-election, Mr Burnham said he did not want to “re-run” the Brexit arguments.



The constituency voted heavily to leave the EU during the 2016 referendum.

Top Tory Alex Burghart said: “The PM’s remarks are proof that he has completely abandoned the people of Makerfield.

“Rejoining the EU will not cut the ballooning welfare bill, fund our Armed Forces or help control immigration.”

News.title: How Trump is plotting ‘short, sharp’ 72hr strike to cripple Iran & force regime’s hand as US deploys third attack team
News.content:
Next

DONALD Trump is planning to cripple Iran with a “short and sharp” strike campaign in a final bid to force the regime’s hand, experts say.

Months into deadlocked peace talks, Tehran remains steadfast in its refusal to back down and meet US demands to dismantle its nuclear programme.



To break the stalemate, the US president has deployed forces to the Middle East as he prepares to unleash one final, debilitating blitz.

Former British army officer Simon Diggins told The Sun: “This particular campaign is going to be short and sharp.”



Current and former officials have reportedly said it is a case of when, not if, Trump issues the order.

They believe strikes will resume before the end of the year, likely after the US midterm elections on November 3.

A renewed offensive will likely see the US return to its initial tactics used at the start of the war – a “high intensity” bombing campaign.

Simon said: “Currently the planning is about a seventy two hour attack. That might be 72 hours across days or a week.



“The 72 hours at the very beginning of the war in February was extremely effective.”

On February 28, US and Israeli forces launched joint strikes on Iran, killing the regime’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, along with senior military commanders in an astonishing blitz.

Trump had suggested on Friday that the US could launch renewed military operations, which he dubbed “another little Epic Fury”.

Simon said: “At the moment, the US have got two US carrier battlegroups in the region.

“Early November, they’ll have a third, which of course coincides with the November midterms elections.



“It gives the US significant additional firepower and everything goes with it.”

Even as the threat of a new war with the US looms, Iran’s hardliners have urged their parliament to withdraw from its nuclear non-proliferation treaty.

The Front of Islamic Revolution Stability, a political faction, said the move should be made “as quickly as possible”.



It is the latest defiant message from the Islamic State since the US launched its war on Iran to block the rogue nation’s nuclear programme.

A fresh wave of strikes will aim to “put the pressure on the Iranian government to concede, particularly on the nuclear programme”.

Simon said: “It will be attacking civilian targets rather than purely military targets,” Simon said.

“They’re looking particularly at energy – things that will have a direct and immediate impact on Tehran’s ability to govern its own people.”

US Central Command is also said to be developing a list of potential targets across Iran‘s nuclear infrastructure.



Pickaxe Mountain, where Tehran is said to be hiding stockpiles of near weapons-grade uranium, would be an obvious target, Simon said.

Known in Farsi as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La, the suspected nuclear lab is situated just 2km south of the Natanz uranium enrichment plant.

It remained untouched by US-Israeli strikes during the 12-day war in June 2025.



Israel believes Tehran moved thousands of uranium-enrichment centrifuges deep inside Pickaxe Mountain shortly after the targeted bombing campaign of nuclear sites that summer.

And last month, experts from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) said satellites had revealed more activity at Pickaxe Mountain in 2026 “than at any point in the site’s history”.

Simon said: “It is Iran’s ultimate safe place for their production of nuclear weapons or nuclear missiles.

“But it’s hard to get to. In the past the Americans have had success hitting these targets with buster bunker bombs.”

Washington’s best bet for the job is its GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator (MOP), deployed for the first time last year.



The coordinated attacks across Iran will be aimed at “bringing about a significant negotiation”, Simon said.

The objectives are threefold – to ban Iran’s nuclear programme, reopen the strait of Hormuz and force regime change, he added.

The US and Iran struck a ceasefire in a mid-June Memorandum of Understanding, to pause the full-scale conflict.

But the two sides remain at odds over the meaning of the MoU’s clauses related to the Strait of Hormuz – a crucial transport route for one fifth of the world oil.

The deadlock over the waterway over the past eight months has sparked huge disruption to global energy supplies, resulting in skyrocketing oil prices.



Any attack launched by the US or Israel would trigger immediate retaliatory strikes against American facilities in the region, Simon said.

But Iranian forces are now more familiar with US tactics.

“We would expect the Iranians to try and do something to try and disrupt this particular attack.



“But they would also conduct what they’ve done in the past, a whole series of attacks.

“Not just on the Strait of Hormuz but attacking the US allies in the region.”

Iran and the Houthis are said to be taking possible renewed attacks very seriously, two US officials told CNN.

Tehran and its militia proxies ramped up attacks across the Middle East following the outbreak of the US-Iran war.

Last week the US ordered diplomats and their families to evacuate Saudi Arabia, amid growing concerns that hostilities could flare up in a fresh conflict involving the Iran-backed Houthis.



The state department is said to be braced to order diplomats to leave embassies across several other Gulf states, three US officials said.

But the US has “changed posture” for its latest campaign, and a fresh wave of attacks will no longer jeopardise the safety of its gulf allies.

Simon said: “The US are not relying on those bases. In the earlier campaigns this year, the US very largely based itself in Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Iraq and Kuwait to conduct attacks.

“That then drew a response onto those countries.



“This time the main campaign will be conducted by US forces themselves using their own carrier battle groups and strikes from there.”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been pushing to carry out new attacks against Iran.

It comes as Trump endorsed Netanyahu ahead of Tuesday’s crucial elections, so that the pair could “finish the job” in Iran.

In the Truth Social post, Trump said: “When you go to the polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!



“We did Operation Epic Fury, and Iran now has No Navy, No Air Force, and both their Military and Economy are in shambles.

“Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started!”

Israel was preparing for the possibility of launching additional attacks against Iran in the last week, US officials told CNN.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Tel Aviv had been lobbying the US to support new strikes but senior American officials held off, signalling instead that the two countries would launch joint strikes soon.

Officials say that Trump has not made up his mind on what he will do after the midterms but he appears to be leaning toward ordering major action.

News.title: Inside Thomas Markle investigation room as cops probing child sex claims warn ‘no-one does this to our children’
News.content:
Next

A FILIPINO police chief analysing a hoard of alleged child abuse images belonging to the Duchess of Sussex’s estranged dad Thomas Markle Snr warned that no one “does this to our children”.

At a press conference held after the last of the material was signed over to police by Markle Snr’s son Thomas Jnr, the police also vowed to find any victims who may appear in the vile stash.



Philippine National Police spokesman Colonel Allen Rae Co said the digital forensic examination had started as they displayed the vast number of items being looked at.

He said of IT searches: “We have to establish the file and its nature, the origin of the files as well as ownership of these materials.



“If there will be evidence found of any wrongdoing, we will have to establish possession during the relevant timeline, as well as the identities of the victims if there are any.”

He added: “We are very saddened by this, and we will not let anybody, whether foreign national or Filipino national, do this to our children.”

The PNP said the initial examination of the material could take about a week.

Meanwhile, the Philippines’ elite National Bureau of Investigation director Melvin Matibag confirmed his organisation had been in contact with counterparts in the FBI over Markle Snr’s case.

Thomas Jnr handed over four large boxes of items last week — including a mass of unviewed material — as Philippines sources said filth found so far could be “the tip of the iceberg”.

At the same time, he provided a sworn statement pledging to have told the truth while he was warned he faced jail if he had lied about any aspect of the case.



He returned to give a supplementary affidavit yesterday before Cebu City prosecutors, giving consent for cybercrime experts to examine the stash.

Thomas Jnr told The Sun yesterday: “It’s been a long process but I’m determined to cooperate fully in the hope that justice will be done.

“It took nine hours to sign all the documentation as I handed over all that stuff but I was relieved to get it off my hands.



“I think it will take months to check all these items and confirm my father is the disgusting monster I’ve now disowned.

“But if it transfers to the US, I’d be prepared to fly to Florida, or wherever he is, to see him in court.”

Window fitter Thomas Jnr became his father’s full-time carer after he suffered a stroke in 2022 and moved to Mexico to support him.

The pair relocated to Cebu City in the Philippines in January 2025 before a life-threatening blood clot led to the amputation of award-winning lighting technician Markle Snr’s left leg.

He was forced to return for treatment in the US, leaving behind a large collection of belongings where his son claims to have found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child abuse images.



A police forensic trawl began yesterday after Philippines interior minister Jonvic Remulla said all signs point to Markle Snr being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind”.

Markle Snr’s belongings — itemised in 80 categories on a police inventory list — were being combed through by Cebu’s Regional Anti Cybercrime Unit 7 last night.

A well-placed legal source said: “The interior minister has estimated that a report on the contents could take just a week but the scale of the task suggests it could take much longer.”



The source said if evidence pointed to a strong case “as seems likely” a report would be sent to the Department of Justice.

They added: “The DoJ will then decide whether any attempt should be made to extradite the suspect in the US or hand the case to the FBI through established channels.

“There is no question in my mind that a specialist working on the material now will be able to confirm the identity of the person responsible for downloading illegal images.”

Horrific abuse content has already been linked to the ex- Hollywood lighting director after searches aided by an IT technician found his CV and phone number on a hard drive.

He is formally under investigation by the Philippines National Police’s Women and Children Protection Centre in an inquiry which looks certain to be expanded to the US and Mexico.



Data checks showed all of the illegal material was downloaded in 2014 and 2020 — long before he moved to the Philippines with his son Thomas Jnr, 60, in January last year.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

FBI investigators have confirmed their interest amid concerns about potential offences while Markle Snr was living in Chicago, Hollywood and Pennsylvania.

Authorities in Mexico were also understood to be standing by — as Meghan’s father lived in the city of Rosarito at the time the hard drives were loaded with horrendous content.

News.title: Army officer, 26, was ‘killed by armoured vehicle during training exercise after order given to reverse at speed’
News.content:
TRAGIC END Army officer, 26, was ‘killed by armoured vehicle during training exercise after order given to reverse at speed’







Next

AN ARMY officer was killed after an armoured vehicle was ordered to reverse at speed during a training exercise, an inquest heard.

Second Lieutenant Max George, 26, died instantly on Salisbury Plain in June 2022 after being struck by a 28-tonne Warrior vehicle.



The tragedy unfolded after the Warrior’s commander gave the order to quickly reverse without realising Lt George was exiting the vehicle.

Members of 5 Rifles had been taking part in Exercise Combat Spirit where two groups of soldiers had been moving in on a target, with Lt George ordered to take command on the ground.



As the Warrior halted the gunner threw a smoke grenade and Lt George was told to exit, the inquest heard.

Lt George, from County Durham, was reaching back inside to grab his weapon and kit when the vehicle surged backwards, knocking him to the ground, the court heard.



Horrified comrades screamed, waved their hands, and sounded horns to abort the move, but their desperate warnings came too late.

Wiltshire and Swindon Coroner’s Court were told that the alarm, which was designed to alert the driver when the Warrior’s rear doors were open, had been faulty since 2018.

Lieutenant Colonel Graham Watson, who led a service inquiry into the incident, told the court that the alarms were installed after two fatal incidents in the 1990s.

He said several faults with the Warrior were known about, but none meant the vehicle should have been taken out of service.



Col Watson said: “One was the rear door alarm cable had snapped, which was first identified on June 20 2018.

“Lt George exited the vehicle and was seen momentarily struggling either with a day sack or trying to free a radio antenna which may have snagged.

“He then went to grab his weapon which was still inside the vehicle and simultaneously the student commander commanded the gunner to reverse the turret to the right in the direction of the enemy.

“The student commander checked through the periscopes and could no longer see the open doors, or Lt George at the rear of the vehicle.

“Believing Lt George was clear the student commander commanded the driver to reverse.



“Lt George was still at the rear reaching for his weapon. He was knocked to the ground.”

Col Watson said between 38 and 43 seconds elapsed between the Warrior stopping and the collision, with witnesses trying to “warn of the impending danger”.

Lt George’s exit from the vehicle created a “clunking noise”, which may have led the vehicle commander to assume he was clear and had shut the doors, the officer said.

“The built in alarm would have alarmed because the rear doors were open, and had that gone off the driver would have almost certainly stopped,” Col Watson said.

“In addition, on the driver’s instrument panel, because the rear doors were open there should have been a light, but again because the wiring loop was damaged that didn’t light up.”



The inquest also heard the exercise was using two types of Warrior – the FV-510 and FV-511 models – and Lt George’s vehicle was not ordinarily used for disembarking troops and close combat.

Col Watson said: “In general, the crew and service personnel within 5 Rifles were not that familiar with the FV-511 and its differences with the FV-510.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said the service inquiry found two causal factors, 22 contributory factors, and 22 other factors in Lt George’s death.

The inquest continues.

News.title: Poppies honour our fallen heroes – so how on earth did wearing one get a veteran barred from Spoons?
News.content:
Next

THE poppy really could do with a new PR.

Certainly it’s been a rough couple of weeks for the sweet botanical beast, and what was once simply a nice flower/symbol of bravery and hope, is now something of a political hot potato.





To recap, first we had some bloke trying to flog his silly “Palestine poppy” on eBay for £1.78 a pop — a complete subversion of all the original badge stood for courtesy of the Cult of Performative Palestine.

And — having already had to overcome a dastardly, centuries-old opium issue (pin your poppy, kids; don’t smoke it), now the poor flower is not allowed into the pub for a pint.

Yep, social media was awash with moral outrage on Sunday night as footage of an over-zealous bouncer refusing entry to a proud, poppy-sporting veteran went viral.

Scott Schillemore, 33, was left baffled, and thirsty, after being told: “You’re not coming in” by a bouncer at The Star in Gosport, Hampshire.

The boozer in question is a Wetherspoons in a historic naval town, for goodness’ sake! And the vet, who lost a pal in Afghanistan, is a former Royal Artillery gunner.

The manager then came out to explain the bizarre measure was a “blanket rule” covering anything, including Pride flags, that could be perceived as political.

Unsurprisingly, people were quick to kick off once footage got leaked by a Reform councillor.

“There wouldn’t be a pub if British men hadn’t fought and died for this country, including family of my own — I will never set foot in a Wetherspoons again,” ranted one user on Instagram.





Others called for the boycott of the chain, citing various shades of “the world’s gone mad” — but with fruitier language.

In the doorman’s computer-says-no defence, earlier in the day there had been a 400-strong anti-immigrant protest, marching through Gosport in anger at small boats.

Although, frankly, I’m fairly sure most of those protesting, many of them likely proud nationalists, would have been wearing poppies themselves.

And people unlikely to take offence to a decorative little red poppy worn on the lapel of, say, a puffer jacket.

For those at the back, let’s remind ourselves why we wear poppies in the build-up to November 11 Remembrance Day in the first place.

An enduring ­symbol of both sacrifice and hope for the brave soldiers who lost their lives in World War One — bright red corn poppies were the first plants to grow across the desolate, churned-up battlefields — the poppy is a lasting legacy of our country’s proud history.

The red petals represent blood shed during wartime, the black centre honours the memory of those who died and the green leaf symbolises both hope and renewal.

And let’s not forget: wearing one raises funds for veterans, current service members and their families through organisations like the Royal British Legion.



Yesterday a scrabbling Wetherspoons publicist — perhaps the poppy can be his next client — was quick to issue an explanation, of sorts.

“Wetherspoon has been a long-standing supporter of the Royal British Legion Poppy Appeal with poppies for sale in our pubs, including The Star,” the spokesperson said, quite frantically.

“There is no ban on poppies in Wetherspoon pubs.”

But they did acknowledge “some standard security measures were implemented due to the demonstrations in the town.”

Too little, too late chaps.

GIVE IT A REST ON MEG

SO many questions surrounding the astonishing – and unbearably bleak – developments around Thomas Markle.

The alleged paedophile monster, who denies all accusations despite mounting evidence, has dominated news headlines over the past five days in the wake of The Sun’s revelations.

I, for one, am now viewing his daughter Meghan in a very different light – and wrote a piece on Friday to this effect.

It caused quite the stir, with hundreds of people messaging me to insist they were furiously “unfollowing”, and that Meghan was, and is, still awful.



Think what you like about the Duchess of Sussex – and certainly she isn’t perfect – but this is a horrifying story about a man’s reported wrongdoing.

Yet people are still rapid to point the finger of blame at the woman.

Why did she not raise the flag earlier after receiving a letter in 2019 about Thomas Snr’s proclivities, for instance?

Well, as Meghan herself has said, she trusted the authorities – the Met police – to do their job and pass on all relevant information.

Had she spoken out, surely, she’d have been at risk of jeopardising any ongoing criminal investigation?

It’s absolutely fair enough people have questions, but let’s give the woman a break.

On a human level, I also cannot imagine how hard it must be to discover your father, once your idol, reportedly is so depraved.

Right now, there is only one monster in this scenario – and it ain’t Meghan Markle.

PLEASE BANISH TRAITORS TEDIUM

WHISPER it, but I think I might be getting Traitors fatigue.



After an absolutely brilliant, water-cooler TV moment opener – Richard E Grant’s blunder – is it just me, or is the cult-like BBC One series now getting a tad, well, dull?

Thankfully with two episodes and ten players left, including comedian Romesh Ranganathan, there’s time, still, for me to be proven wrong.

Here’s hoping.

BYTE SIZED FAILS

FRET not, chaps – AI isn’t coming to replace us all just yet.

Just Eat, the popular online food-delivery service, endured something of a catastrophic cock-up after entrusting an artificial intelligence generator to illustrate its menus.

From a jacket potato, which was literally depicted as a jacket covered in baked spuds, to tiger prawns reimagined as mini big cats in a soup dish, the internet has had a field day.

Other highlights include a “catfish pepper soup” showing a kitten’s head on a fish body, in a bowl of broth, and, my personal favourite, “toad in the hole” depicting an actual toad buried in an earth mound.

A Just Eat spokesperson has since confirmed the images are being removed, with the company pressing pause on the trial until the technology is up to scratch.

OUR social media-loving government had a little backfire over the weekend.



After posting a reminder about the clocks going back, asking “What will you do with the extra time? Comment below”, alongside a pointy finger emoji, jesters were quick to respond.

“Get taxed on it knowing you lot,” remarked one.

“Great – an extra hour of you useless c****”, replied another.

And so it went on.

Great British Public 1: AB and co. 0.

MEME OF THE WEEK

Honestly, at this stage, I won’t be far behind.

STAR TURN FOR PETS ON the subject of dogs, last week I wrote a column item about a miniature dachshund I’d met called Deirdre Barlow. Lots of you subsequently wrote in to share your own wonderfully considered pets’ names. So here is a round-up of my Top 5. Alan Titchmarsh, cocker spaniel Dolly Pawton, tabby cat Lady Penelope, French bulldog Winnie the Poodle Colin the dachshund Plus, a special mention to my parents’ late Shih Tzu, Camilla Parker-Bowles x

GOOD to see local authorities stepping up to the plate in these difficult times.

Yep, Bedford Borough Council sent an official to investigate a 12-year-old girl’s pretend teddy bear cafe.



A video now circulating on X shows an officious, card-bearing woman from the council’s planning department being given a tour of the venue – one showing seven stuffed cuddly toys sitting around a table “supping” from little porcelain cups and saucers.

The teddies were using Monopoly money to “pay” for their treats.

God help us all.

News.title: Lavish lunches, gagging clauses & sweetheart deals – inside Man City’s Abu Dhabi empire and PM’s role in ‘sell-off’
News.content:
Next

IT stands as the gleaming, £300million jewel in the crown of Manchester’s modern makeover.

With its plush, 401-room hotel, buzzing fanzone and swanky dining plaza, Medlock Square is the latest development bankrolled by billionaire Manchester City owner Sheikh Mansour.





Opened last month, it is next door to the £450million Etihad Stadium, home of City superstars such as Erling Haaland and Phil Foden.

There is also the £200million City Football Academy and the £365million Co-op Live arena, all part of the world-class Etihad Campus.

The regeneration of Manchester is the much-vaunted “success story” that has propelled Andy Burnham all the way to Downing Street.

The so-called King Of The North, who was mayor of Greater Manchester before becoming Prime Minister in the summer, is credited with dragging the city away from its crumbling industrial past and transforming it into a booming global metropolis.

But behind the glittering glass towers lies the wholesale sell-off of a great British city to an oil-rich foreign country.

The Prime Minister has faced scrutiny over his cosy, back-scratching relationship with Man City’s Emirati executives.

The Sun discovered Burnham met the club’s Abu Dhabi chiefs at least SEVEN times as mayor — blowing apart his claim of one significant meet-up.

Burnham raised eyebrows after he said that he would be “really concerned to lose” the Abu Dhabi owners as City was found guilty of 114 breaches of Premier League financial rules.





The row has led to serious questions over the scale of Sheikh Mansour’s Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) and the UAE’s investments in the UK, particularly Manchester.

The sheer scale of the desert state’s grip on the city is staggering.

Firms linked to the United Arab Emirates now own almost 40 per cent more land across Greater Manchester than a decade ago.

The number of plots snapped up by UAE-connected outfits rocketed from 51 in 2016 to 168 this year — covering a massive 250 acres.

Sheikh Mansour controls at least 34 of those sites, including the Etihad Stadium and enormous slices of Ancoats and New Islington, giving his firms two thirds of all Emirati-held land.

The remaining land grab is driven by other Gulf corporations — including the Abu Dhabi government’s buyout of three private hospitals in Cheadle, Rochdale and Bolton.

At the heart of the scrutiny is the £1.25billion mega-deal struck between the ADUG and Manchester City Council to regenerate vast swathes of residential areas of the city.

Critics have called for more transparency around the deal, which led to the creation of Manchester Life — a flagship urban regeneration firm majority-controlled by Sheikh Mansour, with the council retaining a minority stake.

Ever since it emerged that the deal included 999-year leases on land grabs, sceptics have asked why the council has jumped into bed with a desert nation globally criticised over its human rights record.

In fairness, the Manchester Life contract was signed a year and a half before Burnham first became mayor in 2017.



Nonetheless, many still accuse him of doing little to unpick the sell-off to a foreign state.

Labour figures have defended the scheme, which saw 1,500 new homes built, the preservation of two historic mills and the creation of 30,000 square feet of commercial space, with solid returns for the council.

They point to how the city’s economy has boomed as a result of the foreign investment.

You only need to walk a few minutes east of Manchester city centre from New Islington into Ancoats to see the scale of change.

Where derelict cotton mills once stood, block after block of shiny new residential developments line a glittering canal marina.

But while Sheikh Mansour — who is the deputy prime minister of the UAE and related to the Crown Prince — got the red carpet treatment, it is claimed other major developers in the northwest of England were ignored.

A 2022 report by academics at the University of Sheffield claims the terms of the deal were startlingly favourable for Abu Dhabi.

The paper stated the joint venture shifted public assets into corporate entities registered in Jersey.



And it calculated that local taxpayers lost out on an estimated £33million in land value plus £1.7million a year in lost ground rent — money that could have fully covered the city’s annual emergency housing bill.

Instead, the profits flow to an autocratic elite halfway across the globe.

Shockingly, despite a big homelessness problem in Manchester, the nine developed Manchester Life sites contain no social or affordable housing.

Two-bed flats routinely sell for over £350,000 — completely out of reach for local working families.

Nathan Evans, leader of the Conservative group on Trafford Council and a member of the Overview and Scrutiny Committee of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority, said he finds the Abu Dhabi takeover “very distasteful”.

“In my view, Manchester is 100 per cent built on Abu Dhabi and foreign money,” he added.

“But I think people are just starting to really have a proper look at it and seriously question why they want to roll Burnham’s model out across the country.

“Every single thing he’s touched, he spins as though it’s a success. But actually, it’s been a mess.”



Mr Evans points to a local police force that was previously under special measures for failing to record up to 80,000 crimes; badly-managed prisons; and rife homelessness — all issues Burnham failed to address during his time as mayor.

The councillor’s wife, Laura Evans, a former Conservative councillor who ran against Burnham in the mayoral elections in 2021 and 2024, agrees.

“Some people might say there’s social value in selling everything off to Abu Dhabi. I don’t think there is,” she said.

Mrs Evans explains that a short walk from the Etihad Complex you will find extremely deprived areas, so East Manchester should not be held up as a shining light. “What about health inequalities?”, she asked.

“You have nice shiny buildings there, but people are dying sooner than the rest of the country. How is that acceptable?

“Did you ever hear Andy Burnham talk about health?”

Life expectancy and health outcomes in parts of Manchester and Gtr Manchester are significantly lower — up to ten years or more — than in wealthier regions of the UK.

Louie French, the shadow sports minister, summed it up bluntly, saying: “The socialist utopia, which Andy Burnham sold the country as his record in Manchester, is in tatters.”



But others disagree, hailing Abu Dhabi’s oil-drenched investments.

Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig, who took over from her close pal Burnham in the summer, insists ADUG has done wonders for Manchester.

She said: “If you ask residents in East Manchester have they benefited from a new library, a new leisure centre, a new sixth-form college, infrastructure investment, the job opportunities that come from them, being a good employment charter signee and an early adopter of the real living wage, then they will have felt that benefit”.

Some of those living in the Manchester Life developments, as well as business owners who have set up nearby, also welcomed the Sheikh’s investment.

Barber shop owner Jonny Mooney, whose brother cuts Andy Burnham’s hair, said: “It’s been going really well.

“We get a lot of business from the surrounding apartments. The investment has been good for the area — we wouldn’t be here without it.”

Mum-of-one Casey Heaton, 26, who lives nearby, added: “It has brought a lot of benefits to the area, with the knock-on effects such as other businesses moving in.

“I don’t really care where the investment has come from. For me, it is all positive.”



John Leech, the Liberal Democrat chairman of the GMCA Overview and Scrutiny Committee, cautioned against complacency.

“There has been regeneration of some of the more deprived parts,” he said.

“And Abu Dhabi has continued to invest significant amounts of money into East Manchester.

“That’s not to say there isn’t any social and economic problems anymore, but we were starting from a low base and there has undoubtedly been very significant improvements.”

Mr Leech said that, while Burnham and his cronies had forged a close relationship with Abu Dhabi, it wasn’t the only cosy bond with developers, pointing to interests from the Far East and major Manchester developers.

“My biggest criticism is that a load of developers have had preferential treatment and have got away without having to provide affordable homes within their developments,” he said.

Burnham built his road to Downing Street on the glittering promise of the “Manchester Miracle”.

But as more architecturally-pleasing towers of glass and steel rise over the city, local taxpayers are left counting the true cost of his foreign-backed boom. The jury is still out.



And if this is the blueprint that Burnham wants to roll out across the nation, Britain had better brace itself for who ends up owning the country.

News.title: Woman, 48, murdered in Dublin home pictured & details of bloody post 5 hours before stabbing amid garda kill probe
News.content:
'TERRIBLE TRAGEDY' Woman, 48, murdered in Dublin home pictured & details of bloody post 5 hours before stabbing amid garda kill probe







Next

IRELAND’S latest murder victim posted a photo online showing blood on her collar just five hours before her brutal Bank Holiday stabbing.

Healthcare advisor Loredana Morosanu, 48, died after being knifed at least twice in her home in Finglas, northwest Dublin.



A suspect who fled the scene was later arrested after cops launched a manhunt and tracked him down.

Ms Morosanu was originally from Romania but had lived in Ireland for at least nine years.



The Irish Sun has learned she posted a shocking picture online on Sunday night which showed a red mark on her right cheek and blood visible on the inside collar of her top.

Five hours later, at around 4.30am today, emergency services learned that Ms Morosanu had been stabbed.





The suspect initially rang 999 before he left the scene at Melville Terrace, Finglas.

It’s understood another person also called for emergency services.

Ms Morosanu was already dead by the time paramedics and cops arrived.

A Garda operation to track down the suspect lasted more than six hours before he was lifted near Charlestown Shopping Centre in Finglas.

The man, in his 40s and also from Eastern Europe, had known the victim for many years.



Cops are investigating whether he knifed her following a row.

A source said: “The woman was stabbed more than once and died at the scene. The man rang emergency services but then fled the scene.

“There were concerns he could go to ground and flee the jurisdiction, you just don’t know in these situations.”

The man is being held on suspicion of murder and can be questioned for 24 hours in total, excluding breaks.

Detectives quizzing him were tonight in contact with the Director of Public Prosecutions, who will decide whether he is charged or released.



It is understood the suspect initially claimed the woman stabbed herself.

An autopsy will today be carried out on Ms Morosanu’s body to establish the exact cause of death and how the stab wounds were inflicted.

Garda technical experts preserved the scene for forensic examination today.

Ms Morosanu is thought to have only moved to the home recently.

It is in the same estate where mother-of-two Jennifer Poole, 24, was knifed to death by evil ex Gavin Murphy in April 2021.



Her brother, Jason, said driving past the murder scene today brought back the pain of losing his sister.

Jason told The Irish Sun: “My thoughts and sympathies are with the family because I know for us looking at it this morning and driving by it, you actually just feel physically sick.

“You can actually see Jennifer’s apartment from the incident and the road was blocked off just at Jennifer’s apartment. It’s all very real. It just brings back April 2021 very quickly. The community is again losing another member in similar circumstances.

“My thoughts are with our family and the people of the community in Melville who have to experience this trauma again on their doorstep again.”

Local Sinn Fein TD Dessie Ellis said the area was in shock, telling us: “It’s just terrible. It’s a terrible tragedy for everyone concerned, for the families and for the friends and neighbours.”



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Gardai are appealing for witnesses or anyone with video footage from near the scene.

They said: “Contact Finglas Garda Station on 01 666 7500.”

Pilots struggle to land at Birmingham airport during Storm Boelo

The forecaster warns the gusts could lead to power cuts and travel disruption, making it difficult for some pupils to attend classes.

‌



Roads and bridges could close as the strong winds hit. The Met Office warning, which will be in place tomorrow between 3am and 9pm, reads: "Strong west to southwesterly winds are expected to spread across much of Scotland and fringe the north of Northern Ireland during Tuesday.

"Gusts of 50-60 mph are possible quite widely and some coastal or exposed areas in the northwest and far north of Scotland could see gusts of 70 mph or more. There is still some uncertainty regarding the peak gusts, but the highest winds are expected in the far north and northwest and most likely over the Hebrides.

News.title: Grandfather's tears at funeral of baby 'stabbed 15 times' and found dead in outhouse
News.content:
Grandfather's tears at funeral of baby 'stabbed 15 times' and found dead in outhouse

Tiny Maria Skopova was found with 33 wounds on the day of her birth in Holywell Heights, Sheffield - her mother is one of four people charged with her murder

View 2 Images The child's grieving grandfather carried the casket into the cathedral for the funeral service (Image: BBC/ Oli Constable)

The devastated grandfather of a newborn girl who was allegedly murdered by four people including her mother was seen breaking down in tears at her funeral.

‌



‌



Little Maria Skopova - previously referred to as Baby S in court - suffered 33 wounds from 15 separate stabbings.

‌



She was found dead in the outhouse of a property on the day of her birth in Holywell Heights, in the Wincobank area of Sheffield.

‌



Maria's mother Andrea Skopova, 20, her boyfriend Peter Horvath Jnr, 19, and his parents, Peter Horvath Snr, 38, and Nina Horvathova, 37, have all been charged with murdering her.

Today (Monday), a funeral was held for Maria at St Marie's Catholic Cathedral in Sheffield. Rev Fr Chris Posluszny, who led the service at St Marie's Cathedral on Monday, said the infant's death had "affected the family so hard", the BBC reports.

View 2 Images Police rushed to the scene in Shefiield (Image: Rahmah Ghazali / Reach PLC)

‌



Royal gardener killed by falling tree during Storm Boelo as tributes pour in READ MORE :

Rain stopped just before the funeral car arrived and the baby's grandfather was seen holding a small bright-white casket. There was a moment of silence on the street outside as he broke down in tears and kissed the casket before carrying it in both arms through the doors of the cathedral.

Inside, he placed the casket by the altar and crouched, sobbing over it, the BBC reports. A card placed alongside it read: "For Baby Maria. The purest souls never stay too long in this world. With love from a mum x."

‌



The service, which was conducted mainly in Slovakian, took place before a further private family service at a cemetery in Sheffield.

Police said the five people charged in connection with Maria’s death would not be attending the funeral. Maria's mother, who is on remand, had asked to be able to watch the service on YouTube from prison, Rev Fr Posluszny said.

‌



Speaking to the BBC before the funeral, the priest said: "There has been a lot of tears, there has been a lot of asking of questions - why? How could this have happened?

"And in some ways, this will be an important moment actually to be able to place the child into the hands of God and also to bury the child and, in a sense, for many of them rebuilding their lives because it has been on hold for weeks and weeks and weeks and I think it has affected all of them tremendously."

Article continues below

The four defendants, who are all Slovakian nationals, were also charged with causing or allowing the death of a child, and perverting the course of justice by cleaning the scene of the alleged crime.

They were all remanded in custody. A 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named because of her age, is charged with the same perverting the course of justice offence. A trial is due to start in April next year.

News.title: Army officer, 26, 'killed by reversing armoured vehicle' in training exercise horror
News.content:
Army officer, 26, 'killed by reversing armoured vehicle' in training exercise horror

Second Lieutenant Max George, from County Durham, was part of 5 Rifles when he was killed during a training exercise at Salisbury Plain

View 2 Images Second Lt Max George died in a horror collision on Salisbury Plain, an inquest heard (Image: MOD)

An Army officer was tragically struck and killed by a reversing armoured vehicle which had a faulty safety alarm, an inquest has heard.

‌



‌



Second Lieutenant Max George, 26, died instantly when the collision happened on Salisbury Plain during a training exercise in June 2022. Lt George was exiting the armoured vehicle, which had an alarm that should have alerted the driver when the Warrior's rear doors were open, Wiltshire and Swindon Coroner's Court heard.

‌



Lt George, who was from County Durham, was fatally injured when the Warrior's commander gave the order to reverse at speed without realising the 26-year-old was still behind the vehicle. The alarm had been broken since 2018, the inquest heard.

‌



The accident happened as members of 5 Rifles were taking part in Exercise Combat Spirit. Lieutenant Colonel Graham Watson, who led a service inquiry into the incident, said alarms were installed after two fatal incidents in the 1990s.

View 2 Images The training exercise was taking place on Salisbury Plain (Image: Getty Images)

Royal gardener killed by falling tree during Storm Boelo as tributes pour in READ MORE :

He said several faults with the Warrior were known about but none meant the vehicle should have been taken out of service. He said: "One was the rear door alarm cable had snapped, which was first identified on June 20, 2018.

‌



"The second one was the rear door locking plunger would not release and is stuck, which meant that the rear doors could not be locked in position. The third fault was the repetition of the first fault that the rear door alarm cable was snapped and required renewing or repairing.

"Those matters were 'fully fit' faults, which at the time of the accident was not incorrect." Lt George was ordered to take command on the ground as two groups of soldiers were converging on a target, the inquest heard.

‌



'He was seen momentarily struggling'

As the Warrior halted, the gunner threw a smoke grenade and Lt George was ordered to exit. Col Watson said: "Lt George exited the vehicle and was seen momentarily struggling either with a day sack or trying to free a radio antenna which may have snagged.

"He then went to grab his weapon which was still inside the vehicle and simultaneously the student commander commanded the gunner to reverse the turret to the right in the direction of the enemy. The student commander checked through the periscopes and could no longer see the open doors, or Lt George at the rear of the vehicle.

‌



"Believing Lt George was clear the student commander commanded the driver to reverse. Lt George was still at the rear reaching for his weapon. He was knocked to the ground."

Between 38 and 42 seconds elapsed between the Warrior stopping and the collision, the colonel added. He said: "There were several attempts by those who witnessed the accident to warn of the impending danger, people shouted, waved their hands, sounded their horn, unfortunately to no avail."

‌



When he exited the Warrior, Lt George made a "clunking noise", which the court heard may have led the commander to believe he was clear and had shut the doors. Col Watson said: "This was part of his reasoning to why he gave the command for the vehicle to reverse after he waited a few seconds after hearing the clunk and not seeing anything at the rear.

"The built in alarm would have alarmed because the rear doors were open, and had that gone off the driver would have almost certainly stopped. In addition on the driver’s instrument panel, because the rear doors were open there should have been a light, but again because the wiring loop was damaged that didn’t light up."

‌



The inquest heard the exercise was using two types of Warrior – the FV-510 and FV-511 models – and Lt George’s vehicle was not ordinarily used for disembarking troops and close combat. Col Watson told the court: "The student commander had done the majority of his training on the FV-510, which is the platoon variant of the vehicle.

"In general, the crew and service personnel within 5 Rifles were not that familiar with the FV-511 and its differences with the FV-510. The training objectives could still be met but by providing the wrong type of vehicles, that should have triggered additional control measures to be put in place to ensure the risk was as low as reasonably practicable."

‌



'A flaw and a safety case'

Col Watson said the service inquiry found two causal factors, 22 contributory factors and 22 other factors in Lt George’s death. He said: "The fact a rear door safety alarm had been fitted to rectify issues discovered in 1998 and 1999 was right and proper, but the fact there was not a maintenance regime that ensured that alarm worked was a flaw and a safety case.

"It was not a high priority. It was not a conscious decision to make it a 'fully fit' fault. I personally believe it was an oversight not to make it a limited role or a not task worthy role. It was a flawed safety case."

‌



Lt George's mother, Vivienne, wrote a pen portrait for her son, which was read during the hearing. She described the 26-year-old as "modest and great fun" and revealed he had won the Queen's Medal for best cadet when he passed out from the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, BBC reports.

He was awarded a first in politics with Russian at Newcastle University and obtained a Distinction in his Masters in Eastern European and Eurasian Studies with Russian at the University of Glasgow. His mother said: "Max had effortless leadership qualities and his potential was enormous. His loss has left a hole in our lives, he was the very best of all of us."

Article continues below

The inquest continues.

News.title: DARREN LEWIS: 'I despair for our moral compass when police view Black babies as dangerous threats'
News.content:
DARREN LEWIS: 'I despair for our moral compass when police view Black babies as dangerous threats'

From a one-year-old shot dead in his mother’s arms to boys handcuffed face-down on London streets, writing this column leaves me wondering how much longer we can let this brutality destroy our children

View 2 Images Kohen Wiley, 1, was shot dead by officers in the incident

Sometimes doing this column there are so many stories that lead you to despair for society’s moral compass. And it’s hard to know where to start with two in particular.

‌



‌



Do I focus on the fatal Stateside shooting of one-year-old Kohen Wiley in a Mississippi supermarket car park, by a police officer among several responding to a report of shoplifting?

‌



Do I focus on the claim from the ­officer’s lawyer that his client “had no choice but to discharge his weapon” and that the “outcome of the investigation was not only expected, but it was overdue”?

‌



Do I point out that the heartbreaking fallout continued as the country’s president was busy remarking on the “beautiful ass” of rapper Nicki Minaj?

View 2 Images Kohen was just a year old when he was fatally shot (Image: Facebook)

Or do I opt instead for the ridiculousness that is the other ­developing story around police reportedly called by upset parents to deal with – wait for it – a three-year-old excelling at football against their kids in Florida?

‌



Apparently officers were called to a youth sports field in Winter Park, resulting in the as-yet unnamed boy and his family being escorted away. To be fair to the local law enforcement officers, they appeared not to have been aggressive from the footage still going viral on social media.

But you don’t need me to explain to you the profound trauma, social and ­developmental implications of calling the police to deal with children, anywhere.

‌



This column has discussed it on many occasions, from Child Q – the ­menstruating teenage girl scandalously strip-searched by Met Police officers after being wrongly accused of possessing drugs a few years ago.

To, well, Kohen Wiley. At just one, the latest victim of ­America’s trigger-happy gun culture. The common denominator in both (and most) cases: young Black children and their families treated by law ­enforcement with scant sensitivity.

‌



And the obvious question is: how long can this go on? How often can the justice systems allow law enforcement to operate in a manner that wrecks ­families and shatters communities?

I wrote in this column just two months ago about the bewildered young – innocent – Black boy, no older than 10 or 11, made to lie face down by a Met Police officer who’d hand­cuffed him unne­ces­sar­ily in East Lon­don.

‌



Regular readers will also know that Black chil­dren are up to eight times more likely to be strip-searched, face higher rates of stop-and-search and exper­i­ence inflated risk assess­ments in the justice sys­tem when evaluating their potential to ­reoffend.

In other words, even as young­sters, the data shows that Black people are seen by police as more of a threat.

‌



Just as the drugs accusation sparking the Child Q violation was found to be false, Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya, has not been charged with any crime after claims she and a friend had stolen nappies.

She’d denied the allegation and, with a friend, had left the supermarket, holding Kohen. The police officer responsible for killing the child, 33-year-old Sgt Hunter Foster, has since resigned. He’d fired into the moving vehicle the Wileys were inside. Kohen had been sitting on his mother’s lap.

‌



Foster’s lawyer argued in a statement to the BBC that the car driver was attempting to kill law enforcement. The Wiley family’s lawyer, Ben Crump, argued that the distressing bodycam footage, released last week showed Foster firing at the car from the right hand side, disputing that the officer was in imminent danger. An independent autopsy commissioned by the family reached a similar conclusion.

Kohen’s death is just the latest among the hundreds of children killed by US police in the past 10 years alone.

‌



A sobering study, published four months ago by Yale researchers found between 2003 and 2024, 270 child deaths had been caused by law enforcement.

Kohen would have celebrated turning two this coming Sunday. Instead he has become yet another addition to a damning statistic that makes you want to weep.

News.title: 'Bank bosses’ obscene pay must be tackled as working families struggle to make ends meet'
News.content:
'Bank bosses’ obscene pay must be tackled as working families struggle to make ends meet'

As families across the country struggle with rising bills, Britain’s biggest bank bosses continue to pocket millions — and so Wednesday’s Budget is a chance for Labour to make the banks pay their fair share

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

The obscene rewards paid to Britain's banking bosses expose just how deeply unjust our economy has become. While millions of families struggle to pay their bills, the average chief executive of Britain's four biggest banks pockets more in two days than an ordinary worker earns in a year. Last year, Barclays boss C.S. Venkatakrishnan trousered an astonishing £15 million, including £12.7 million in bonuses. Such eye-watering payouts make a mockery of the sacrifices demanded of working people. And on Wednesday, Chancellor John Healey has an opportunity to do something about it. The Tories slashed the surcharge on bank profits from eight per cent to three per cent, handing the financial giants a grotesque, lucrative advantage. Restoring it could raise £2.25 billion annually, money desperately needed for our NHS, police, schools and public services. Those who have grown rich beyond imagination should contribute more to the country that helped make their fortunes. Working families have shouldered the burden for far too long. Tomorrow's Budget must prove whose side Labour is really on.

‌



‌



Henry Nowak’s family deserve answers and accountability

Henry Nowak was just 18, with his whole life ahead of him, when a murderer robbed him of his future and his family of their beloved son. The horror of his death was compounded by disturbing footage showing the dying teenager being handcuffed by police. So Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's announcement of an independent review is welcome, albeit long overdue. Serious questions remain about what authorities knew of Henry's killer, whether warning signs were missed and how police treated the teenager in his final moments. Everyone demands a full and honest answer. The review must leave no stone unturned, however uncomfortable its findings. Henry's family have already endured a devastating loss and a deeply disappointing fight for justice. They deserve answers, accountability and meaningful change.

Back of the net
