Sports.title: Ballon d'Or plunged into CHAOS as esteemed event announces Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal ALL as winners on official website just hours before the ceremony
Sports.content:
Ballon d'Or plunged into CHAOS as esteemed event announces Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal ALL as winners on official website just hours before the ceremony

Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal were all bizarrely listed as winners of the Ballon d'Or on the organisers' website hours before the ceremony began in London.

The trio have all been viewed among the leading candidates to land football's biggest individual prize for the first time.

Prior to the event at the London Palladium, the Ballon d'Or's official website appeared to mistakenly publish three separate articles announcing them individually as the winner.

Daily Mail Sport alerted the organisers to the mistake at 5.23pm and it triggered a series of frantic phone calls and WhatsApp messages.

Shocked organisers have since launched an investigation, with articles announcing Kane and Mbappe as winners subsequently being removed.

The article listing Yamal as the winner was still live on the website over 30 minutes after organisers were informed by Daily Mail Sport.

Ballon d'Or organisers published three articles announcing different winners of the Ballon d'Or, including England captain Harry Kane

Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe were also listed as winners on the website, with shocked organisers only becoming aware after being alerted by Daily Mail Sport

A Ballon d’Or statement read: 'Portraits of some Ballon d’Or nominees prepared by were inadvertently published online.

'These articles had been prepared in advance for all nominees in the event of a win.

'They DO NOT, in any way, reveal the podium, which remains unknown to everyone at this time.'

Kane's article featured the headline 'Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d’Or: Here are his best and most meaningful strikes from a 61-goal season.'

The article examined Kane's stunning year as he helped Bayern Munich win a domestic Treble, as well as reaching a century of goals for the German side in record time.

'A record-breaking welter of league and cup goals in 2025/26 has propelled Harry Kane to Ballon d’Or success. Here we identify his most iconic and greatest finishes in what has been a bountiful year,' the article stated.

Another announced Yamal as the Ballon d'Or winner, stating that the Barcelona and Spain star had set an 'unprecedented record' by becoming its youngest winner and labelling him as the 'new king of football'.

'In fact, at just 19 years of age, Lamine Yamal has just become the youngest winner in the history of the Ballon d'Or, which was established in 1956,' the article read.

'To truly appreciate the scale of his achievement, one need only recall that not even Lionel Messi – the record holder for the most trophies – had managed to win the Ballon d'Or at that age.

'The Argentine star won it for the first time in 2009, when he was 22 years and 160 days old.

'The all-time record for the youngest winner, until this magical evening in London, belonged to Ronaldo Nazário, who won the Ballon d'Or at the age of 21 years and 92 days.

All three articles were subsequently taken down, with Yamal's last to be removed from the website over 30 minutes after organisers were informed of the error

'Now, this historic record belongs to the new king of football and the brand-new winner of the most prestigious trophy on the planet.

'It belongs to Lamine Yamal Nasraoui Ebana.'

The third stated Mbappe as the winner, lauding him as 'consistency personified at the very highest level'.

'A record-breaking World Cup and another welter of goals for Los Blancos has brought Kylian Mbappe his first Ballon d'Or triumph,' the article read.

'Here we celebrate the French star's consistency, not just last season, but every season since first emerging as a true phenomenon.'

The error took place ahead of official coverage of the ceremony, which will be headlined by the winner of the Ballon d'Or.

England captain Kane is bidding to become the first English player to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001.

Yamal and Mbappe are also hoping to claim the gong for the first time, with the pair having had best finishes of second and third respectively.

Sports.title: Who should replace Michael Carrick as Man United boss as pressure mounts? Bringing in Unai Emery would be the best thing INEOS have done, writes NATHAN SALT... but would Eddie Howe simply be Carrick 2.0?
Sports.content:
Who should replace Michael Carrick as Man United boss as pressure mounts? Bringing in Unai Emery would be the best thing INEOS have done, writes NATHAN SALT... but would Eddie Howe simply be Carrick 2.0?

Michael Carrick is on the brink of the sack and the sorry cycle of managerial churn in the corridors of Old Trafford is set to pick up once again.

Fans turned on key figures such as director of football Jason Wilcox and CEO Omar Berrada in the closing stages of Sunday’s 3-0 defeat to AFC Bournemouth and they will be under enormous amounts of pressure to get the next appointment right.

Behind the scenes there has long been a difference of opinion on which direction to go next.

As exclusively reported by Daily Mail Sport, Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell have been at odds as tensions grow between the pair, with Vivell pushing for former Bayern Munich and Germany manager Julian Nagelsmann, while Wilcox wants a Premier League proven manager. Eddie Howe is his preferred candidate.

So, with that in mind, Daily Mail Sport assesses the five candidates on the club’s internal shortlist to see who the best fit for Manchester United, now at such a low ebb just above the relegation zone, is…

Fans turned on key figures such as director of football Jason Wilcox and CEO Omar Berrada in the closing stages of Sunday’s 3-0 defeat to AFC Bournemouth

Eddie Howe (out of work)

The front-runner as it stands given he is the preferred choice of the director of football.

There is an irony in that given former director of football, Dan Ashworth, lobbied for Howe before Ruben Amorim arrived, only to find himself out of a job for not agreeing to hire the Portuguese boss.

That aside, Howe’s appeal is that there is no compensation required to get him as he currently continues his break from the game after leaving Newcastle following a successful five years in the North East in which he ended their 70-year trophy drought with a League Cup.

Privately, Howe is keeping his cards close to his chest but he knows that he checks a lot of the boxes, not least that he’s shown he can cut it in the Premier League and Champions League.

One of Howe’s biggest strengths is that he’s viewed as someone who can build a team from the ground up and privately, figures at United believe he has a track record of improving players through coaching on the training ground.

United sought a low-key character after the fireworks of Amorim but numerous figures close to the dressing room are keen to see an inspirational leader walk through the door and that isn’t really Howe’s MO.

The next manager needs to galvanise a club that is hurtling towards the bottom three with an apathy kicking in that this doomed group are merely rinsing and repeating the same problems.

Where other contenders such as Antonio Conte would achieve that in the short term, Howe’s temperament is much closer to Carrick’s and that may be one reason why some behind the scenes will be hesitating.

Odds: 4-6 (favourite)

Wilcox is a fan and he has enormous sway – for now at least – on the appointment of the next manager. Howe is available to start straight away and won’t cost a penny in compensation. For a club as cheap as United, that’s worth its weight in gold.

Howe’s temperament is much closer to Carrick’s and that may be one reason why some behind the scenes are hesitating

Julian Nagelsmann (out of work)

The other leading contender, pushed heavily by Vivell in the boardroom.

Nagelsmann’s stock took a hit after a disastrous World Cup in charge of Germany but even with that, there has long been a fascination in England about the suave 39-year-old.

He has long been viewed as one of Europe’s rising young stars on the coaching scene and therefore it’s no surprise to know that Chelsea, Liverpool and Tottenham Hotspur have all looked at him when job openings came up.

Tactically he is incredibly detailed and is closer to the Amorim and Ten Hag mould, where Howe, from a personality point, is closer to that of Carrick.

Nagelsmann is also free to begin work right away – a key reason he too is near the front of the queue – and one feather in his cap is that he’s had two enormous high-pressure jobs previously in Bayern Munich and Germany.

He could walk into a dressing room and not be overawed by what he finds having had the two biggest jobs in German football and that shouldn’t be underestimated given the next man is walking into a dressing room completely devoid of confidence and belief.

It was Monday when club captain Bruno Fernandes was liking a post on social media claiming he had been pushed to a point where he no longer cares.

‘I strongly believe that if you want to be successful, empathy and taking care of the person behind the player is of greater importance than any tactical aspects,’ Nagelsmann said in his early managerial days.

‘I place great emphasis in giving my players a clear tactical plan to help and support in match situations. But the relationship I have with them is very, very important to me.’

He’s never managed in the Premier League and the worry is that this could be Amorim Mark II, even with so much potential behind him.

This one comes down to the power battle between Wilcox and Vivell and it’s unlikely one the latter will win.

Odds: 5-2

A Premier League job feels inevitable and he’s got lots of admirers in the building at United. This just feels like this could be the wrong timing given many at United are still reeling from the gamble they took on an up-and-coming manager in Amorim.

Tactically Nagelsmann is incredibly detailed and is closer to the Amorim and Ten Hag mould, where Howe, from a personality point, is closer to that of Carrick

Antonio Conte (out of work)

The last of the out of work managers to have seen their name crop up in discussions about who and what comes next.

One thing to say is that Conte wants the job and nobody on the shortlist would inject as much short-term adrenaline into the entire club than the Italian. He’d put rockets up all the right people to get a much-needed response.

The issue is that he’s highly combustible and while Sir Jim Ratcliffe has previously gravitated to those who challenge him – Amorim did that and Ratcliffe liked him for it – this feels like a candidate that may be a bridge too far for the thinner-skinned execs put in place by Ratcliffe.

‘My name has been linked with numerous clubs, but there are currently no negotiations at an advanced stage,’ Conte wrote on Instagram in the past week following a damning report in Italian paper La Repubblica.

‘I have read reports of financial demands and requests for full control that I have supposedly already made to the clubs mentioned, as well as reservations about what has been described as my "strong personality". These reports are unfounded.’

Conte is a hybrid candidate that can point to tangible success in England at both Chelsea, where he won the Premier League, and at Tottenham where, for as toxic as it ended, he wasn’t wrong about the issues that the club badly needed to fix.

Players in the dressing room are looking for an inspirational leader to get behind – that’s a quality numerous sources have put to Daily Mail Sport in recent hours and days – and Conte is undoubtedly the man for that job.

He’s won the Premier League, won Serie A, won the FA Cup, and has a resume that he knows what he’s doing.

But the current United structure is very rigid, and the manager isn’t the ultimate shot-caller.

Also, this squad would need major surgery to get it close to playing the intense football Conte would want to play. Feels very unlikely.

Odds: 5-1

Even with his statement dismissing a lot of the concerns attached to his name, he’s seen as too combustible to fit in around all the cooks in the kitchen that is this shambolic boardroom.

Players in the dressing room are looking for an inspirational leader to get behind and Conte is undoubtedly the man for that job

Unai Emery (Aston Villa)

INEOS continue to preach a desire to bring a ‘best in class’ mantra to Manchester United and as laughable as that is given their work to date, bringing in Unai Emery would be the best thing they’ve done to this point.

Emery is at the very top when it comes to the Premier League’s managerial rankings given what he’s done at Aston Villa, who are a major player in the Champions League so far this season.

Villa have no desire to lose Emery – naturally – and while his release clause, if one exists, is no doubt so sky high that it’s prohibitive from United coming in and poaching the Villans' beacon of light in the dugout.

Emery works in a very particular way and that is also a question mark, beyond the enormous compensation that would be required. It would likely usurp the £20million Chelsea had to pay Brighton to get Graham Potter and his staff.

The Spaniard has an enormous amount of power and that would have to be curbed at United unless they went in a totally different direction: one that bestows all of the power to the manager.

His colder personality, compared to say, Howe, is a mark against his name when it comes to getting buy-in from a dressing room that grumble at the most minor inconvenience.

He will try his luck at one of the game’s top, top jobs at some stage but United feels like a stretch given, at the very least, they won’t put the money up for compensation, never mind back him sufficiently in the transfer window to overhaul a squad that is failing miserably.

Odds: 17-2

A top, top manager and perhaps the best candidate on the shortlist given everything he’s achieved. He wrongly gets mocked for his command of English but he’s tactically immense and can make a credible case to be the No1 boss in the Premier League. He’s just too expensive, and United’s hierarchy is notoriously cheap.

Emery has an enormous amount of power and that would have to be curbed at United unless they went in a totally different direction, one that bestows all of the power to the manager

Fabian Hurzeler (Brighton)

The candidate of choice for Wilcox if money was no object.

Hurzeler is the hot young coach taking the Premier League by storm now, with Brighton in the top three with five wins from the first eight games.

At just 33, he’s a rising star and he’s shown no signs of being overwhelmed since arriving as the Premier League’s youngest-ever coach when he pitched up at 31 from St Pauli in 2024.

Hurzeler spoke earlier this season after knocking Carrick’s United out of the Carabao Cup about how powerful the Brighton structure is and that cannot be underestimated. Everyone is so aligned it has allowed him to focus on coaching, which he’s doing to great success.

The German has built an aggressive, intense, high-press side at Brighton that so often runs over their opponents, all qualities that continually seem to be lacking from United’s sides in recent seasons.

Hurzeler is innovative, exciting and looks to have a bit of steel to him as well. There was a point last season where fans jeered and booed him, and privately some players had their doubts, but he never did as he turned it around.

The thorough dismantling of current league champions Arsenal earlier this season was a sign of how far he’s come and that he can mix it with the best, even with much more limited resources.

But compensation for Hurzeler would likely surpass the £20million it took to get Potter out given Hurzeler signed a three-year contract extension in May.

There are those close to him, too, that have intimated that he is the right coach at the wrong time and that he is not interested in jumping off the Brighton ship right now, not least given he has the chance to deliver European success in the Conference League, as well as a top five finish this campaign.

United’s squad is miles away from what Hurzeler needs to make his vision a success at Old Trafford but his stock is unlikely to diminish anytime soon and so don’t be surprised if Hurzeler eventually finds his way to Old Trafford… it just won’t be now.

Odds: 40-1

Brighton are clicking on every front right now and are a club heading in the right direction, where Manchester United are not. Opportunities for top jobs will keep coming and so he won’t have the overwhelming sense of ‘now or never’ like others do. He’s also just way too expensive right now.

Sports.title: Burnley appoint chief football officer as they ramp up search for new manager - as frontrunner Rob Edwards drops out of the running to replace Nicky Hayen
Sports.content:
Burnley have appointed Diego Lopez as their new chief football officer as he assesses candidates to become their next manager.

Rob Edwards and Carlos Corberan were among the early contenders under consideration, though former West Brom and Valencia coach Corberan - who knows Lopez well - is understood to be waiting for a Premier League opportunity and has told him he is not interested in the position.

Meanwhile, Daily Mail Sport understands Edwards has now ruled himself out of the running, leaving Burnley to pursue a managerial candidate from overseas.

Lopez, who was previously with Genoa, has been handed responsibility for football operations, recruitment and sporting structure and the immediate search for a new manager.

Burnley parted company with manager Nicky Hayen following a damaging 4-1 defeat against Lincoln City on Saturday.

Lopez, 37, joins with Burnley 22nd in the Championship after a poor start to the season in which they have won just one game in 12. They are without a win at home for over a year.

Club chairman Alan Pace said: ‘We wanted someone with deep experience in recruitment and player development, a strong knowledge of European markets and a clear understanding of how those come together to strengthen a club over the long term. Diego has a proven record of exactly that.’

Burnley have appointed Diego Lopez as their chief football officer as they search for a manager

Former Wolves and Luton Town boss Rob Edwards has ruled himself out of the running

Hayen won the Belgian title with Club Brugge in 2024 and was brought in by Pace during the summer with the hope of securing a swift return to the top flight.

Corberan, also 43, left Valencia in September and has previously coached Huddersfield as well as West Brom. But Daily Mail Sport understands he is only interested in Premier League jobs after coaching in La Liga and, despite links, is not speaking to Burnley today.

Burnley are also exploring another option based abroad.

Lopez, who was sport director at Lens and previously worked as a head scout at Monaco, Lille, Excelsior Mouscron and Bordeaux, said: 'I am eager to start exploring the great potential of this club. I understand our mission and I believe in what Burnley can become in the coming years, if we all work in the same direction with full determination.

'From my first conversations with Alan, it was clear there is real ambition here and a plan to match it.'

Sports.title: England Under 15s WALK OFF during World Cup clash with Ireland after youngster accused rival of calling him a 'monkey' in alleged racist slur
Sports.content:
England's Under-15 World Cup match against Ireland descended into chaos after an alleged racist incident in Azerbaijan.

Young Lions boss Matt Thorpe withdrew his players in the 40th minute after one of them claimed an opponent had called him a 'monkey' moments after the England youngster pushed his opponent in the back.

A member of the Irish backroom staff shouted 'no, he didn't' while the English player remonstrated, sparking a shouting match between the two benches.

The England player approached his bench and waited on the touchline as Thorpe spoke to the fourth official. And just before play could resume, the England coach ordered his team off the pitch.

England were trailing 4-1 at the time but it is unclear whether the incident will affect the result, given it played out in the final knockings of the game - consisting of two 20-minute halves.

England's Under 15s walked off midway through their World Cup clash with Ireland

The Young Lions claimed one of their players was labelled a 'monkey' by an opposing player

Daily Mail Sport understands the FA are in contact with FIFA and working to establish the full details.

A full debrief with the players was delayed until after their final group match, a 2-0 win against Zimbabwe, which the affected player started.

The FA are taking the matter extremely seriously and will now fully investigate the circumstances, with player welfare their top priority.

A FIFA spokesman told Daily Mail Sport: 'FIFA is aware of an incident at the FIFA U-15 World Cup & Festival match between England and the Republic of Ireland. The match was abandoned by the referee following England's refusal to continue.

FA Ireland (FAI) did not respond to Daily Mail Sport's request for comment.

'The official reports are being gathered, and the matter will be referred to the independent Disciplinary Committee who will decide in due course.'

The Young Lions won their first three group games at the experimental eight-versus-eight tournament 16-1 on aggregate and topped the group before their match with Ireland, who were behind on goal difference.

This was not the first England youth match disrupted by racism allegations. Last year, England's Under-17s had their friendly victory over Venezuela stopped twice after multiple players were accused of racial abuse.

FIFA have comprehensive rules for dealing with racist incidents. Players who cover their mouths during a confrontation can receive a straight red card.

The rule was introduced after Benfica's Gianluca Prestianni was accused of calling Vinicius Jr a monkey while covering his mouth during a Champions League match earlier this year. Prestianni was retrospectively handed a six-match ban for the incident.

Meanwhile, abusive and discriminatory language – if heard by the referee – results in a straight red card.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino was in attendance at the tournament on Monday

In July, the FA announced stricter measures to combat on-field discrimination in England, including a minimum 10-match ban for any player found guilty.

FIFA have a three-step procedure to address discriminatory incidents in stadiums, triggered when players make an X symbol to the referee.

Initially, the referee stops the match while spectators are warned to stop the abuse. It then escalates to a temporary pause before eventual abandonment if the conduct continues.

That protocol was notoriously implemented during England's 6-0 European Championship qualifying victory away to Bulgaria in 2019 when England's black players were tormented by monkey chants and Nazi salutes from the home support.

The game was stopped twice in the first half but the Three Lions opted to finish the game, having walked off the pitch just before half time.

Sports.title: VOICE OF THE PADDOCK: This season has been a snoozefest, the most sanitised, anaemic shadow of F1 imaginable. And Russell's refusal to even try to unsettle Antonelli sums up its 'Drive to Survive' problem
Sports.content:
VOICE OF THE PADDOCK: This season has been a snoozefest, the most sanitised, anaemic shadow of F1 imaginable. And Russell's refusal to even try to unsettle Antonelli sums up its 'Drive to Survive' problem

We will come on to how this is the biggest snoozefest of a Formula One season in recent memory, but first praise where it is due.

There is a lot of hurrahing and golly-goshing about Kimi Antonelli, and rightly so. If he were, God forbid, never to turn a wheel again, the Italian would still be crowned Formula One world champion aged 20 at some point in the next few weeks.

In my and my colleagues’ description of what he needs to clinch the title in Mexico City on Sunday, we have reported that he must finish ninth to be certain of it. True, after his crushing victory in Austin last weekend lifted him 123 points ahead of any pursuer with 125 up for grabs.

But, to put it more starkly, either George Russell or Lewis Hamilton would have to win every one of the remaining five races and Antonelli fail to score as much as a couple of points.

So, it is game over. Put your feet up, Kimi, in San Marino, where he lives. And he blazed to his incoming title in blistering style, blowing away Russell into a place he never expected to be – understudy to the Italian he thought he had the measure of as Mercedes team-mates of contrasting F1 experience (the 28-year-old Russell’s eight seasons versus Antonelli’s two). Russell finished eighth on Sunday in the same equipment.

Antonelli has attacked all year at almost every corner, while still modifying the exuberance of his rookie fireworks of last year to accumulate wins brick by brick, seeing things through with a lightness of touch that is remarkable to witness.

Kimi Antonelli's crushing victory in Austin means the world championship is all but his

George Russell (left) has refused to verbally joust with his Mercedes team-mate despite falling behind him

Yet, yet, yet, this is a boring season. The sport has reached the apogee of Netflix’s Drive to Survive genre, the most sanitised, anaemic shadow of Formula One you could imagine. Ha, and to think that great Rabelaisian James Hunt won the title 50 years ago last week in a more buccaneering era with scraps and taunts and honest opinions overflowing, as well as a line of British Airways stewardesses outside his bedroom door.

Antonelli, a brilliant driver just out of his teens, is chilled but also a product of corporate Mercedes, trained up to his eyeballs to be circumspect since he joined them aged 11. He has not uttered one memorable line all year.

Nor has Russell, someone I know better and have always liked, jousted with Antonelli verbally.

Again, corporate Mercedes is at play, when Russell might otherwise have ripped into the team and stamped his feet for clearly favouring Kimi. (I repeat again and again, Russell has not been sabotaged; I just don’t believe he is Toto Wolff’s favourite son.)

So there has been no intra-team tension displayed, as well as no contest on track for months. Russell has won just three times to Antonelli's nine.

Why has Russell not got out his elbows as Nico Rosberg did when he used every possible psychological device to beat Hamilton in 2016 rather than keep talking about being the team player. It seems a sad and fatal statement of submission. Bernie Ecclestone wondered: ‘I don’t know if George has that killer instinct you need.’

Ferrari have been bumping along as so often, Hamilton’s win in Barcelona revealing itself to be the false dawn it always looked like being. He is past his best at 41 and, in Fred Vasseur, has a team principal not up to the task. They are going nowhere as fast as they would like. Hamilton’s team-mate Charles Leclerc, so talented, has an infuriating magnetism to walls.

Red Bull and McLaren have been making ground, fair play to them, but Mercedes had already bolted.

Corporate Mercedes is at play, when Russell might otherwise have ripped into the team and stamped his feet for clearly favouring Kimi

The absence of compelling team principals like Christian Horner (left, with his rival Toto Wolff) has reduced the drama in F1

Then, we have the appalling half-electric engines that have rendered overtaking a manufactured joke. A move is practically all down to when the power can be deployed, with passing and repassing. A proper emergency solution rather than putting a plaster on the sore should be found as soon as possible, not delayed until 2030 or 2031. This failure to revert to V8 engines is causing huge damage to the sport’s credibility.

Finally, we have a different set of team principals from the old days. They are engineers. Repartee has gone, neutralising the needle that was the intrigue which enlivened boring afternoons. Christian Horner taking on Wolff could often be better sport than the race itself. That’s vanished.

There are signs of revival, though, with Max Verstappen suggesting he and Red Bull can pose a threat in 2027. McLaren canter on well under astute leadership from Zak Brown and Andrea Stella.

Verstappen against Antonelli, with Lando Norris, provides hope after this year’s gruel.

And none of the whines above are meant as a word of criticism about Antonelli, essentially already a history-making world champion, and a deserving one at that.

Austin experience getting better and better

I rated Austin my seventh favourite race on a list we published last year.

The rankings merely reflected my mood at the time. Some venues were harshly treated, such as Barcelona, placed last, because I was fed up with the concrete jungle of a track that has not progressed in terms of facilities, and, really, because I had been there ad nauseam for testing and the like for more than 20 years.

Engineers loved it for its representative data collection. Which is nice for them.

I was bored with it, at any rate. And while Barcelona is a fine city, the Sagrada Familia is tanks of petrol away from Circuit de Catalunya and the volume of traffic turned my hair grey a while ago.

But, to be honest, if you took the relatively short flight to Spain as a fan you could have a fabulous weekend. And I have had some there, for sure.

But coming back to Austin, it not only remains high among my favourites but continues to evolve and develop.

It has always been a brilliantly designed track, put together by German Hermann Tilke, though Sunday’s race was not a classic.

The track in Austin, designed by Hermann Tilke, is brilliant, even if Sunday's race was not a classic

The attendance over the weekend was a huge 467,000 but getting in and out of the Circuit of the Americas was easy

Getting out of the circuit used to be a nightmare of snail’s pace pain, but this year it was as smooth as a production line. Perhaps I got out at the right times, and was lucky, but it seemed a masterful improvement in organisation. These things matter in terms of fan experience. It is paying off. The attendance over the weekend was a huge 467,000.

I have reported on this race from the start and have a nostalgic fondness for it. I was in the Four Seasons hotel, next to Lady Bird Lake – the southern boundary rope of Downtown Austin – with track owners Bobby Epstein and Red McCombs, the late Texan billionaire businessman. Red walked with a stick, as I remember, even back then.

Red loved Bernie Ecclestone and called him an ‘English gentleman’. Bernie rang me as I took a coffee with the Americans. It was the eve of the inaugural race in 2012 and Epstein, who kindly showed me around the track of which he was understandably so proud a few days before the crowds arrived, was as nervous as a kitten about how it would all play out.

‘How are preparations going?’ asked Ecclestone from his London office hours before he flew across the Pond. I told him everything was in hand. ‘They are good people,’ he added. Epstein and Co got it right now and still are.

It is my favourite of the American races. Then comes Miami, then Las Vegas.

For the record, my top six races to attend, in an assessment admittedly skewed by my own nostalgia and bias, were, as of last year: 6th Monza; 5th Silverstone; 4th Singapore; 3rd Brazil; 2nd Monaco; 1st Melbourne.

Sitting here now, writing this by Lady Bird Lake, as two rowing eights go by as dawn breaks, I might swap around Austin for Singapore. The rest stay where they are.

Sports.title: Jeremy Clarkson in hot water after he aimed barb at Argentinian F1 driver - despite being a GUEST of his team at the US Grand Prix
Sports.content:
Jeremy Clarkson is in hot water again after Alpine took exception to a remark he made towards Argentinian driver Franco Colapinto.

Clarkson has a stormy history with Argentina after a controversial stunt in 2014 when his number plate appeared to reference the 1982 Falklands War.

He and his fellow Top Gear presenters had to flee the country after he drove a Porsche 928 with the number plate H982 FKL, which angry locals threw bricks at.

And the 66-year-old has again sparked controversy after joking that he would give Colapinto a grid penalty purely because of his nationality.

To make matters worse, Clarkson was a guest of Alpine for the Grand Prix in Austin, Texas, when he made the remark.

'Franco's got a grid penalty for being Argentinian... Probably. Well I'd give him one for that,' he said in an interview with Sky Sports' Martin Brundle.

Clarkson was invited onto the grid in Austin as a guest of Alpine but has since been criticised for insulting one of the team's own drivers

He then clarified: 'That's just because of what happened when we went there.'

Colapinto's manager Jamie Campbell-Walter said: 'Jeremy Clarkson’s comments about Franco’s nationality were completely unacceptable.

'There is no place for remarks like this in Formula One, regardless of who makes them or whether they are intended as a joke.'

Colapinto, whose career-best Grand Prix finish across his 45 races is sixth, had to deal with a 10-place grid penalty for Sunday's race at the Circuit of the Americas as a result of power unit component changes.

Clarkson's run-in over the Falklands is one of the most memorable scandals to have hit Top Gear. Rock-throwing protesters had vowed to 'barbecue' him after his stunt.

Veterans of the conflict laid siege to the hotel where Clarkson and fellow presenters Richard Hammond and James May were staying after news of the number plate appeared online.

Clarkson said at the time: 'I've been to Iraq and Afghanistan, but this was the most terrifying thing I've ever been involved in.'

Franco Colapinto has urged his Argentinian supporters to refrain for further abusing his team

Jeremy Clarkson, 66, has said he won't be sticking to his healthy diet after getting the all-clear from prostate cancer - because he 'hasn't worked his a**e off for 40 years to have no joy'

It comes after the Falklands War became a major flashpoint during the summer's World Cup, with Argentina's players claiming the archipelago belongs to them, not Britain, following their semi-final win over England.

Argentina's President Javier Milei has also amplified the messaging, saying in September that his nation 'needs to recover' the islands.

Clarkson is in remission from aggressive prostate cancer after being diagnosed in mid-June.

He said he was 'unwell for a short amount of time' after doctors 'found a little something' during his annual prostate check.

Jeremy told The Times it was 'not nice' to have to tell his children he had cancer but simply went into hospital for a procedure and was back in his tractor a fortnight later.

He is now feeling leaner after losing two stone down to weight-loss drug Mounjaro rather than 'steely will' and in series five, Jeremy's girlfriend Lisa Hogan advised him to adjust his diet and start eating healthier foods such as Greek yoghurt.

'Sure, I can eat less and more healthily. I can become a herbivore,' he said. 'And yes, I can go for 20-mile hikes and do 20,000 steps a day.

'But the truth is, there has to be some joy in life as well. And not drinking and not eating a pork chop means there is less joy in life. And I haven't worked my a**e off for 40 years to have no joy in my old age. So I'm having joy in my old age.'

Asked if he is going to stick to his new low-fat protein rich regime, Jeremy defiantly said: 'No,' while breaking out a NiQuitin lozenge.

Jeremy has two grandchildren through his daughter Emily and her husband Alex Andrew: Arlo, aged three, and Xanthe, 18 months.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
