World.title: Trump hits back at Obama over Saddam ‘Cheesecake Factory’ jab
World.content:
Photo by SAUL LOEB / AFP.

US President Donald Trump hit back at Barack Obama on Monday after the former president jokingly said his successor’s White House looked as if it were a cheesecake restaurant run by Saddam Hussein.

“For you to say it’s a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president,” Trump said in a three-minute diatribe when asked about Obama’s comments over the weekend.

“Guys like Obama, they would pass the front door, they would see the broken masonry… He doesn’t notice dirt and filth where the walls haven’t been cleaned for years,” Trump told reporters as he headed for his latest midterm election rally.

Cheesecake Factory is a popular restaurant chain known for its lengthy list of indulgent dishes and an eclectic interior design.

Obama made a series of scathing criticisms of Republican Trump’s “chaos and cruelty” as he hit the stump for Democrats in Ohio and Michigan ahead of next week’s midterm elections.

But it was Obama’s jabs at billionaire Trump’s prized renovations at the White House — including building a massive ballroom and adding gold-leafed ornamentation throughout the Oval Office — that really appeared to sting.

“He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” Obama said on Saturday, referring to the Iraqi dictator who was executed in 2006 following the US invasion of Iraq.

Trump has long had a bitter rivalry with Obama.

He launched his own political career by pushing the racist and false “birther” conspiracy theory that the Democrat was lying about being born in the United States.

But Trump’s rant over the cheesecake comments was also a sign of the 80-year-old’s increasingly short temper as the midterms loom.

On Sunday night, Trump sent his longest ever post on his Truth Social network — a 1,300-word screed in which he railed not about Iran or the economy but about US comedian Bill Maher.

Last week Trump also lashed out at a series of reporters as he faced questions about the midterms, in which Republicans face losing control of Congress, and his dealings with Russia.

AFP

World.title: Ballon d’Or: Yamal edges Cubarsi, wins Kopa Trophy 3rd time in a row
World.content:
Barcelona and Spain forward Lamine Yamal has won the men’s Young Talent of the Year award for the third consecutive year.

Yamal expressed gratitude after receiving the award but admitted that he believed his Barcelona teammate Pau Cubarsí deserved to win it instead.

The 19-year-old thanked his teammates at both club and international levels, acknowledging their contributions to his success.

Yamal, who has established himself as one of football’s brightest young stars, continues to earn recognition for his performances for Barcelona and Spain.

Ahead of the 2026 Ballon d’Or ceremony at the London Palladium in England, football stars from different clubs around the world and journalists have gathered at the venue for the 70th edition of the award.

Harry Kane has been tipped as favourite to become England’s first Ballon d’Or winner in 25 years when the award is presented, but he faces stiff competition from La Liga pair Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappé.

This 2026 edition marks the first time the showpiece is staged outside France.

Vanguard News

World.title: NDC opens new Abuja base, targets 2027 electoral victory
World.content:
Sen. Seriake Dickson, National leader of the NDC.

…As Dickson hails new national secretariat as Noah’s Ark 2

By Henry Umoru

The National Leadership of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, has inaugurated its newly acquired national secretariat in Abuja as part of efforts to strengthen its operations ahead of the 2027 general election.

The facility, located in the Jabi area of the Federal Capital Territory, was unveiled shortly after an emergency meeting of the party’s National Executive Committee (NEC), as it marks a significant step in the party’s efforts to strengthen its organisational structure and establish a permanent administrative base as preparations for the forthcoming elections gather momentum.

The new secretariat is expected to serve as the party’s administrative centre and headquarters for its presidential campaign as preparations for the 2027 elections gather momentum, just as the development marks a step in the NDC’s efforts to establish a permanent national base for coordinating its activities and managing its expanding political structure.

It is a strategic centre for coordinating its activities, strengthening communication among state chapters and mobilising supporters across the country and is also expected to play a central role in organising the party’s presidential campaign and coordinating other electoral activities ahead of the 2027 general elections

In his remarks, the National Leader of the party, Senator Seriake Dickson, described the facility as its new “Noah’s Ark” ahead of the 2027 general elections as he congratulated members and supporters on the acquisition, describing the new secretariat as a unifying centre that would provide a befitting home for the party’s growing membership.

He referred to the facility as the NDC’s newly acquired “Noah’s Ark,” a description underscoring its importance as a rallying point for members and supporters as the party pursues its political ambitions.

The inauguration attracted the party’s National Chairman, Senator Moses Cleopas; National Leader, Senator Seriake Dickson; and Senator Victor Umeh, representing Anambra Central in the National Assembly.

Also present was the party’s Rivers State governorship candidate, Dumo Lulu-Briggs, alongside other party leaders and members.

With this, the NDC has positioned itself as an alternative political platform for Nigerians seeking a change from the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC).

With the new facility, the party is expected to strengthen coordination between its national leadership, state chapters and other structures as election preparations continue.

World.title: OPHK troops destroy ISWAP enclaves in Lake Chad, kill 16 terrorists
World.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi

Troops of Operation Hadin Kai have neutralised 16 suspected Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) fighters during coordinated air and artillery strikes on three suspected terrorist locations in the Tunbunma area of South Lake Chad, following intelligence on the presence of key terrorist leaders and fighters.

According to the Joint Task Force, the operation followed sustained and relentless offensive against terrorist networks in the Lake Chad Basin.

“The operation was conducted between 1 am and 2 am on 26 October 2026, using air and ground weapon systems to engage the identified locations.

“Battle Damage Assessment indicates that 16 ISWAP fighters were neutralised across the targeted locations.

“Among those reportedly killed were Abu Zubiru, an Arab national, and two associates, Baana Nglewa and Jindullah Sadiq, alongside other fighters.

“Additionally, Abu Saleem, identified as the Wali of Tunbunma, sustained severe injuries alongside seven others.

“Operation Hadin Kai reaffirms that there is no hiding place for terrorists and remains committed to restoring peace and normalcy while conducting intelligence-led operations against terrorist elements in the North East.

“Members of the public are encouraged to provide timely and credible information to security agencies to support ongoing counter-terrorism operations.”

World.title: Microsoft offers voluntary exit packages to 60,000 staff
World.content:
Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, the company said on Monday, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as the tech giant seeks to cut costs while pouring money into artificial intelligence.

Staff on select teams in the United States, Canada, India and Britain at vice president level and below will be eligible, a Microsoft spokesperson said, while some groups of employees, including some working on data centers, sales and marketing, are excluded.

“The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter,” Amy Coleman, an executive vice president and chief people officer, told employees in a memo.

It’s the second voluntary buyout offer that Microsoft has offered employees this year.

In April, the company reportedly offered around seven percent of its US workforce the option to retire early.

Around 30 percent of those eligible took the voluntary retirement plan, according to CNBC.

Microsoft had 223,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 228,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings.

Around 27 percent of Microsoft’s workforce is eligible for the new buyout offer.

The company is expected to report quarterly earnings later this week.

AFP

World.title: Niger APC raises 525-member campaign council, targets 2m votes for Tinubu/Bago
World.content:
By Clare Nnabuike

Niger State Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago has declared that his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), is targeting 2 million votes to defeat the opposition parties in the 2027 presidential and governorship elections.

The governor made this known on Monday at the inauguration of a 525-member State Presidential/Gubernatorial Campaign Council of the APC in Minna, where he revealed that the council is drawn from commissioners, special advisers, local government chairmen, councillors, state and national lawmakers, ministers, directors-general and coordinators.

Bago described the structure as spanning party units to the state level and including political appointees, with total membership exceeding 100,000 over the years.

“If everybody would bring its own votes, it would give us more than 1 million votes. But our target is beyond that. The ambition this time around is to bring out over 2 million votes, and by the grace of God we will do that,” he said.

The governor urged the party to welcome returnees who had earlier defected to other parties, crediting the APC’s emergence as a coalition of parties that defeated the main opposition.

He called for constructive media coverage and warned against overheating the polity or triggering insecurity, saying the campaign would highlight the federal government’s economic policies, improved revenue and job creation.

Bago cited recent infrastructure and security gains, including better roads and freer movement of goods in parts of the state, as part of what the government has done and disclosed that the North Central Presidential Campaign office in Minna would be commissioned next week, with possible attendance of the President, Vice President, Senate President, Speaker or National Chairman.

Minister of Information, Idris Malagi, in his remarks, praised the choice of leadership of the council and said the APC would campaign on the administration’s record of transforming the Nigerian economy over the past three and a half years. He urged the newly appointed members to prioritise the collective good of the state and party unity

The chairman of the APC North Central, Hon. Mu’azu Rijau, while congratulating the council leadership, stressed that the 2027 campaign council should not underestimate opponents, saying the party aimed to re-elect Governor Bago alongside its senators, House of Representatives members and state assembly members.

Director-General of the campaign council, Ahmed Ibeto, accepted the assignment on behalf of members, pledging hard work, strategic coordination, grassroots engagement, unity, discipline and compliance with electoral guidelines.

He said the council would establish operational frameworks across directorates, local governments, wards and units, and would value experience while welcoming new ideas.

World.title: Kwara Youth Coalition Backs Call for Independent Audit of KWASSIP
World.content:
By Hammed Shittu in Ilorin

The 52-Youth Coalition in Kwara State has thrown its weight behind the call by the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) governorship candidate in the 2027 election, Prof. Abdulmumin Yinka Ajia, for an independent audit of the Kwara State Social Investment Programme (KWASSIP).

This, the coalition said, would go a long way in providing full details of the day to day financial operations of the agency.

The group, in a statement issued on Monday and made available to journalists in Ilorin, signed by the Director of Contact and Mobilisation of the coalition, Comrade Yusuf Eniola Obe, explained that, “the coalition fully supported the demand for a comprehensive and transparent account of every naira allocated to and expended by the agency since its inception.

“And the full details of the financial operations must include annual appropriations, actual fund releases, expenditure records, administrative costs, and outstanding balances”.

According to the coalition, “We commend the NDC candidate for raising these concerns and add our voice unreservedly to his call.

“Public funds channelled through the Kwara State Social Investment Programme belong to the people of Kwara State.

“Every kobo of those funds must be accounted for, openly, honestly, and without the evasion and opacity that has characterised this agency’s operations from the beginning”.

The coalition added, “the call for accountability coming from the NDC governorship candidate shows that Kwarans, across every political divide, are concerned about the opaque nature of KWASSIP operations and are interested in knowing how their collective resources are being spent”.

They described the level of alleged opacity surrounding KWASSIP as troubling, alleging that when the agency’s Director General, Dr. Abdulwasiu Tejidini, was asked to account for the total funds received by the agency, he was unable to answer.

The group noted, “That the Director General of a public agency cannot account for the funds his agency has received is not merely embarrassing, it is alarming.

“A Director General who does not know how much money his agency has received has either been deliberately kept in the dark or is deliberately keeping the public in the dark.

“The scenario is unacceptable and demands investigation. This is more reason the agency must be audited”.

The coalition condemned allegations that the programme had been used to make substantial payments outside established application and beneficiary selection processes, with some amounts reportedly falling outside the programme’s recognised benefit categories — a development the group described as a brazen misuse of public funds for political purposes.

“What is being described is not a social investment programme. It is a political slush fund, a mechanism for settling political obligations, rewarding loyalists, and inducing voters ahead of the 2027 general elections with money that belongs to the most vulnerable Kwarans the programme was supposedly designed to serve. This is a betrayal of public trust of the most cynical and contemptible kind,” the statement alleged.

The coalition issued a stern warning to officials of the agency and all those involved in the alleged misappropriation of KWASSIP funds, reminding them that the era of unaccountability in Kwara State is drawing to a close.

“We want to send a clear and unambiguous message to every official at KWASSIP and every political actor who has used this programme as a personal political instrument:

“The PDP if its formed the next government in Kwara State, and when it does, there will be a full and thorough accountability exercise.

“Every naira that cannot be accounted for, every payment made outside due process, and every political obligation settled with public funds will be investigated and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. Prepare your records. You will need them,” the coalition warned.

The group therefore called on the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC), and other relevant anti-corruption agencies to take immediate note of the allegations surrounding KWASSIP operations and commence preliminary investigations.

World.title: Ribadu Urges African Leaders to Develop Local Solutions to Combat Terrorism
World.content:
*Reiterates calls for international collaboration, intelligence sharing

Linus Aleke in Abuja

The National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu, has urged African leaders to take the lead in developing local solutions to combat terrorism and other emerging security threats across the continent.

Ribadu also reiterated the need for stronger global and regional cooperation, intelligence sharing and the responsible use of emerging technologies to combat terrorism and violent extremism in Africa.

Speaking at the High-Level African Lessons Learned Forum on Counter-Terrorism Cooperation, Intelligence Sharing and Emerging Technologies in Abuja on Monday, the NSA stressed that no country could effectively tackle transnational terrorist networks in isolation, given their ability to operate across borders, communicate through digital platforms and finance their activities through international channels.

He said terrorist groups were exploiting porous borders, local grievances, illicit financial networks, digital platforms and online radicalisation to expand their operations across the continent.

Ribadu noted that Nigeria’s experience over the past 15 years had shown that military operations alone could not provide a sustainable solution to terrorism.

He said the country had continued to pursue a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach to counter-terrorism and the prevention and countering of violent extremism.

According to him, “Our partners remain important, and we value their continued support. However, sustainable solutions must be rooted in African ownership, African priorities, African institutions and the lived experiences of our communities.

“While security operations remain necessary, they must be complemented by intelligence coordination, law enforcement, financial intelligence, justice, strategic communications, prevention, rehabilitation, reintegration, reconciliation, community resilience, education, youth engagement, research, training and technology-enabled analysis.”

He also highlighted the growing influence of artificial intelligence, encrypted platforms, drones and synthetic media on the security landscape, noting that although terrorist groups could exploit these technologies, they also offered opportunities for early warning, threat analysis, digital investigations, border security and the protection of vulnerable communities.

“Our task is to ensure that technology is used responsibly, lawfully and effectively in support of peace and security,” he said.

Similarly, the United Nations (UN) Deputy Secretary-General, Amina Mohammed, called for stronger intelligence sharing, public trust and the responsible use of emerging technologies to strengthen Africa’s fight against terrorism and violent extremism.

Speaking virtually, Mohammed said terrorism continued to devastate families and communities across Nigeria’s North-East, the Lake Chad Basin, the Sahel and parts of East and Southern Africa.

“In Nigeria, we know the cost of this scourge, the toll it is taking on families and communities across the North-East and the Lake Chad Basin,” she said.

She added that the violence was claiming lives, displacing communities, disrupting economic activities and undermining development in vulnerable areas.

She also cautioned that military operations alone would not end terrorism, urging governments to complement security measures with rehabilitation, reintegration, justice and community support.

The Country Representative of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), Cheikh Touré, also called for African-led counter-terrorism strategies, warning that terrorist groups were increasingly exploiting cross-border networks, organised crime and emerging technologies.

Touré said Africa had become a major centre of global terrorism, with the Sahel accounting for more than half of all terrorism-related deaths worldwide.

He noted that four of the five countries responsible for nearly 70 per cent of global terrorism deaths in the previous year were African: Burkina Faso, Nigeria, Niger and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

“In the past decade, terrorism has gained a foothold in Africa that few of us would have predicted,” he said.

Earlier, in his welcome address, the National Coordinator of the National Counter-Terrorism Centre (NCTC), Major General Adamu Laka, said the forum was designed to enable African countries to share experiences, identify effective strategies and strengthen cooperation against terrorism.

Laka said terrorist groups were increasingly exploiting technology, illicit financial flows, corruption and criminal networks to advance their activities.

He stressed that military action must be complemented by prevention, rehabilitation, reintegration, criminal justice and community resilience.

World.title: Kwara PDP Guber Candidate Urges IGP to Probe Alleged Arrest, Detention of Party Members
World.content:
By Hammed Shittu in Ilorin

The governorship candidate of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Kwara State, Engr. Sulaiman Bolakale Kawu, has called on the Inspector-General of Police, Mr. Tunji Disu, to urgently investigate the alleged arrest, detention and repeated police invitations involving members of the party in the state.

The call was made in a statement issued in Ilorin on Monday by the media office of the PDP candidate, following reports of arrests and the alleged use of tear gas during a peaceful procession at the Emir’s palace in Ilorin, the state capital.

The media office accused the Kwara State Commissioner of Police, Mr. Ojo Adekimi, of allegedly being behind the actions, warning that failure to investigate the incidents could heighten political tension in the state.

It described the development as a potential threat to police neutrality, respect for the rule of law and the protection of fundamental rights ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The office also urged the police authorities to investigate the reported deployment of tear gas against participants in the procession, which was attended by Kawu, Senator Saliu Mustapha and other PDP political candidates.

According to the statement, the incidents could create the impression that the police command was being used to intimidate opposition members and suppress legitimate political expression rather than address established security concerns.

Particularly concerning, the statement said, was the reported imprisonment of Kadri Usman Elesin and Taiye Alaboke without proper arraignment before a competent court or a meaningful opportunity to respond to the allegations against them.

The media office recalled that the two men, identified in earlier reports as Taiye Laufe, also known as Taiye Alaboka, and AbdulKadir Usman, were arrested on October 24, 2026. It said both men were from Agaka Isale, Ilorin, the family house of Kawu.

It further alleged that the men had remained in detention despite efforts by their families and legal representatives to secure administrative bail, expressing concern over reports that they had subsequently been taken to prison without due judicial process.

The statement called on the relevant authorities to establish the legal basis for their imprisonment, clarify whether they had been formally charged and arraigned before a competent court, and ensure that their constitutional rights were protected.

It also listed several individuals reportedly invited by the police on different dates in October. They include Kayode Jack, Shuaib Baba Agaka, Amuda Ajia Eru, Shuaib Tunde, Idris Samad, Fazawa Anafi Agaka and Alhaji Aloa Moshood Imam.

The media office maintained that the reported arrests, repeated police invitations, alleged imprisonment without proper arraignment and reported use of tear gas against peaceful protesters should be investigated collectively to determine whether they constituted legitimate policing or interference with opposition political activities.

“The police are not an extension of the ruling party, nor should any opposition party be made to feel that its political activities constitute an invitation to harassment by security agencies,” the statement said.

It stressed that the Nigeria Police Force must remain accountable to the Constitution and the law rather than serve the political interests of any individual or party.

The statement warned that perceived partisanship by security agencies could undermine public confidence in the electoral process ahead of the 2027 elections.

“An election cannot be regarded as free and fair merely because votes are cast and counted.

“The environment leading to the election must also be free from intimidation, selective arrests and the abuse of security institutions to create an advantage for the party in power,” it said.

The media office urged the Inspector-General of Police to order an independent investigation into the arrests, detention and reported imprisonment of the two men, as well as the alleged use of tear gas against peaceful protesters.

It also called for an investigation into whether any police officers acted on improper political instructions and whether constitutional safeguards relating to personal liberty, fair hearing, peaceful assembly and the treatment of suspects were observed.

The statement further demanded appropriate disciplinary action against any officer found to have abused his authority or compromised the impartiality expected of the Nigeria Police Force.

While stressing that its position was not intended to obstruct lawful police investigations or shield anyone from accountability, the media office maintained that no citizen should face intimidation, unlawful detention or disproportionate use of force because of political affiliation or participation in peaceful political activities.

It also called for a review of the leadership of the Kwara State Police Command if an independent investigation established that the commissioner had failed to maintain the neutrality, professionalism and restraint required of his office.

The statement said that the credibility of the 2027 electoral process depended not only on the conduct of political parties and candidates but also on the ability of security agencies to demonstrate fairness, impartiality and respect for the fundamental rights of all citizens, irrespective of political affiliation.

Meanwhile, efforts to obtain the reaction of the Police Command Public Relations Officer, SP Toun Ejire Adeyemi, proved unsuccessful, as calls made to her telephone were not answered.

A text message sent to her number had also not received a response as of the time of filing this report.

World.title: NDC Discloses N8.5bn Income, N2.4bn Spending in Seven Months
World.content:
*Party unveils campaign council, inaugurates national secretariat

Sunday Aborisade in Abuja

The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) on Monday disclosed that it generated N8.529 billion from nomination forms, membership dues, levies and contributions within its first seven months of operation, while spending N2.402 billion on primaries, publicity, staff salaries and other activities.

The party presented the financial figures at its National Executive Committee (NEC) meeting in Abuja, where its National Chairman, Senator Moses Cleopas, said the disclosure was intended to promote transparency and accountability in the management of the party’s resources ahead of its first anniversary.

The NEC Meeting was attended by the National Leader of the party, Senator Henry Seriake Dickson; the Presidential Candidate of the party, Mr. Peter Obi; his Vice, Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso; serving and former members of the National Assembly and other notable leaders of the party, among others.

Cleopas said the party decided to account for its finances before the statutory deadline for submitting its audited accounts to the relevant government institutions, insisting that members had a right to know how funds entrusted to their leaders were being managed.

He said the decision was not prompted by allegations or criticisms on social media but reflected the party’s commitment to accountability and responsible leadership.

According to him, the party’s leadership considered it necessary to provide members with an early account of its financial position, even though the NDC had yet to complete its first year of operation.

He said, “One of the critical instruments that destroys leadership or communal living, as I have been taught, is the management of public funds. When you have a responsibility to sit over a public forum, you also owe the people who entrusted you with that privilege an obligation to be open to them.

“They must know what you are doing from time to time. Any attempt to foreclose that will lead to suspicion and give room for people to say what is not true.

“When you find yourself in a leadership position, accountability must be your sense of duty, especially when it has to do with common wealth.

“That is what Nigeria is suffering from. Nigeria is so blessed. We cannot say that we do not have resources in this country. The question we are asking is: where are our resources? What are our resources being used for that will bring relief or blessings to Nigerian citizens?”

The national chairman said the NDC would submit its properly audited financial statement to the constitutionally authorised institutions when the appropriate reporting period ended.

He explained that the party’s financial management process involved a committee comprising the national chairman, national secretary, financial secretary, treasurer and auditor, with the party’s legal adviser co-opted when necessary.

The National Treasurer, Dr Peter Onigah, presented the financial statement at the meeting, outlining the funds received and expenditure incurred during the period under review.

The disclosure comes as the NDC intensifies preparations for the 2027 general election, with the party also inaugurating its presidential campaign council, present certificates of return to its candidates and commission its national secretariat at the Jabi Area of Abuja.

Cleopas said the activities were part of efforts to strengthen the party’s structures and demonstrate its readiness for the forthcoming elections.

He said the inauguration of the presidential campaign council followed consultations aimed at identifying people willing to commit their time and resources to the party’s electoral project.

“It is not a matter of rushing to announce a campaign council. It is a matter of getting people who are committed, people who are ready to serve this nation in that capacity,” he said.

The chairman also cautioned party members against interpreting the initial list of campaign council appointments as a complete representation of all those who would eventually be involved.

“Some are calling to ask, ‘Why is my name not there? Why is my name not there?’ We are not finished. Let them wait for us,” he said.

Cleopas said the party presented certificates of return to its candidates to prevent individuals who did not win its primaries from parading themselves as candidates and misleading voters.

He described the NDC as a party intended to outlive its founding leaders, urging young Nigerians to identify with it and prepare for future leadership responsibilities.

Cleopas said, “This party is intended to be a generational party for as long as we remain on earth. This party is intended to outlive us. And if that is the vision we have, there is a particular set of people we must target.

“We have the youth to target in this country. The reason is that they must be prepared for leadership. So, this is a party of mentorship,” he said.

Umeh Seeks Funding for State Chapters

At the meeting, Senator Victor Umeh, representing Anambra Central, commended the party’s leadership for making its financial position available to members, describing the disclosure as an important step towards building public confidence.

Umeh said providing financial information would help members understand the party’s operations rather than rely on speculation.

He, however, called on the national leadership to ensure that state chapters received an appropriate share of the funds generated through their activities.

Responding, Cleopas said the issue of funding for state chapters was already under consideration, assuring members that the party would address the matter in line with its constitution and organisational objectives.

The chairman also disclosed that the party’s reconciliation committee had visited the six geopolitical zones to engage aggrieved aspirants and other members dissatisfied with the outcomes of its primaries.

He said the national secretariat was holding regular meetings to resolve outstanding disagreements and prevent internal disputes from undermining the party’s preparations for the elections.

Cleopas urged candidates, party leaders and supporters to put aside their differences and work collectively for the success of all NDC candidates.

He said the party could not afford to allow personal disagreements to weaken its electoral prospects, particularly when its presidential and vice-presidential candidates would require the support of lawmakers and other elected representatives to implement their programmes if elected.

The chairman argued that supporting only the party’s presidential candidate while abandoning its candidates for governorship and legislative seats could undermine the party’s ability to govern effectively.

He said, “Don’t you also know that they need a majority, if not all, in the National Assembly from our party? If you don’t know so, how will they get the president they want? How will they get the Senate president or the speaker of their choice?

“You may not like the face of the candidates, but they are your party’s candidates. We must work together so that we can have the Nigeria of our dreams.”

NDC Insists on Candidate Compliance, Vote Protection

The NEC meeting also heard updates from party officials on preparations for the 2027 elections, including efforts to resolve disputes involving candidates and strengthen the party’s grassroots structures.

The National Vice-Chairman for the North-east, Dr Dallamiya Nzukumbe, said preparations were progressing, although the party had encountered some disagreements between candidates and party leaders in certain areas.

He said the leadership was working to resolve the disputes and ensure that the party’s structures remained focused on the elections.

Nzukumbe also urged Nigerians to reject the notion that their votes would not count, calling on voters to remain at polling units after casting their ballots to ensure that votes were counted and results properly documented.

“We will vote, we will wait, and we will escort,” he said, stressing that the party wanted an electoral process in which votes cast at polling units were accurately reflected in the final results.

He said voters in the North were particularly concerned about insecurity, the disruption of farming activities and attacks on schools, adding that residents wanted to return to their farms, travel safely and send their children to school without fear.

“The children in the North must go to school,” he said.

Another party official, speaking on preparations in the southern part of the country, said the party was working to resolve outstanding disputes arising from its primaries and restore harmony among members.

He said the NDC was intensifying voter education and sensitisation on electoral responsibilities, particularly the need for voters and party agents to protect their votes after voting.

According to him, the party was documenting its agents and working with candidates at different levels to ensure adequate representation at polling units and collation centres.

He urged voters not to leave polling units immediately after casting their ballots but to remain until the votes were counted and the results properly recorded.

Cleopas, in his closing remarks, also addressed concerns over the omission of some candidates’ names from the relevant electoral processes.

He said the party was pursuing both administrative and legal avenues to address the matter and expressed confidence that candidates who had fulfilled the requirements of the law would be able to contest the elections.

“The party is not folding its hands. The party is interfacing on administrative fronts and legal fronts,” he said.

He added that the leadership was conscious of its responsibility to candidates who had completed the required processes and would continue to pursue the matter.

The NDC chairman urged members to remain united as the party moved from internal preparations to the next phase of its electoral activities.

He said the party’s immediate priorities included commissioning its national secretariat, inaugurating the presidential campaign council, presenting certificates to its candidates and resolving outstanding grievances before the 2027 general election.

World.title: At 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit, Tinubu Says His Govt Is Rewriting Nation’s Decades-old Story of Economic Underperformance
World.content:
.Stresses economic reforms are restoring confidence, laying foundation for sustainable growth

Deji Elumoye in Abuja

President Bola Tinubu on Monday disclosed that his government is rewriting Nigeria’s decades-long story of economic underperformance through far-reaching reforms designed to dismantle structural barriers, unlock the nation’s enormous potential and deliver jobs, productivity and shared prosperity.

According to him, the administration is currently undertaking what it came into office to achieve: rewriting the story of a nation that has performed below its potential for far too long.

Speaking in Abuja while formally declaring open the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit, the President, who was represented by Vice President Kashim Shettima, noted that his government began on a difficult note because there is no shortcut to economic growth.

His words: “Distinguished ladies and gentlemen, we came to rewrite the story of a nation that has performed below its potential for far too long. But there is no shortcut to economic growth. This is why we began with a difficult reset. For us, rescuing the economy means rescuing livelihoods and transforming the fortunes of young jobseekers, farmers, manufacturers, entrepreneurs and innovators.

“We cannot harness the immense opportunities offered by our growing population without first stabilising the economy. We must also create the conditions for the public and private sectors to invest, expand and generate productive employment.”

Tinubu observed that the summit’s theme, “Growth That Works: Delivering Jobs, Productivity and Shared Prosperity,” built on the ambition of the previous edition of the annual event to achieve a prosperous and inclusive Nigeria by 2030.

He noted that his administration has “since set in motion a series of reforms to dismantle the structural barriers that have prevented our abundant human and natural resources from yielding prosperity.

“These reforms are restoring confidence, strengthening our economic foundations and laying the groundwork for sustainable growth,” he added, noting that the administration is encouraged by what it has accomplished so far.

Acknowledging that creating jobs was only half the task, the President stressed the need to “improve the quality of work, reduce underemployment and harness the potential” of the nation’s underutilised workforce.

“Our pursuit of prosperity demands greater productivity from every worker, enterprise and investment. We must judge infrastructure by the economic activity it generates and education by the skills and productivity it delivers.

“We must judge industrial policy by the competitiveness of our firms and investment incentives by the capital, technology, exports and jobs they attract.”

Tinubu outlined what he described as the achievements of his administration’s reforms, saying they have been well documented. He cited figures from the National Bureau of Statistics indicating that Nigeria’s inflation-adjusted GDP grew by 3.89% in the first quarter of 2026, compared with 3.13% a year earlier.

On economic diversification, he stated that “non-oil activities accounted for 96.08% of GDP, while manufacturing grew by 3.29% and the oil sector by 2.57%,” emphasising that the gains have reinforced his administration’s confidence in the path of recovery and diversification.

The President stated, however, that his administration’s ambition must go beyond favourable statistics, even as the development narrative is changing and investor confidence is returning.

Outlining the administration’s gains so far, he said, “In the first quarter of 2026, our capital importation reached $10.37 billion, an increase of 83.83% over the corresponding period in 2025. This comprised both portfolio and foreign direct investment. We will, therefore, continue to ease regulatory burdens, strengthen transparency and policy predictability, and expand access to finance.

“Our tax reforms seek to build a modern, equitable system that finances development and gives businesses certainty. This discipline must guide our investments in all sectors of the economy, including energy, agriculture and solid minerals. We are reforming the electricity market to improve supply and attract investment in generation, transmission, distribution and alternative energy.”

On agriculture, Tinubu said the administration is connecting farms to storage facilities, processing centres and markets while expanding irrigation, mechanisation, finance and rural infrastructure.

He added that the government is also seeking “to move beyond extraction into domestic processing, industrial production and exports” in the solid minerals sector.

The President, however, noted that despite the gains of his administration’s economic reforms, the task remains far from finished, even as young Nigerians have demonstrated their capacity to compete globally in technology, financial services and the creative industries.

On her part, United Nations Deputy Secretary-General, Dr. Amina Mohammed, assessed the reforms implemented under the Tinubu administration, acknowledging the gains while urging their urgent consolidation and stabilisation, as well as the effective management of expectations among citizens and other stakeholders.

She also applauded the African Development Bank (AfDB) for its new financial architecture for development across the African continent, particularly its prioritisation of financing programmes that target impactful development.

In his remarks, Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Dr. Taiwo Oyedele, presented the Nigerian Economic Policy Framework, which he described as a national economic doctrine that establishes how Nigeria makes economic decisions and measures real progress.

The minister invited members of the Nigerian Economic Summit Group (NESG) and private sector experts to make valuable contributions to the development of the framework by rigorously critiquing the draft proposal with facts and figures.

He said the principles underpinning the framework include enterprise, open but fair markets, and whole-of-government coherence.

Oyedele also listed key areas of focus in the proposed framework, including economic stability, human capital development and productivity, among others.

Earlier in his welcome address, Chairman of the NESG, Mr. Olaniyi Yusuf, said participation at the 32nd summit reflected stakeholders’ commitment to contributing to inclusive and impactful growth, while acknowledging the Federal Government’s efforts to improve the ease of doing business in the country.

He said that although the reforms of the Tinubu administration may have introduced significant changes to Nigeria’s economic structures, the task before economic experts at the summit and beyond was to ensure stabilisation rather than seek a reversal of the policies.

Yusuf added that the 32nd edition of the summit must help Nigeria move from policy consensus to a framework that resolves practical issues, noting that deliberations would be guided by proposals for job creation, improved productivity and shared prosperity for all.

Also speaking, Chairman and Founder of BUA Group, Abdul Samad Rabiu, commended the economic reforms of President Tinubu’s administration, saying they had begun to address longstanding challenges confronting Nigerian businesses.

Rabiu acknowledged the difficulties experienced by ordinary Nigerians but noted that improvements in access to foreign exchange had created a more predictable environment for businesses.

“For many years, one of the greatest challenges facing businesses was access to foreign exchange. You could have all the naira but be unable to obtain the foreign exchange needed to buy raw materials and machinery,” he recalled.

World.title: NMDPRA Expands Gas Supply Access to Power, Fertiliser Plants with New Network Code
World.content:
*Targets 9 fuel laboratories nationwide by H1 2027

*Authority, NNPC advance talks to pilot national strategic fuel reserve

Peter Uzoho

The Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA)! has expanded gas supply access to power plants, fertiliser plants and shippers with the launch of Revision II of the Nigerian Gas Transportation Network Code (NGTNC).

Authority Chief Executive of NMDPRA, Mallam Rabiu Umar announced the new code Monday at the opening of the 20th Oil Trading and Logistics (OTL) Africa Downstream Week in Lagos after signing the document with key partners.

The partners comprise power generation plants, fertiliser plants, shippers and investors.

Umar said the new code will deepen domestic gas utilization and ensure open, fair access to gas transportation infrastructure.

“The Network Code basically is the rulebook for gas transportation. As we know, there’s one pipeline that different producers put their gas into. And for there to be equity, there needs to be a code, or if you like, rules of engagement on how you put your gas inside, how the gas is measured, and how you nominate gas.

“The pipelines deliver their full value only when access to them is open and fair. It is therefore a pleasure to announce, as you have witnessed, that the Authority has launched officially the revision 2 of the Nigerian Gas Transportation Network Code,” he said.

Speaking under the summit’s theme “Secure Energy, Shared Prosperity,” Umar said the code revision comes as gas demand rises, with about three-fifths of gas processed in September deployed to power plants, factories, NLNG and the West African Gas Pipeline (WAGP) while demand for cooking gas outstrips supply.

He said infrastructure to support the expansion is advancing, with the Oben-Obiafu-Obrikom (OB3) pipeline, the Escravos-Lagos Pipeline System (ELPS) midline compressor nearly complete and the Ajaokuta-Kaduna-Kano pipeline now more than 80 per cent built.

Once on stream, Umar said the gas pipelines would double national gas transport capacity from 2.2 to 4.4 billion cubic feet per day and linking southern supply to northern demand.

“Since revision 1, more shippers have come onto the network, and the imbalance on the Western network has fallen by about 30 per cent. Revision II builds on these gains, and I invite every shipper, transporter and investor to make full use of that,” Umar said.

He explained that the Revision II provides clearer rules for shippers and buyers, including provisions on shrinkage factor, noting that high shrinkage from wrong gas injection creates avoidable losses.

The code also lays the initial rules for regional pipelines, including the West African Gas Pipeline, the proposed Trans-Saharan Pipeline to Algeria and the Trans-African Pipeline to Morocco, requiring harmonised standards for cross-border gas movement.

On downstream security, Umar said a year ago more than half of petrol in Nigerian tanks was imported, but last month three in every four litres were refined domestically.

This he said, means energy security built at home as Nigerian crude refined in Nigeria is supplying Nigerians.

He however cautioned that much of current supply comes from one large refinery which ran above nameplate capacity in September, stressing the need for diversity through modular refineries, the four national refineries and competitive imports.

He said import licences will be issued only on published merit-based criteria and transparent shortfall determination.

On consumption trends, Umar said Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) consumption has risen by almost half since 2021, while Compressed Natural Gas (CNG), which was almost non-existent six years ago, is expanding, with presidential directive to double penetration by year-end to enhance energy flexibility.

He disclosed that petrol stock cover stands at 24 days, below the 30-day threshold, while cooking gas is tighter, with diesel and aviation fuel comfortably above thresholds.

According to him, global guideline by the International Energy Agency (IEA) is 90 days, but Nigeria targets 30 to 45 days first.

“Over the past eight months, a war in the Gulf has shaken the world’s fuel supply and pushed crude oil to around $100 a barrel. Through it all, Nigeria kept its fuel flowing, because more of that fuel is now made here at home,” Umar said.

He revealed advanced talks with the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) to pilot the national strategic stock at the

Nigerian Pipelines and Storage Company Limited (NPSC) depots in Ibadan, Enugu and Suleja, to cushion the economy against price and supply shocks.

“Secure energy is energy we produce, we move, we store and price well for ourselves. Shared prosperity is what follows when the value of that energy stays and circulates within our economies and across our continent,” Umar said.

He also announced quality assurance expansion, with the first of nine fuel laboratories launched in Port Harcourt, two more by year-end and nine functional by mid-2027 in partnership with Bureau Veritas and Ace Energy and Power Solutions towards a National Reference Laboratory.

He said all Premium Motor Spirit (PMS) supplied in Nigeria was on-spec, with market data published monthly, and that NMDPRA does not set prices under the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) but ensures fair competition.

With 215 trillion cubic feet proven gas reserves and 600 TCF prospective, Umar said Nigeria needs $30 to $50 billion fresh investment in processing, fertiliser, LPG and flare commercialisation.

He proposed an aligned fuel standards and a West Africa reference price to reduce dependence on European benchmarks like Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Antwerp (ARA) benchmarks.

World.title: The Shadow In The Twilight: An Ode to Pa Reuben Famuyide Fasoranti (1926–2026)
World.content:
By Marindoti Oludare

There are men whose lives are measured in years, others whose lives are measured in accomplishments, and a rare few whose lives are measured by the generations they have inspired. Pa Reuben Famuyide Fasoranti belonged to that rare breed of men whose very existence became a moral compass for society. He lived for a century, but the measure of his life was never in the number of years he lived. It was in the principles he upheld, the lives he touched, the institutions he built, and the causes for which he never ceased to fight.

For as long as I can remember, Baba Fasoranti has been one of the men I looked up to. He represented everything I believed public service ought to be: integrity without compromise, leadership without arrogance, political conviction without blind loyalty, and an abiding belief that the welfare of the people must always be the supreme purpose of government.

It was this admiration that, in the lead-up to the 2023 presidential election, made his endorsement of Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu one of the most consequential influences on my decision to join the campaign for his presidency. I believed that a man who had spent his life advocating true federalism, restructuring, state police, and public accountability would not lend his moral authority lightly. If Baba believed that Tinubu could advance these causes, I believed there was good reason to join that effort.

Today, as we mourn his passing, I find myself reflecting not only on the extraordinary life he lived but also on the promises we owe his memory, some of which remain painfully unfulfilled.

Baba was born on May 11, 1926, into a Nigeria still under British colonial rule, long before independence, long before the First Republic, and before many of the political institutions we now take for granted had been conceived. To say that he participated in Nigerian politics for almost as long as modern Nigerian politics has existed is hardly an exaggeration. His life traversed colonialism, nationalism, independence, civilian administrations, military dictatorships, and the return to democracy.

Yet his journey began not in the corridors of power but in the humble pursuit of knowledge.

As a young man, he dreamed of becoming a medical doctor. But the educational limitations of his time stood between him and that ambition. At Ondo Boys’ High School, where he received his secondary education, the absence of adequate science teaching denied him the opportunity to pursue the subjects needed for medicine.

For many young men, such a disappointment might have ended in bitterness or resignation. For Baba, it became the foundation of a lifelong mission. He would dedicate himself to ensuring that the generations coming after him did not have their ambitions determined by the limitations of the schools they attended.

He went on to study at Yaba Higher College and University College, Ibadan, before pursuing advanced studies in education in Britain and Australia. He became a teacher, an administrator, and subsequently a principal. In 1957, he became the founding principal of Anglican Grammar School, Iju-Itaogbolu, which began with only 30 students. He would later help establish Omolere Nursery and Primary School, Akure High School, and St. Frances’ Academy, named in memory of his beloved wife.

The young man who could not study medicine because his school could not adequately teach the sciences devoted his life to building schools where other people’s children could pursue their dreams.

What greater testimony to selfless leadership could there be?

Baba’s political life was equally remarkable. He was an admirer and disciple of Chief Obafemi Awolowo, whose philosophy of progressive governance, education, social welfare, and federalism resonated deeply with his own convictions. But Baba was no political sycophant. His loyalty was to principles, not personalities.

Perhaps no episode demonstrates this better than his extraordinary encounter with the political establishment of the Action Group in Akure.

When Awolowo’s political machinery supported a candidate for the chairmanship of the Akure Local Council whom Baba and his associates believed did not represent the wishes of their people, he refused to surrender his convictions to party authority.

Instead, he and his supporters established the Alarm Clock Party, challenged the established political order, and defeated the Action Group candidate at the polls.

Imagine the audacity of that young man! A committed disciple of Awolowo, standing against the candidate preferred by the very political leader he revered, not out of personal animosity but because he believed that the people of Akure deserved the right to determine who represented them.

And perhaps even more remarkable was what followed. Having made his point and secured the mandate of his people, Baba returned to the Action Group. He had not abandoned his political philosophy; he had merely refused to abandon the people for the sake of party convenience.

There lies a lesson for today’s political class: loyalty to a political party must never become disloyalty to the people. A party is merely the vehicle through which the people exercise their democratic rights. It must never become an instrument for suppressing those rights.

The story of Baba’s service in the Akure Local Council also provides an enduring lesson in public morality. While serving as council chairman and simultaneously working as a school principal, he refused to draw two salaries. He considered his income as a principal sufficient and chose to offer his political service without collecting remuneration from the council.

At a time when public office has become, for too many, an invitation to personal enrichment, such a disposition almost sounds unbelievable. But Baba belonged to a generation that regarded leadership as a duty to be discharged, not a privilege to be exploited.

His years in local government are also remembered in Akure’s history of early public infrastructure, including local recollections of pioneering road development around Arakale. For him, the measure of political authority was not the prestige of occupying an office but the visible improvement in the lives of those who elected him.

This philosophy followed him into the Second Republic when he served as Commissioner for Finance under the administration of Chief Michael Adekunle Ajasin between 1979 and 1983.

Together, Ajasin and Fasoranti represented a tradition of public probity that has become distressingly scarce in contemporary Nigerian politics. The resources of the state were held in trust for the people, and public officials were expected to account for their stewardship.

Their reputation for integrity was tested when the military overthrew the civilian government in December 1983.

The succeeding military administration subjected members of that government to imprisonment, investigation, and prosecution. Chief Ajasin was famously tried twice and acquitted twice, yet remained in detention. Baba Fasoranti also endured imprisonment and prosecution in the aftermath of the coup.

It was an era in which allegations against the political class became a convenient justification for military intervention, and men who had devoted their lives to public service could find themselves deprived of liberty by those who claimed to be rescuing the nation.

Baba emerged from these ordeals without abandoning his principles. He would go on to participate in the struggle against military dictatorship, lending his voice to the campaign for the restoration of democratic government.

The same man who had challenged his own party over the wishes of the Akure electorate would later stand against military rule in defence of the sovereignty of the Nigerian people.

His was not a convenient democracy that mattered only when his preferred candidates won. It was a conviction that the people’s mandate must remain sacred.

And so I wonder what Baba would make of the political developments in our country today, where party nominations are sometimes determined not by the wishes of the electorate but by the influence of powerful individuals far removed from the communities whose futures they seek to control.

What would he say to political imposition, the manipulation of electoral processes, and the growing belief that power belongs to those who can control the machinery of a party rather than those who can win the confidence of its members?

I believe his life has already answered these questions.

A man who once challenged Awolowo’s preferred candidate to defend the democratic rights of Akure people would hardly have wanted future generations to surrender those same rights without resistance.

Baba’s life was not without profound personal tragedy. He lost his beloved wife, Frances, in 1991. He endured the death of a daughter while he was in military detention. Then, in July 2019, another daughter, Funke Olakunrin, was brutally murdered by gunmen along the Benin-Ore highway.

For any father, the loss of a child is an unbearable burden. To lose a daughter to the same insecurity against which one has spent years warning one’s country is a cruelty beyond words.

Yet Baba did not allow his personal grief to diminish his concern for the suffering of others. If anything, the tragedy reinforced the urgency of his lifelong advocacy for the protection of lives and property.

This brings me to one of the most poignant images of Baba’s final years: the frail, elderly statesman, confined to a wheelchair, who nevertheless found the strength to travel to Abuja and appeal directly to President Tinubu for the restructuring of Nigeria and the establishment of state police.

Dr. Marindoti Oludare, Pa Reuben Fasoranti, and Marindoti’s dad, Dr Patrick Oludare, at the home of Papa in Akure, on July 6, 2023

On April 17, 2024, Baba led an Afenifere delegation to the Presidential Villa. At an age when most men would have withdrawn completely from the affairs of the world, he was still pleading for a country where its citizens could live without fear.

He was not asking for a contract. He was not seeking a political appointment. He was not requesting a favour for his children or grandchildren.

He was asking for a safer Nigeria.

There is something profoundly moving about a man nearing a hundred years of age, who has already lost a daughter to violence, continuing to spend what little strength remains in his body demanding the security of other people’s children.

That, to me, is the essence of Baba Fasoranti.

And it is here that my admiration must coexist with my disappointment.

President Tinubu has taken steps toward the establishment of state police, including supporting constitutional changes and legislative proposals. These developments deserve acknowledgment. But I remain deeply saddened that the reform did not become a functioning reality while Baba was alive to witness it.

Indeed, the irony of history could hardly be more painful. On October 23, 2026, just three days after Baba’s death, the Presidency announced that the proposed constitutional amendment to establish state police had secured the support of 24 state Houses of Assembly, crossing the constitutional threshold necessary for the reform to advance.

Three days after he departed.

Baba had lived a hundred years. He had waited through colonialism, military dictatorship, and successive civilian administrations for the emergence of a truly federal Nigeria. Yet he departed before seeing one of his most enduring aspirations become reality.

I wish President Tinubu had moved with greater urgency, not merely for Baba’s sake but for the countless Nigerians whose lives remain vulnerable to insecurity. Baba deserved to witness more than promises and proposals. He deserved to see the machinery of a restructured security system take shape in his lifetime.

Nevertheless, this disappointment must not become an excuse to abandon the struggle. Rather, it must strengthen our resolve to complete it.

We who remain must now take up the mantle.

We must insist on state policing that is genuinely accountable to the communities it serves, with proper safeguards against political abuse, independent oversight, and a firm commitment to protecting every Nigerian, regardless of ethnicity, religion, political affiliation, or social standing.

We must continue the struggle against corruption, that malignant disease which robs our schools of classrooms, our hospitals of medicines, our roads of durability, and our security institutions of the resources required to protect the people.

We must resist the manipulation of elections and the imposition of candidates, for a society that permits its people’s votes to be stolen cannot credibly claim to honour the memory of a man who once defied his own political leader to defend the right of his people to choose.

We must remember that political leadership is not measured by the number of convoys surrounding an officeholder, the size of the allowances he collects, or the fortunes accumulated by his associates. It is measured by the opportunities created for the next generation and by the dignity with which the ordinary citizen is treated.

Above all, we must restore integrity to public life.

For me, Baba Fasoranti will remain a North Star, a constant moral reference by which to judge not only those who seek to govern us but also our own conduct as citizens.

At a hundred years of age, he had nothing more to prove. He could have spent his final years in the comfort of his family, receiving tributes and enjoying the gratitude of a society he had already served beyond measure. Instead, he continued to concern himself with the unfinished business of Nigeria.

Therein lies the final lesson of his remarkable existence: a life of service never truly retires, and a conviction worth holding is a conviction worth defending until one’s final breath.

Now Baba has entered the twilight of eternity.

The sun that illuminated a century of Nigerian history has finally dipped below the horizon. The voice that once rose in defence of the people of Akure, that challenged political imposition, that upheld probity in the management of public resources, that resisted military tyranny, and that pleaded for the security of our country has fallen silent.

But there is something about the twilight that we must remember.

As the sun descends, the shadows of great things stretch farther across the earth.

And so it shall be with Baba Fasoranti.

Though he has sailed beyond the horizon into the quiet embrace of the night, his shadow remains cast upon our nation. It will stretch across our political institutions, across the schools he founded, across the roads of Akure, and across the conscience of every Nigerian who still believes that public office should be an instrument of service rather than self-enrichment.

His body may have surrendered to the passage of time, but his ideals have not. His voice may have fallen silent, but his example still speaks. His eyes may have closed to the troubles of our nation, but the light of his convictions must continue to illuminate our path.

And when the darkness of corruption, electoral manipulation, insecurity, and political expediency threatens to overwhelm our country, may we look toward the North Star of his example and find the courage to do what is right.

Let us not merely mourn Baba. Let us become worthy of him.

Let us complete the work he could not finish.

Let us build the Nigeria he believed in.

For Baba Fasoranti may have departed into the twilight, but his shadow will remain with us long after the night has fallen.

And so long as we keep his ideals alive, the darkness shall never claim his light.

Rest peacefully, Baba.

Your struggle is now ours. Your mantle has fallen into our hands. And we must not let it fall to the ground.

World.title: Shoga: City Boy Movt’s Efforts Contributed To Success Of APC’s Kaduna Rally
World.content:
.Says inauguration of Abuja–Kaduna highway opens economic platform for N’West

Folalumi Alaran in Abuja

Director-General of the City Boy Movement (CBM), Hon. Oluwatosin Shoga, has attributed the large turnout of youth at Saturday’s flag-off of the All Progressives Congress (APC) re-election campaign of President Bola Tinubu in Kaduna as an affirmation of the Movement’s sustained grassroots enlightenment and mobilisation efforts in support of the President.

According to him, the impressive youth participation at the rally demonstrated growing interest among young Nigerians in the Tinubu’s development programme and their determination to participate actively in determining Nigeria’s political and economic future.

In a reflection titled, “Beyond the Road: Unlocking Opportunities, Empowering Young Nigerians, and Building a Prosperous Future,” released in Abuja, the CBM boss attributed the enthusiasm witnessed at the Kaduna rally partly to sustained grassroots engagements, including the Movement’s mobilisation activities and street walk in Kano.

His words: “The City Boy Movement was proudly on the ground, engaging with young Nigerians and grassroots supporters who came out to demonstrate their commitment to the future of our country.

“The enthusiasm witnessed in Kaduna, alongside our grassroots engagement and street walk in Kano, reinforces our conviction that young Nigerians want to be part of a national conversation about development, opportunity, and a more prosperous Nigeria.”

Shoga stressed that the Movement’s activities extended beyond mobilising electoral support for Tinubu, adding that its central mission was to educate and empower young people to understand government policies and take advantage of emerging economic opportunities.

He referenced the inauguration of an 81-kilometre section of the Abuja–Kaduna highway during the campaign flag-off, describing the development as a demonstration of the Tinubu administration’s commitment to improving infrastructure and stimulating economic activities in the North-West.

According to him, the strategic road corridor linking Abuja, Kaduna, Zaria and Kano offers opportunities for agricultural transformation, industrial expansion, regional trade, private investment and employment generation.

He noted that improved connectivity could benefit farmers, traders, transport operators and young entrepreneurs by facilitating access to markets, reducing transportation difficulties and encouraging investments in logistics, manufacturing, food processing and related businesses.

“The objective is not simply to build infrastructure. It is to create the conditions in which people can build businesses, earn sustainable incomes, create jobs, and improve their standard of living”.

Shoga, however, emphasised that infrastructure development must be complemented by sustained security operations, effective intelligence gathering, reliable electricity and investment-friendly policies to unlock the region’s full economic potential.

“A good road connects destinations. A secure road connects people to opportunity. Together, infrastructure and security can help unlock the economic potential of an entire region”, he further said.

World.title: Orania residents to ‘refugees’ – Leader calls on Afrikaners to stay behind
World.content:
Orania Movement leader Joost Strydom has appealed to Afrikaners to remain behind in South Africa . Images via Facebook: Orania

More residents of Orania are choosing to leave the Afrikaner-only town to take up refugee status in the US.

The programme is open to South Africans of minority race groups – predominantly white – who are “victims of racial persecution”.

ORANIA RESIDENTS TAKING UP REFUGEE STATUS – HERE’S WHY

According to a new report, a small percentage of residents in Orania have been granted refugee status in the US.



Orania Movement leader Joost Strydom predicts this to be around 5% of the 2 900 population he believes have left the Afrikaner-only town to pursue bigger and better opportunities in America

Strydom stated that families were interested in applying to the refugee resettlement programme, as the US boasted a “powerful economy” compared to Orania.

He added in a Facebook post: “America has a lot to offer. This is the most powerful economy in the world. There are definitely many safe places in the USA, and there are welfare services for Africans who arrive there. Housing, food, and medical care are paid for by the U.S. government for a number of months, and there are other benefits.

He continued: “There are many places out there with better service delivery and obviously without an ANC government. Orania can’t compete with all those economic benefits. Orania is still small and is still very strong under the ANC government’s influence”.

Strydom added that many Afrikaner families saw Orania as a “stepping stone” to other opportunities.

We are also saddened by each of these individuals who had to seek greener pastures beyond their native land. The reality is that with every person who leaves, fewer and fewer Afrikaners remain in South Africa.



CALL TO STAY AND ‘BUILD’

Joost Strydom appealed to those considering leaving from Orania or elsewhere in South Africa on the refugee programme, or of their own accord, to consider staying behind.

He shared: “We cannot give you anything; we ask that you come and help build. Come and help build for those who choose to live in South Africa. Come help build for Afrikaners who believe that we belong here on this continent.

“Yes, we are sad about everyone leaving…they made a choice. If we want to survive as Africans in Africa, we must choose to build on something where our people can have opportunities again, where our children can go to school and study in Afrikaans, and where we can protect our culture”.

Strydom listed attractions such as Orania’s high-quality education, training facilities, and booming tourism sector.

He added, “All these things contribute to us being able to build a bigger and stronger economy. We choose to stay here and build a future for our people. What is your choice?”.

WHAT RACIAL PERSECUTION DO THEY FACE?

Orania is located in the Northern Cape, with a population of around 3000 individuals.

The Afrikaner-only town was built on private property in 1963. It is self-sufficient, with its own businesses, schools, hospitals, and even currency.

So, how do residents qualify to enter the refugee programme?

Like other applicants, those from Orania must meet the following criteria…

Be South African

Be of Afrikaner ethnicity or be a member of a racial minority in South Africa

Must be able to articulate an experience of persecution or fear of future persecution.

In line with US President Donald Trump’s claims of “racial discrimination”, South Africans interested in the refugee resettlement programme must prove that they have been “persecuted” in their applications.

In the Statement of Interest form, applicants are required to specify if the “persecution” was based on race, religion, nationality, political opinion, membership of a social group, or a fear of “future harm”.

Other questions included when the prospective “refugee” would like to travel to the US, how many family members they would like to bring, and if interested parties have a valid passport.
