Several Democratic incumbents targeted by redistricting have stuck it out to fight for their seats. A Republican strategist involved with midterm races, but who wasn't authorized to speak publicly, pushed back on the characterization that redistricting didn't work, saying that it "creates new battlefields" but doesn't "create outcomes." ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Sponsor Message

In a stunning political comeback, leftist Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in the presidential runoff election in Brazil. Lula defeated Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, by more than 4 million votes. It's the first time since Brazil restored democracy in 1989 that a candidate who finished second in the first round has gone on to win the presidency.



🎧 Lula's win appears to have put the brake on a right-wing sweep in Latin America, NPR's Carrie Kahn says. Seven conservative presidents have been elected in the past 18 months. Kahn says one message helped rally voters in the final weeks of Lula's campaign: that the return of a Bolsonaro to power would be an existential threat to Brazilian democracy.

Large demonstrations against the government continued over the weekend in France, where more than 100,000 people showed up in Paris, and more than 400,000 came out nationwide. What started with students demanding better conditions has grown into a much bigger movement. Unions and public-sector workers have joined, calling for more public spending and protesting growing inequality. Similar protests have erupted across Europe, from Spain to Serbia.



🎧 The reasons behind the protests vary, from schools and housing costs to corruption, NPR's Eleanor Beardsley says. But they have something in common: most are leaderless movements by young people frustrated with the world they're being left to. In Serbia, crowds celebrated in the streets of Belgrade after a student-led movement known as the "student-list" defeated the party of longtime strongman Aleksandar Vucic in Sunday's parliamentary elections. The win followed two years of protests over government corruption and lack of accountability.

Sponsor Message

Healthcare helpline

Oona Zenda/KFF Health News

Out-of-pocket maternity expenses are difficult to predict. A federal requirement for insurers to provide personalized cost estimates under the No Surprises Act was supposed to take effect in 2022, but federal regulators haven't made it happen despite pressure from Congress. Until the cost of maternity care gets more transparent, here are some tips to help you budget for the cost of pregnancy:

👶 Enroll your baby in your insurance before your deadline. For most employer health plans, that's within 30 days of birth.

👶 Check what your maximum out-of-pocket expense is. That's the most you'll pay each year for covered, in-network expenses before your insurance pays 100% of the costs.

👶 Choose in-network providers whenever possible.

👶 Go over every bill, and don't be afraid to appeal errors.

👶 Ask your hospital or other providers about financial assistance.

Deep dive

toggle caption i National Oceanic and Atmospheric/National Oceanic and Atmospheric

When Hurricane Isaias made landfall in Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm, Google DeepMind's AI model outperformed the traditional model, correctly predicting it would hit the Florida Panhandle rather than head west toward Louisiana. Hurricane forecasters say they're increasingly relying on AI technology, and that it's rapidly transforming the field.



🌀 The National Hurricane Center first started incorporating Google DeepMind into its official forecasts last year. By the end of the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, it was among the best at predicting a storm's strength and path.

🌀 Traditional physics-based prediction models use real-time atmospheric data like temperature, humidity, pressure and wind shear. AI models rely more on history and patterns from analyzing thousands of past storms.

🌀 AI models can feel like a black box; meteorologists depend on them but don't always know why their predictions are correct.

🌀 Humans still interpret the results of these models and translate them into clear guidance people can act on.

3 things to know before you go

The latest edition of NPR's Breakfast Around the World series takes us to the ancient city of Aleppo in northern Syria, where a sweet semolina pudding called mamounieh evokes memories both bitter and sweet. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported 4,588 confirmed measles cases across the U.S. this year through Oct. 22 — more than double the number for all of 2025. Cases are particularly high in Pennsylvania. The general fertility rate for U.S. women fell by 1% to a record low in 2025, according to the CDC. Birth rates declined among women in their 20s but rose among women ages 30 to 45.

Sponsor Message

This newsletter was edited by Majd Al-Waheidi.

World.title: Trump escalates anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed in Michigan
World.content:
Trump escalates anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed in Michigan

toggle caption i Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

PORT HURON, Mich. — President Donald Trump intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric against Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, portraying him as a threat to national security and questioning his loyalty to the United States in remarks that drew a sharp rebuke from a former top Arab American ally.

Trump called El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official, a "jihadist" who was "on the side of the terrorists" and would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate." He also repeatedly invoked the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate chamber and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers aboard United Flight 93.

El-Sayed, who would become the nation's first Muslim senator if elected, has called attacks on his loyalty to the country "shameful" and repeatedly denied any ties to extremist groups. The Republican president's remarks were condemned by Bishara Bahbah, a founder of Arab Americans for Trump, the group that helped lead the president's outreach to Arab American voters in 2024.

Sponsor Message

"The president's statements are out of line," he said in a phone interview. "They are crossing a red line. They are racist."

With Republicans on the defensive over inflation, soaring fuel prices and the Iran war, the president has been trying to generate turnout by claiming that El-Sayed and other Democrats are existential threats to America, instead of electoral rivals. Michigan's Senate race between El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers is among a handful of contests that could determine control of the chamber.

Trump made his remarks in Port Huron, a Canadian border city about an hour north of Detroit and near communities where he made significant gains among Arab American voters in 2024. He became the first Republican presidential candidate since 2000 to win Dearborn, a city with one of the nation's largest concentrations of Arab Americans.

Trump, who imposed a travel ban targeting several predominantly Muslim countries during his first term, has increasingly leaned into anti-Muslim rhetoric as Election Day approaches. He also attacked Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota at Sunday's rally, where he declared that he had come to Michigan "to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator."

Responding to Trump, who also regularly mocks his name, El-Sayed told supporters at a rally in Grand Rapids later Sunday that he doesn't care how Trump pronounces or misrepresents it.

Sponsor Message

"I don't even care that he remembers my whole name because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November," El-Sayed said, drawing cheers. "I will be Senator Muhammad to you, bro."

El-Sayed's faith, associations and past statements become campaign flashpoints

Central to Republicans' strategy against El-Sayed in the final weeks of the campaign has been an effort to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamic movement with branches that the U.S. government has designated as terrorist organizations.

There is no evidence that El-Sayed has any affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood. His half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, wrote on social media in 2012 that "my family has long been MB" and described a conversation with her mother about her involvement in the Muslim Brotherhood in the early 1970s.

El-Sayed was born in the United States to Egyptian immigrant parents who divorced when he was young. He was raised by his father, not his biological mother.

Trump on Sunday also targeted El-Sayed's ties to popular streamer Hasan Piker, who appeared alongside the Democrat multiple times during the primary campaign, including at his election night event.

Piker in the past has said that "Hamas is a thousand times better" than Israel, describing some Orthodox Jews as "inbred" and that "America deserved 9/11."

El-Sayed has faced criticism for his own rhetoric. He has repeatedly refused to answer questions about whether Iran or Israel poses a bigger threat to the country. Earlier this year, he said "hurt people hurt people" after an attack on a synagogue in the Detroit area. The attacker had lost four relatives in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon the week earlier. El-Sayed later apologized, saying he was not trying to justify what happened.

"To anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful, I'm really sorry," he said. "That was not my intention."

Sponsor Message

Founder of Arab Americans for Trump calls the president 'racist'

Bahbah, whose organization has since changed its name to Arab Americans for Peace, said Trump's remarks were unacceptable to Arab and Muslim communities, including Christian Arabs.

"The remarks are out of line and crazy. I mean, no sane individual would say these things," Bahbah said.

Dearborn helped Trump win Michigan in 2024 after many voters in the city were outraged by the Biden administration's handling of the war in Gaza.

"The president of the United States saying that about a person because of his religion, that is just not acceptable," said Bahbah. "And people are going to remember that on Nov. 3."

Sen. Bernie Sanders, speaking at the Grand Rapids rally, said Trump and his allies were using Islamophobia because they have "nothing to say" about the issues most important to working people, such as health care, housing and income inequality.

"All they can do is foment hatred and divisiveness," Sanders said.

The campaign has been one of the most contentious this year

Rogers and El-Sayed have been locked in a bitter race to fill the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

During their second and final general election campaign debate, Rogers questioned El-Sayed's loyalty to the United States.

"Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?" Rogers asked.

El-Sayed said that questioning was "shameful."

"I'm proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray," he said.

Speaking before Trump's appearance Sunday, Rogers repeated his allegations linking El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood.

"The Muslim Brotherhood celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year," Rogers said on stage. "Abdul El-Sayed's."

toggle caption i Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

Rally doesn't deliver a new economic handout, but gets boost from Minaj

Trump has routinely announced new investments in factories at his campaign rallies, but he did not do so as part of his speech in Michigan, a state defined by the auto industry.

Sponsor Message

The president instead repeated investments already being made by domestic automakers. Those automakers could see their finances slump if the president expands his trade war with Canada, which has been an essential partner for the U.S. automotive sector.

While it lacked a fresh promise for Michigan's economy, Trump's rally did deliver a bit of star power.

Rapper Nicki Minaj appeared on stage and urged people to get out and vote for the state's Republican ticket. Her appearance followed an awkward moment from Trump, who has increasingly been fixated on commenting about other people's body parts.

After praising the body of Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican in a close election contest, Trump turned his eye toward Minaj and commented on her posterior.

The president then signaled for Minaj to stand for the crowd and she did, after which Trump said, "I hope Nicki wasn't insulted, but we love Nicki. She's been with us for a long time."

World.title: How AI is transforming hurricane forecasts
World.content:
How AI is transforming hurricane forecasts

toggle caption i NOAA/NOAA

Hurricane forecasters are increasingly using artificial intelligence to make predictions — and they say the technology is rapidly transforming the field.

When the first hurricane of the Atlantic season formed this month, an AI model beat out traditional models at predicting where it would go.

In early October, Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 storm. Conventional forecasting models initially predicted it would head further west, toward southeastern Louisiana.

But Google DeepMind's artificial intelligence model called it right out of the gate: the hurricane was going to hit the western Florida Panhandle.

"Google DeepMind, in particular, has really proven itself the last few years as the gold standard model," says Michael Lowry, a longtime meteorologist and hurricane expert in Miami, who has previously advised both the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the National Hurricane Center (NHC).

Sponsor Message

"That model has been, by far and away, the best performing computer model that we've ever seen. Period."

A different kind of model

The National Hurricane Center first started incorporating the Google DeepMind model into its official forecasts last year.

By the end of the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, it was already one of the best at predicting a storm's path and strength, says Brian McNoldy, a hurricane researcher for the University of Miami.

Usually, new models take years to refine after first being introduced.

"It's something we're not used to – to have a model, the new kid on the block, very quickly becoming the best model out there," McNoldy says. "This pretty much came out of the gate in first place, and that's a pretty impressive feat."

Traditional physics-based hurricane models use real-time atmospheric data, like temperature, humidity, pressure and wind shear, as measured by satellites and aircraft. Then they use complicated equations to predict what path a storm might travel and how strong it could get.

An AI model operates very differently: it relies more on history. It identifies patterns by analyzing thousands of past storms along with atmospheric data.

"The AI models don't really know anything about the atmosphere other than the current picture," Lowry says. "Beyond that, it's not leaning on the governing equations of the atmosphere, the physics, to make predictions."

Sponsor Message

Most of the people designing and developing these models aren't even meteorologists, Lowry notes: "They're software engineers, and they're developing neural networks."

A "neural network" is a set of computer algorithms modeled on the human brain and trained to find patterns in massive amounts of data.

As a result, the models can seem like a "black box," Lowry says: "We don't know why they might get a forecast right. We also don't know why they might get a forecast wrong."

It can be unsettling for meteorologists to depend on a system they don't totally understand – especially during storms when millions of people might be relying on their forecasts.

"It makes us a little uncomfortable, because we like to know why you're getting the right answer," McNoldy says. "And I feel like we don't – or at least I don't know why."

Not all AI models have performed well, though. There are lots of unproven weather forecasting AI models out there, Lowry says.

The two that have so far proven to be the most accurate, despite some pitfalls, are the models developed by Google DeepMind and by the U.K.-based European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF).

toggle caption i Gerald Herbert/AP

Relying on a "blend" of models

Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center use several proven models – both AI and traditional – when putting together their official forecasts.

"Every storm has different forecast challenges," says NHC Director Michael Brennan. "That's why we take that consensus approach and use that blend of the best models."

And it's still humans who have to interpret the results of those models before deciding what to tell the public.

The NHC provides updates every six hours during active hurricanes. The models by themselves can sometimes show drastic changes from one update to the next. Forecasters have to translate those shifting predictions into clear guidance that people can act on.

Sponsor Message

"That's one thing that the human forecaster provides a lot of, is continuity," Brennan says. "We're using our expertise and our understanding to translate that hurricane forecast into the hazard space, and that's what people really need to pay attention to."

Scientists expect rapid advances

The Google DeepMind model still needs some work, Brennan says. While it topped other models in tracking the path of Isaias, it didn't do as well as the NHC's blended forecast in determining the intensity, or strength, of the storm.

Brennan's team gives regular feedback to Google DeepMind to help improve the model. Google didn't respond to questions from NPR for this story.

The "future of forecasting has always been changing," Brennan says. "It's never just one thing that's driving those improvements."

It wasn't that long ago when forecasters couldn't predict how strong a storm would be even within a couple of days, he notes. That changed, because of advances in prediction models and better data collected by satellites and planes.

"Errors are about half of what they were, say, at the time of [Hurricane] Katrina, in terms of intensity forecasting," Brennan says.

The exciting thing about AI, says meteorologist Michael Lowry, is how quickly it's improving. AI updates take only months or even weeks, unlike traditional models, which are updated annually at best.

"They are making advancements in skill and hurricane predictions over the course of a year that would have taken us 10 years, a decade or more, to make," Lowry says.

But even with AI coming in fast and strong, Lowry says he's not worried about artificial intelligence replacing people.

"For me, I don't feel some sort of existential crisis with AI," Lowry says. "If anything, I think it is a boon for our business."



Edited by Rachel Waldholz

World.title: 'It's time to abolish the Indian Act,' Manitoba premier tells PM during historic meeting with chiefs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew is calling on the federal government to abolish the Indian Act.

Kinew shared that request during a scrum in Ottawa on Monday, as First Nations leaders and Canada's first ministers meet to discuss Indigenous rights for the first time in two decades.

"I don't know how many folks in Canada have seen one of these before, but this is a status card, and it says your friend Wab Kinew is an Indian, within the meaning of the Indian Act," he said, holding up his own card in front of reporters during a midday break in the historic meeting.

"I'm not sure if that lines up with your vision of Canada, that we still have a race-based form of identification in this country. But this is a reality."

Kinew said he raised the issue with Prime Minister Mark Carney earlier Monday, calling it "long overdue that we have a relationship with Indigenous Peoples in Canada that reflects who we are as Canadians today.

"I think it's time to abolish the Indian Act," Kinew said. "And it needs to be done with First Nations people and First Nations governments."

WATCH | Indian Act should be scrapped, Wab Kinew says: Abolishing Indian Act 'long overdue,' says Wab Kinew | Duration closed caption 1:31 Holding up his Indian status card, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says it's time to abolish the Indian Act. Kinew said on Monday that his colleagues at a meeting between First Nations leaders and first ministers gave the idea an 'open-minded reception.'

The controversial legislation has governed the lives of First Nations people for the last 150 years .

Coming into effect in 1876, the act controlled almost every aspect of First Nations people's lives, dictating things like how communities were governed and who could be considered an "Indian."

While the act has had many amendments, it remains the overarching legal document for First Nations in Canada.

Later Monday, Carney said he shared Kinew's view and is "committed to a process that moves Canada beyond the Indian Act."

He said he's asked his ministers to work in partnership with First Nations to "chart that path together."

WATCH | PM says he's 'very open' to abolishing act: Carney 'very open' to abolishing Indian Act | Duration closed caption 3:35 Prime Minister Mark Carney said 'there's many reasons' to move on from the Indian Act, speaking after Monday's meeting between First Nations leaders and first ministers. Carney said the solution 'could be moving beyond, it could be reforming, it could be abolishing' the 1876 law in order to establish a modernized relationship.

Speaking alongside Carney, Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak talked about the diversity of First Nations in provinces and territories across Canada.

"And that question is going to be up to them to decide," she said. "I look forward to hearing from First Nations in assembly this December, right here in Ottawa," when the AFN hosts its special chiefs assembly in the capital.

'Nothing to lose but your chains'

Monday's closed-door meeting, which saw Carney and most of Canada's premiers sit down with chiefs from the Assembly of First Nations in Ottawa for a discussion, is the first such gathering since the Kelowna Accord talks of 2005.

That meeting brought premiers and then prime minister Paul Martin together with Indigenous leaders to discuss ways to close the socioeconomic gaps in Indigenous communities.

The Kelowna agreement was not implemented after the Conservative government under former prime minister Stephen Harper took office only a few months later.

Woodhouse Nepinak sa id Monday's meeting is intended to help build prosperity for coming generations.

It comes as Carney's government works to speed up major project approvals and development — efforts some First Nations chiefs have said threaten their rights.

Tensions between Ottawa and First Nations spiked soon after Carney was elected in 2025, when his government passed legislation to create a new office tasked with streamlining major project developments and approving projects within one year.

Kinew said he supports Carney's work at the international level, "saying that we are going to be a leader when it comes to human rights and democracy, and a leader among middle powers." But he called the Indian Act's continued existence inconsistent with that message.

The premier said though doing away with the Indian Act would bring changes, things like treaties and constitutional rights would still be able to exist for First Nations people.

"You can have self-determination, and you can have strong Indigenous nationhood, while at the same time not having the paternalism and the barriers that come with the Indian Act," Kinew said.

"You have nothing to lose but your chains."

World.title: Canada-U.S. trade talks intensifying but wide gap remains, sources say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With the U.S.-Canada trade war dominating the final days of the U.S. midterm campaign, trade discussions between the two countries have intensified. But sources tell CBC News and Radio-Canada that doesn't mean a deal is imminent.

A source familiar with the discussions told Radio-Canada that there are "substantive conversations, but there are still key elements that remain unresolved."

"We are not on the verge of an agreement just yet," the same source said.

Another Canadian government source told CBC News on Monday that while discussions between officials from both countries have become more frequent in recent days, the state of play is best understood by reviewing comments made last week by Janice Charette, Canada's chief trade negotiator.

"Pens are down, and the doors are open," Charette said at the Toronto Global Forum on Thursday. "Canada stands ready to continue discussions."

Charette said that while conversations are taking place at "multiple levels," they aren't happening at the negotiating table.

"We're having conversations to see whether or not we can come back to the table for a set of detailed negotiations," she said. "We don't know exactly when that's going to happen."

Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters on Monday that his government's position hasn't changed since talks fell apart in August and that he's only looking to sign a deal that's "in the interests of Canadians."

"We have very clear bottom lines, red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in August," the prime minister said.

"To the extent any progress has been made, it's because the U.S. is coming closer to our position."

According to several Canadian sources, the gap between the two sides has been too wide in recent days to reach an agreement.

"Canada remains in constructive dialogue with our U.S. counterparts on a range of priorities," a spokesperson from Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc's office said on Sunday.

"We stand ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada's interests."

A Canadian source told CBC News that LeBlanc had to stay in Ottawa this weekend because calls with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer increased in the past few days.

Some industry stakeholders received calls from senior members of the federal government over the weekend to discuss the current status of trade discussions, according to two industry sources.

U.S. trade spin and the midterms

U.S. President Donald Trump and other senior U.S. officials have suggested in recent days that progress is being made toward a deal with Canada.

"We'll have ​that settled pretty soon. They're willing to give us anything ​at this moment," Trump told a campaign rally in Port Huron, Mich., on Sunday.

And Kevin Hassett, the director of the National Economic Council and a key economic adviser to the White House, suggested on Fox News that trade talks had been hampered by the referendum vote in Alberta but since then "negotiations have picked up."

"They're gathering steam. Secretary Lutnick has been talking to his Canadian counterparts all week. I think it's very close to finally having a deal on that," Hassett said.

WATCH | More about Trump's stop in Michigan: Trump campaigns in battleground Michigan with trade talk swirling | Duration closed caption 2:55 U.S. President Donald Trump campaigned in Michigan with less than 10 days before the midterm elections. The U.S.-Canada trade war has become a key issue in several battleground states.

While the White House may want to send a political message that progress is being made on the trade front, it is far from clear whether the U.S. administration is prepared to make Canada an acceptable offer.

Polls show Trump's dispute with Canada is deeply unpopular among American voters in both major parties.

Canadian sources that have spoken with Radio-Canada caution it's in the Americans' interest to "spin" the narrative that a deal with Canada is possible — especially with the midterm elections a week away.

David Axelrod, a former chief strategist to U.S. president Barack Obama, suggested in a post on social media Monday that "an 11th-hour trade deal [with] Canada is an option [Trump] still might pursue to help his Senate candidates in northern states."

On Friday Trump removed some tariffs from some goods — while hitting other products with new tariffs — in order to help Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins whose campaign has been frustrated by the trade war's impact in her state.

Ford says 'we'll see what happens'

"They're going for an election down there and I don't think Trump's doing too well," Ontario Premier Doug Ford said on his way into a meeting between first ministers and First Nations leaders in Ottawa.

"I think the trade deal with Canada is affecting him."

The premier said he hopes talks are progressing, but for now it's a "we'll see what happens" situation.

Asked if Carney has asked him to reconsider the province's U.S. booze ban to move trade talks along, Ford said "not yet."

But he said a fair deal for steelworkers, autoworkers and manufacturing workers would have him put American booze back on LCBO shelves "in a heartbeat."

World.title: Police locate vehicle allegedly used by Toronto mother to abduct 3 children
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Toronto police say they have found a vehicle believed to have been used to abduct three children from Scarborough on Friday, but the children and their mother have not been found.

In a news release Monday, police said the mother of the three children, Somerda Miclescu, 22, was believed to be driving a 2017 White Ford Expedition vehicle with Ontario licence plate DJJS 875.

Police did not say where or when they found the vehicle.

Daniel, six, Irina, three, and Anastasia, four months, were having a semi-supervised visit with a relative on Friday, when polices say their mother took them and fled. Police say the children's mother does not have legal custody of them.

"Efforts to locate them remain ongoing," police said in the release.

Police described the mother as 5 feet 7 inches, about 180 pounds, with long, black hair. Police said she was last seen wearing a long black skirt and a dark-coloured top.

Somerda Miclescu is wanted by police for allegedly abducting her three children. (Toronto Police Service)

Police first responded to a call at about 11:30 a.m. Friday for an abduction in the Midland Avenue and Eglinton Avenue East area.

Police have named Ionut Stroe, 25, who owns vehicle in which Miclescu fled, as a person of interest.

Stroe is also wanted for four counts of failing to comply with a release order, unrelated to the abduction.

Police described him as being around 5 feet 11 inches, 235 pounds, with a tattoo on his right forearm.

World.title: This 3-year-old scored 10 goals. Then police showed up at his soccer game
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the viral video posted by his parents, a three-year-old central Florida boy dribbles the ball up the field, dodging the other pint-sized players and kicks it into the net as his parents cheer.

Then the boy, named Nevada, does it again. And again. And again.

Later in the same video, which has been viewed more than one million times on TikTok since it was posted Sunday, Nevada stands on the sidelines as his father says, "they called the police on a three-year-old because he was too good."

"Because he had the ball for too long, and nobody else could get the ball, so they called the police."

The reaction online was swift, with people equally enraged over the allegations and admiration for the preschooler's skills. In the TikTok comments, some called on the parents to sue, others alleged that calling the police was racist, and many commented on the "heartbreak" in the little boy's face when the police show up.

"I'm LIVID," children's entertainer and vocal children's rights advocate Ms. Rachel posted on Instagram Monday morning, calling on soccer stars and other athletes to support the child and his family.

" This is racist, sick, traumatizing and disgusting," she added.

Former NFL quarterback Robert Griffin III called the incident "crazy," writing on X that "punishing a 3 year old child for being too good at a sport is RIDICULOUS."

CBC News has reached out to Nevada's parents but has not yet heard back. The family already had a sizeable social media following on TikTok and Instagram, where they've documented Nevada's soccer skills over the years.

The Winter Park Police Department confirmed to CBC News Monday that officers were called to a children's soccer game Saturday after a league official "requested response to a disturbance between league officials and the parents of a player."

A screen shot of a post on Threads by children's entertainer Ms. Rachel on Monday. (@msrachelforlittles/Threads)

So, what actually happened?

The official called 911 at 9:53 a.m., according to the police incident report viewed by CBC News.

In a recording of the call provided by police, the official can be heard saying he has "an unruly parent here, calling me names and having me on Instagram."

He says the parent is being "really disruptive, like following me around and calling me names. I want her to be gone."

He describes her as a Black woman wearing pink.

The incident report says the official told police the parents were upset about their son's playing time, while the parents said their child "was being scorned for playing too well and was being taken out of [the] game."

The Winter Park Police Department said the league had asked the family to leave and offered to refund its fees. When police arrived, the official asked officers to communicate that to the family, the department said.

A screen grab of an Instagram post by illustrator and activist Nikkolas Smith, in support of 3-year-old soccer player Nevada, posted on Monday. (@nikkolas_smith/Instagram)

"The family stated the game was over and they were leaving," the police statement says, adding that the family was co-operative and no one was arrested, trespassed or forced to leave the park.

The video posted by Nevada's parents shows a Black woman wearing pink speaking with two police officers. One tells her the league office should be reaching out soon about a refund.

In a separate video, the parents claim the soccer officials repeatedly pulled Nevada from the 30-minute game after he scored and that, as a result, he played only about 12 minutes — but still scored 10 goals.

Boy is 'traumatized,' says mother

The soccer league, i9 Sports Maitland/Winter Park, told CBC News in a statement Monday that it was aware of concerns about "an incident at a local i9 Sports program" and takes them very seriously.

"We have reached out to the family and have begun a review that includes speaking with those involved," the league said.

In an interview with The Breakfast Club, Nevada's mother, identified as Martasia Griffin, said Nevada has been targeted all season because of his talent and that, at this particular game, some parents complained that no one else could get the ball.

She said the league director agreed it was unfair to other children and offered Griffin a refund.

"I cannot explain to my three year old son that he cannot play today because he's so good. I continued to let him play until the police walked in," Griffin said.

Nevada, she told HuffPost in another interview Monday, is "traumatized."

An Instagram post by former U.S. soccer player Eddie Johnson in which he supports 3-year-old Nevada. (Eddie_Johnson7/Instagram)

"He still wants to play soccer. He just doesn’t want to go back to that place. I don’t think that’s how he should be thinking, that as a 3-year-old he did something wrong."

Former U.S. professional soccer player Eddie Johnson posted about Nevada several times on social media Sunday and Monday, saying the boy would be joining his soccer program and criticizing how he was treated at the game.

"They wanna dim his light," Johnson posted to his Instagram stories.

"They thought they were taking your dreams away, but in reality (made) you the most famous three-year-old in the world right now."

World.title: Microsoft gives voluntary buyout offer to about 60,000 employees
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Microsoft said on Monday it is offering voluntary buyouts to many staff members as the technology giant looks to contain costs and help fund its ‌massive AI investments.

The offer was extended to about 60,000 employees according to Microsoft. The company had 223,000 full-time employees ‌globally as of June 30, according to its annual filing, meaning more than a quarter of its global workforce would have received the buyout offer.

Staffers across the Windows maker would be eligible for the offers, including those working in AI experiences, Copilot, finance, human resources, Xbox and Windows + Devices, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters, requesting anonymity ​as the matter was private. Units such as marketing, ​commercial business and security will be excluded, the source added.

In a memo, Microsoft's executive vice-president and chief people officer Amy Coleman said the offer will be available to eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Microsoft declined to tell CBC News how many Canadians were offered the buyout.

"This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company ​a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also ⁠gives participating organizations another ⁠way to adapt their workforce to changing needs," ‌chief people officer Amy Coleman said in a staff memo.

WATCH | Block CEO says AI tools behind cuts to nearly half its workforce: Block cuts nearly half its workforce, CEO cites AI tools | Duration closed caption 2:03 Tech company Block, which owns payment platform Square, announced it will lay off thousands of employees because of the potential of artificial intelligence. But some industry watchers say blaming AI can be an easy excuse.

The company said it was a time-limited, voluntary program and built on insights gained from a previous voluntary retirement program. The eligible employees will receive details within the next few hours, it added.

Like other tech giants, Microsoft is spending hundreds of billions of dollars on AI data centres and chips, drawing scrutiny from investors over whether the returns will ⁠justify the staggering cost. The company, slated to report first-quarter results after markets close on Wednesday, has forecast $175 billion US in capital expenditures for the 2026 calendar year.

Shares of Microsoft, which had risen about 10 per cent this year, were up about 1 per cent on Monday. The development was first reported by Business Insider.

The company earlier this year offered ​voluntary buyouts to about 7 per cent of its U.S. workforce, or about 9,000 employees.

In July, Microsoft announced it would ⁠cut 4,800 jobs, or about 2.1 per cent of its global workforce, overhauling its Xbox gaming business and ⁠divesting up to five studios as it looks to boost returns after years ⁠of ⁠heavy investment in the division.

World.title: How this Brooklyn bar owner had Conan O’Brien in stitches on SubwayTakes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Interview with Debbie Shields: As It Happens 5:53 Meet the Brooklyn bar owner who stole the show on Conan O'Brien's episode of SubwayTakes

It's not everyday you go from running a comedy night at a bar to doing improv with an Emmy-winning comedian on the New York City subway.

Debbie Shields wasn't expecting to strike up a conversation with comedian Conan O'Brien when she set out to run errands, but her quick-witted humour meant she was prepared.

"I mean, if you give it to me, I give it right back to you," she told As It Happens host Nil Köksal.

Shields has become an internet sensation after her exchange with O'Brien aired on the most recent episode of SubwayTakes.

O'Brien was a guest on the popular internet talk show hosted by comedian Kareem Rahma, where regular New Yorkers and celebrities humorously discuss their controversial opinions while riding the subway.

Toward the end of his episode, O'Brien apologized to Shields as she moved into an empty seat next to Rahma. She and O'Brien shook hands and jumped into a spontaneous scene together, with O'Brien joking that the two used to be married.

Shields quickly responded that they had two kids. "One's in medical school, the other one's in jail," she said, causing the former late night host to crack up.

WATCH | Debbie Shields riffs with Conan O'Brien on SubwayTakes:

Some viewers said they loved her wit and ability to keep up with O'Brien. He was impressed, too.

O'Brien told New York Magazine he's open to working with Shields again. "I'll do a sitcom with her," he said. "Or we can just hit the road, do a two-person show."

Shields told Köksal she'd love to collaborate with him again. Here is part of their conversation.

Debbie, what is your relationship status with Conan O'Brien now? Is remarriage in the cards? He walked out on you again?

He just did his interview and walked off the train. "Bye Debbie."

Typical. How are the kids feeling?

They're fine. They're used to him not being around.

In all seriousness though, how are you doing with all of this attention?

It's crazy right now. SXM radio, I was in the New York Times, 1010 radio.

Internationally, are they interested, too?

Yeah, somebody called me from Japan, 1:30 in the morning, Australia, England. Oh boy, it's been busy.

On that day on the train, did you have any idea what you were walking into?

Not at all. I was going to see my accountant for my business.

O'Brien appeared delighted with the random encounter. (Emma McIntyre/Getty Images/SiriusXM)

Did you just see that shock of orange hair and the pasty skin? He would say that about himself, so I feel like can say that.

No, I saw a camera crew. And when I saw the camera crew, my friend said, "Oh, that's Conan O'Brien." I was like, "Oh, OK." But I was looking for a seat because I'm always looking for a seat on the train. So I got me a seat and I told him "You hold the seat and I'm just going to go over and say hi." And that's all it took.

And you did not miss a beat, a millisecond even. Have you always had that kind of comedic timing?

Yeah, I mean if you give it to me, I give it right back to you. That's how it goes.

That's the New Yorker in you, I would imagine. But you are at another level, though.

Thank you.

You didn't seem nervous, but were you at all nervous inside?

No, I was having a ball.

He was, too.

Yeah, we had a good time doing that.

You were a fan of Conan before. What about him do you like?

Yes, I like his style of comedy. He's witty, he's fast, he's risky, he is risque. I just like him.

Did you have any idea about the show SubwayTakes?

No, I didn't know anything about that show, nothing.

It's really cool when you meet a celebrity whose work you admire and the exchange goes really well. Sometimes, it could be not as pleasant. You go about your day, you went to your accountant. And then when did you start getting a sense that this was more than this great memory for you?

Tuesday evening. Somebody told me, "Oh, you're on Conan, we saw it." I was in my bar and people started showing me. Then Wednesday morning, it went crazy. People were calling me at eight in the morning. "Oh, you were all over the internet. You've got five million hits." Then somebody called me at like about 10 in the morning, "You're on television, on channel five. You're on channel four." And I'm like, "Oh my God." It was surreal.

That's what I do with people, even in my bar. The name of my bar is Confessions Bar, I have comedy on Friday nights. I introduce the host of the comics and I really go off on the people. I make them laugh, I talk about their outfits, whatever it is, and they all love me. I like to see people happy. And if I lay my head to rest today, I want people to remember that I made people laugh.

Oh, they're sure going to remember, Debbie. Conan's at the top of that list. Do you think he's going to drop by?

He's been in touch with me. Kareem's team has been in touch with me to do another show with him.

Oh my goodness. What would be your dream show?

Saturday Night Live.

I think at least Conan could arrange that for you. Conan said he'd do a sitcom with you.

Yes he would, and I would love to do one with him.

What does this tell you about life?

Life is funny, you never know where your blessings are coming from. That's why you have to live your life in a certain way. So when the aura of God, or whatever you want to see or call it, sees that you're doing your best and you're trying really hard and you genuine, he always throws you a ball.

You've got the comedy night at Confessions, are you incorporating this new part of your life and your ex-husband into the bar?

Yes, we invented a drink called Baby Daddy O'Brien. We've got whiskey, Triple Sec, lemon, lime, and blood orange.

Can we expect you to bring your show to Toronto sometime?

That would be fun. I love Toronto. I love Canada. I've been to Canada so many times.

I'm sure people would love to see you riding the subway here, too, Debbie. Thank you for this.

My pleasure. You just always laugh your ass off.

That's the key to life.

World.title: Quebec's Spa Nordik introduces new safety measures following sexual assault allegations
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Nordik Spa Village in Chelsea, Que., has announced new measures to protect clients amid a class action lawsuit alleging sexual assault that implicates 36 massage therapists over a 19-year-period.

In a list outlined on its website, the spa says massage therapists will now undergo criminal background checks and get training on consent and the prevention of sexual violence.

They'll also be "required to maintain good standing with a recognized professional association."

Massage services will be relegated to their own floor with security personnel, the spa says.

Other measures include an electronic consent form that clients will be able to update throughout their massage and a requirement for therapists to obtain consent before massaging "sensitive areas."

The spa defines those as the "buttocks [and] upper inner thighs" and the "pectoral area."

Clients will also have the option to have the audio of their session recorded. A new complaint process for clients is also being implemented, the spa says.

Founder 'deeply shaken'

In a statement shared on social media, Groupe Nordik founder Martin Paquette wrote that the company is committed to the safety of its clients, adding that he was "deeply shaken," and "angry" when he learned of the allegations.

" No one should ever have to go through something like that in a place dedicated to well-being," he wrote.

Paquette also called for stronger government oversight of Quebec's massage therapy sector.

"Unfortunately, what has happened at our establishment is not unique to Nordik," he said.

World.title: Walter Koenig, Ensign Chekov on original Star Trek series, dead at 90
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Actor Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, the youthful Russian navigator on the original Star Trek television series and in several movies, has died. He was 90.

Koenig died Monday at his home in the North Hollywood neighbourhood of Los Angeles, talent agent Zachery McGinnis said in a statement.

In Star Trek, which ran on NBC from 1966 to 1969, Chekov was the sole Communist-bloc member of the starship Enterprise's bridge staff. His friendly, supportive presence showed how the rival nations (in the far-off future in which the show was set) were capable of working together.

The TV show has also inspired multiple spinoff TV series with new casts, and conventions that draw thousands of fans.

Speaking heavily Russian-accented English, Chekov embodied fierce pride, love of poetry and great loyalty.

"My heart is heavy," Koenig's castmate George Takei said in a post on social media. "Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man and a loyal friend."

George Takei as Sulu, left, and Walter Koenig as Chekov are shown in an archival photo from the set of Star Trek: The Original Series. (Getty Images)

"Walter's legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it," McGinnis said. "Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before."

McGinnis said Koenig died surrounded by his daughter and niece.

The baby face of the Enterprise

Series creator Gene Roddenberry said Chekov's character, who joined the show in its second season, was a response to Russian complaints about the program.

"They put in Pravda that, 'Ah, the ugly Americans are at it again. They do a space show, and they forget to include the people who were in space first,'" he said, according to The Fifty-Year Mission by Mark A. Altman and Edward Gross, an oral history of the Star Trek franchise's first 50 years.

Koenig would become the baby-faced heartthrob of the main cast.

"They wanted somebody who would appeal to eight- to 14-year-olds and the decision was to make him Russian. My fan mail came from eight- to 14-year-olds who weren't that aware of the Cold War and what was going on anyway," Roddenberry told Altman and Gross.

"At the time, the whole thing of getting fan mail was so novel to me that I read every single letter I got. I was literally getting about 700 letters a week, so that took up a lot of my spare time."

Adventure over predictability

Koenig played Chekov in seven Star Trek movies starting in 1979, as well as innumerable other spinoffs, including writing a Star Trek book, Chekov's Enterprise, in 1980.

After Star Trek ended, Koenig continued acting and wrote scripts for Family, The Incredible Hulk and other shows. He also taught part-time at UCLA and other schools.

Members of the Star Trek crew (from left): James Doohan, DeForest Kelley, Walter Koenig, William Shatner, George Takei, Leonard Nimoy and Nichelle Nichols toast the then-upcoming film Star Trek V: The Final Frontier during a news conference at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles, Calif., on Dec. 28, 1988. (Bob Galbraith/The Associated Press)

Koenig also worked in the burgeoning field of computer games, including some with a Star Trek theme. In 1995, he took a role in the CD-ROM game Maximum Surge.

"I'm at a point where I could opt in my life for complacency and a bit of predictability, or I could have one last holler — one last try for adventure," Koenig told The Associated Press in 1995. "I'm of the opinion that adventure is still a very enticing and exciting option."

He returned to the science fiction genre with occasional appearances in the syndicated 1990s TV series Babylon 5.
