Sheinbaum also pointed to electronics production as a growth driver.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Sheinbaum’s Monday press conference came a day after Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won the presidential run-off election in Brazil, Latin America’s most populous country.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@claudia_shein)

Lula’s surprise victory over Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, halted a right-wing wave that has recently swept over Latin America.

Sheinbaum made it abundantly clear that the triumph of the 80-year-old incumbent Brazilian president pleased her. She said she would speak with Lula at midday Monday to congratulate him.

Lula’s victory in Brazil after finishing behind Bolsonaro in the first round earlier this month means that the Sheinbaum administration retains an important ideological ally in the region at a time when various other Latin American countries, including Argentina, Chile, Colombia and El Salvador, are ruled by right-wing governments.

At today’s mañanera, Sheinbaum also commented on another significant development on Sunday — Guadalupe Taddei’s announcement that she would resign as president of Mexico’s National Electoral Institute (INE).

Taddei decided to leave the role she has held since 2023 amid corruption allegations related to the INE’s awarding of lucrative contracts to companies linked to José Alfredo Hernández Casillas. According to recent media reports, Taddei has a close personal relationship with Hernández.

Sheinbaum celebrates Lula’s victory in Brazil

“We are happy!” Sheinbaum declared at the very start of her mañanera as she made an L sign with her thumb and index finger.

“We’re very happy with Lula’s triumph in Brazil,” she said.

“Many congratulations to President Lula and the people of Brazil. It’s a breath of fresh air for Latin America and the Caribbean. We’re very, very happy,” Sheinbaum said.

Later in the press conference, she described Lula’s victory as “very important.”

“It’s the triumph of a president, of a people’s movement, of a government that represents its people,” Sheinbaum said.

“It’s the defeat of a rightist movement,” she added.

🇧🇷 La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum expresó su gran alegría por el triunfo electoral de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva en Brasil, calificándolo como “una bocanada de aire fresco” para América Latina y el Caribe. Destacó que esta victoria representa el triunfo de un movimiento popular sobre uno de derecha y reconoce el trabajo del pueblo brasileño para revertir el resultado de la primera vuelta. Asimismo, mencionó que sostendrá una llamada telefónica con Lula para felicitarlo y que evaluarían el momento oportuno para retomar proyectos conjuntos, incluyendo la colaboración entre PEMEX y Petrobras. Más información: https://t.co/JnS6s9oW56 #VideosLaJornada — La Jornada (@lajornadaonline) October 26, 2026

Sheinbaum described Lula’s administration as “similar” to hers before saying that “it makes us feel very happy that a movement like the one Lula represents in Brazil won.”

Sheinbaum endorses Taddei’s decision to resign

Sheinbaum described Taddei’s decision to step down as INE president as “good.”

She noted Taddei made her decision amid allegations of corruption.

“Obviously, an investigation has to be carried out. … There has to be an audit in order to review the suspicions or the allegations there have been regarding abuses or privileges within the INE,” Sheinbaum said.

She subsequently reiterated the view she expressed on Friday, saying that there must be “no hint of corruption” at the INE.

Sheinbaum stressed that there will be no interruption to the INE’s work despite Taddei’s decision to resign. The electoral authority’s main focus is currently the federal, state and municipal elections that will be held on June 6, 2027. The “electoral process” ahead of those elections officially began last month.

Sheinbaum touts strong economic growth in August

Sheinbaum said that year-over-year economic growth of 3.5% in August was “very good news.”

The national statistics agency INEGI reported the growth rate last Friday. It also reported that Mexico’s economy grew 0.6% in August compared to July. Earlier last week, INEGI published preliminary data showing that Mexico’s economy expanded 3.7% year-over-year in September.

Sheinbaum noted that construction, including housing and public infrastructure projects, is helping to drive growth. Construction activity increased 7.9% in August compared to the same month of last year, according to INEGI.

Sheinbaum also noted that the production of electronics is providing momentum to Mexico’s economy. Mexico’s export revenue has surged this year, in large part due to a sharp increase in the shipment to the United States of AI servers and other computer and electronic equipment. However, much of the content in such products is sourced from Asia, particularly Taiwan, limiting Mexico’s share of their total value added.

World.title: Mexico sends ultrarunners and a photo exhibit to El Salvador to promote Indigenous sporting culture
World.content:
A delegation of high-performance Mexican athletes will travel to El Salvador to participate in next month’s Cordillera Challenge, a 130-kilometer mountain race with over 6,300 meters of positive elevation gain.

The participation of the four runners is part of a government-sponsored agenda seeking to strengthen sporting and cultural ties between both countries.

María Lorena Ramírez Hernández, an Indigenous ultramarathon runner originally from the Sierra Tarahumara in the state of Chihuahua, will lead the delegation.

The 31-year-old Ramírez, a 2025 National Sports Award recipient, gained international recognition after winning the UltraTrail Cerro Rojo in 2017, an ultra-distance race of 80 kilometers (50 miles), while wearing huaraches, a type of traditional sandal. She finished with a time of 7 hours, 20 minutes.

The Cordillera Challenge — a 130-kilometer, multi-day endurance race taking place from Nov. 6-8 — will traverse some of El Salvador’s most stunning natural landscapes, including Lago de Coatepeque (a 115-meter-deep crater lake), the Izalco and Ataco volcanoes and the coastal sandbar known as Barra de Santiago.

Mirna Beatriz de la Cruz, leader of México Imparable, a government initiative that links sport and cultural identity to promote athletic talent and give visibility to Mexico’s Indigenous peoples, will also attend the 3-day event.

Upon establishing México Imparable in August 2025, President Claudia Sheinbaum described the initiative as “a symbolic action that represents the strength and resilience of all the Mexican people, particularly the indigenous communities.”

México Imparable’s agenda in El Salvador includes the photo exhibition “Mexico, Land of Champions,” which will be inaugurated on Nov. 3 at the National Library in San Salvador.

The exhibition — sponsored by the Mexican Embassy — includes images of daily life, traditions and the rich cultural heritage of the Sierra Tarahumara’s Indigenous communities.

Through portraits of its inhabitants, their customs, their relationship with the land and their connection to sport, the exhibit seeks to introduce the Salvadoran public to the cultural diversity of the Rarámuri and highlight their contribution to Mexico’s heritage.

With reports from El Mundo and Diario Latino

World.title: Mexico in 10 objects: Stone heads, silver dollars and tacos
World.content:
In January 2010, Neil MacGregor of the British Museum started to broadcast his new series, “A History of the World in 100 Objects.” It was a magnificent success, and a bestselling book followed. Since then, there have been numerous other titles, from “The History of Football in 100 Objects” to “A History of Food in 101 Objects.”

The idea is such fun that MND asked contributor Bob Pateman to put together his very own “A History of Mexico in 10 Objects.”

1. The Olmec stone heads — the start of Mexican civilizations

The Olmecs, the Mexican mother culture, thrived in the lowlands of southeastern Mexico between 1500 and 400 B.C. San Lorenzo and La Venta became the biggest communities on the continent, the builders of palaces and pyramids.

The most striking of their artwork was the giant heads carved from boulders that had been brought from the distant Sierra de los Tuxtlas mountains. Mysterious and haunting, 17 of these heads have been discovered.

Item selected: Colossal Head 1 was the first to be discovered and is the largest, at 2.84 meters (9 feet 4 inches) and 25.3 metric tons. With its direct stare and elaborate headdress, it is also one of the most haunting.

Where it is: Colossal Head 1 can be seen in the Xalapa Museum of Anthropology in the city of Xalapa, Veracruz.

2. The Mexica statue of Coatlicue

Pre-Hispanic Mexico was a mosaic of different societies that interacted through trade, politics and war. The Mexica flourished for little more than 200 years, but during that time they acquired previously unheard-of levels of wealth and power.

There is no lack of amazing objects to represent them, with gems ranging from feather headdresses to giant stone calendars.

Item selected: The giant statue of the earth and mother goddess Coatlicue. This was carved around A.D. 1500 at the height of Mexica power. It stands 2.5 meters tall and weighs between 2 and 3 metric tons. It is an interwoven collage of snakes, claws, skulls, and human hearts and hands. Threatening and powerful, Coatlicue was clearly a god you didn’t mess with!

Where it is: The National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City.

3. A memory of a lost empire — the Florentine Codex

Although the Mexica did not have an alphabetic writing system, they produced wonderful books that recorded their myths, economic records, history and laws in pictograms and glyphs. Written on bark, skin or cloth, they were targeted by the Spanish, and only a handful escaped the flames.

Item selected: Ironically, the Spanish, who tried so hard to burn all the Mexica “books,” produced one of the finest. Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagún worked with Nahua elders and artists to document the culture and history of the Mexica people. It was a mammoth work, 2,500 pages organized into 12 books, recording the story of an empire that was in the process of being destroyed.

Where it is: The Florentine Codex is housed in the Laurentian Library of Florence.

4. A Spanish silver dollar

The Spanish colonies in the Americas became rich from their silver mines, and for 350 years Mexico led the way. Much of the raw metal was turned into coins known as the Spanish dollar or, later, the Spanish peso. The amount of silver in each coin was equal to eight Spanish reales, and for smaller purchases, a coin could be cut into bits, which is why pirates referred to them as pieces of eight.

Mexico sat at the center of an international trade network that stretched from China to the Ottoman Empire, and the Spanish dollar became the world’s first international currency.

Item selected: Produced in the millions, the coins can be acquired for as little as US $100. However, everything depends on rarity and the history of the coin, and the highest auction price is US $587,500 for a coin minted in Mexico in 1538. This was the first dollar-sized silver coin ever struck in the New World, and this particular example was salvaged from the underwater wreckage of the Golden Fleece, a vessel that sank in the northern Caribbean around 1550.

Where it is: Only three coins of this standard are known to exist, and all are in the possession of unknown private collectors.

5. Bell of Dolores — Campana de Dolores

View this post on Instagram A post shared by JBorcegui (@borcegui)

On Sept. 16, 1810, the Roman Catholic priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla entered the parish church in Dolores and rang the bell to gather the villagers. This is seen as the symbolic start of an 11-year war that would bring Mexican independence from Spain.

Every year, the bell is rung on the night of Sept. 15 as the president of Mexico starts Mexico’s Independence Day celebration.

Item selected: The bell dates to 1768 and was cast in bronze in the small town of Dolores. It is 1.77 meters in height and weighs approximately 750 kilograms.

Where it is: Since 1896, the bell has hung above the central balcony of the Palacio Nacional.

6. The world’s oldest tequila bottle

Tequila can trace its roots back to the drink pulque. The Spanish brought in the technology to distill a clearer, more alcoholic version, which became known as mezcal.

This was displayed at the 1893 World’s Fair in Chicago, where it was labeled as “mezcal from the village of Tequila.” The name was reduced to simply tequila, and a legend was born.

Today, the tequila industry is worth around US $12 billion, and the drink is deeply interwoven into Mexican history and culture.

Item selected: The oldest known tequila bottle. Before 1880, tequila was sold in large wooden barrels to bars or to regional distributors, and you took it home in your own bottle or jug. A José Cuervo bottle dating to 1905 is the oldest verified surviving bottle of tequila.

Where it is: Displayed in The Tequila House in Parral, Chihuahua, as part of a collection of more than 3,000 vintage bottles.

7. Looking good! — A mariachi outfit

Mariachi music traces its origins to Jalisco, emerging from a combination of Spanish strings and Mexican folk music with just a trace of African influence.

The first mariachi bands performed in the simple white cotton shirts, trousers and leather sandals of the farms, but during the early 1900s, musicians started to adopt the dandy dress of the Mexican cowboy. Costumes reached a new height in the 1940s when mariachi bands appeared in Mexican movies.

Item selected: The iconic mariachi costume is the black charro suit and tejana hat that Pedro Infante wore in the 1955 movie “Los Gavilanes.”

Where it is: A collection of authentic costumes, hats and cinematic memorabilia — including the famous mariachi outfit — is on display in the Museo El Rincón de Pedro Infante, in the actor’s hometown of Mazatlán.

8. A painting from Mexico’s most beloved artist

Mexico has produced some wonderful artists, from the masterful landscapes of José María Velasco to the blending of styles and cultures in the work of Rufino Tamayo. However, nobody has captured the love of the country more than Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera, and, as time goes by, it is Frida who is emerging as the real superstar of the partnership.

Her paintings have pride of place in art galleries around the world, and the auction record for one of her paintings stands at US $54.7 million for her 1940 self-portrait “The Dream (The Bed).”

Item selected: “Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird.” Painted in 1940, this is a complex work full of symbols. The thorn necklace is a reference to both Christ and her own pain. While the hummingbird is usually a symbol of love, this one is dead and still, a reflection of Frida’s own disastrous relationships. With its colors, animals and plants and the artist’s simple peasant dress, there is also something notably “Mexican” about the work.

Where it is: “Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird” is in the permanent collection of the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas at Austin.

9. Tacos — the food that fuels Mexico

The origins of the taco are debated. Some argue that they predate the arrival of the Spanish; others that the idea came across from Spain, perhaps with miners or even with Hernán Cortés himself.

Whatever the origins, there is nothing more Mexican than a small corn or wheat tortilla filled with a piping hot and juicy filling. It is the food that fuels the country every morning.

Item selected: What represents Mexican street food better than small, semi-mobile taco stands? It is not only a place to eat, but a spot to stand and chat.

Where it is: We are looking for a small stand with umbrellas, a few plastic chairs and a bright advertising sign. Shouldn’t be too hard to find!

10. The title belts of Julio César Chávez

View this post on Instagram A post shared by World Boxing Council (@wbcboxing)

Sport has a special place in Mexican society, from bullfights to lucha libre to the passion generated by big soccer games. Sport has also helped Mexico stake its place on the world stage, hosting the 1968 Olympics and three World Cup tournaments.

If there is one sport that is special to Mexicans, it is boxing, and for many, the greatest Mexican fighter of them all is Julio César Chávez. Over a 25-year career, he was a six-time world champion across three different weight classes. To get there, he had to go through many personal challenges, the kind of background that endears a fighter to Mexican fans.

Item selected: A world championship belt. When British fighter Tom Cribb defeated his American challenger, Tom Molineaux, in the early 1800s, King George III presented Cribb with the first championship belt in boxing history. There are no pictures of the gift, but it is said to have been made from lion skin with a silver buckle. This started a tradition that continues today, with boxers receiving a championship belt on winning a world title.

Where it is: Two of Chávez’s six belts are believed to have gone to private collectors. Four remain in his private collection.

Bob Pateman lived in Mexico for six years. He is a librarian and teacher with a Master’s Degree in History.

World.title: MND Local Guadalajara: Salman Rushdie to keynote the 2026 FIL Book Fair, Día de Campo Music Festival and plans for a new urban park
World.content:
Exciting music and book festivals are coming to town, while city leaders commit to addressing a critical shortcoming in Guadalajara: the lack of green spaces for public recreation.

A new urban park is coming to land that once housed the Oblatos prison

The Guadalajara City Council recently announced that it will renovate this public land with the aim of creating a new urban forest, with designated areas for sports facilities and family fun.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Verónica Delgadillo G (@verodelgadillog)

This initiative is critical to address the dire shortage of parks and other green spaces for residents’ enjoyment in the Guadalajara Metro Area (GMA). On World Environment Day in 2019, María Guadalupe Garibay Chávez of the University of Guadalajara shared findings that the GMA has a mere 1.4 square meters per resident of public green space, falling well short of the World Health Organization’s recommended 9 square meters per resident.

The city plans to invest more than 100 million pesos (US $4.9 million) in the project, with work to be carried out in phases so that park activities can continue during construction.

One of the most visible — and welcome — changes will be the elimination of vast areas of concrete. The project calls for removing approximately 6,300 square meters of concrete, with more than 600 trees planted in its place.

A swimming pool and other sports areas

While the construction of a new swimming pool is a showpiece, the project also calls for the renovation of multipurpose courts, the frontenis area and the baseball diamond. There will be new spaces for calisthenics and boxing, with other areas repurposed to create children’s play areas.

In addition to sports facilities, the new park will provide a variety of areas to socialize and gather with friends and family. Park trails and walkways will be renovated, with the goal of expanding the availability of green spaces for city residents.

Outside park boundaries, improvements are planned for street lighting, sidewalks and intersections to make accessing the park safer and easier.

The new park, which has not yet been named, will be located at Calle Sebastián Allende 200, Colonia La Penal, on Guadalajara’s east side near the Cristóbal de Oñate station on Line 2 of the light rail.

The FIL Guadalajara prepares to welcome Salman Rushdie as keynote speaker

The FIL Guadalajara, Latin America’s premier book festival, has an exciting program in the works for its 40th edition. British American writer Salman Rushdie is slated to open the program with a keynote lecture Nov. 28 at the Juan Rulfo Auditorium of Expo Guadalajara.

The announcement was made earlier this month by the FIL’s director, Marisol Schulz, who noted that this year’s festival will encompass “more than 3,000 activities that over nine days will center the conversation on literature, thought, scientific outreach, art, music, film, gastronomy, comics, the publishing business, programs for professionals and, of course, the formation of readers.”

In total, more than 900 authors from 41 countries are expected to take part in this year’s FIL, where Italy returns as the guest country of honor after 18 years.

This year’s FIL will also pay tribute to Juan Rulfo, 40 years after his death, with an immersive pavilion devoted to the universe of “Pedro Páramo” and a panel featuring Juan Carlos and Juan Pablo Rulfo, writer Élmer Mendoza and photographer Rogelio Cuéllar.

Nicaraguan writer Gioconda Belli is set to receive the 2026 FIL Prize for Literature in Romance Languages, and Italian author Alessandro Baricco will open the Salón Literario Carlos Fuentes.

Ticket availability

No tickets will be sold specifically for Rushdie’s keynote address. Entry requires a general admission ticket to the FIL paired with mandatory online pre-registration due to the strict security protocols necessary to ensure the author’s safety.

Keep an eye on the official FIL Guadalajara website or its press announcements as the fair approaches for the exact date the pre-registration link goes live.

For more information about the general program and specific events, visit the website’s calendar page.

Dates: Saturday, Nov. 28, 2026 – Sunday, Dec. 6, 2026

Location: Expo Guadalajara, Jalisco

Cost: General admission tickets are available online from the FIL website or in person at FIL’s main office, with prices starting from 40 pesos (US $2) for adults and 30 pesos (US $1.50) for children.

Día de Campo Festival returns to Guadalajara

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Aperol Día De Campo (@aperoldiadecampo)

Returning to Guadalajara next month for its fifth edition is the Día de Campo festival. Unlike the typical music festival experience these days, Día de Campo bills itself as an intimate, low-key event — a chill day in the park with fantastic music, not a drunken bacchanal.

This year’s festival is moving to a new venue, Titanes GDL, which sits across from Parque Metropolitano. It is reachable by taxi from downtown Guadalajara in about 20 minutes.

Headlining Día de Campo this year is Santa Pirata, a new side project by Arcade Fire’s frontman Win Butler. The band includes Haitian musician and Arcade Fire member Paul Beaubrun and DJ Cosmo Gonik. Santa Pirata blends DJ sets with live instrumentation, featuring Butler on drums and Beaubrun on bass and guitar.

Also performing this year in its Guadalajara debut is Chet Faker. Australian musician Nick Murphy has been performing under the moniker Chet Faker for the past 15 years, combining soul, R&B and electronic music with catchy, danceable beats. The artist is touring in support of his new album, “A Love for Strangers.”

Other confirmed artists for Día de Campo 2026 are Argentina’s Grammy-nominated Bándalos Chinos, known for its synth-pop, funk and indie rock, Norway’s Kakkmaddafakka, CocoRosie and Alanis Yuki.

Date: Nov. 29, 2026, starting at 1 p.m.

Location: Titanes event space next to Parque Metropolitano in Zapopan

Cost: Available on Boletomóvil starting at 1,323 pesos (US $65).

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Made in Mexico: How Carlos Fuentes captured Mexico’s political soul
World.content:
Mexican author Carlos Fuentes entered my life with the soft insistence of a truth you recognize before you can name it. In a house where books functioned as liturgy and political arguments were my family’s daily prayer, politics and fiction braided until nationhood itself could only be discussed through story.

Friends learned to avoid politics and religion in polite conversation. But at our table, it was compulsory.

Encountering Carlos Fuentes

Between my mother’s journalistic and analytic perception and my father’s artistic view of the world, I first encountered Carlos Fuentes. It was an introduction that felt less like discovery than initiation.

I first found “La Muerte de Artemio Cruz” (“The Death of Artemio Cruz“) rummaging through my parents’ bookshelves as a teenager, that furtive, holy act of taking what the house has to offer.

The book is a slow, terrible confession. It follows a revolutionary soldier who becomes a wealthy businessman and, on his deathbed, confronts the compromises that made his life

possible.

I asked my father if I might read it. He agreed with the tolerant risk of someone who knows the power of literature. I was too young to understand everything — too young for many of the dates and alliances and the dense historical scaffolding — but not too young for the voices.

The blunt honesty of Fuentes’ interlocutors cut into me. Their phrases echoed family stories, private grievances and the way a father’s silence sometimes explained more than his sermons.

I went to sleep that night with the book heavy under my pillow, feeling the first tremor of an allegiance.

Fuentes liked to say that the Latin American novel rescues what official history neglects. It is an attractive aphorism: literature as a salvage operation, novels as lifeboats ferrying the lives, rumors and embarrassments that governments prefer to let sink.

But his claim is more than rhetoric. Read Fuentes and you find not an inventory of facts but a map of forces — the informal routines, petty calculations and generational betrayals — through which Mexican politics actually works. He is not interested in vindicating every detail of the public record. He excavates the subterranean arithmetic of power. The small acts and grand illusions that produce regimes.

A ‘gypsy in a black tie’

If Fuentes’ vantage feels panoramic, it is because it was cultivated that way. Born in 1928 in Panama to a cultured, liberal diplomatic family, he spent his early years amid the humid expanses of Montevideo and Rio de Janeiro. Those tropical afternoons — book-lined, humid and full of foreign tongues — were where Fuentes first fell in love with literature. Alfonso Reyes, the Mexican humanist and a central pillar of the country’s intellectual life, became an early mentor who guided him through the literary world.

The young Fuentes absorbed European and Latin American canons with equal appetite, continued his journey to Washington with his family. They stayed eight years in the American capital amid tense Mexico–U.S. relations following President Lázaro Cárdenas’ 1938 nationalizations.

Made in Mexico: Carlos Fuentes

Watch this video on YouTube

Distance sharpened his sense of Mexico as a nation, and of his identity as Mexican in a foreign country, as he turned into a schoolyard enemy thanks to the “Tata Lázaro initiative.” Watching his country from abroad, he did not simply miss home. He began to interrogate it. He traced a family history animated by wider European convulsions — ancestors who fled Germany and Spain and settled in Veracruz, establishing a coffee hacienda, and he learned how much a personal identity could be a palimpsest of political choices and historical happenstance.

Then a pivotal evening at a New York cinema, where he watched “Citizen Kane” with his father, supplied a kind of formal revelation: narrative could reveal the way private lives braided into public histories. He decided then to write within those intersections.

The acquisition of a global perspective

Fuentes’ early reading list — Stevenson, Dumas, Miguel Zévaco, Jules Verne — reads less like a curriculum than a confession. He wanted plot and spectacle, but with an eye to the moral and historical sediment underneath.

A teenage posting in Chile broadened that sensibility further. Latin American politics did not respect borders. The authoritarian and reformist rhythms he observed in Chile and Argentina taught him that patterns reverberated across the continent, that the fate of one republic often presaged the anxieties of another.

He returned to Mexico, weary of the peripatetic diplomat’s life — the “gypsy in a black tie” as he called it — and enrolled at UNAM to study law at Alfonso Reyes’ encouragement. The law sharpened him. Fuentes would later borrow Stendhal’s praise for the Napoleonic civil code — “clear, concise and effective” — and insist that legal training gave a novelist a discipline of clarity.

Yet his impulse was to use that clarity to break forms with novels that could capture the messy simultaneity of Latin American time.

At age 26, he published his first book, “Los Días Enmascarados” (“The Masked Days”), 1954, a collection where myth and the fantastic meet a restless modernity. His true breakthrough came with “La Región Más Transparente” (“Where the Air Is Clear”), 1958, a book that announced, with a kind of civic thunder, a new way of seeing Mexico City.

From that moment, he was no longer an apprentice. He was a national habit.

A life stranger than fiction

Fuentes’ public life was as complicated as his fiction. His unique voice made him central to Mexican culture to the point where presidents listened carefully to what Fuentes and other Mexican intellectuals had to say about their regimes. Later, he accepted the ambassadorship to France (1975–1977), a decision tied to a friendship with President Luis Echeverría that earned both praise and censure.

When the following president, Gustavo Díaz Ordáz, took office, he resigned from his role as ambassador in protest to the Tlatelolco massacre in 1968, an act that marked him among writers who believed conscience could not be compartmentalized.

He would reflect on this episode as a reminder that the line between cultural influence and political entanglement is rarely neat. Fuentes moved in circles of power even as he remained a sharp critic.

The restless writer

He was, by any measure, prolific, writing more than seventy books — including novels, essays, short stories, scripts and plays — along with a steady stream of articles across the Americas.

Critics who catalog his work point to recurring obsessions: the mestizo nature of Mexican identity, the ways power shifts under pressure, and, when left to its own inertia, the precariousness of state narratives that tidy over contradictions.

But to reduce Fuentes to a set of themes is to miss his artistry, which is the ability to render political life in the language of human habit: betrayal as domestic pattern, corruption as genealogy and revolution as a choreography of broken promises.

If a reader wants a beginning, here are five texts that make his method and moral urgency plain.

1. “La Región Más Transparente” (“Where the Air Is Clear”), 1958

A portrait of Mexico City through a chorus of characters — peasants, intellectuals, opportunists, dreamers — this novel critiques a hopeful bourgeoisie who believes concentrated wealth will somehow be redistributed by fate. The city is staged as myth and machinery, a place where pre-Hispanic ghosts brush against neon and where national identity is debated in salons and tenements alike. Fuentes anticipates the rupture generation’s disillusionments, sketching a metropolis both magnet and mirror.

2. “La Silla del Águila” (“The Eagle’s Throne”), 2003

Set, proleptically, in 2020, told through letters after a communications collapse, it narrates a corrupt election, the corrosive compromises of those who seek higher office, and the blunt interventions of foreign powers — most pointedly the United States. It is less a speculative thriller than a study in how institutions erode when informal networks take precedence over civic duty.

3. “Tiempo Mexicano” (“Mexican Time”), 1971

An essayistic meditation on temporality and national memory. Fuentes argues that Mexican time is not linear but circular and overlapping. Epochs coexist and narrate one another. He examines who is given the right to remember and how state and culture conspire to shape collective consciousness. Here, his faith in youth and his hope that new generations could craft a more democratic nation glimmer most clearly.

4. “Nuevo Tiempo Mexicano” (“A New Time for Mexico”), 1994

Written in the wake of 1994’s ruptures — the Zapatista uprising in Chiapas and the peso’s collapse — this book is more sober. Where earlier essays were buoyed by the possibility of reform, “A New Time for Mexico” reflects on the hard limits of institution-building amid enduring inequality and the new economic realities shaped by NAFTA.

5. “El Espejo Enterrado” (“The Buried Mirror: Reflections on Spain and the New World”), 1992

Perhaps my favorite, a sweeping cultural history that traces five centuries of Hispanic America. Fuentes is at once historian and storyteller. He narrates the persistence of colonial and Indigenous legacies as the subterranean currents of identity. The book is elegiac and exuberant, a reminder that culture is not a surface polish but an accumulated architecture.

Why read Fuentes?

Because he converts complexity into clearness without flattening it. He is not a historian in the archival sense. Dates and citations are subordinated to moral geometry.

But he is remarkably precise in diagnosing how power, memory and myth conspire to produce national life. His prose wants to unsettle complacency. He hoped readers would argue with his books, not to annul them but to enlarge the conversation.

Fuentes belonged to an erudite generation that could look at Mexico from both inside and outside. The diplomat’s gaze that knows protocol and the exile’s view that knows perspective.

He understood how the Mexican Revolution’s promise had been domesticated: the postrevolutionary bourgeoisie reproducing prerevolutionary hierarchies, the Institutional Revolutionary Party’s (PRI) transformation from the Party of the Mexican Revolution (PRM) into an apparatus that welded party to state, and how industrial growth often masked social exclusion.

Clarity and cultural insight

But perhaps his clearest insight is cultural. The revolution’s deepest achievement was not the redistribution of land or the construction of institutions alone, but the knitting together of a fragmented populace so disparate communities could finally perceive one another.

To read Fuentes is to feel history as a kind of weather: sudden, changeable and always shaping the small gestures of private life. His novels let you listen to Mexico’s interiors — the whispered bargains, the private prayers and public betrayals. They teach patience.

Political truths are rarely delivered in headlines. They arrive through accumulations of habit and choice, through the intimate narratives that novels can, more truthfully than manifestos, deliver.

If you find a copy of his work, take it. Fuentes will not hand you a neat syllabus of reform. Instead, he will offer scenes and voices that make the stakes of politics unavoidable. His writing insists upon engagement.

Not mere consumption, but conversation, argument, indignation, laughter and, sometimes, renewal. In that stubborn insistence lies his lasting invitation: to read Mexico not as a place to be explained, but as a country alive with stories that refine what we think we know.

María Meléndez is a writer and art historian. She works at the Mexican Cultural Institute of the Embassy of Mexico in Washington, D.C.

World.content:
Brazil Markets · Company Earnings

Gerdau made almost 40% more adjusted profit than a year ago on only 3.9% more sales. That gap is the whole story of its third quarter, which the company reported on Monday, 26 October 2026, after the New York close.

Gerdau is a Brazilian steelmaker whose shares trade in Brazil’s stock market and, as American depositary receipts (ADRs, dollar-priced certificates), on the New York Stock Exchange under GGB. The result also says something about Brazil’s economy, where steel tracks building and factory demand.

A Bigger Profit From Barely Bigger Sales

Adjusted net income, which strips out one-off items, reached R$1.52 billion (about US$282 million at R$5.39 per dollar, the 26 October close from RT, a market-data provider). That is up 39.7% from the third quarter of 2025.

Reported net income, the accounting figure, was R$1.56 billion (about US$290 million), up 43.4% from R$1.09 billion a year earlier, according to the unaudited statements Gerdau filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the American market regulator.Net sales rose 3.9% to R$18.69 billion (about US$3.5 billion).

Adjusted EBITDA, a measure of operating profit before interest, tax and depreciation, came in near R$3.77 billion (about US$700 million), roughly 20% of sales.Gerdau reported adjusted EBITDA of R$3.4 billion in the second quarter, so the latest figure is higher again.

Profit growing far faster than sales usually means a company is earning more on every tonne it sells, or spending less to make it.

The shares trade without the right to the dividend from Wednesday, 11 November. For ADR holders in the United States, the record date is Thursday, 12 November and the payment date is Tuesday, 22 December.

The notice states the amount in reais, so the dollar value depends on the exchange rate that day.

A Quiet Day Before a Loud Reading

The numbers arrived after the market had closed. The ADR ended Monday at US$4.75, down 6.9% on the day, so that fall came before anyone saw these results.

Tuesday will be the first test of how investors read the quarter. Gerdau has scheduled a videoconference for noon in Brazil, 11 a.m. New York time.

In plain English: “Adjusted” means the company removed one-off gains and costs to show its usual earning power. “EBITDA” is profit from running the business, before financing costs and taxes.

What It Means for US Readers

For an American holding GGB, the quarter shows earnings rising much faster than revenue, and a cash payout on 22 December. Because the dividend is declared in reais, the dollar amount depends on the exchange rate on the payment date.

Steel is also a clue to the wider economy. When a large producer earns more on flat sales, it can point to better pricing or lower costs, though one quarter proves little.

What Is Not Known

The full earnings release carries steel volumes, the split between North America and Brazil, debt and the outlook. The Rio Times had not confirmed those figures against the company document at publication, so we do not report them here.

Whether investors treat the profit jump as lasting will show in Tuesday’s trading. We will update this story if the call changes the picture.

World.content:
The former Bolsa de Mercadorias & Futuros building in downtown São Paulo, whose business is now part of B3. Photo: Fulviusbsas / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Brazil Markets · Stocks · Published Monday, 26 October, 4:53 p.m. ET · Source: B3 exchange trading data, market prices

Key Facts —Stocks. The Ibovespa, Brazil’s main stock index, closed down 13.88% at 176,608 points. —Currency. The dollar ended at about 5.41 reais (R$5.41), up 8.4% from R$4.99 on Friday. —Pause. B3 halted trading with a circuit breaker, the first since March 2020. —Why. Markets had bet on a win by his rival; President Lula won re-election on Sunday. —Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index, with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

Brazil woke up on Monday to a stock market in free fall, a day after re-electing its president. By the closing bell, the Ibovespa had lost 13.88% of its value in a single session, its biggest daily fall since March 2020.

The index ended at 176,608 points, down from 205,082.56 on Friday. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated the conservative senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, in Sunday’s runoff, an outcome many investors had not priced in; for the wider picture, see our guide to Brazil’s economy.

In Plain English Ibovespa: the main gauge of Brazilian stocks, like the S&P 500 for Brazil. B3: the São Paulo exchange where Brazilian shares trade. Circuit breaker: an automatic pause in trading after a steep fall, meant to stop panic selling. Real: Brazil’s currency.

How Bad Was the Day?

At its worst the index touched 169,516 points, a fall of 17.34% from Friday’s close. The losses were so fast that B3 triggered its circuit breaker, a step it had last used in March 2020, when the Covid-19 pandemic hit markets.

The pause did not stop the slide for long. Shares recovered a little by midday and closed about 4% above the day’s low, but still far below where they started.

Friday’s close of 205,082.56 sat only a little below the index’s record close of 209,067 points on 9 October. Monday wiped out the rally of recent weeks in a few hours.

Who Lost Most, and Who Gained?

Banks and the state oil company took the heaviest blows. Itaú Unibanco, Brazil’s largest private bank, fell by double digits, while Petrobras, the state-run oil giant, lost about 8%.

A few companies that earn dollars rose against the tide. Vale, the iron-ore miner, gained about 4%, and Suzano, a pulp and paper exporter, jumped about 10%.

Why Did the Real Sink Too?

The dollar peaked at R$5.60 during the day and closed near R$5.41. A weaker real makes imports and dollar debts costlier for Brazilian firms, while it helps exporters.

Stocks and the currency fell together, a pattern that often means investors are pulling money out. That double blow is what makes Monday’s move so painful for investors who hold Brazilian assets in dollars.

What It Means for US Readers

Americans who own Brazil through the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ), a fund tracking large Brazilian companies, saw it close down 19.8% at US$34.15 on Monday. Holders of Brazilian companies traded in New York as American depositary receipts face the same repricing, with the weaker real on top.

Measured in dollars, the Ibovespa lost roughly 20% on the day, by our calculation from R$4.99 on Friday and R$5.41 on Monday. That is the number a US investor actually felt.

Travellers and expats gain purchasing power. At R$5.41 per dollar, a R$500 hotel night costs about US$92, against about US$100 on Friday.

What Is Not Known

It is not clear whether the sell-off will extend on Tuesday or whether foreign investors return after the first shock. Nor is it known how the government or the central bank will respond.

Prices here are Monday’s closing levels, which may be revised by later data. This report covers market reaction; official election results come from the TSE, Brazil’s electoral court.

The dollar rose about 8.4% to roughly R$5.41, from R$4.99 on Friday. It touched R$5.60 earlier in the session.

World.title: Cuba’s Airports Run Out of Jet Fuel
World.content:
CUBA · BREAKING

Updated Monday, 26 October, 4:22 p.m. ET · Source: Cuban aviation authorities, airport and airline notices

Key Facts — What Ten Cuban airports list Jet A-1 aviation fuel as unavailable for refueling until 04:00 UTC on 1 November 2026.

— Who Empresa Cubana de Navegación Aérea (ECNA), Cuba's state-run air navigation company, issued NOTAMs A3459/26 through A3468/26.

— Where Affected airports include Havana, Varadero, Cienfuegos, Santa Clara, Camagüey, Cayo Coco, Holguín, Santiago de Cuba, Manzanillo, and Cayo Largo.

— When The current notices replaced an earlier series that had been due to expire on 1 October.

Official Notices Extend Restriction

Cuba's state-run Empresa Cubana de Navegación Aérea (ECNA), the country's air navigation authority, issued ten aviation notices declaring Jet A-1 fuel unavailable at major airports. The NOTAMs, numbered A3459/26 through A3468/26, state simply: 'JET A1 FUEL NOT AVBL.'

The notices replaced an earlier series that had been due to expire on 1 October, and they run through 1 November.

The affected airports include José Martí International in Havana, Juan Gualberto Gómez in Varadero, and eight other principal gateways serving tourism and international travel. The restriction applies specifically to aircraft refueling, not to airport access or all flight operations.

Airlines Adjust Operations

The fuel shortage does not constitute a blanket flight ban, but it creates significant operational constraints for carriers serving Cuba. Airlines may still operate if aircraft arrive with sufficient fuel, alter payloads or routes, or arrange technical refueling stops abroad.

Short-haul routes from Florida, Mexico, or Caribbean destinations may be viable if aircraft can carry enough fuel for both outbound and return legs. Long-haul services, however, often require technical stops in third countries, increasing costs and extending travel times.

Shortage Dates to February

Reports place the broader aviation-fuel problem as far back as February 2026, when authorities declared a lack of Jet A-1 at nine international airports. Authorities renewed the notices before the initial period expired, and successive extensions continued through the spring and summer.

Reports now count ten airports; the original February notices covered nine. Some reports attribute the shortage to wider difficulties obtaining petroleum products.Reports attribute the shortage to disrupted Venezuelan oil supplies and tighter U.S. sanctions.

Traveler Impact and Outlook

The fuel restriction has raised concern for international and tourism-oriented services using Varadero, Cayo Coco, Cayo Largo, Holguín, and other listed airports. Travelers are advised to confirm schedules, stops, and connections with their airlines, particularly those traveling from the United States and Europe.

Air China scheduled an extra flight, CA590, on 19 October at the request of the Chinese embassy in Cuba, for passengers stranded after earlier cancellations.The expiry date of 1 November is the end of the current notices, not a guarantee that fuel supplies will resume.Authorities may issue new notices if the shortage continues.

What It Means for US Readers

U.S. travelers with planned trips to Cuba should confirm flight status directly with their airline, as schedules and routing may change with little notice. The fuel restriction affects refueling at ten major Cuban airports, but does not automatically close those airports or cancel all flights.

Short-haul routes from Florida may remain viable if aircraft can carry enough fuel for both outbound and return legs. Travelers should verify whether their carrier has arranged technical refueling stops or adjusted departure times before heading to the airport.

What Is Not Known

Whether fuel will actually return on 1 November is not known; the date is the expiry of the current notices, not a guarantee that supplies will resume. The precise cause and scale of the shortage are also not established in available reports.

No authoritative tally is provided for cancelled, delayed, diverted, or fuel-stopped flights. The available reports do not provide a consolidated figure for stranded passengers, financial losses, or the volume of fuel unavailable.

The available reports identify ECNA as the issuing institution but do not name an official who authorized the extension or explain the procurement failure. Claims that U.S. actions or a Caribbean naval blockade caused the shortage are reported but not substantiated by an independent primary-source assessment.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are Cuban airports closed?

No. The notices state that Jet A-1 fuel is not available for refueling, but they do not order the closure of the terminals. Flights may still operate if airlines make alternative arrangements for fuel.

Which airports are affected?

Ten airports are affected: Havana, Varadero, Cienfuegos, Santa Clara, Camagüey, Cayo Coco, Holguín, Santiago de Cuba, Manzanillo, and Cayo Largo. These include Cuba’s principal international gateways and several tourist destinations.

When will fuel be available again?

The current notices expire at 04:00 UTC on 1 November 2026, which is the start of that day in Cuba. However, the expiry date is not a guarantee that supplies will resume, and authorities may issue new notices if the shortage continues.

World.title: Ebola Alert Spreads Beyond Nigeria
World.content:
AFRICA · HEALTH

Key Facts — What is happening Cameroon, Benin and Madagascar tightened their Ebola checks after Nigeria confirmed its first case on Tuesday 20 October 2026, and none of the three has recorded a case.

— Why it matters Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country and a major air hub, and the Bundibugyo strain, a rare Ebola species, has no approved vaccine or specific treatment.

— The numbers Nigeria is the fifth country to detect the virus, after the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Uganda, France and Kenya. The WHO counted 9,704 confirmed cases and 4,687 deaths as of 20 October, nearly all in the DRC.

— Who is who Malachie Manaouda is Cameroon’s public health minister, Benjamin Hounkpatin is Benin’s health minister, and Patrick Amoth is Kenya’s health director general.

— What to watch A first case in Cameroon, Benin or Madagascar would signal wider spread. Cameroon’s health minister will also submit a budgeted response plan to the Prime Minister.

— Prediction markets Polymarket, an online prediction market, puts the chance that the World Health Organization (WHO) calls Ebola a pandemic in 2026 at 2.5% (26 October, 3:05 p.m. ET).

— What it means for you US rules announced on 21 May route travellers from Congo, Uganda and South Sudan through Washington Dulles airport for screening. No such rule for Nigeria was found, so travellers should check notices from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Ebola has reached Nigeria, and Cameroon, Benin and Madagascar are tightening health checks before any case arrives. None of the three has recorded a case so far.

The Ebola outbreak in Nigeria, confirmed on Tuesday 20 October 2026, has put its neighbours and far-off Madagascar on alert. Cameroon, Benin and Madagascar are tightening health checks, and none of them has recorded a case.

Ebola is a deadly virus that spreads through contact with the body fluids of sick people. For US readers it matters because Nigeria is a major air hub and this strain has no approved vaccine.

The Ebola Outbreak in Nigeria So Far

Nigeria confirmed on Tuesday 20 October that a woman in Abuja, the capital, had tested positive for Bundibugyo Ebola. The World Health Organization (WHO), the United Nations health agency, says she had recently arrived from Uganda; investigators are still tracing her full travel history.

The WHO says she is in isolation after seeking care at a private clinic in Abuja. Congo, formally the Democratic Republic of the Congo, declared the outbreak on Friday 15 May 2026.

Nigeria is the fifth country to detect the virus, after Congo, Uganda, France and Kenya. Bundibugyo is a rare Ebola species with no approved vaccine or specific treatment, the WHO says.

Cameroon Calls Its Preparedness Insufficient

Cameroon shares more than 2,000 kilometres (about 1,240 miles) of land and sea border with Nigeria, with daily trade and direct flights. Public Health Minister Malachie Manaouda said on Thursday 22 October that Cameroon has no case but a very high risk.

A crisis meeting in Yaoundé, the capital, judged preparedness insufficient and set seven priorities, including hospital alerts and stronger border controls. Manaouda will submit a budgeted plan to Prime Minister Joseph Dion Ngute.

Benin Moves to Pre-Alert

Benin moved to a pre-alert phase on Wednesday 21 October. Health Minister Benjamin Hounkpatin inspected Cotonou airport, where thermal cameras now scan arrivals, and the government says Benin has no case.

Why Madagascar Watches Travellers From Kenya

Kenya, not Nigeria, is the reason, because it announced a fatal imported case on Tuesday 6 October. Kenya now has nine confirmed cases and one death as of 20 October, all in one cluster.

An unnamed health ministry source said five direct flights a week link Madagascar to Kenya, so the danger is imminent. Arrivals from Kenya fill in a health form at Ivato airport in Antananarivo, the capital, and get 21 days of follow-up.

The same source said 500 to 600 passengers arrive weekly on that route and the ministry has no facilities to quarantine them. Staff phone them often, while travellers from Congo face a mandatory 21-day quarantine in requisitioned hotels.

Africa’s Health Agency Calls Ministers Together

A news agency reports that Africa CDC, the African Union‘s health agency, invited ministers to a virtual meeting on Wednesday 28 October. It quotes director general Jean Kaseya, who said Ebola now affects three regions of Africa; no second source was found.

The WHO counted 9,704 confirmed cases and 4,687 deaths as of 20 October, almost all in Congo. The WHO urges readiness but advises against travel or trade bans.

What It Means for US Readers

On Thursday 21 May the US ordered travellers from Congo, Uganda and South Sudan to enter through Washington Dulles airport for screening. No opened source shows it still applies or covers Nigeria, or shows a US travel ban tied to Nigeria.

Travellers to Nigeria, Cameroon, Benin or Kenya should check notices from the CDC and the State Department before flying. Companies with staff in Abuja or Lagos should expect extra airport health checks.

What Prediction Markets Say

Traders on Polymarket, a prediction market, bet 2.5% that the WHO calls Ebola a pandemic in 2026 (26 October, 3:05 p.m. ET). The bet pays only if the WHO uses the word pandemic officially.

Another bet gives 22.5% for a case in the Republic of the Congo, which borders Cameroon. Volume is about US$789,000 on the first bet and US$17,000 on this one.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

It is not known where the Nigerian patient caught the virus, and the WHO says investigators are still reconstructing her travel. Case totals change daily, so the figures here are the WHO count as of 20 October.

Madagascar’s flight and passenger figures come from unnamed ministry sources and are not independently checked. The Africa CDC meeting and Kaseya’s remarks rest on one news agency text, and the outcome is unknown.

What Comes Next

One news agency says Africa CDC ministers meet on Wednesday 28 October. An outbreak ends only after 42 days with no new case.

Related Coverage

The patient is covered in Nigeria Flies Ebola Patient to Switzerland, and contacts in Nigeria Ebola Contact Tracing After the Evacuation. See also Nigeria Pays Ebola Contacts US$75 a Week and Congo’s Ebola Vaccine Trial in Bunia Explained.

Kenya is covered in Kenya Ebola Quarantine Release Sunday and What Happens Next. Country news is on the Nigeria and Cameroon pages.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there Ebola in Cameroon, Benin or Madagascar?

No case has been confirmed in any of the three as of Monday 26 October 2026. Each has raised its alert after Nigeria and Kenya confirmed cases.

Why does Madagascar monitor travellers from Kenya?

Kenya has nine confirmed cases and one death, and five direct flights a week link it to Madagascar. Travellers face airport checks and 21 days of health follow-up, not quarantine.

Which Ebola strain is in Nigeria?

It is Bundibugyo virus, confirmed on 20 October 2026. The WHO says no approved vaccine or specific treatment exists for this strain.

Does Ebola spread on planes?

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of sick people or contaminated objects, not through the air. The WHO advises against travel or trade bans on affected countries.

Should US travellers avoid Nigeria?

No source opened shows a US ban on travel to Nigeria. Check CDC and State Department notices and airline rules before flying.

COLOMBIA · MARKETS

Key Facts — What is happening Colombia launched new dollar bonds due 2032, 2037 and 2056 on Monday, 26 October 2026, its first dollar bond sale since January. The amount and interest rate were not public when this was written.

— Why it matters Colombia is selling dollar debt while its credit rating sits below investment grade at two of three major agencies, and the government is also cutting 2026 spending and swapping peso debt.

— The numbers Each bond costs at least US$200,000. Spending cuts of 13.8 trillion pesos (about US$4.4 billion) were announced on 23 October, and the January sale raised US$4.95 billion.

— Who is who Abelardo de la Espriella, Colombia’s conservative president since 7 August, and Finance Minister Miguel Gómez Martínez lead the sale, which BBVA, Itaú and J.P. Morgan banks run.

— What to watch Watch for the final amount, interest rates and investor demand once pricing is complete, then for the third peso bond swap set for Thursday, 19 November.

Colombia has launched its first dollar bond sale under its new president. The amount and the interest rate are not yet public.

Colombia launched a new sale of dollar bonds on Monday, 26 October 2026. These Colombia global bonds are the country’s first dollar debt sale since January.

It is also the first under President Abelardo de la Espriella, a conservative who took office on 7 August. The size of the sale and its interest rate were not public when this was written.

Global bonds are debt that a government sells to investors around the world in US dollars. Colombia borrows abroad this way, rather than in pesos at home.

What the Colombia Global Bonds Offer

On Monday morning Colombia filed three draft offering documents with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, the American market regulator. They describe bonds due in 2032, 2037 and 2056, so investors would lend for about five, ten or 30 years.

The drafts leave the amount, the interest rate and the price blank, because those are set once investors place orders. Each bond costs at least US$200,000, so buyers are mostly large funds and banks.

The bonds are a direct, unsecured promise of the Colombian state, backed by its full faith and credit. Interest is paid twice a year, with the first payment in 2027.

Three banks run the sale: BBVA of Spain, Itaú of Brazil and J.P. Morgan of the United States. The documents say the money goes to general budget needs, not to a named project.

Why Colombia Is Borrowing Again

In January, under former President Gustavo Petro, Colombia sold US$4.95 billion of global bonds in three parts, its largest such sale ever. Those bonds, due 2029, 2031 and 2033, pay 5.375%, 6.125% and 6.5% interest.

In February, the public debt office said Colombia would not return to this market in 2026 except to manage existing debt. The new government has since worked on its payment calendar at home.

On Friday, 23 October, the Finance Ministry finished a second peso bond swap, and a third is set for Thursday, 19 November. In a swap, investors hand in bonds due soon for bonds due later.

On 23 October the president also announced Decree 1585, cutting 2026 spending by 13.8 trillion pesos (about US$4.4 billion). Conversions here use the 26 October rate of about 3,170 pesos per US dollar.

How Credit Rating Agencies See Colombia

Credit rating agencies grade how likely a government is to repay. S&P Global Ratings gives Colombia BB- and Fitch Ratings gives it BB, both below investment grade.

Moody’s, the third agency, rates Colombia Baa3, the lowest investment-grade step. The agencies pointed in part to the three-year suspension of Colombia’s fiscal rule, its legal limit on deficits.

What It Means for US Readers

US investors can hold Colombian sovereign bonds, but the US$200,000 minimum puts the new issue mainly with institutions. The final rate will show how much extra yield investors demand from Colombia, which two of three agencies rate below investment grade.

That price also serves as a benchmark for Colombian companies that borrow in dollars, including firms with shares listed in New York. For background, read about the peso bond swap and a bank’s view of Colombian bonds.

Colombia is also a close US security partner. Wider context is in Colombia explained and on the Colombia hub.

In Plain English

Global bonds: dollar debt that a government sells to international investors.

dollar debt that a government sells to international investors. Prospectus supplement: the offering document that lists a bond’s terms and risks.

the offering document that lists a bond’s terms and risks. Finance Ministry: the department that runs Colombia’s budget and public debt.

the department that runs Colombia’s budget and public debt. Investment grade: a rating that signals low default risk; Colombia is below it at two agencies.

What Is Not Known

The amount, interest rate, price and investor demand are not yet public. The ministry has not said how the sale ties to its swap programme.

One market report put early rate guidance near 7.35% for 2032, 7.9% for 2037 and 8.45% for 2056. A bank economist estimated that Colombia needs about US$3 billion this year, and the ministry has confirmed neither.

What Comes Next

The final terms should appear once pricing is complete, in a pricing document filed with the SEC. The next scheduled step is the third peso bond swap on Thursday, 19 November.

The government also plans to send Congress an adjustment bill to cut public spending. The bond sale adds debt and does not by itself reduce the deficit.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are Colombia global bonds?

They are US dollar bonds that Colombia sells to investors worldwide. The new ones mature in 2032, 2037 and 2056.

How much is Colombia borrowing?

The amount is not yet public. The draft documents leave it blank until investors place orders.

Why is Colombia borrowing in dollars?

The documents say the money is for general budget needs. The government is also cutting 2026 spending and swapping peso debt.

Is Colombia’s debt investment grade?

Only at Moody’s, which rates it Baa3. S&P and Fitch rate it below investment grade.

Can ordinary US investors buy the bonds?

Each bond costs at least US$200,000, so the sale mainly targets institutions. Smaller investors usually reach such bonds through funds.

World.title: Peru Extends Lima State of Emergency
World.content:
PERU · SECURITY

Key Facts — What is happening Peru extended the emergency in Lima and Callao by decree on Sunday, 25 October, for 60 days from Wednesday, 28 October.

— Why it matters Gunmen killed five people in the two cities on Sunday, 25 October, while soldiers keep backing the police under the emergency order in both cities.

— The numbers Sixty days, which by the newsroom’s own day count end on Saturday, 26 December; four rights can be limited; five people were shot dead on Sunday.

— Who is who The National Police leads and the Armed Forces help; President Keiko Fujimori heads the government, Luis Galarreta the cabinet.

— What to watch Whether killings and extortion fall, and whether the government renews the order again before late December.

— Power Index Peru ranks 5th of 14 in Peru ranks 5th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 54.7 points (October 2026 edition).

— What it means for you US visitors should check the State Department’s current Peru advisory, and organisers of mass events in Lima need official permission.

Peru has renewed the emergency covering its capital and main port for 60 more days. Soldiers keep supporting the police while gunmen kill on the streets.

Peru has extended the Lima state of emergency for 60 more days, covering the capital and Callao, the neighbouring port city. The decree, published on Sunday, 25 October, takes effect on Wednesday, 28 October.

The order lets the National Police call on the army against extortion and contract killings. It also allows limits on four civil rights, so mass events need official permission.

What the Lima State of Emergency Allows

Supreme Decree 142-2026-PCM extends the emergency declared by Decree 123-2026-PCM. Peru’s cabinet, the Council of Ministers, is led by Prime Minister Luis Galarreta.

President Keiko Fujimori, who took office on 28 July 2026, heads the government. The order runs 60 calendar days, which by the newsroom’s own day count ends on Saturday, 26 December.

Under Article 137 of the constitution, the decree allows limits on four rights. They are protection of the home from entry, freedom of movement, freedom of assembly, and personal liberty and security.

Large public religious, cultural and sports events need permission from the competent authorities, who assess each request. Smaller gatherings need no prior approval, and coverage of the decree mentions no curfew.

Who Is in Charge on the Streets

The National Police, known as the PNP, keeps control of internal order, with support from the Armed Forces. Police choose where to operate using intelligence, crime statistics and crime maps.

A joint police and military body, the Unified Command against Organized Crime, stays in place. El Comercio, a Lima daily, reports that the decree calls it a temporary, focused force led day to day by the police.

President Fujimori announced that command on Wednesday, 7 October, with 1,350 personnel and an elite unit. Both police and soldiers must follow the legal rules on the use of force.

The government also created a high-level cabinet commission on security and public order, reported by the official gazette on 14 October. The crime commission report explains what it does and what it cannot do.

Why Lima and Callao Stay Under Emergency

The decree says the aim is to confront crime and other situations of violence. Lima daily El Comercio reports that the police command asked for the extension on 14 October, citing homicide, contract killings and extortion.

Extortion means gangs demand regular payments from businesses, often backed by threats of shooting. El Comercio also counts this as the fifth extension decree of 2026, a tally the official summary does not confirm.

On Sunday, 25 October, five people were shot dead in separate attacks across the two cities in under 24 hours. Killings were reported on Loreto street, in Oquendo, in Ventanilla and in a settlement bordering San Martín de Porres.

Gunmen on a motorcycle also wounded a 71-year-old bus driver in San Juan de Miraflores, who was reportedly stable, according to relatives. In central Lima, a retired police officer and his son were wounded.

Police are investigating every case and have not confirmed motives. They do not rule out extortion in the central Lima attack.

What It Means for US Readers

The US State Department, Washington’s foreign ministry, publishes a travel advisory for Peru with a numbered risk level. That page could not be opened for this report, so check its current level before booking.

Visitors may see more police and soldiers in Lima and Callao. Coverage of the decree describes no new checkpoints.

Companies that organise conferences, concerts or sports events in Lima need authorisation for mass gatherings. The sources reviewed do not say how long approvals take.

Staff travelling to Lima can find local guidance in the Peru security explainer and the Lima city page. The Peru hub tracks the wider political picture.

What Is Not Known

The decree coverage gives no crime targets or earlier results, so whether the extension will reduce killings is open. The 14 October police request and the fifth-extension count rest on one newspaper.

The motives for Sunday’s attacks are unconfirmed. Police say the cases are still under investigation, and the current US advisory level is unverified.

A 60-day order that began on 28 August would end on Monday, 26 October by count. The sources do not say how Tuesday, 27 October is covered.

What Comes Next

The extension takes effect on Wednesday, 28 October. The government must decide before late December whether to renew it again.

An extension does not by itself mean a curfew or a wider military role. The decree keeps the police in command.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Lima state of emergency?

It is a government order limiting four civil rights in Lima and Callao to fight crime. The National Police lead, with Armed Forces support.

How long does the extension last?

It lasts 60 calendar days from Wednesday, 28 October. By a simple day count, that runs through Saturday, 26 December.

Is there a curfew in Lima?

Coverage of the decree mentions no curfew. It describes limits on movement and assembly, and permission rules for mass events.

Is it safe for US travellers to visit Lima?

The current State Department advisory for Peru could not be opened, so check its level before travelling. Sunday attacks hit streets, cars and a bus across both cities.

Why was the emergency extended?

The decree cites crime and other situations of violence. Five people were shot dead on Sunday, 25 October, in separate attacks.

World.content:

MEXICO · TRADE

Key Facts The country Mexico is the largest trading partner of the United States, and its trucks carry goods across the border every day.

What happened An indefinite national strike began Monday 26 October 2026, with rigs parked near Mexico City and protests planned in about 20 states.

Who is striking Canacar, the national freight chamber, with Fematrac, Amotac and Indeco announced it, while Segob says most other trucking groups chose talks.

What they want Safer highways, an end to extortion and a bigger tax credit on tolls.

Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 71.4 points (October 2026 edition).

The Mexico truckers strike began on Monday 26 October 2026, as drivers parked rigs near Mexico City, with protests planned in about 20 states. Organizers call the protest peaceful, and parked or slow trucks can still delay freight for factories, stores and the US border.

US readers have trade at stake, because organizers estimate that up to 21,000 daily crossings, worth about US$1.8 billion, could stop. Our preview of the strike explained why most trucking groups chose talks, and this report covers the day itself.

Why the Mexico Truckers Strike Began

Drivers and haulage firms behind the Mexico truckers strike complain about robberies, extortion and protection payments on Mexican highways, and about roads in poor repair. They also want compensation for stolen trucks that are never recovered, a review of detentions they call unjustified, and rules on tow-truck and impound-yard fees.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

La Razón, a Mexican daily, reported 3,646 complaints of robbery against transporters from January to September. Canacar says carrying cargo has become a way of risking life and property.

A second grievance is the toll credit, which lets carriers deduct up to half of what they spend on toll roads. Deputies approved cutting the revenue ceiling for the credit from 300 million pesos (about US$16 million) to 250 million pesos (about US$13.4 million).

Canacar says the credit is a partial refund of toll costs, not a privilege, and asks the Senate to keep the old ceiling. Mexico’s finance ministry, known as Hacienda, judged the benefit too generous.

Who Is Striking and Who Stayed Out

Canacar, the National Chamber of Freight Transport led by Augusto Ramos Melo, called the strike with three smaller alliances named Fematrac, Amotac and Indeco. Mr. Ramos appealed directly to President Claudia Sheinbaum to step in, saying the strikers are her allies.

Several groups stayed out of the Mexico truckers strike, among them ANTAC, a national truckers’ association that sees no defined goals. Conatram, a national confederation of truckers, said none of its members would join blockades.

Amontac, an alliance of trucker groups, said it would wait on a security deal, and the Canapat bus chamber will keep working. Segob says most organizations accepted a dialogue table.

Where Trucks Parked on Monday

Around Mexico City, the Monday trouble spots include the highways to Querétaro, Pachuca, Puebla and Toluca. El Financiero, a Mexican daily, reported the first protest at the Tepotzotlán toll plaza north of the capital, with about 10 rigs on side lanes.

No blockades were announced inside Mexico City itself, but strikers planned to block toll booths and key points between the capital and Mexico State. Commuters were advised to use the Metro, suburban trains and other public transport.

Route lists published by Infobae, a Mexican news site, also name roads in Jalisco, Nuevo León, Veracruz, Morelos, Guanajuato and Baja California. Reports put the number of states with planned protests at about 20.

Infobae’s list places trucks beside the Tijuana customs post, on side lanes at Nuevo Laredo and in slow traffic at Reynosa-Río Bravo, with no closures. It said the Pacific port of Manzanillo had no blockades, and drivers should check with the National Guard and the federal toll agency Capufe.

What the Government Says

According to El Financiero, Sheinbaum said the protest responds to a change in the revenue law and called the striking sector “very small”. El Financiero also reported that Hacienda considered the earlier tax benefit “very excessive”.

No deal with Canacar had been announced at the time of writing. Segob calls the chamber’s stance “inexplicable” and says its dialogue table stays open.

What the Mexico Truckers Strike Could Cost

Canacar has warned that disruption could cost about 7 billion pesos (about US$370 million) a day. That is an industry estimate and has not been audited.

Organizers say trucks carry about 1.6 million tonnes of freight a day on Mexican highways. Even a partial stoppage can therefore ripple to shops and factories.

What It Means for US Readers

A partial Mexico truckers strike should mean delays, not a shutdown, for US importers of Mexican parts, produce and goods. Organizers estimate that up to 21,000 daily crossings worth about US$1.8 billion could stop, but nothing shows Laredo, Tijuana or Reynosa closed.

Shippers should ask their carriers about Monday and Tuesday schedules and watch Mexican highway alerts. Travelers driving in Mexico should avoid toll plazas near large cities until the situation clears.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how many trucks joined the Mexico truckers strike, how long it will last or whether Canacar will accept the dialogue table. No figures on delayed shipments or lost trade were available at the time of writing.

The size of the daily loss rests on the organizers’ own estimate. Whether the Senate will change the toll credit is also open.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Mexico truckers strike still on?

Canacar kept its call for an indefinite national strike from Monday 26 October 2026, and no deal had been announced at the time of writing. Segob says most other groups agreed to talks instead.

Does the Mexico truckers strike close the US border?

Route lists describe parked or slow trucks near Tijuana, Nuevo Laredo and Reynosa, but no closures were reported there. Organizers say they do not plan to shut roads completely.

What do the truckers want?

They want safer highways, an end to extortion and cargo theft, better roads and a higher revenue ceiling for the toll tax credit. They also want President Sheinbaum to step in.

Who is not joining the strike?

ANTAC, Conatram, Amontac and the Canapat bus and tourism chamber said they would stay out. Segob says most groups chose dialogue.

Could the strike delay deliveries?

Parked or slow trucks can delay freight for factories, shops and the US border. How much depends on how many trucks join and for how long.

World.title: Belize Network of NGOs call for integrity in public office; urges Alexis Rosado to step down as ICJ co-agent
World.content:
Belize Network of NGOs call for integrity in public office; urges Alexis Rosado to step down as ICJ co-agent

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Network of NGOs (BNN) is calling for greater accountability and integrity in public office, urging Alexis Rosado to step down as Belize’s Co-Agent in its case before the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

“The BNN aligns with the current call for Alexis Rosado to step down as Belize’s Co-Agent in Belize’s case before the International Court of Justice,” the BNN said.

The BNN said public officials and individuals serving in government roles must be held to high standards of conduct and remain accountable to the public.

BNN cited Section 121 of the Constitution of Belize, which states that public officials must not “demean their office or position” or undermine public confidence in the integrity of government.

In addition, the BNN said those who receive compensation and benefits from taxpayers have a responsibility to uphold public trust and maintain standards of integrity while serving in an official capacity.

The network also called for consistent protocols to address situations in which public officials or individuals entrusted with public responsibilities face serious criminal charges or allegations.

BNN said these measures should include temporary removal from official duties until the matter is determined by the judiciary.

It stressed that its position on Rosado is not intended to prejudge guilt or innocence, but to uphold expectations of accountability in public service.

“Public trust must be earned and protected,” BNN stated, adding that integrity in public office is “not discretionary or optional.”

World.title: Climate awards 2026 recognize partners advancing Climate action in Belize
World.content:
Climate awards 2026 recognize partners advancing Climate action in Belize

By Zoila Palma: The Climate Change Department hosted the Climate Awards 2026 on October 26, recognizing organizations, institutions, and partners contributing to a more sustainable and climate-resilient Belize. The department emphasized the importance of collective action and strong partnerships in addressing environmental challenges and protecting the country for future generations.

World.title: Julian Cho Society receives Climate Action award for Indigenous-led initiatives
World.content:
Julian Cho Society receives Climate Action award for Indigenous-led initiatives

By Zoila Palma: The Julian Cho Society (JCS) has received the Climate Action Award from the Climate Change Department in recognition of its contributions to climate action.

The award recognizes the organization’s continued efforts to advance Indigenous-led initiatives that strengthen community resilience, protect biodiversity, and safeguard the lands and natural resources relied upon by Maya communities.

JCS said climate action for Indigenous Peoples goes beyond environmental protection, encompassing the preservation of ancestral lands, traditional knowledge, and food systems.
