World.title: Belize welcomes BermudAir with new Fort Lauderdale–Belize City route
World.content:
Belize welcomes BermudAir with new Fort Lauderdale–Belize City route

By Zoila Palma: Today, Belize welcomed BermudAir following the airline’s inaugural flight from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, to the Philip Goldson International Airport (PGIA). The arrival marks a new air connection between South Florida and Belize, offering travelers another option for visiting the country.

The milestone was celebrated at PGIA, with the Belize Tourism Board (BTB) joining BermudAir in marking the launch of the new route.

The service is expected to provide greater convenience for travelers seeking to explore Belize’s tourism attractions, including its barrier reef, rainforests, Maya temples, and cultural experiences.

BermudAir will operate flights between Fort Lauderdale and Belize City every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. The new service adds another connection between Belize and the United States, an important market for the country’s tourism industry.

The airline’s arrival was welcomed as another opportunity to strengthen Belize’s accessibility and support tourism growth.

World.title: Halloween vs. Day of the Dead: Two traditions, two very different meanings
World.content:
Halloween vs. Day of the Dead: Two traditions, two very different meanings

By Zoila Palma: Although Halloween and Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, take place around the same time and feature imagery such as skeletons and spirits, the two celebrations have different origins, traditions, and meanings.

Halloween is widely associated with costumes, trick-or-treating, and spooky entertainment, while Day of the Dead is a cherished Mexican tradition centered on remembering and honoring deceased loved ones.

Halloween’s origins are linked to the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain, which marked the transition into winter and was associated with beliefs about the dead and the spirit world. Over time, the celebration evolved, particularly in North America, into a holiday featuring costume parties, haunted attractions, horror stories, and children collecting candy from house to house. Today, Halloween is celebrated in many countries, with traditions varying across communities.

Día de los Muertos, meanwhile, has roots in Indigenous Mesoamerican traditions and developed through centuries of cultural exchange with Spanish Catholic observances, including All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day. Celebrated primarily on November 1 and 2, the holiday brings families together to remember those who have died.

Many create ofrendas, or altars, decorated with photographs, candles, marigolds, sugar skulls, and the favorite foods and drinks of deceased relatives. Traditional foods, including tamales and pan de muerto, also play an important role.

One of the biggest differences between the celebrations is how they approach death.

Halloween often embraces frightening imagery and supernatural themes for entertainment, while Day of the Dead emphasizes remembrance, family connections, and the celebration of life.

Although both holidays may feature skeletons and colorful costumes, Día de los Muertos carries deep cultural and spiritual significance for many Mexican families, serving as a way to preserve memories and honor loved ones who have passed away.

World.title: International News: Mexico kicks off Day of the Dead celebrations with spectacular La Catrina parade
World.content:
International News: Mexico kicks off Day of the Dead celebrations with spectacular La Catrina parade

By Zoila Palma: Mexico began its Day of the Dead festivities on Sunday, October 25, with a La Catrina parade celebrating one of the country’s most recognizable cultural symbols.

The elegant female skeleton, often depicted wearing elaborate dresses, flower crowns, and wide-brimmed hats, has become a prominent figure in celebrations honoring deceased loved ones.

La Catrina’s origins date back to Mexican illustrator and engraver José Guadalupe Posada, who created a satirical skeleton figure known as La Calavera Garbancera in the early 1900s. The image criticized people who rejected their Indigenous roots while imitating European fashions and lifestyles.

Decades later, renowned Mexican muralist Diego Rivera popularized the figure in his 1947 mural Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in Alameda Central Park and gave her the name La Catrina.

Today, La Catrina is closely associated with Día de Muertos, or Day of the Dead, a Mexican tradition dedicated to remembering and honoring people who have died.

The observance commonly includes family altars featuring photographs, candles, marigolds, favorite foods, and other offerings intended to celebrate the lives and memories of loved ones.

Although skeletal imagery is also associated with Halloween, Day of the Dead has its own distinct cultural and spiritual significance.

Beyond her striking appearance, La Catrina represents the idea that death makes everyone equal, regardless of wealth or social status.

Her presence during the festivities blends humor, artistic expression, and remembrance, reflecting a cultural tradition that acknowledges grief while celebrating life and the enduring connections between families and those they have lost.

World.title: International News: Global food prices expected to rise as war and drought disrupt supplies
World.content:
International News: Global food prices expected to rise as war and drought disrupt supplies

By Zoila Palma: Global food inflation is expected to accelerate in the coming months and remain elevated into 2027 as war-related shipping disruptions and drought linked to El Niño threaten food supplies.

Rising costs are already forcing vulnerable families in several countries to reduce spending on essential food items, particularly in low- and middle-income nations across Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa, Reuters report.

The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization’s chief economist, Maximo Torero, warned that the impact could worsen, saying, “We will see a bigger impact towards the end of the year, at the beginning of next year and potentially throughout next year.”

Several countries are already experiencing significant price increases.

Rice prices in Indonesia have reached record highs, while unsubsidized bread in Egypt has become more expensive and sugar, onions, and pulses in India have risen in price following production shortfalls.

The FAO Food Price Index averaged 136 points in September, its highest level since November 2022. Meanwhile, wheat prices have increased by more than 30 percent in 2026, while rice prices in key Asian exporting countries have risen by 10 to 13 percent.

The pressure on food prices is being driven by disruptions to grain shipments in the Black Sea, insecurity in the Red Sea, higher fuel and fertilizer costs, and reduced agricultural output due to dry weather.

Freight rates on some major shipping routes have risen by about 50 percent, adding to the cost of importing food.

Economists warn that shrinking stockpiles and renewed demand from major food-importing countries could push prices higher, increasing pressure on household budgets and raising concerns about shortages and potential social unrest

World.title: Belize participates in Regional Parliamentary meeting on security and organized crime
World.content:
Belize participates in Regional Parliamentary meeting on security and organized crime

By Zoila Palma: Belize participated in the Second Gathering of the ParlAmericas Parliamentary Network on Security, held from October 21 to 23, 2026, at the National Congress of Chile in Valparaíso.

Hosted by the National Congress of Chile and ParlAmericas, the gathering focused on “Public Security in the Americas and the Caribbean: Parliamentary Responses to Organized Crime and Violence.”

President of the Senate, Carolyn Trench-Sandiford, represented the National Assembly of Belize and served as moderator of one of the working sessions.

Participants examined regional security trends, shared national experiences, and discussed ways parliamentary action can strengthen public security policies while upholding human rights and the rule of law.

Discussions addressed illicit economies and the financing of criminal networks, the effects of insecurity on communities, and the balance between effective crime-fighting measures and human rights protections.

On October 22, Trench-Sandiford moderated a session titled “Public Security and Justice: Institutional Capacities to Address Crime,” which featured presentations by representatives of the Justice Studies Center of the Americas and the Inter-American Children’s Institute.

The final day focused on intelligence systems, parliamentary oversight of public security, and the use of artificial intelligence to strengthen state capabilities.

World.title: Sinclair rejects claims that plea bargaining absent from Firearms Act
World.content:
Jamaica Labour Party Deputy General Secretary, Senator Charles Sinclair (File photo)

Government Senator Charles Sinclair says a narrative created by some individuals in the legal fraternity that no provision exists for plea bargain under the current Firearms Act is inaccurate and misleading.

“What I find interesting is that no one appears to have spoken about the possibility of using the Plea Negotiation and Agreements Act in order to achieve for their client reduce sentence below the minimum mandatory,” Senator Sinclair, a prominent defence attorney, told journalists on Monday.

“The 2022 legislation made a consequential amendment to the Plea Negotiation and Agreements Act and included in particular, I mean section 5, a provision which would be described as section 5.2a, whereby there can be pre negotiations done with the CROW and for persons to receive a sentence below the minimum mandatory of 15 years,” he added.

On page 130 of the Act, Section 5(2a) says in the case of an offence under the Act, a plea bargain arrangement may be accessed if there is the provision of information that assists the Crown in the prevention, detection or investigation of, or in proceedings relating to, the offence concerned or any other offence.

Senator Sinclair says there is precedent for an accused successfully using that section of the law to obtain a reduced sentence.

“I am fully aware that this particular amendment was used successfully in the gun court in relation to a person who was charged with possession simpliciter, and that person received, by virtue of the plea agreement that was done and the agreement of the judge, obviously, at the end of the day, received a sentence significantly below the minimum mandatory sentence of 15 years,” Senator Sinclair said.

He made the comments against the background of renewed concerns being expressed by lawyers over the Act following the recommendation by the National Security Council (NSC) that individuals convicted of illegal possession of a firearm should face a new minimum mandatory sentence of 20 years imprisonment.

READ: TOUGHER GUN LAWS

Senator Sinclair says there may be a lack of awareness in the legal field about provisions of the law which allow for pleas bargain arrangements.

“So, whilst the discussion is taking place in relation to the minimum of 15 years, which potentially, having regard to the comments, can be increased to 20 years in the event that there is an amendment to the 2022 legislation, the possibility still exists for a lesser sentence by virtue of plea negotiations, and I would encourage persons to look at it and to seek to use it in moving forward,” Sinclair further commented.

World.title: TOUGHER GUN LAWS
World.content:
.

A month after defence attorneys mounted an islandwide silent protest and scaled back their services over what they described as “shortcomings” in the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 (Firearms Act), the National Security Council (NSC) has recommended that individuals convicted of illegal possession of a firearm should now face a new minimum mandatory sentence of 20 years imprisonment.

Justice Minister Delroy Chuck was flayed in mid-September after he indicated that while legislators are set to review the mandatory minimum sentences under the 2022 Firearms Act, a repeal is unlikely as security forces and other key stakeholders are crediting the law for the sharp decline in murders and shootings in recent times.

The current Firearms Act, which prescribes a mandatory 15-year sentence for violations, took effect in November 2022 and, among other things, provides penalties ranging from 15 years to life imprisonment for possession of illegal weapons, and establishes a dual regime — distinguishing between prohibited weapons or unregulated firearms and connected activities, and firearms that are duly authorised or registered.

Among the concerns raised primarily by members of the defence bar were that the mandatory minimum provisions in the Act counteract the Plea Negotiations and Agreements Act (plea bargaining legislation), with many accused opting to head to trial rather than plead guilty at their first appearance.

During the planned silent protest on September 23, attorneys had called for a review of the mandatory sentencing provisions of the Act to allow judges to exercise their discretion in circumstances in which a lesser sentence was warranted.

Following meetings with the justice minister, the attorneys expressed disappointment over the Government’s seemingly unrelenting stance on the mandatory minimum issue.

At the time Advocates’ Association President Tamika Harris had reiterated that attorneys were not seeking to downplay the seriousness of gun crimes and those involved in criminality.

“What we are asking for, in simple words, is that firearms and imitation firearms are dealt with separately, so that children who are at play are not at risk of being criminalised. The court must be able to distinguish,” Harris said.

Sunday, the NSC said the council had further proposed that adults who groom children to use, store, transport, or acquire illegal guns will face a new criminal offence under the pending amendments to the Act “to address the gap whereby gangs seek to recruit and enlist minors in the commission of gun crimes”.

The NSC, in a statement released on Sunday, said the changes are in keeping with the Government’s commitment to refine the Act “to make it tougher while protecting the innocent and vulnerable”.

According to the statement, the National Security Council has also agreed that further consideration should be given to how cases involving children found with illegal firearms are handled.

It said concerns raised regarding imitation firearms will be “clearly addressed to distinguish between toy guns and guns designed to realistically imitate a weapon”.

According to the ministry, the review will also examine matters surrounding firearms with expired licences.

In the meantime, however, it said before the new provisions take effect, the Government will provide a gun amnesty and cash buy-back programme, giving anyone holding an illegal gun the opportunity to surrender it.

The Ministry of National Security and Peace has been directed to have the draft legislation ready by the end of November 2026 for wider consultations.

Chairman of the NSC, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness, said the amendments strengthen the law while keeping it fair.

“We have seen what criminals are capable of, and we will not stand by while they put guns in the hands of our children,” he said. “We are determined to send a strong signal against illegal guns and those who promote them, while making sure the law is fair to the most vulnerable. Make no mistake, this Administration is drawing a line in the sand against gun crime, and we are determined to eliminate the gun culture from our society.”

Meanwhile, the NSC also received a briefing from Commissioner of Police Dr Kevin Blake on the intensified effort to interdict and seize illegal drugs entering Jamaica.

Blake indicated that the police has seized 8,734.37 kilogrammes of cocaine since the start of the year. That amounts to 74 per cent of the 11,852.01 kilogrammes seized over the 10-year period between 2016 and 2025.

The NSC commended the security forces and the Jamaica Customs Agency for their work in keeping the country safe by finding and recovering illegal drugs, weapons, and other contraband.

The NSC noted that, given the effective closure of various drug trafficking routes by United States operations in the region, there will be greater attempts to use Jamaica’s geographic location for trans-shipment.

World.title: Fi We Children urges child-centred approach to proposed Firearms law amendments
World.content:
In this 2023 file photo Edith Dalton James High School students stand outside the school's premises after being locked out due to uniform and grooming violations.

WHILE welcoming indications that the 2022 Firearms Act will be amended so that adults who groom children to use, store, transport, or acquire illegal guns will face a new criminal offence, advocacy outfit Fi We Children Foundation (FWCF) is discouraging a further proposed change which will see individuals convicted of illegal possession of a firearm facing a new minimum mandatory sentence of 20 years’ imprisonment instead of the current 15 years minimum mandatory.



In a release issued to the media on Sunday, moments after the Ministry of National Security announced the changes which were proposed by the National Security Council in a statement, the foundation said while it welcomed the recognition that further consideration must be given to cases involving children found in possession of illegal firearms, it was cautioning that any amendments to the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 “must distinguish between children exploited by criminal networks and adults who deliberately recruit, coerce, or manipulate them into gun-related activities”.

The national security minister had indicated that the NSC has also agreed that further consideration should be given to how cases involving children found with illegal firearms are handled.

It said concerns raised regarding imitation firearms will be “clearly addressed to distinguish between toy guns and guns designed to realistically imitate a weapon”.

Sunday, the foundation said it approved of the NSC’s intention to clarify the law concerning imitation firearms, but urged the Government “to ensure that the legislation clearly distinguishes ordinary toy guns from realistic imitation firearms and actual weapons, using objective and proportionate criteria”.

“Children should not acquire a criminal record merely for engaging in ordinary childhood play with toys that are not firearms. An overboard approach risks disproportionately exposing boys, in particular, to criminal justice intervention for conduct that should not automatically be treated as criminal,” it said.

The foundation said it will be making recommendations to the joint select committee considering the proposed legislative amendments, advocating for a child-centred, evidence-based, and rights-compliant approach that protects public safety without criminalising vulnerable children or undermining judicial discretion.

It said it was particularly concerned about children recruited by gangs to carry, use, store, or transport illegal firearms.

And the foundation said while it supports the proposed creation of a specific offence targeting adults who groom or recruit children into firearms-related criminal activity, such provisions must be accompanied by effective investigation, child sensitive interviewing, appropriate safeguarding measures, and access to diversion and rehabilitation where warranted.

“While FWCF recognises that gun violence remains a severe national concern requiring decisive action, we caution against adopting draconian measures as quick fixes to complex social and criminal justice challenges,” it said.

“The proposed 20-year minimum sentence for adults convicted of illegal firearm possession also raises broader questions about the appropriate role of mandatory sentencing. FWCF maintains that mandatory minimum sentences can unduly restrict judicial discretion by limiting a court’s ability to consider the individual circumstances of an offence and the offender.”

The proposed changes come just a month after defence attorneys mounted an island-wide silent protest and scaled back their services over what they described as “shortcomings” in the Act.

That protest was sparked after Justice Minister Delroy Chuck indicated that while legislators were set to review the mandatory minimum sentences under the Act, a repeal is unlikely as security forces and other key stakeholders are crediting the law for the sharp decline in murders and shootings in recent times.

World.title: NSC clamps down on blue plates abuse
World.content:
A vehicle with blue demonstration licence plates, which police said crashed after its driver eluded cops twice on Winston Jones Highway in Manchester last year. At that time, a senior cop pointed to the importance of the Government’s plan to overhaul the system of motor vehicle dealerships using demonstration licence plates, pointing out that they were only able to identify the driver of the speeding vehicle because the car crashed after ignoring a police command to stop on the highway. A police source said the driver of the car identified himself as a car mart dealer.

THE National Security Council (NSC), in responding to a proposal from Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) for a new regime for issuing dealer and demonstration licence plates, which it says are now being unlawfully used to regularly operate vehicles on public roadways without permanent registration and vehicle identification, has directed that the current plates be discontinued and a new form of temporary vehicle identification be considered for the specific purposes of demonstration or dealer transit.

According to the TAJ, the current regime “facilitates scammers and other criminals in the commission of crimes and provides an avenue to evade taxes”.

On Sunday, the NSC, in issuing a statement about the development, said the recommendation is that the new system be electronically enabled to link the plate with the specific vehicle to which it will be temporarily assigned and the identification plate itself be Global Positioning System (GPS)- and Radio Frequency Identification (RFID)-enabled.

“This will ensure control of the plates issued and enable the police to immediately verify the dealer to whom the identification plate was issued, the particulars of the vehicle assigned to it, and the location of the plate should it be suspected of involvement in an incident,” the ministry outlined.

It said the new system will network the TAJ, the Island Traffic Authority, the Jamaica Constabulary Force, and the Jamaica Customs Agency, allowing for easier cross-verification.

Last September, Transport Minister Daryl Vaz, in announcing that changes were being contemplated, declared that the current arrangement has become a matter of national security, made moreso by the fact that the TAJ does not have an accurate count of the demonstration plates in circulation at the time.

“This gap in oversight has presented opportunities for cloning and unauthorised use by criminal elements. As a result, the Government is losing revenue, and the lack of control over this system poses a serious threat to public safety and national security,” Vaz stressed then.

He further disclosed that it would cost an estimated $10 million for the design and implementation of the management system, the total recall of the existing plates for which a deadline will be issued, submission of the legislative changes, and finalising the new fee structure.

Demonstration plates are popularly referred to as blue plates. They come with the designation DC for cars and DT for trucks. Issued by TAJ, they should only be affixed to motor vehicles with insurance coverage, but this is reportedly often not the case as cited by individuals involved in motor vehicle crashes with vehicles with the plates affixed.

Some people are also known to have the plates affixed to the same vehicle for months at a time.

World.title: Private investigator wants psychiatric evaluation for firearm applicants
World.content:
GRANNUM... a psychologist can go above and beyond to determine whether a person is mentally prepared to carry a firearm.

JOINING lawyers’ call for legislative review of the Firearms Act, private investigator Alton Grannum wants it to be made law that people applying for firearm licences and permits of any kind be psychologically evaluated as part of the Firearm Licensing Authority’s (FLA) vetting process.

Grannum, a certified polygraph expert, said the numerous instances of misuse of guns by licensed firearm holders and permit holders point to underlying issues masked by having an unblemished police record and squeaky-clean public image.

“A police record only indicates that you don’t have a criminal record, which, if clear, moves you to the next stage of investigators conducting interviews plus background checks in your community.

“However, nobody knows you from a mental standpoint, how mentally stable a person you might be, which can only be determined by a psychologist,” argued Grannum, who, as part of his mission to promote responsible use of firearms, is set to stage a ‘Rules of Engagement’ conference and exhibition December 7-8, at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel.

Trained in the Reid technique, a structured, three-phase method used by international law enforcement to gather information, assess behaviour and obtain confessions from suspects, Grannum also believes polygraph testing should be mandatory during interviews for firearm licences.

“A psychologist can go above and beyond to determine whether a person is mentally prepared to carry a firearm. Both should be mandatory — polygraph testing and psychiatric evaluation.

“When you go into the FLA and tick all the boxes after being asked certain questions, you may pass and appear qualified. However, when carrying a firearm, a feeling of empowerment can cause one’s true nature, mindset, and tendencies to come to the fore,” Grannum reasoned.

“When some people have a firearm, they believe they are invincible. This behaviour can be detected by a psychiatrist and, to an extent, during interviews while being polygraphed,” Grannum stated.

“Not only is the element of fear non-existent, they become aggressors,” he added, pointing out that “the firearm now becomes a boost” despite whatever forewarning might have been transmitted by the FLA to successful applicants.

A member of the American Polygraph Association since 2012 with 26 years of close-protection experience in the security industry, Grannum noted that psychologists are trained to elicit certain responses from subjects while polygraphs detect abnormalities in responses.

Grannum said refreshers such as the upcoming Rules of Engagement conference and exhibition for anybody in possession of a weapon, licensed firearm holders, or members of the security forces, private and public, can never be too much.

“Such a conference, which is really a seminar with different speakers, will present real-life scenarios that are played out daily in our lives, such as domestic quarrels arising from infidelity as well as business arrangements,” Grannum said, pointing to a recent incident in Harbour View during which a 63-year-old businessman, a licensed firearm holder, shot a fellow elderly businessman as well as the man’s dog during an argument. He afterwards confronted responding police officers by whom he was shot and killed.

“We also had an incident of a former Member of Parliament admitting to shooting his wife and was sent to prison for 20 years and 10 months in March,” Grannum added.

“A person can pass a psychological evaluation, still go out there and do something stupid. Nothing in life is 100 per cent foolproof. However, it is a missing step that needs to be added. A psychologist can assess emotional stability, how an applicant manages frustration, anger, stress, and rejection, particularly situations involving conflict,” he emphasised.

World.title: Desmond’s to be honoured
World.content:
The cast of black British comedy Desmond’s.

LONDON, England — One of Britain’s most influential television comedies will on Saturday be celebrated with the unveiling of a Nubian Jak blue plaque honouring Desmond’s, the ground-breaking Channel 4 sitcom that brought black British and Caribbean life, humour, and culture into millions of homes across the UK.

Created by Trix Worrell and starring the unforgettable Norman Beaton — who died in December 1994 — and Carmen Munroe, Desmond’s broke new ground when it arrived on television in 1989.

Set in a Peckham barbershop, the series brought together generations, cultures, and communities through unforgettable characters.

More than a sitcom, Desmond’s helped reshape how black people were represented on British television. It brought Caribbean culture and the realities of multicultural Britain into the mainstream; making audiences laugh while challenging stereotypes and bringing communities closer together.

Its barbershop became an iconic meeting place where cultures collided, generations debated, and everyday life provided comedy that audiences across Britain could recognise and enjoy.

The idea for the plaque was brought to the Nubian Jak Community Trust by a young Birmingham-based English fan of the show, who grew up watching repeats of Desmond’s with his father. What began as a personal connection to a much-loved comedy has become a tribute to a programme whose influence reached far beyond the screen.

Aron Shabir, inspiration behind the Desmond’s plaque, said: “Desmond’s holds a special place in my heart, with fond memories of watching it with my father. Starting this campaign has shown me how much the programme still means to so many people. This plaque will preserve its history, celebrate the people who made it special and ensure its legacy is remembered by future generations.”

The Desmond’s plaque will celebrate the cast, creators and cultural legacy of a series that helped broaden British television. It will also bring UK Black History Month 2026 (October) to a close.

Dame Carmen Munroe, who played the character Shirley (Desmond’s wife), said: “…I am proud to have been part of a series that reflected the lives, humour, and experiences of ordinary people… What made Desmond’s special was its honesty, warmth, and ability to bring audiences together through laughter. I am delighted that this lasting tribute will celebrate the cast and creators, and the important place the series holds in British television history.”

Dr Jak Beula, founder and CEO of Nubian Jak Community Trust, said: “The trust is delighted to honour and remember the casts of Desmond’s 35 years after they first appeared on our TV screens. The plaque is also of personal satisfaction to me having met Norman Beaton in my teenage years. He made me promise that we would meet up again one day when I was an adult and had made something of my life. We had no way of knowing the occasion would be on his birthday, and as a tribute to his most successful TV series.”

Jeremy Lester Beaton, son of (Desmond) Norman Beaton, said: “My brother and I are honoured that the

Desmond’s series is being honoured in this way… I’m sure dad is smiling wherever he is, with a cigar and raising a glass to the plaque.”

Robbie Gee who played the character Lee Stanley, said: “1988.. I was cast as Lee Stanley…working with my idols, Norman Beaton, Carmen Monroe, Ram John Holder, and Christopher Asante… pioneer’s in the acting world… To this day I am beyond grateful and still cherish every moment, every experience, every lesson that I learnt from them…”

The noon event is set for 204 Bellenden Road, Peckham, London.

World.title: Hanover health upgrade
World.content:
Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton (centre) having dialogue with team members in front of the dietary department at Noel Holmes Hospital which is currently under construction.

FORT CHARLOTTE, Hanover — Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton has revealed that close to $1 billion is being spent by the Government to rehabilitate and upgrade health facilities in Hanover following Hurricane Melissa, which devastated a number of the parish’s facilities last October.

Tufton said the sum being spent on Noel Holmes Hospital and 17 health centres (clinics) across the parish is separate from the undisclosed amount that will be allocated to construct a new hospital approximately four years from now.

“That is the Government’s commitment to the people of Hanover,” assured Tufton, who was providing an update on medium- and long-term recovery progress a year after the Category 5 storm.

The update was delivered during a press conference held at the Type-C hospital following a tour on Friday.

The National Health Fund (NHF) is currently spending more than $300 million on renovation work at the hospital, which is now 82 per cent complete.

The staff quarters, paramedics, outpatient clinic, and general stores are 100 per cent complete. However, the maternity ward and operating theatre are currently at 90 per cent completion and are expected to be handed over next month.

Similarly, the newly constructed pharmacy and dietary buildings are expected to be handed over in December of this year and January of 2027, respectively.

With millions being spent to rehabilitate the facility while dialogue takes place between the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and the Ministry of Finance for the construction of the new hospital, the minister addressed questions surrounding the current expenditure.

“We can’t care for people under a tent or in the open during the interim. When it comes to life and the preservation of life, we can’t compromise. We have to provide some very basic things, and inpatient care, dietary, pharmacy — those are just obvious things that have to be here,” Tufton argued.

Land is currently being sought for the construction of a new 150-bed facility — a significant expansion from the hospital’s current 60 beds — which will offer a wider range of services.

Tufton noted that finding a suitable location to build a resilient facility is not the only reason for the relocation.

“It is also a recognition that, as a parish, Hanover will continue to grow [and] the population will expand. There are many housing developments and hotels planned, so it will naturally become a more robust parish. We in public health, and as a government, have to plan for the future. You have to look 20 years down the line, and this facility has outgrown its useful life, even though it continues to provide critical care and remains very important to the parish,” Tufton explained.

Between April and September of this year, the hospital saw increased demand for most of its services, with the exception of outpatient visits and baby deliveries, compared to the same period in 2025.

Similarly, all 17 clinics recorded a combined usage increase of 5.1 per cent for the same period.

Staffing levels have also expanded significantly across the parish, increasing from 278 before the hurricane to 314 at the health centres and from 189 to 270 at the hospital.

Rehabilitation work has already been completed on nine health centres — Cascade, Cave Valley, Chester Castle, Copse, Grange/Kendal, Green Island, Hopewell, Lucea, and Sandy Bay. Work is expected to be completed at Nyerere by the end of this month, and at Mt Pelier and Ramble by November and January, respectively.

Meanwhile, no repairs were required for the Dias, Kingsvale, Logwood, and Mt Peto health centres. Askenish Health Centre continues to operate from rented premises, where structural repairs remain the responsibility of the landlord.

The minister also revealed that seven of the parish’s health centres will undergo major smart upgrades — the installation of water catchment systems, back-up generators, solar power, disability access, stronger wind pressure resistance — in the next phase.

“We look forward to exciting times in the parish of Hanover. I think Hanover from a health perspective has potential, and we’ve seen some manifestations of that, and the government is certainly spending money,” asserted the minister.

World.title: COULD IT BE?
World.content:
Jamaica striker Khadija Shaw (left) and United States player Alana Cook battle for possession during the 2022 Concacaf Women’s Championship match at BBVA Bancomer Stadium in Monterrey, Mexico, on July 7, 2022. (Photo: AFP)

Khadija “Bunny” Shaw stands on the verge of history today, with the Reggae Girlz captain in contention to become the first Jamaican to claim football’s most prestigious individual prize, the Ballon d’Or.

Shaw is among 30 players shortlisted for the 2026 Women’s Ballon d’Or which will be announced this afternoon at the award ceremony in London.

The 29-year-old received her third-ever nomination after an incredible season with Manchester City in England’s Women’s Super League (WSL). She won her third-straight WSL golden boot after scoring 21 goals in 22 appearances as City won the title for the first time in a decade. She also led them to their first FA Cup title win since 2020.

Shaw’s Ballon D’Or nomination is another accolade after winning the Professional Footballers Association (PFA) Women’s Player of the Year and the WSL Player of the Season earlier this year.

National senior women’s head coach Hubert Busby believes Shaw is further cementing her legacy and raising Jamaica’s profile on the global stage.

“When you really take a minute to pause and you think about the amount of tremendous players, male and female, on the globe, and just to be recognised, that is amazing,” he told the Jamaica Observer. “When you think about football being the most popular sport in the world and obviously she’s playing at one of the most high-profile clubs in the world, but it’s her consistency, the fact that she continues to do what she does at the highest level, it’s an amazing opportunity for us as Jamaicans to just revel in that one of us is being recognised globally for those achievements.”

“I think more so than that, it just goes to show that put in the right environment, given the right resources, and obviously God-given talent and she’s been able to go out there and with all the talent she’s had, she’s worked really hard to make it to this level. I just think of just spell volumes what she means to Jamaica football and what she means to Jamaicans on the island and in the diaspora,” he added.

Although Shaw is among the favourites, she will have to contend with Spain and London City Lionesses superstar Alexia Putellas who won all four titles on offer at Barcelona last season including the Champions League. Barcelona trio Ewa Pajor, Patri Guijarro and Caroline Graham Hansen as well as Lyon’s Melchie Dumornay are among the leading contenders for the award.

In an anonymous survey conducted by sports media outlet The Athletic, in which reporters polled several stakeholders in football, Shaw finished second with 276 points after featuring in the top three on most of the ballots.

However, Shaw’s fate will be decided by an international jury of specialised journalists. One journalist from each of the top 50 nations in the FIFA rankings will vote for the women’s award, meaning Jamaica will be represented, with the Reggae Girlz currently ranked 40th in the world.

Busby is keeping his “fingers crossed” as he hopes to see Shaw crowned the world’s best.

“It’s an amazing achievement to be recognised by your peers and by sports journalists around the globe as being one of the best footballers each and every year for the last couple of years,” he said. “Hailing from obviously Spanish Town, Jamaica, she gives and provides opportunities for girls on the island to dream so I think it’s just an amazing achievement she does and we’re looking forward and hoping that she takes home the prize.”

Shaw, who has an incredible 67 goals in 49 caps for Jamaica, finished 24th in the 2023 ranking and 15th in 2024. She’s the only Jamaican, male or female, to have been recognised for the award.

World.title: Frontex set for new powers to deport beyond EU borders in latest overhaul
World.content:
The push comes just months after EU lawmakers approved a new “return regulation” aimed at accelerating deportations and allowing member countries to establish controversial deportation hubs outside the EU.

With the legal framework largely agreed, Brussels is now turning its attention to enforcement — and to the agency expected to help make the new rules work in practice.

Political pressure has also been mounting. In June, the leaders of 19 EU countries urged the Commission to support the establishment of return hubs outside the bloc, including through EU funding, as first reported by POLITICO.

The proposed Frontex overhaul, which is on the College of Commissioners’ agenda and is expected to be approved by the EU executive on Oct. 27, would help put that broader shift into practice by giving the agency more resources, greater operational flexibility and an expanded role in carrying out returns beyond EU borders, including transfers between third countries.

Emergency response

But deportations are only part of the equation.

The Commission also wants to transform Frontex into a force that can intervene in border emergencies within 24 hours, according to the two officials.

World.title: European defense ministers warn Putin isn’t looking for peace
World.content:
The meeting came amid a renewed U.S. effort to push Ukraine into peace talks with Russia and growing doubts about Washington's support for Kyiv.

U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said last week he would offer Russia's Vladimir Putin direct talks with President Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy to secure a ceasefire.

"No results whatsoever comes for those who want to negotiate with Putin," German defense minister Boris Pistoripus said. "The results are what? It doesn't lead to anything. There is no signal whatsoever that Putin is looking for peace."

The U.K.'s Wes Streeting added: "While none of us seek confrontation with Russia ... We do have to be aware of the threat posed by Russia."

While pledging "total transparency" with the U.S., France's Catherine Vautrin said the E5 members would "work together concretely," focusing on arms production and interoperability.

"Produce more, produce faster, produce equipment suited to today’s conflicts – but we must already be planning for the conflicts of tomorrow," Vautrin said. "On that, EU financial initiatives can help us move in this direction."

World.title: French government fails to convince students to stop protests
World.content:
Students have demanded up to 250,000 extra places in higher education and universities, better conditions in educational institutions, more teachers and a major overhaul of the selection process for university entry.

On Monday, the government told students it would look into reforming France’s university admissions platform, Parcoursup, which student groups consider opaque and a source of inequality, starting in 2028. It also promised more money to renovate schools, an extra 15,000 places in higher education in industry, health and technical education, and a maximum of 28 students per classroom in the first year of high school.

Those measures, widely reported by French media and confirmed by student representatives who attended the meetings, will be detailed at a press conference later this evening.

But university students are not impressed.

“Once again, the government is missing the point. If the government’s strategy is to show contempt for our demands, then we will remain mobilized in the streets and on university campuses, and we won’t back down,” university union UNEF said earlier in the afternoon, when news of the government’s proposals began to circulate.

Student demonstrations and blockades in schools and universities earlier this month were among the first expressions of broader social unrest, which later turned into protests over the cost of living and spiraled into riots two weeks ago.

World.title: Europe is living in a new ‘era of darkness,’ Finland’s Stubb warns
World.content:
“In a sense, I began my studies during an era of light and you begin your studies in an era of darkness,” he said. “We used to be able to say that the three biggest killers of mankind, disease, famine and wars, have been defeated. That is not true anymore. The light has given way to darkness.”

Stubb, who has studied and written extensively on geopolitical upheaval, has been intimately involved in European efforts to navigate U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term — particularly when it comes to the question of a peace deal for Ukraine.

He told his audience they would graduate into “a dog-eat-dog world” in which there are, by some estimates, 65 conflicts or wars playing out — “more than at any time after the Second World War.”

Global security will “depend on what the big powers — namely the U.S. and China — end up doing. Will they choose co-operation or confrontation?” he said.

“The key question for all of us is to create a European security structure which makes sure that Russia does not attack its neighbors again,” he said. NATO will remain a vital security alliance but new processes should also be developed, he said, including “confidence building” measures between Russia and Europe to build “trust.”

Stubb urged the audience of future diplomats, politicians and officials not to be pessimistic, but to be ambitious for a new “era of light,” despite the challenges. He said that in 30 years’ time, the European Union could grow to 40 member countries from the current 27 — including the U.K. rejoining the bloc alongside Norway, Moldova and Ukraine.

World.title: Von der Leyen’s big Commission shake-up moves a step closer
World.content:
“We need to be able to act effectively and to act quickly,” she said about the needed changes in the EU Executive’s machinery. “That means simpler procedures, clearer structures, better cooperation across departments so that our colleagues can focus their efforts where it makes the greatest difference.”

The external group, consisting of Day and eight other experts with experience in national administrations and international organizations including the OECD and OSCE, put forward nine interrelated recommendations aimed at making the Commission more agile and better equipped to adapt to future challenges.

Among its main proposals is a shift away from working in siloed departments toward greater collaboration across directorates-general, including through cross-DG portfolios.

This part of the exercise is politically sensitive. Behind the push to modernize the Commission lies the prospect of a far-reaching reorganization of its departments, potentially redrawing the responsibilities of powerful directorates-general that oversee billions of euros in EU spending.

As POLITICO first reported, several major Commission departments face an uncertain future under plans to overhaul how the bloc manages and distributes EU funds, raising the prospect of mergers or other structural changes.

Among the departments potentially affected is the Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy (DG REGIO), which oversees cohesion policy funding, accounting for almost a third of EU spending. Other departments facing uncertainty include the Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development (DG AGRI), responsible for Common Agricultural Policy money; DG EMPL, which oversees employment and social funding; DG MARE, which handles fisheries funding; and DG RTD, responsible for research and innovation.

World.title: Belgium postpones terrace smoking ban
World.content:
The minister’s move initially prompted backlash from the Belgian hospitality sector; the statement added the postponement would allow enough time for venues to adjust to the new rules.

Several other EU countries are moving forward with similar bans — albeit with different success rates. France recently introduced a smoking ban on beaches, gardens and near schools.

Spain, meanwhile, approved a draft bill in July that would extend the ban to outdoor terraces and other public spaces, including restrictions on e-cigarettes — but which faces pushback from restaurant owners.

Belgium introduced a slate of new anti-smoking laws last year, including curbs on smoking in airport rooms and a ban on flavored vapes, aiming to achieve a “smoke-free generation” by 2040. Outdoor smoking bans are one of many measures advocated by the World Health Organization (WHO).

According to the Belgian Cancer Foundation, nearly a quarter of Belgians smoke and 19% do so daily.

It is unclear how long Belgium will postpone its outdoor smoking ban. Once published, the country's national parliament still has to approve the Council of State's amendments.

World.title: ‘Disturbing and pathetic’: German politicians slam Audi CEO’s appearance at Trump rally
World.content:
At the rally in the U.S. state of Georgia, Trump announced Audi plans to invest around $4 billion to build a new factory and begin producing cars in the U.S. for the first time. Döllner joined Trump on stage and thanked him for his support.

The announcement comes as Volkswagen faces a deep crisis amid a major restructuring in Germany, with factory closures and mass layoffs expected.

MEP Dennis Radtke from the center-right Christian Democratic Union party also lambasted Döllner’s appearance at the Republican campaign rally. "Donald Trump's policies are massively damaging German industry, including the automotive industry," he told German media outlet Handelsblatt.

"The fact that German companies invest abroad is initially a completely normal and understandable process. However, to turn this into an election campaign staging for Donald Trump is disturbing and pathetic," he added.

German union leaders joined in the condemnation of Döllner. Christiane Benner, first chair of IG Metall, Germany's biggest industrial trade union, said Monday: “The way in which Gernot Döllner presented himself and Audi in the USA is highly embarrassing, politically unacceptable, and unworthy of the company — and, above all, unworthy of the people who work at Audi.

“Döllner is flagrantly violating the company’s own internal policies, which explicitly mandate political neutrality in the lead-up to elections,” she added.

World.title: Liz Truss claims Brits would be on Mars by 2040 if she hadn’t been ousted
World.content:
LONDON — Liz Truss claims the U.K. would have managed successful missions to Mars within years — if only her 49-day premiership hadn’t been cut short.

The assertion comes in the former British prime minister’s new book “Bank Job,” which was published Monday and claims to explain “how the Bank of England broke the bond market and brought down the government” when her mini-budget in 2022 precipitated market turmoil.

In its closing chapter, the book paints a vivid picture of what Truss believes life in 2040 would be like if her policies had been given a chance to bed in. “Several missions to Mars have now been launched from Britain’s space port,” Truss’ book imagines.

World.title: Trump says Brazil election looked 'rigged' without giving evidence
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that the Brazilian election over the weekend looked "rigged," without providing evidence, after leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva beat right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.

 

Speaking to the media, Trump said the vote "looked terrible" and "like another rigged election."

"I didn't take sides," Trump told reporters when asked for his thoughts. "Elections have to be indisputable, and it looked very bad to me."

Bolsonaro initially refused to recognise Lula's victory, saying it was "impossible" to acknowledge the result and that the election should have been annulled. He has since said he would "organise the opposition."

In a video post shared on social media on Monday, he added that he had been banned from leaving Brazil and had been "served a notice to surrender my passports."

Trump welcomed Bolsonaro - who is the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro - to the White House earlier this year, later calling him a "smart young man who loves his country, Brazil, very much."

The Trump administration has hailed a recent wave of right-wing election victories across South America.

"In South America, it was all leaning big left. It's all right now," Trump said last week. "I endorsed many of those people. Every single one that I endorsed won.

World.title: Microsoft offers around 60,000 employees voluntary buyouts
World.content:
US tech giant Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to employees around the globe, its chief people officer announced on Monday.

 

In a memo sent to staff, Amy Coleman called the "Voluntary Exit Offer" an "important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter."

The offer will be made available to employees on select teams across the US, Canada, India and the United Kingdom "at level 70 and below," meaning some senior staff could be included.

"This is a time-limited, voluntary program that gives those who are eligible the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources," the memo continued.

It added that eligible employees would receive an email with a link to their offers in the coming hours.

Around 60,000 staff are reported to be eligible.

In July, Microsoft announced it was eliminating around 4,800 roles, or roughly 2.1% of its global workforce at the time, as the company sought to shift its focus and cut costs as the AI era continues to take hold. Those cuts mostly affected the firm's commercial and Xbox gaming divisions.

Microsoft also offered some staff the option to retire early this year.

The company has said that more than 30% of those eligible for the early retirement scheme chose to participate and that it would "continue exploring similar approaches in the future."

World.title: Anthropic's IPO filing shows off soaring revenues as the company warns of AI's 'risks to humanity'
World.content:
US firm Anthropic gave the world a window into its remarkable finances on Monday after it submitted its S-1 paperwork ahead of a planned initial public offering.

 

The artificial intelligence company revealed soaring revenues and high costs as it warned of the risks posed by AI.

The listing will be a key yardstick for investor appetite in an increasingly controversial industry that has quickly woven itself into the fabric of daily life.

Anthropic's net losses hit $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, the filing showed, while revenue jumped to around $16.3 billion over the period.

An IPO could bring in as much as $100 billion for the company behind Claude, with it potentially valued at upwards of $1.5 trillion, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Anthropic was valued at $965 billion in May.

"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the company said in the S-1 form. "If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort."

But Anthropic also warned of the dangers posed by its technology, saying AI could bring "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" if it is not "developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures."

"The political environment and our engagement with policymakers and public positions on AI regulation and safety could subject us to heightened scrutiny, political backlash, or disproportionate regulatory action," it added.

Gary Marcus, an emeritus professor at New York University and a staunch critic of the AI industry, accused Anthropic of attempting to "skirt the truth" with the filing by leaving out certain figures.

"Anthropic ducked Q3 in its S-1," he wrote in a post on X. "That omission tells you all you need. Demand has drop, economics haven’t gotten worse. And a company that is allegedly built around trust is trying to skirt the truth."

Anthropic reportedly told investors earlier this month that Q3 revenue had hit $16.8 billion, up from $11.6 billion in Q2.

World.title: María Corina Machado seeks talks with Delcy Rodríguez after return from exile
World.content:
María Corina Machado says she is willing to talk with Delcy Rodríguez after returning to Venezuela.

 

Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado said on Monday that she is ready to meet the country's interim president following her unexpected return from exile.

Machado landed in Caracas on Sunday after almost a year in exile, where she was greeted by a crowd of supporters in a direct challenge to the US-backed government.

Thousands of people gathered along roads, toll booths and streets in the capital, waving Venezuelan flags and shouting "Freedom!" as a smiling Machado entered Caracas accompanied by a convoy of cars and motorbikes.

The Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado arrives in Caracas on Sunday 25 October 2026. AP Photo/Ariana Cubillos

Dressed in her usual white T-shirt and jeans, she leaned out through the sunroof of a vehicle to greet the crowd and shake hands with her supporters.

On Monday, Machado reached out to the interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, and signalled her willingness to engage in talks with the former vice-president of her main political rival, Nicolás Maduro, prior to his capture by the United States.

Machado "has said she is willing to sit down not only with Delcy (Rodríguez), but with whoever she needs to sit down with, before the country, with full transparency and with an agenda", her spokesperson Claudia Macero told local broadcaster Unión Radio.

The European Union welcomed her return: "We trust that the Venezuelan authorities and all political actors will seize this opportunity to move towards an inclusive dialogue, led by Venezuelans themselves, that leads to free and fair elections," said the EU foreign affairs spokesperson, Anouar El Anouni.

Finally back home

Machado's return once again places the most influential figure in Venezuela's opposition at the heart of the country's turbulent politics.

"María, if you come back, my daughter has to come back too!" a supporter shouted on Sunday, referring to one of the millions of Venezuelans who have left the country to escape repression and a stagnant economy.

Supporters of María Corina Machado celebrate her return to the country on Sunday 25 October 2026. AP Photo/Pedro Campos

Machado slipped out of Venezuela clandestinely last December to receive the Nobel Peace Prize, after spending almost a year in hiding.

Since then, the 59-year-old leader had tried to return to the country at least seven times without success, according to party sources. She is now coming back to a very different Venezuela.

Nine months ago, Maduro was captured in an extraordinary US military operation and imprisoned in the United States. Yet, to the disappointment of the democratic opposition, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, took over as interim president with Washington's backing.

From her exile in Panama, Machado had been forced to follow from afar the US-backed talks on political transition, in which she did not take part. The interim government has promised to hold elections, although it has not yet set a date.

Machado has repeatedly praised US President Donald Trump for ordering the risky military operation, and even gave him the medal from her Nobel Prize.

Trump, for his part, has repeatedly voiced his satisfaction with Rodríguez, who is meeting key US demands, especially regarding access to Venezuela's oil.

On Sunday, Trump said he had been unaware of Machado's return, but added: "I think she is a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize, so what else can I say?" "We are doing very well in Venezuela," he said.

Huge oil reserves

Last week, thousands of people demonstrated in Caracas and other cities to demand Machado's return and the holding of elections.

Many leaders of her party, Vente Venezuela, have also recently returned from exile, to which they were driven by the post-election crackdown that left 28 people dead and more than 2,400 detained, including dozens of Machado's associates.

Her party is calling for elections to be held in 2027 and for Machado to be allowed to stand as a candidate, something she was barred from doing in the last presidential election.

Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves. Yet current output, at one million barrels a day, is far below the three million it was pumping decades ago, after years of corruption and mismanagement.

Rodríguez has granted Washington access to a significant share of the country's crude reserves and has signed agreements with foreign companies to explore, produce and export oil and gas.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV confirms Latin America trip after recovering from surgery
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV will travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from 6 to 17 November, as originally planned. The Press Office of the Holy See has officially confirmed the visit after doctors verified the favourable progress of the Supreme Pontiff following his recent operation.

 

According to the Vatican statement, the procedure went ahead without complications and subsequent tests confirmed that the illness was contained, so he does not need any additional oncological treatment.

Two weeks after the operation, the latest medical check-ups show a favourable recovery and there are no contraindications to making the trip.

Since returning to the Vatican, Leo XIV has gradually resumed his activities, although he keeps to a schedule adapted to medical recommendations and sets aside time to rest. Doctor Luigi Carbone, responsible for reporting on his progress, has confirmed that he is in good health.

The Holy Father has expressed his joy at returning to Latin America, a region with which he has a close personal bond. "It fills me with happiness to return to the continent where I have lived so many moments of my life," he said. During his visit, he will seek to strengthen ties with Catholic communities and convey a message of faith, hope and peace.

World.title: Russia: flames engulf buildings after Ukrainian drone attack in Voronezh region
World.content:
Videos posted on Russian social media showed flames rising from apartment blocks and from the 25-storey Galereya Chizhova business centre, with thick black smoke drifting over neighbouring districts. Other footage showed burning private homes, a damaged commercial building, residential blocks with blown-out windows and at least ten cars ablaze in a car park. Residents picked through the wreckage, where drone engine fragments were found.

 

Alexander Gusev, the governor, said air defences brought down 113 drones over the region, more than 70 of them directly above the city. Russia's defence ministry claimed 290 across the country.

Debris also started fires at several industrial plants — local reports named the Voronezhsintezkauchuk rubber works and the VASO aircraft factory — as well as two dacha settlements, a school sports ground, a garage cooperative and an apartment building. The Novovoronezh nuclear plant said it was operating normally.

Most of the injured were aboard the Anapa–Moscow train when debris struck near Somovo station, Russian Railways said. Five passengers were hurt, two seriously, and rail traffic through the city was suspended. Gusev confirmed three people were killed.

Kyiv has not commented. Independent monitors could not establish whether the explosions beside apartment blocks were direct hits or falling debris, a distinction the governor's account leaves open. A strike on Voronezh three days earlier hit the Baltimor military airfield.

World.title: Zelenskyy calls out monthlong wait for Hegseth to sign off on Patriot missiles
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on much coveted Patriot interceptor missiles.

 

In an update on weapons supplies shared on social media, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been awaiting approval to receive missiles for both the Patriot and NASAMS systems.

"We are working on several tracks – with the United States, Europe, and other partners that have stocks of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles," he wrote.

"In particular, we have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr. Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS," Zelenskyy continued, adding that he had instructed his team to raise the issue with Washington once again.

"Conversations with other countries are also ongoing," he said.

Kyiv has repeatedly pressed the need for more interceptors to be delivered to its forces as Ukraine continues to defend against deadly Russian missile attacks and jet-powered drone strikes.

On Sunday, Zelenskyy said Russian forces had fired 48 missiles - including ballistic missiles - at Ukraine over the past week, as well as around 1,600 guided aerial bombs and close to 2,300 attack drones.

"Unfortunately, almost every day, these brutal strikes leave people killed and injured," he wrote on X. "We need to unblock the deliveries of Patriot interceptors already approved by European countries."

The Patriot missile platform is one of the world's most advanced air defence systems and can be used to defend against a variety of threats, including aircraft and ballistic missiles.

Ukraine receives the majority of its Patriot missiles through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which facilitates the purchase of military equipment and munitions from the US by allies and partners.

As of June 2026, allies had committed to funding more than $6 billion of defence equipment for Ukraine through the scheme, per NATO.

Munitions stockpiles under strain

Global munitions stocks have come under significant pressure in recent months amid the US' war in Iran.

A report from the US Department of Defence's inspector general, published in September, said American forces had fired $22.3 billion worth of munitions from the start of Operation Epic Fury in late February to the end of June.

Yurii Ihnat, a colonel in the Ukrainian military, said in an interview published on Monday that the number of Patriot missiles used in the Middle East could have supported several years of combat operations in Ukraine.

It is unclear how many of the missiles Ukraine is waiting for Hegseth to sign off on, although Ukrainian media reports suggest that it is a sizeable figure.

World.title: Azerbaijan hijab ban exposes strain in ‘brotherly’ ties with Turkey
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, a staunch advocate of Muslim rights, has been notably silent on Azerbaijan’s recent hijab ban in schools. For years, Erdogan and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev have shared a close alliance, but the ban is putting the Turkish president in a tight spot.

Advertising

School uniform rules introduced in September in predominantly Muslim Azerbaijan, which is a secular state, have been used to bar pupils wearing the hijab. Teachers have also reported being excluded. The new rules do not explicitly mention hijabs, but prohibit clothing deemed incompatible with school uniforms or secular education.

With Turkish social media awash with videos of Azerbaijani children wearing hijabs and pleading to be let into their schools, the ban has sparked outrage among Turkey’s religious conservatives.

Yet Erdogan, a vocal defender of Muslim rights both at home and on the world stage, has remained silent on the issue.

"He's unusually muted because Azerbaijan and Turkey, of course, had this extremely good relationship,“ said Turkish political analyst Sezin Oney. "If it were another country, he would have had a harsher reaction.”

‘We're fighting a daily battle': Iranian women dare to shed hijab in public

Baku's response

Erdogan, who is religiously conservative, rose to political prominence in the 1990s by challenging a similar ban in Turkish universities, and went on to become a global advocate of Muslim rights.

Oney predicts his silence on Azerbaijan will damage this reputation.

"[It's] a far cry from the days when Erdogan could stand up against the powerful of the world. That was the image he projected, and now he cannot even stand up to Aliyev."

Aliyev has publicly dismissed criticism of the hijab ban by one of the Turkish president’s advisors and Baku has issued international arrest warrants for several prominent Turkish Islamist and conservative figures, along with banning others from entering the country after similar criticism.

Azerbaijani officials accuse the critics of threatening its sovereignty and national security.

Shifting status

Aliyev and Erdogan have enjoyed close ties for more than two decades, built on economic and defence cooperation, with the mantra of ‘two states, one nation’.

“Erdogan and Turkey [still] see Azerbaijan as a little brother,” explains Tbilisi-based defence and security expert Eugene Kogan.

“I think that's not the perspective that comes from Baku because they say quite clearly that their relationship is no longer between a big brother and a little brother, and their relationship is now of equals.”

He added: “I think this phrase 'equal' is not fully accepted in Ankara. So that puts a strain on bilateral relations between the two countries."

Energy-rich Azerbaijan is growing in economic importance, in comparison with Turkey’s struggling economy. It is also among Turkey’s largest foreign investors.

Earlier this month, the two countries signed arms agreements worth more than $500 million. Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR says it has invested around $19.5 billion in Turkey.

“SOCAR is the flagship of investments in Turkey – it's huge," said Turkish analyst Atilla Yesilada of Global Source Investments.

“Turkey has a chronic deficit in plastics and petrochemicals. In fact, there are plans to establish a huge petrochemical complex in the Adana or Antalya area with a cost of $10 billion. I don’t think domestic capital has that kind of funding. Eventually, if Turkey wants to cover its petrochemical deficit, it needs SOCAR to get involved."

Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea

Relations with Israel

Azerbaijan’s deepening relationship with Israel, despite its Turkish ally’s condemnation of Israel’s war in Gaza and broader escalating tensions, is another source of friction with Ankara.

International media reported that Azerbaijan signed a $235 million arms deal with Israel’s Elbit Systems this month, although neither side has commented on the reports.

Azerbaijan also remains a key oil supplier to Israel, with oil piped through Turkey and shipped from the Turkish Ceyhan port. In 2024, Erdogan moved swiftly to suppress mounting protests against these exports – protests led largely by religious conservatives who form a crucial part of his political support.

However, Kogan believes Israel will not try to exploit any rift between Baku and Ankara. “The stability of relations between Ankara, Baku and Tel Aviv is very, very important for Tel Aviv,” Kogan said.

Turkey-Azerbaijan alliance strained by opposing stances on Israel

Baku last year hosted talks between Turkey and Israel aimed at defusing tensions over Syria.

'[Isreal] understands that it could come to war [with Turkey] and Baku can still act as a meeting point for both countries. I cannot really think of another meeting point between Ankara and Tel Aviv at the moment,” Kogan said.

With Turkey the main export route for Azerbaijan’s oil and gas, mutual dependency remains a powerful means to contain any tensions.

Gasimov suggests the current rift is part of a learning process.

“I wouldn’t read it as reshuffling or rebalancing, but rather as a new chapter that may have opened up now, if the two sides learn from it and are ready to accept these kinds of differences."

As Turkey wrestles with mounting financial and economic woes, Erdogan is expected to look for ways to smooth things over with his affluent neighbour. But the full impact on their ties of this dispute remains to be seen.

World.title: UN sounds the alarm over Israel's West Bank military operation
World.content:
The UN has sounded the alarm on Israeli action in the West Bank city of Hebron after hundreds of families were displaced at the weekend. Israel has ordered the military to demolish homes after soldiers were killed there.

The Israeli military operation in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron was met with sharp criticism from the head of the UN as well as the UN's human rights commissioner in comments made on Monday.

The criticism comes after an Israeli military operation was launched in the occupied West Bank in response to a shootout on Friday that left two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinian gunmen dead. Three more Israeli soldiers were also injured.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the military to demolish buildings in the West Bank city of Hebron and to close off the West Bank. It came just days before Israel's general election on Tuesday.

What did the UN say about Israeli operation in the West Bank?

The United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres said on Monday that "settlements are expanding, evictions are unrelenting with Palestinians driven from their lands," in a post on X.

"We are seeing an increasingly coercive environment, with the spectre of ethnic cleaning looming ever larger," he wrote.

The UN Human Rights High Commissioner Volker Türk also issued a statement condemning Israeli actions, saying the "aggressive operation" has resulted in the forcible displacement of thousands of Palestinians, "demolished homes and commercial property, and deprived residents of the ability to move freely."

"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law. Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing," he said.

Israeli army demolishes Palestinian buildings in Hebron To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A UN report, also released on Monday, that accuses Israel of committing war crimes in the West Bank , was rejected by the Israeli Foreign Ministry as "propaganda."

The ministry said that the findings were "not a human rights report but a propaganda document detached from reality, aimed at undermining Israel's right to self-defense, delegitimizing the Jewish state, and legitimizing jihadist terrorism against its citizens."

What is the Israeli operation in the West Bank?

Israeli troops entered the Deir Baha neighborhood, where the assailants lived, and ordered residents to pack up and leave.

The Hebron municipality said that more than 3,000 people, including 200 babies, were ordered to leave.

The Israeli military said at the weekend that its troops were carrying out precise, targeted and thorough searches to "locate and dismantle terrorist infrastructure and locate weapons, alongside questioning suspects" in Hebron.

The military said the operation was expected to continue "for several days" and would focus on Deir Baha.

The largescale response to the firefight in the West Bank comes in the run-up to elections in Israel on Tuesday that could bring an end to Netanyahu's premiership.

Netanyahu has frequently painted himself as the only person who can keep Israel safe but his opponents have accused him of lacking a plan.
