1. Within one year of the treaty’s entry into force, the parties must establish a Joint Information and Coordination Centre for their interior affairs agencies.

2. The Joint Information and Coordination Centre for Interior Affairs Agencies is responsible for:

organising the exchange of operationally significant information between the law enforcement agencies of the Russian Federation and the Republic of Abkhazia, as well as maintaining the necessary operational and forensic records;

compiling and maintaining a specialised database on organised criminal groups whose illegal activities affect the interests of the contracting parties;

collecting, consolidating and analysing information on efforts to combat organised crime and other serious offences;

assisting with the international search for and extradition of people who have evaded criminal prosecution or the enforcement of a sentence;

facilitating the implementation of necessary coordinated measures to combat serious crimes that threaten the security of the contracting parties;

developing and submitting proposals to the contracting parties on improving the effectiveness of their cooperation.

None of these provisions, nor the treaty as a whole, states or implies that the Joint Information and Coordination Centre (JICC) may be used to “monitor and analyse the crime situation and operational environment in the Republic of Abkhazia, as well as the activities of Abkhazia’s interior affairs agencies”, as stated in Article 1 of the new agreement.

That last point is particularly absurd. Why have an entire ministry if it needs to rely on an external organisation to monitor its activities? Not to mention that Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry may have internal matters that the JICC should know nothing about.

The 2014 treaty also says nothing about the JICC, let alone specialised units of Russia’s Interior Ministry, tackling “economic crime and corruption” in Abkhazia.

Nor does it mention any Russian Interior Ministry units directly engaging in “countering the spread of criminal ideas on social media and messaging platforms”. Yet Article 4 of the new agreement between the two interior ministries explicitly includes this provision.

Incidentally, many have interpreted this clause as an attempt to monitor online spaces for dissenting views.

There is also the fact that the very definition of what constitutes “criminal” content online may differ significantly between our two countries. In Russia, for example, even this text, published on Facebook, a platform owned by Meta, is illegal.

And, of course, the 2014 treaty nowhere states that the Russian and Abkhaz interior ministries will “conduct joint operational and preventive measures in border areas” — activities that infringe on our sovereign jurisdiction. Yet Article 6 of the new agreement explicitly provides for them.

And so it goes with many other provisions…

International treaties are not folk songs from which you can create a new work by developing the main theme. They are complete legal documents, and their provisions cannot be freely reinterpreted.

For this reason, and because the two instruments differ substantially in their content, the new agreement cannot be said to “derive” from the 2014 treaty, as some “experts” are trying to argue. If anyone really wants to establish a new legal framework for the work of Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry, they should try doing so openly and through the lawful procedure. Then we can see how that works out.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Serbia protests timeline: how students brought Vucic’s 12-year rule to end
World.content:
The end of Vučić’s rule

Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s former president and the ruling party’s candidate for prime minister, conceded defeat in the snap parliamentary election held on 25 October. He said the “Student List” had won.

“Judging by the preliminary results, it is clear that we have lost this election. The Student List has won — they will get between 135 and 140 seats, while we will have around 105,” Vučić said.

The snap election, which Vučić called before stepping down as president, followed a wave of student-led protests that had lasted for almost two years.

The demonstrations began after a disaster at the railway station in Novi Sad in 2024 that killed 16 people. Protesters blamed corruption and negligence for the tragedy and demanded that those responsible face justice.

Vučić’s party had been in power in Serbia for 12 years.

Here is a chronological account of how the protests began, grew into a student movement, challenged Aleksandar Vučić’s government and brought Serbia to the 25 October 2026 election, in which Vučić conceded defeat.

From a spark to a change of government

Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have dominated Serbian politics since 2012. Vučić became prime minister in 2014 and was elected president in 2017.

Government supporters portrayed him as a guarantor of stability, economic development and a foreign policy that balanced relations with the West and Russia. Critics, however, pointed to the concentration of power, the ruling party’s influence over the media, corruption and concerns about the independence of state institutions.

Public discontent periodically spilled onto the streets. Protests included demonstrations over electoral fairness and rallies against a proposed lithium mining project. Until 2024, however, the government had largely managed to prevent the emergence of large-scale, sustained protest movements.

1 November 2024: the tragedy that changed everything

On 1 November 2024, a concrete canopy collapsed at the railway station in Novi Sad, a city in northern Serbia, killing 16 people.

The station had undergone renovation shortly before the disaster, prompting immediate questions. How could recently refurbished infrastructure collapse? Who was responsible for the quality of the work? How transparent were the public procurement procedures and the renovation project itself?

Authorities opened an investigation, but for many people, the fact that an investigation had begun was not enough. Suspicions grew that the collapse might not have been merely a technical failure, but could also involve corruption and attempts to evade accountability. Further concerns over access to project documents only deepened those suspicions. Protesters demanded that those responsible be identified.

The tragedy, which claimed 16 lives, became more than a moment of mourning. It turned into a test of accountability for state institutions. People wanted to know not only what caused the canopy to collapse, but also who had allowed potential wrongdoing to take place and why the oversight system had failed.

November 2024: students take to the streets

On 22 November, students at the Faculty of Dramatic Arts in Belgrade were attacked during a silent protest in memory of those killed in the disaster. The incident gave the protests a new focus: students demanded that authorities identify the attackers and hold them accountable.

University students soon began disrupting classes. The movement spread from Novi Sad and Belgrade to other cities across the country.

The way the protests were organised was also significant. Students made decisions at general assemblies known as “plenums”. From the outset, the movement had no single central leader whose removal would have allowed the authorities to bring the entire campaign to a halt.

What were the students demanding?

Make all documents related to the station’s reconstruction publicly available;

Identify those responsible for the disaster and hold them accountable under the law;

Punish those involved in the attacks on students and drop charges against detained protesters;

Increase funding for higher education by 20%.

In other words, the movement was never solely about calling for the government to resign. Its main goals were transparency, justice and accountability from state institutions.

By December, the protests had evolved beyond a reaction to the Novi Sad tragedy. University blockades, daily demonstrations and public support for the students had turned the movement into a nationwide campaign.

One of its most powerful symbols was the minute of silence. Every day at 11:52 — the exact time the canopy collapsed — protesters stopped to honour the victims. They also held 16-minute silences in memory of the 16 people who died.

The movement drew its strength from the fact that it differed from a typical political opposition campaign. Students stressed that political parties should not dictate their demands. This helped bring a wide range of social groups into the protests.

January 2025: the first major political outcome

On 28 January 2025, Prime Minister Miloš Vučević announced his resignation. Around the same time, the mayor of Novi Sad also stepped down.

This marked a significant political concession. The authorities could no longer maintain that street protests were failing to achieve any tangible results.

However, the students continued their protests. In their view, the resignation of individual officials did not answer the key questions: who was responsible for the disaster, how independent was the judicial system, and how should the system of government be reformed?

This marked an important turning point. The protests showed that a sustained, organised mass movement could impose significant political costs on the authorities.

The students adopted a new strategy. Rather than limiting their demonstrations to the capital, they began organising marches, cycle rides and meetings with local residents across the country.

This strategy was important for several reasons:

The protests spread beyond the capital. The movement built ties with residents of smaller towns and regional communities;

Students positioned themselves as representatives of society as a whole. They won support from university staff, teachers, ordinary citizens and people from a wide range of professions;

The movement built its own communications network. Citizens critical of the government ensured that the flow of information no longer depended solely on traditional media.

By this stage, the student protests had become one of the largest popular movements in Serbia’s recent history.

Miloš Vučević

15 March 2025: the historic rally in Belgrade

The rally on 15 March 2025 marked a pivotal moment for the movement. Hundreds of thousands of people gathered in Belgrade.

The independent organisation Archive of Public Gatherings estimated that between 275,000 and 325,000 people took part. Serbia’s Interior Ministry gave a significantly lower figure. The discrepancy itself became a subject of debate.

Why was this event important?

First, it showed that the students enjoyed support well beyond university campuses;

Second, the government faced a challenge not only from the traditional opposition, but also from a broad coalition of citizens united by a common demand for justice and state accountability;

Third, the movement had grown so powerful that the question of Serbia’s political future could no longer be ignored.

Once again, the protest showed that calls for a change of government were coming from beyond political parties. A sense emerged across society that the existing system could be changed.

Spring and summer 2025: when the demands turned into a political struggle

On 5 May 2025, the student movement called for snap parliamentary elections. This broadened the scope of the protests. Vučić’s government, meanwhile, said the demonstrations aimed to destabilise the state and alleged that foreign powers were involved. The student movement rejected these accusations, identifying its main goals as fighting corruption, establishing independent institutions and holding fair elections.

Tensions continued to rise throughout this period. Reports emerged of arrests, clashes and acts of violence against protesters. Government opponents accused the authorities of controlling the media and weakening democratic institutions — allegations the government denied.

One of the movement’s most significant decisions was to create a political alternative from within the protest movement.

Students began selecting candidates to represent them in the parliamentary election. They formed an electoral list called “Student List — Students Win”. The aim was to broaden the movement’s representation by including people from different professions and social groups.

On 9 September 2026, Vučić called a snap parliamentary election for 25 October. He made the announcement amid a prolonged political standoff, as the student movement was already preparing to contest the election.

22 октября 2026 года: сотни тысяч сторонников движутся к предвыборной финишной прямой

За несколько дней до выборов, назначенных на 25 октября, студенческое движение провело в Белграде масштабный заключительный митинг. Сторонники из разных городов страны направились в столицу.

Согласно данным, опубликованным накануне выборов, между студенческим списком и правящей партией развернулась упорная борьба. Вучич предрекал победу, хотя и признавал, что она достанется нелегко.

Это стало кульминацией движения, которое продолжалось почти два года: протест, начавшийся с требований справедливости после гибели 16 человек, теперь стремился обеспечить себе большинство в парламенте.

25 October 2026: Vučić concedes defeat

On election night, something that many in Serbian political circles had long considered unthinkable happened.

Vučić announced that his political camp had lost the election and that the Student List had won. He estimated that the Student List would secure between 135 and 140 seats in parliament, while his own camp would get around 105.

According to Reuters, preliminary projections gave the Student List 138 seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with 104 for Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party. The Student List had therefore secured a parliamentary majority. Voter turnout stood at around 70%, one of the highest levels since 1992.

According to Serbian political sociologist Gazela Pudar Draško, writing in The Washington Post, the student movement had taken the protests to a new level: citizens had moved beyond simply expressing discontent and begun taking direct part in political change. Students across the country had created an alternative model of political mobilisation by building relationships with local communities and making decisions collectively.

Radomir Šajčić, a professor at the University of Belgrade, commented on the victory at the students’ campaign headquarters. “Tonight we celebrate our victory, and tomorrow we will start building the future!” he said, Reuters reported.

The end of Vučić’s rule

World.title: Two teenagers arrested in Tbilisi over alleged plot to attack school: what we know
World.content:
School attack plot in Georgia

Two 14-year-olds have been arrested in Tbilisi on suspicion of planning an attack on a school and acts of violence against pupils. They attend different schools and communicated with each other through social media.

According to the prosecutor’s office, the teenagers had already chosen a specific school and planned their actions.

One of the teenagers has already been remanded in custody. The court is due to hold a hearing on the second suspect today.

What we know about the case

The Georgian outlet Sando Tskaro was the first to report the teenagers’ arrests. According to its report, police detained 14-year-old S.T. on the afternoon of Thursday, 22 October.

The following day, 23 October, police arrested the second teenager at his home. The first suspect exercised his right to remain silent, while the second denies the charges against him.

Police searched both teenagers’ homes. They seized a number of items, including a starter pistol, ammunition, pepper spray, gloves, a helmet and a knife.

The father of the first suspect, S.T., told Sando Tskaro that he did not know who the teenager was with whom his son had allegedly planned to commit the crime.

According to the father, the teenagers communicated through video calls on Telegram and TikTok.

He said they had discussed the 2011 terrorist attacks in Oslo. They had also talked about films based on real events that depicted acts of violence.

The prosecutor’s office has largely confirmed this account. It issued an official statement only after the information had already appeared in the media.

According to the statement, the teenagers met in April and May 2026. They chose a specific school in Tbilisi, studied its layout and began preparing an attack.

The prosecutor’s office says the teenagers planned to place a dummy explosive device outside the school. This would have allowed them to enter the building undetected, cause a disturbance and use weapons to injure people inside.

“They acquired various items and created all the necessary conditions to commit the crime. However, they failed to carry out their plan because law enforcement officers uncovered their activities,” the prosecutor’s office said.

Defence lawyer’s position

Gia Darchia, the lawyer representing one of the teenagers, told Radio Liberty that the prosecution had no evidence in the case.

According to Darchia, the case file contains only two days’ worth of messages from October, none of which mentions organising anything.

According to the defence, the items seized from the suspects’ homes as evidence were intended for personal use. They included souvenirs given to them by their parents and ordinary household objects. The lawyers argue that any claims that the teenagers were “preparing to commit a crime” are therefore entirely “unserious”.

“These people did not know each other. They had never even seen each other and had made no attempt to meet. What is more, they had never been to the school they allegedly planned to attack.”

The lawyer says his client would not even recognise the second suspect if someone showed him to him. He notes that his client had never seen a photograph of the other teenager, who used an avatar on social media. He also stresses that the teenagers never communicated via video calls.

The defence lawyer says the investigation began after the second suspect published a social media post calling for violence. However, the case file contains neither a screenshot nor any other visual evidence that the post existed. The lawyer argues that neither the investigative materials nor interviews with the suspects indicate any links between the teenagers and radical groups. Nor had anyone observed any suspicious behaviour on their part.

“They had no intention of blowing anything up or harming anyone. There is no basis for talking about any kind of organised activity,” he says.

The lawyer representing the second suspect has declined to comment to the media at this stage.

Authorities have opened a criminal case under Article 225, parts 1 and 2, of the Criminal Code. The article covers organising group actions involving violence, looting, damage to or destruction of other people’s property, and the use of weapons. It also covers preparing to take part in such actions.

The article provides for a prison sentence of six to nine years.

World.title: ‘Georgia without Ivanishvili’: Opposition launches new wave of protests – photos and video
World.content:
New wave of protests in Georgia

On 25 October, thousands of people gathered in Tbilisi for a major opposition-organised protest under the slogan ‘Georgia without Ivanishvili’.

Waving flags and blowing horns, protesters gathered outside Tbilisi State University before setting off on a mass march towards Rustaveli metro station.

With this rally, the opposition announced the start of a new wave of protests in Georgia. The next rally is scheduled for 28 November.

The date is symbolic: exactly two years earlier, the ruling Georgian Dream party publicly announced that it was suspending EU accession talks.

The announcement sparked ongoing pro-European protests, with demonstrators demanding fresh, free and fair parliamentary elections.

Key messages from opposition leaders

The rally’s organisers, leaders of the pro-Western opposition, addressed the demonstrators.

“This day, 28 November, represents a defeat for all of us as long as Bidzina Ivanishvili remains in power. The postponement of our integration into the European Union is a defeat for all of us. The indefinite delay of a brighter future for our children is a defeat for all of us,” said Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change.

“Ivanishvili’s group is trying to formally strip us of one of the most important achievements secured by the United National Movement – multiparty elections in Georgia. They now seek to legally establish a one-party dictatorship,” said Levan Tsutskiridze, leader of the Freedom Square party.

“It may seem that Bidzina Ivanishvili is making such a brazen decision that we should all despair. In fact, the opposite is true. By banning any alternative, Ivanishvili is acknowledging a crisis of his own legitimacy. He is admitting that he no longer trusts the Georgian people – that he fears the free choice of Georgian citizens, and quite rightly so,” said Tamar Chergoleishvili, leader of the Federalists movement.

Young people and other protesters were also among the speakers.

“Look at one another – you are surrounded by people who refuse to give up, who continue to fight for a better future for our country,” student Luka Mishveladze told the crowd.

Background

The 25 October rally was part of Georgia’s pro-European protest movement, which has been ongoing for nearly two years. The demonstration was announced and organised by the opposition.

The date was no coincidence: on 24 October 2024, Georgia held crucial parliamentary elections, with the country’s European future at stake.

The election results remain disputed both domestically and internationally. The vote marked the beginning of a major political crisis in Georgia, leading to strained relations with Western partners, sanctions and the suspension of multimillion-dollar aid packages.

The protests were met with violent police crackdowns, including beatings, torture and arrests of activists. Several packages of repressive laws were adopted, while pressure on the media and civil society intensified, including measures that effectively blocked access to funding.

Western institutions adopted numerous resolutions criticising these developments.

The political crisis entered a new phase when the ruling Georgian Dream party moved to ban pro-Western opposition groups it deemed unacceptable.

Almost all the parties that organised the 25 October rally and announced a new wave of protests were among those facing a proposed ban.

World.title: Why are Abkhazia residents with dual citizenship asked to show Russian passports at Moscow airports?
World.content:
Abkhazia‘s Foreign Ministry has said that some residents of the breakaway republic who hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship are experiencing difficulties crossing the Russian border at Moscow airports.

Russian border guards have reportedly been refusing to allow dual nationals to enter or leave the country using their Abkhaz passports, instead demanding Russian documents.

As Abkhazia is a largely unrecognised republic, its passports are also not widely recognised internationally. Travelling on an Abkhaz passport is virtually impossible, except to a handful of countries, including Russia. For Abkhazians, obtaining a Russian passport is therefore practically the only way to travel internationally. However, this generally means a Russian international passport rather than a domestic identity document. Most do not hold Russian internal passports because they permanently reside in Abkhazia, where Russian passport holders account for around 70% of the population.

The ministry added that people holding only Abkhaz citizenship do not encounter such problems at airports. Similar incidents have not been reported at other border crossing points either.

Russia explains its position by saying that, for dual nationals, a Russian passport is not merely the primary document required to cross the border, but the only acceptable one. However, the explanation has been met with scepticism in Abkhazia, where some suspect the border guards may have other motives.

The issue was discussed by Abkhaz and Russian foreign ministers Oleg Bartsits and Sergei Lavrov during a recent meeting in Moscow. However, no solution has yet been found. According to Abkhazia’s Foreign Ministry, the matter remains subject to “consultations with the competent authorities of the Russian Federation, taking into account the provisions of existing bilateral agreements”.

In the meantime, the ministry has advised Abkhaz citizens experiencing difficulties at border crossings to formally report the incidents to the ministry, providing detailed accounts of what happened.

From the perspective of international practice, border guards at Moscow airports are not doing anything unlawful.

As a general rule, people holding two or more citizenships are required to present the passport of the country whose border they are crossing, if they are citizens of that country. This requirement is enshrined in national legislation and strictly enforced in countries including Georgia, the United States and many others.

This raises the question: what exactly is the problem, why are Abkhaz citizens unhappy, and why are they reluctant to present their Russian passports at the border if they have them?

For some Abkhazians with dual citizenship, the right to use an Abkhaz passport is a matter of principle and national pride. While this argument carries little legal weight, it is highly significant in Abkhazia.

Others simply want the option of crossing the border using their Abkhaz documents in certain circumstances, such as when their Russian passport has expired and they have not yet received a replacement.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Azerbaijan-banned Turkish media representative detained in Istanbul
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. Muhammed Emin Yıldırım, the Istanbul representative of the Köklü Değişim magazine and media group, who was declared persona non grata by Azerbaijan and banned from entering the country, has been detained.

The media group announced this on the social media platform X.

It was reported that he was detained by Istanbul police over his social media posts.

“We are closely monitoring the legal proceedings through his lawyer,” the media group added.

It should be noted that 31 Turkish citizens have been declared persona non grata in connection with statements made on various social media platforms and online outlets that were directed against Azerbaijan’s sovereignty, national security, constitutional order, people and leadership, as well as calls for the violent seizure of power and the incitement of violence on the grounds of religious radicalism, religious hatred and hostility. Muhammed Emin Yıldırım is also on the list.

World.title: Azerbaijan, UNESCO discuss prospects for developing cooperation (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. On October 26, Azerbaijani Deputy Foreign Minister Elnur Mammadov met with UNESCO Deputy Director-General Asa Regner, who is visiting the country.

This was reported by the Press Service Department of Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

According to the report, the meeting addressed the current state and prospects for developing cooperation between Azerbaijan and UNESCO, as well as intercultural dialogue, education, science, artificial intelligence, cultural heritage, sustainable tourism, the Man and the Biosphere Programme, and support for African countries and small island states.

It was noted that the Framework Agreement signed in 2013 and the Azerbaijan–UNESCO Trust Fund established that year play an important role in advancing cooperation. Azerbaijan’s interest in continuing to support UNESCO programmes and projects in line with the country’s national priorities was also emphasized.

Satisfaction was expressed with UNESCO’s active participation in the 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue. It was noted that the organization had hosted three panel discussions as part of the forum.

Elnur Mammadov provided information on the Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2025–2028 and the Digital Development Council. It was noted that artificial intelligence technologies are being applied to promote the country’s development and digitalize public services.

Asa Regner thanked Azerbaijan for the successful organization of the 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue and for its cooperation. She highly appreciated Azerbaijan’s support for African countries, gender equality, girls’ education and small island states, which are among UNESCO’s priority areas.

The meeting also included an exchange of views on other issues of mutual interest.

World.title: Six years pass since Armenia's rocket attack on Azerbaijan's Barda district
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. Six years have passed since Azerbaijan's Barda district was once again subjected to rocket attack by the Armenian armed forces during the Second Karabakh War.

The Armenian forces once again shelled Garayusifli village in Barda, located outside the frontline zone, with Smerch rockets on October 27, 2020.

As a result, civilians Ofeliya Jafarova, Aybaniz Ahmadova, Ehtiram Ismayilov, Aysu Isgandarova and Almaz Aliyeva (born in 2013) became martyrs, and 13 more people were injured.

The rocket fire completely destroyed several residential houses and caused significant damage to the villagers.

During the Second Karabakh War, Barda district and city center were subjected to rocket and artillery fire by Armenian armed forces three times (October 5, 27, and 28). As a result, 29 people became martyrs, 112 were wounded, and vehicles and civilian infrastructure facilities located in the area were significantly damaged.

In light of this fact, the General Prosecutor's Office of Azerbaijan initiated criminal proceedings under articles 120.2.1 (premeditated murder by an organized criminal community), 120.2.4 (premeditated murder with particular cruelty or in a generally dangerous way), 120.2.12 (premeditated murder with intent to incite national, racial, religious enmity, or hatred), 100.2 (waging a war of aggression), and other articles of the Criminal Code of Azerbaijan.

A preliminary investigation was entrusted to the Investigation Department of the Prosecutor's Office.

In total, during the war that began on September 27, 2020 and lasted 44 days, as a result of the military aggression of the armed forces and illegal armed groups of Armenia against Azerbaijan, 93 civilians were killed (including 54 men, 27 women and 12 children), and 444 people were injured (including 268 men, 109 women and 67 children).

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 27, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Chronicle of the 31-st day of the second Karabakh war:

- First Vice President of Azerbaijan Mehriban Aliyeva shared a post on her Instagram account.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry has released information on the latest situation on the front.

- The chief of staff of the Armenian motorized infantry division was killed. The list of destroyed military equipment of the Armenian armed forces has been announced.

- Tartar city and the villages of the Tartar district were shelled.

- The Azerbaijani army liberated four cities, four settlements and 165 villages in just one month.

- The territories of Goranboy, Tartar and Barda districts were shelled. The death toll from Armenian missile attack in Barda has reached four. One of the dead in Barda was an 8-year-old child.

- The Defense Ministry said that over the past day, Armenian armed forces repeatedly violated the humanitarian ceasefire.

World.title: Leyla Aliyeva and Alena Aliyeva visit Capybara Azerbaijan farm in Shamakhi (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. On October 26, Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, and Alena Aliyeva visited the Nasimi Gardens complex in Shamakhi.

Leyla Aliyeva and Alena Aliyeva first viewed the artworks displayed in the area. The guests then visited the Capybara Cafe, which was created based on the capybara concept.

Capybara Cafe offers visitors a unique and relaxing atmosphere. The cafe's interior and offered products are designed in line with a unified concept, where every detail resembles capybaras. Even the desserts on the menu are presented in the shape of capybaras.

For guests wishing to purchase souvenir gifts, a souvenir shop operates inside the cafe.

Subsequently, Leyla Aliyeva and Alena Aliyeva visited the Capybara Azerbaijan farm and were briefed on the conditions created there, while also feeding the capybaras. Recognized as the first capybara farm ever established in Azerbaijan, the Capybara Azerbaijan aims to introduce visitors more closely to these unique animals, contribute to the development of ecotourism, and support the formation of a responsible and caring attitude toward animals. The farm has quickly turned into a top destination for numerous visitors in a short span of time.

Considered the world's largest rodents native to Central and South America, capybaras have gained immense popularity in various countries in recent years. Being incredibly friendly animals, capybaras attract people's attention with their unusual appearance and social characteristics, fostering greater love for animals and nature in general. Taking into account the above-mentioned factors, the Capybara Azerbaijan farm was constructed using advanced technologies.

The existing infrastructure at the farm was designed to create conditions matching capybara’s natural habitat as closely as possible. Both indoor and outdoor pools, as well as individual baths, have been built for capybaras. The farm is equipped with a modern water filtration system, an automatic humidification system ensuring optimal humidity, and special UV lamps simulating natural sunlight.

At this venue, which garners great interest from both children and adults, it is possible to get in touch with a piece of exotic nature. Visitors can feed capybaras and gain interesting information about their lifestyle, behavior, and natural habitat.

The guests also visited the Magic Village section, another popular project consisting of themed houses built in the style of hobbit homes.

World.title: Leyla Aliyeva and Alena Aliyeva attend Khinisli nursery-kindergarten in Shamakhi city (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. The Khinisli nursery-kindergarten was inaugurated in the city of Shamakhi on October 26.

Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, and Alena Aliyeva attended the opening ceremony and familiarized themselves with the conditions created at the facility.

Constructed by the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, the preschool educational facility has a capacity of 110 seats. The nursery-kindergarten features bedrooms located in separate wings for boys and girls, as well as group, computer, and medical rooms, music and gymnastics halls, and a cafeteria.

The facility is fully equipped with the necessary furniture and equipment, while the rooms are provided with visual aids.

Gazebos and a playground with amusement rides have been installed for children’s recreation.

In her interview with AZERTAC, Saida Zahidova, Director of the nursery-kindergarten, said that since the old kindergarten building, constructed in 1969, had become unfit for use and a new building was needed. In the new nursery-kindergarten, built by the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, children will be involved in the educational process across six groups.

Along with state programs implemented in the country for the construction of new children education facilities and the reconstruction of existing ones in line with the most modern requirements, the Heydar Aliyev Foundation constantly keeps this issue in spotlight. Since 2014, by implementing the program "Development of Preschool Educational Institutions," the Foundation has contributed to the training, education, and development of knowledgeable and well-educated children. The program covers regions alongside the capital, Baku, including Shamakhi. Overall, several new nursery-kindergartens and schools have been built and commissioned in Shamakhi in recent years.

World.title: Choreographer behind Kylie's grand final show prepares to reveal final work
World.content:
After nearly 20 years at the helm, Rafael Bonachela will premiere his final work as artistic director of Sydney Dance Company (SDC) for its 2027 season.

The Spanish-born choreographer, known as "Rafa", will present his as-yet-unnamed work as part of a triple bill called Wild Order.

"[My new work] will carry something of the shared history I have with collaborators like [composer] Nick Wales and the dancers, but also the curiosity and desire to create that brought me here in the first place," Bonachela says.

"I'm thinking a lot about, 'Why did I come here?' To create work and take a company into the future."

Bonachela's announcement of his final commission for SDC comes after he revealed in March he would leave the company in mid-2028.

"It just felt like, as a contemporary dance company, change is important; renewal is important," he says.

"For the love and care of the company, an organisation I've been so incredibly lucky to be guiding and curating and creating work for, it felt time for somebody else to take that on.

"I'm excited more than anything to be able to still have some time to share with the artists I'm working with, and with audiences."

The 2027 season reveal also follows the Australian premiere in September of his seminal 2004 duet E2 7SD, which won him the Place Prize for new choreography.

In the same month, he helped choreograph Kylie Minogue's AFL grand final performance, which featured 16 SDC dancers.

Rafael Bonachela with Kylie Minogue and ensemble dancers from Sydney Dance Company at the AFL Grand Final in September. (Supplied: SDC)

It's the latest collaboration between the choreographer and the pop star, who first worked together in 2002 on Minogue's iconic BRIT Awards performance Can't Get You Out of My Head. He then went on to choreograph her Fever concert tour.

The rest of SDC's 2027 season includes a collaboration between four choreographers, titled Future Reverie; the return of INDance, which spotlights independent choreographers; and a showcase of the company's Pre-Professional Year dancers.

Rafael Bonachela on Creative Types The artistic director of Sydney Dance Company has come a long way from his hometown in Spain to the top of contemporary dance in Australia.

It will also take SDC bills around Australia, to regional New South Wales, Queensland, and Tasmania, and overseas, to Spain, Germany and Serbia.

"For me, 2027 is about creative possibility, bold new work that's going to be created for us, fresh collaborations; but also, lineage and connections that have been there from the very beginning [of my time at SDC]," Bonachela says.

With such a busy year ahead, the artistic director hasn't had time to figure out what he will do after he leaves the company.

"It's as scary as it's exciting," he says. "I don't know where the next chapter of my career will take me.

"I know that I want to continue to choreograph. I want to continue to create work."

Looking back to look forward

Understandably, Bonachela has been thinking about legacy as he approaches his final full season as artistic director.

This year, Rafael Bonachela felt inspired after he travelled to USC Glorya Kaufman School of Dance in LA to make a new work. (Supplied: SDC/Toby Burrows)

That's most pronounced in the first show, Future Reverie, which brings together choreographers Richard Cilli, Antony Hamilton, Sela Vai and Charmene Yap.

The artistic director recalls Hamilton's Black Project 1 was one of the first he saw after moving to Australia as part of Dance Massive in Melbourne in 2013.

"It was something I had never seen before," he says.

He was thrilled to see Hamilton, performing with Lane, seeming to combine his training as a ballet dancer with street dance, visual arts and graffiti.

"It was so urban and contemporary," Bonachela says. "It gave me great hope for my time here."

Hamilton, now artistic director of Melbourne dance company Chunky Move, would choreograph the award-winning Forever & Ever for SDC in 2018, which the company took to Finland last year.

After its 2018 premiere, Forever & Ever was remounted for a national tour five years later, then toured Germany. (Supplied: SDC/Pedro Greig)

"Sydney Dance Company has the capacity to perform the breadth of work of the incredible artists that we have here in Australia," Bonachela says.

Meanwhile, Cilli and Yap are former SDC dancers who continue to work with the company: Cilli as rehearsal director and Yap as rehearsal associate.

They have also choreographed for the company, including for the defunct emerging artist showcase New Breed.

Bonachela recalls them both joining the company early in his stewardship.

"There is a lineage of dancers that have dedicated significant time to Sydney Dance Company who are known worldwide," he says.

"People don't just think about me; they also think about Richard and Charmene. I could keep going with names of dancers … They're carrying the spirit of what we've built for Sydney Dance Company."

Charmene Yap, pictured in SDC's Lux Tenebris in 2016, was recently announced as co-artistic director of Co3 in Perth. (Supplied: Peter Greig)

The final choreographer, Vai, has never worked with SDC, but Bonachela is excited to see how she draws on her hip hop and contemporary dance for the work.

"There's risk in bringing four different voices to collaborate on one work, but, for me, that's what contemporary dance is about," Bonachela says.

It reflects the artistic director's commitment to platforming Australian artists.

"Once I really knew the Antonys, the Melanies, the Stephanie Lakes, the Tra Mi [Dinh]s, I started to commission more Australian work because I knew the people, what they were doing, and that we could work together," Bonachela says.

"And then when we've gone to the world … [We are] lucky and privileged to be able to take [Australian] dance to the world."

Beyond the choreographers, Future Reverie also brings together the SDC ensemble with students from its Pre-Professional Year.

"It's about different generations sharing the same space, the same dancefloor," he says.

Making opportunities for dancers

Bringing Pre-Professional Year students to the main stage is one way Bonachela's final full season as artistic director creates opportunities for dancers.

How to 'get' contemporary dance It can be a lot of things – audacious, thrilling, arousing, funny, joyous, even brutal. If you haven’t discovered contemporary dance yet, there’s a lot you’re missing out on.

Another is in Wild Order, which features the return of two works that premiered as part of New Breed: WOOF by Lane, the incoming artistic director of Lucy Guerin Inc, and From the Horizon Thereafter by SDC dancer Ngaere Jenkins.

From the Horizon Thereafter will be the first current ensemble member's work to be performed on the main stage and will join WOOF in the company's repertoire.

For Bonachela, highlighting these works as part of Wild Order is a way to pay tribute to the impact of development programs like New Breed.

From the Horizon Thereafter was the choreographic debut of New Zealand-born dancer Ngaere Jenkins. (Supplied: SDC/Pedro Greig)

"It had a huge impact on Australian dance because it's giving opportunity to independent choreographers and company members to create work for the company," he explains.

He recalls how important it was to him when he was in London working as a dancer for Rambert, the company created by Polish-born ballerina Marie Rambert, to be chosen for its choreographic workshop program.

"You sort of don't believe that's happening or you're even as good as you should be," he says.

Bonachela also knows how difficult it is to be an independent choreographer, having left Rambert in 2006 to run his own company.

" I know why I am where I am," he says. "Because the people that believed in me gave me those opportunities. "

While New Breed is no more, INDance continues to platform independent choreographers, while the upcoming Orbit program offers the opportunity to tour independent works.

WOOF premiered as part of New Breed in 2017, before it toured Australia in 2019. (Supplied: SDC/Pedro Greig)

"That commitment to supporting independent artists is continuing, and I hope it does forever," he says.

"As a company, I think we have the responsibility to do that."

World.title: Veteran rugby prop cited for allegedly grabbing opponent's genitals
World.content:
Veteran Ireland prop Leinster's Tadhg Furlong has been cited for allegedly grabbing the genitals of Munster's Gavin Coombes during their United Rugby Championship match last weekend.

Coombes alleged during the game on Saturday that his testicles had been grabbed, but an immediate television review ordered by referee Andrew Brace was inconclusive, with no evidence of the incident.

However, since the incident was noted in the referee's report, it can be reviewed by the citing commissioner Peter Ferguson.

"Leinster Rugby's Tadhg Furlong has been cited for an incident that occurred in the 37th minute of the United Rugby Championship [URC] Round 4 fixture at the Aviva Stadium against Munster Rugby on Saturday, 24 October," a statement from the URC said on Monday.

"The Citing Commissioner in charge has made a complaint about an act of foul play by the Player [Tadhg Furlong No. 3] against opponent Gavin Coombes [No. 8].

"The Player has been cited under Law 9.27 — A player must not do anything that is against the spirit of good sportsmanship, including but not limited to grabbing, twisting or squeezing the genitals.

"Arrangements for the disciplinary process are currently in progress and will be announced in due course."

Coombes has been backed in his allegation by Munster coach Clayton McMillan.

"All I know is that I back our players 100 per cent — that if they make an allegation like that, they wouldn't do it lightly — and that's not the sort of person Gavin is, so we'll see where that goes," McMillan said.

Furlong faces the possibility of a lengthy ban if found guilty. The 33-year-old is a British & Irish Lion and key member of the Ireland team, approaching 100 test caps. He is in the squad for November's Nations Championship fixtures, and a ban would be a blow to his personal reputation as well as to the Irish team.

Leinster head coach Leo Cullen said: "Obviously, once that accusation is made, it becomes a serious matter for the citing commissioner. So my comment is not going to help in any way here. But from what I've seen, I can't see anything."

In the URC last season, Bulls hooker Jan-Hendrik Wessels was handed a nine-week suspension for grabbing the testicles of Connacht's Josh Murphy.

Reuters

World.title: Country residents paying three times to keep local doctors
World.content:
A West Australian country town is handing over 16 per cent of its annual rates income in a bid to keep a local doctor.

The arrangement in Narembeen, 280 kilometres east of Perth, is one of several detailed in a new report by the Local Government Rural Health Funding Alliance, aiming to shine a light on the increasingly unsustainable conditions country councils face to attract and retain local GPs.

The Shire of Narembeen pays the local medical practice $370,000 a year, while also providing its building, a car and a house under its current agreement.

It is an arrangement Shire President Holly Cusack concedes is unsustainable financially.

But the alternative for the community if the GP closed — a 120km round trip to the nearest doctor — is worse.

Holly Cusack says the financial burden is unsustainable. (Supplied: Holly Cusack)

"One of our top priorities is a doctor in town, so we will keep providing that," she said.

"But all the other sort of things we provide for our community, they'll all start falling off."

Paying three times

Narembeen and six other local governments commissioned the recent Alliance report, which used information from 30 councils across Australia.

It found the seven councils collectively spent about $1.7 million each year to attract and retain a GP.

The council provides a medical practice, a house and a car to the local GP. (Supplied: Holly Cusack)

The report said rural ratepayers effectively paid for their medical care three times: through the Medicare levy, the consultation fee and their council rates.

Cr Cusack said the combination of high costs and small populations added to the challenges facing doctors.

She said the federal government had a responsibility to fund the gap, rather than leaving it to local councils.

Solution pitched

In Kalbarri, 780km north west of Narembeen, a community group has hatched a plan to bring back medical services without overwhelming costs to ratepayers.

A Kalbarri charity has proposed a creative way to retain a GP practice. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

The town's only GP closed in June, leaving more than 1,500 people facing a two-hour round trip to see a doctor.

The Kalbarri Development Association (KDA) crowdfunded more than $70,000 to set up a not-for-profit, bulk-billing clinic that would be run by a community board.

KDA chair Merilynn Eastland said it was unacceptable that many country towns paid to prop up private GP businesses.

"We thought, 'Well, stuff that,'" she said.

"Any money we made would come back to the community, it doesn't go into any individual pockets."

Kalbarri residents rallied for the doctor service in August. (Supplied: Kalbarri Development Association)

Ms Eastland said the initial funds would be used to try to lease the Shire-owned clinic and cover set-up costs.

"We believe at the end of 12 months we will be well and truly profitable," she said.

Ms Eastland said similar not-for-profit clinics were operating across the country, and represented a way forward for smaller communities.

The tender for the clinic is expected to be awarded at the next Northampton Shire meeting, in November.

Locals fight to keep GP

The challenge facing smaller towns is laid bare in Donnybrook, where locals are fighting to secure one of the town's two remaining medical practices.

Regional residents are often forced to travel out of town to see a GP. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

Donnybrook Medical Services (DMS) says the cost and terms of its lease from the local council, coupled with operational costs, were a threat to its viability.

The clinic had leased the building from the Shire of Donnybrook-Balingup since 2021, with the lease expiring this year.

Local Samantha Wright started a petition to keep the practice in town, which has attracted more than 400 signatures.

"There is genuine concern and panic that if Donnybrook Medical Services were to close, we would lose seven doctors from this community," she said.

"I've got a daughter with additional needs and a chronic disease … I'm a single mum of four children and it's hard enough as is."

Samantha Wright started a petition to keep the medical practice in town. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet )

The shire said it was reviewing DMS's interest in purchasing the site from the WA government and the building from the council.

A state government spokesperson said the closure of any regional GP was concerning, and it would continue to advocate for federal government action.

World.title: Breaking: Earthquake reported by residents around Adelaide
World.content:
Residents from around Adelaide have reported feeling an earthquake this morning, with one saying he heard a rumble when his pot plants started shaking.

Geoscience Australia's website shows a magnitude-4.9 quake with an epicentre in waters south of Adelaide.

Callers to 891 ABC Adelaide reported rattling and shaking this morning, for several seconds.

"I just made a cup of coffee and hopped back into bed and then the whole bed moved and my coffee split," Kate from Reynella in Adelaide's south said.

Brian from Goolwa said he noticed all the pot plants started vibrating and "heard a bit of a rumble".

Josh said he was at Mount Barker when he noticed windows rattling and "the dog went a bit crazy".

"Went about three seconds, definitely an earthquake I think," he said.

Willunga local Mark said he did not hear anything but "the house just started shaking crazily".

"It's not real stable and vibrates when the washing machine's spinning but I got up to check that wasn't on," he said.

"I was sitting at the breakfast table and the next minute the wood started to shake," Goolwa local Heather said.

"It was like several motorbikes starting up at once and everything, the ground, shook. Really moved," another resident, from nearby Hindmarsh Island, said.

Closer to the city, Annie from Glenside, said the apartment vibrated.

"I'm on the third floor of a multi-storey apartment and it just moved from north to south for about four shakes from side to side," she said.

World.title: Fines of up to $120k for dumping pet fish in Adelaide river
World.content:
Adelaide residents are being urged not to release noxious koi carp or their unwanted goldfish into the River Torrens, following sightings of more than a dozen suspected koi at Hackney, and a smaller number upstream at Dernancourt.

The group of bright orange, black and muti-coloured fish at Hackney appeared last week between the St Peters Weir and Hackney Bridge.

Stuart Collard from Green Adelaide, the organisation responsible for managing the environment of the Torrens, said it was illegal to keep koi carp in South Australia and it was unusual to see such a large number in the river.

Some of the large group of koi spotted by an ABC reporter in the River Torrens at Hackney last week. (ABC South East SA: Caroline Horn)

"We haven't seen those numbers, or in fact many records at all, of koi within the river," he said.

Mr Collard said Green Adelaide suspected the fish had been released by members of the public.

Koi are considered a noxious species under the SA Fisheries Management Act and cannot be owned without a permit from the Minister for Primary Industries.

It is illegal to dump koi, goldfish or any non-native fish, into South Australian rivers and people can be fined up to $120,000 for doing so.

Stuart Collard is urging people not to dump koi, goldfish or other non-native fish into the River Torrens. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Goldfish dumping

Mr Collard said Green Adelaide regularly caught goldfish while carrying out surveys in the river.

"People do release them and we understand that there's a self-sustaining population within the river," he said.

"It's not the right place for these species to be."

Nets are being deployed at Dernancourt to try to catch the rogue koi carp. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Nets are currently being used at Dernancourt to try to catch the population of koi recently spotted in that part of the river.

Mr Collard said, like European carp, koi carp competed with native fish for food.

He said as bottom feeders, they stirred up the sediment that disturbed plants at the bottom of the river, impacting their growth.

"It's really important for these types of invasive fish species that we get on top of those populations early so that they don't expand and take up more space within the river," he said.

Matt Jacobs from the Glenelg Nature Trust undertaking work to catch the koi at Dernancourt. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Platypus dreams

James Johnston from the Invasive Species Council said it was disappointing to hear of the koi carp being spotted in the river, particularly with the funds and effort being used to try to help native fish, rakali and other species thrive.

The South Australian government announced in August that it would provide $4 million in additional funding to try to return platypus to the Torrens.

Work is being done to prepare the River Torrens for the reintroduction of platypus. (ABC News: Malcolm Sutton)

The unique animals were last recorded in the waterway in the 1880s, but Mr Collard said the river was getting close to being able to sustain a population again, with those reintroduced likely to be relocated from Victoria.

World.title: Live: Anthropic to hit stock market with 'eye-popping' growth and massive losses
World.content:
Anthropic has filed to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

Here are some of the key metrics or findings from the filing, from Dan Ives at Yorkville Ives:

In September 2025, 950 customers spent at least $100,000 a year on them. This grew to 11,900 a year later, including the US's 10 largest companies and more than half of the top 500.

The company has Net Revenue Retention of approximately 900%, which means that for every $1 of revenue on average from a customer, Anthropic is generating about $9 from them a year later. Almost 2,000 customers spend more than $1 million, and roughly 250 more than $10 million.

"Concentration is easing: no single customer exceeded 10% of revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, and roughly 79% of Q3 revenue came from outside the top five, up from roughly 64% in Q1, even as each top-five account hit a record. Revenue is overwhelmingly consumption-based ($13.1 billion in 1H26) with subscriptions at $3.2 billion, up from $180 million, and remaining performance obligations were $10.8 billion," Ives says.

Let's take a look at how revenue has changed in recent years:

$41 million in 2023

$386 million in 2024

$4.6 billion in 2025.

The first half of last year it made $1.2b, and increased it to $16.3b for the first half of this year.

With this said, Ives says "there are some concerning (not unexpected) risk factors" in the filing.

"Anthropic has asked its cloud partners for more compute than they were willing to provide, and those same partners build competing models and could curtail, reprice, or terminate access, all while the take-or-pay commitments above are owed regardless of actual usage and have been partly debt-funded. The filing also discloses past failed or underperforming training runs, warns that scaling laws may plateau, and flags that safety-driven release delays such as holding back Mythos through Project Glasswing could slow capability gains versus competitors and may become more frequent and costly as models advance."

The filing also flagged some potential liability of the AI agents including misuse by bad actors, models acting in unintended or autonomous ways that no user directed, and contractual protections and insurance that may prove insufficient.

World.title: Sydney University hires Jacinda Ardern as lecturer and mentor
World.content:
Former New Zealand prime minister Dame Jacinda Ardern has been appointed a lecturer and mentor at the University of Sydney.

The 46-year-old has been hired as a professor of practice "with a focus on empathetic leadership, social cohesion and civic trust", the university said.

In her role, Dame Jacinda will explore new ways to address global health challenges, inclusion and wellbeing, as well as lead guest lectures and masterclasses.

Jacinda Ardern and vice-chancellor Mark Scott at the university. (Supplied: The University of Sydney/ Stefanie Zingsheim)

According to the university, the position would not be a full-time teaching role.

Dame Jacinda said she was hoping to "explore and develop ways to better serve our communities".

"I've found myself especially focused on the question of leadership since leaving office – and how we can better support and encourage the kind of leadership needed to tackle our many global challenges," she said.

University of Sydney vice-chancellor and president Mark Scott said he had "long admired the courage and humanity" Dame Jacinda brought to public life.

"For our students, the opportunity to learn from Dame Jacinda is exceptional. They will meet not only a former prime minister, but a thoughtful teacher with a great deal to share about public leadership and service," he said.

Dame Jacinda was elected prime minister of New Zealand at 37 and served in office between 2017 and 2023.

During her tenure, she led the country through the Christchurch terrorist attack, the Whakaari White Island volcanic eruption and the COVID pandemic.

In 2023, she was awarded a damehood for her services to the state, a few months after she announced her shock resignation as prime minister.

Dame Jacinda and her family moved to Australia in February, reportedly buying a $5.3 million home with her husband, Clarke Gayford, on Sydney's northern beaches.

World.title: Prison officers fear deaths in custody under Queensland bill
World.content:
Prison officers fear there could be deaths in custody and increased assaults on staff under a proposed Queensland bill exempting them from having to consider prisoners' human rights.

The bill removes a requirement for corrective services staff to comply with, or properly consider, prisoners' human rights.

If passed, prisoners would have no basis to complain to the Queensland Human Rights Commission.

The ABC has spoken with current and former officers who oppose the changes and fear they will only make their jobs more dangerous if jails become more crowded and prisoners' human rights are not respected.

Their names have been changed for safety reasons and because of their employment.

The proposed exemption would mean prison staff would not have to consider prisoners' human rights. (correctiveservices.qld.gov.au)

Jordan works in a regional Queensland jail and is concerned prisons could move to triple bunking, where three prisoners are housed in a cell built for one.

The ABC understands triple bunking is not currently occurring throughout the state. But Together Queensland, a union that covers prison guards, warned last week that "triple bunking" would have to be considered once new breach bail laws come into effect due to an expected influx of prisoners.

"We don't want it. It's going to be bloody awful," Jordan said.

"Putting three people in a [small] square cell is a f***ing bad idea."

Do you know more? Contact regional Queensland investigations reporter Eden Gillespie at Gillespie.Eden@abc.net.au

at Gillespie.Eden@abc.net.au If your information is sensitive, you can also reach her at eden.gillespie96@proton.me

Threats to staff had escalated, Jordan said, as prisoners became increasingly frustrated by overcrowding.

"I'm worried there will be deaths in custody," he said.

"[Prison staff] are thinking, are we going to get flogged [by prisoners] because they're pissed off?"

Jordan said prisoners were already being kept in cells for up to 20 hours a day and waiting up to eight months to see a dentist, even without the human rights exemption.

"If we don't facilitate the stuff that they need, they don't get that, and that's not right," he said.

"We have a much better day if they are happy. We have much better rehabilitation opportunities for them if we can get them to their courses, their visits and into medical."

Prisoners are already being held in cells for up to 20 hours a day, according to one corrective services officer. (Supplied: Daniel Soekov, Human Rights Watch)

Trent, a former correctional officer, is also worried about the potential of triple bunking prisoners.

He said officers must look through a small window overnight to check whether prisoners are breathing.

"One hundred per cent [there could be a death]," Trent said.

"There's no way you're going to be able to see all three prisoners by looking through that window with one of them sleeping on a mattress directly below the door on the floor."

Brett Thompson from the Queensland Homicide Victim Support Group told a parliamentary committee that victims' rights are often overlooked. (ABC News: Kristian Silva)

But some advocates say it is victims' rights that are being overlooked.

"Human rights, weirdly, does not seem to consider the person who had the rights, whose life has been taken in the first place by someone else," Brett Thompson, the chief executive of the Queensland Homicide Victims' Support Group, told the parliamentary committee earlier this month.

He was responding to concerns raised by the Bar Association that limiting prisoners' human rights and parole options could leave the community less safe.

Queensland Corrective Services (QCS) did not respond to the ABC's questions about triple bunking, cell hours or dental wait times.

"QCS is firmly committed to keeping Queenslanders safe and ensuring the safety and security within correctional centres," a QCS spokesperson said.

"[We] are delivering more beds to increase capacity and have increased staff by more than 2,000 officers in less than 24 months."

Queensland Corrective Services supported the exemption, saying it was necessary for staff and community safety. (Supplied: Queensland Ombudsman)

QCS told the parliamentary committee the proposed changes were needed to keep officers and the community safe, particularly when managing dangerous sex offenders.

The exemption would apply to those on remand and all prisoners, not only those convicted of murder or sex offences.

Corrective Services Minister Laura Gerber said: "The Crisafulli government will always put the rights of victims ahead of the rights of offenders."

World.title: ‘Outrageous’: Payman asks if PM is waiting for attack on her in bitter staff feud
World.content:
PoliticsFederalWorkplace culture ‘Outrageous’: Payman asks if PM is waiting for attack on her in bitter staff feud James Massola October 27, 2026 — 9:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Independent WA senator Fatima Payman has stunned a parliamentary committee hearing by asking if Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was waiting for a Helen Haines-style attack on her before finally granting the senator additional staff. Payman refused to withdraw the comment, stating she would only do so if she were granted the additional political staffers. One Nation senator Pauline Hanson and senator Fatima Payman at a press conference in September. Alex Ellinghausen On the same day when MPs lined up to deliver tributes to Haines, who last week had both her legs amputated after she was rammed by a four-wheel-drive outside her office, many politicians called for the temperature to be turned down on political debate. Payman, who has been targeted more than most MPs with abuse and extremist threats, has been asking for nearly two years for Albanese to allocate her two additional “adviser” level staff – who are paid better than electorate staff that all MPs have – to cope with the demands of being an independent representative.



Last Thursday, a Queensland Bunnings worker pleaded guilty to six counts of using a carriage service to menace or harass Payman, including a phone call in March where he hoped the senator would be run over by a truck. Last November, a Ballarat man pleaded guilty to threatening the senator by email, writing that there was a bullet with her name on it. Payman’s office estimates it has referred over 100 incidents to Australian Federal Police. In a Senate estimates hearing late on Monday evening, Payman asked Special Minister of State Don Farrell why senators including Lidia Thorpe and Tammy Tyrrell received extra personal staffing allocations after leaving their original political parties. Loading “Has the prime minister refused to make a decision on my request because, unlike all the other defectors, I defected from the Labor Party? Am I being made an example of?” Payman asked.



Farrell said he would raise the matter with Albanese again, prompting a furious response from the WA senator. “I’ve been raising it for two years ... my staff are expected to do the job of an office that has seven full-timers, so I don’t know how the ‘same job, same pay’ thing that Labor keeps bragging about applies to my team? “They can’t take this any longer. And is the prime minister waiting for something like what happened to Dr Helen Haines to occur to my office, to me, for him to take our request seriously?” The comment drew an immediate rebuke from Farrell and Labor committee chair senator Karen Grogan.



“I personally think that’s an outrageous suggestion, Senator Payman,” Farrell said. Related Article One Nation Hanson demands PM play fair and double her staffing allocation Payman shot back: “I can’t believe that I’m saying that, or making that suggestion, because it’s been two years.” Grogan then interrupted and suggested that Payman take a moment “to think about those kind of accusations” and said the senator had made an outrageous statement. Farrell suggested Payman “go further and withdraw that suggestion about the prime minister’s motivation. Because it’s absolutely not the case”.



But Payman refused to withdraw her comment and said: “With all due respect, I haven’t made any accusation.” Grogan replied: “I think you just did.” Payman said: “I mean, you can take it as an accusation, minister. But once you’ve discussed it [staffing allocations] with the prime minister, and if he thinks that’s an accusation, then I’ll withdraw it.” The visibly upset WA senator then added: “I’ve been waiting two years, chair, and I am tired of looking in my staff’s eyes and saying you’ll just have to deal with this because the prime minister is petty and is taking it out on me.” Grogan said the comments were unparliamentary and that she would be “delighted” to raise it with Senate president Sue Lines. “We should be better than that, and particularly on a day like today, we should all be better than that, but you’re not going to be,” Grogan replied.



Albanese has sole discretion over the amount of staff allocated to independent and opposition parties, and most independents have either one or two additional adviser-level staff. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership Albanese granted Greens 15 staff just before party blocked inquiry into PM’s powers Earlier in the hearing, Payman asked Farrell a series of questions about the allocation of extra staff to independent MPs, including why independent MP Nicolette Boele and Greens leaders Larissa Waters – and then David Shoebridge – all had their requests for extra staff met while she did not. The new Greens leader had his request to maintain the additional advisers allocated to Waters within two weeks, compared to the 23 months Payman has been waiting. Days later, the Greens voted with Labor to block One Nation’s motion calling for a staffing inquiry. Farrell replied: “I’m sure the prime minister, as he always does, gives it due consideration and at this point has not made a decision to allocate additional staff to yourself.”



One Nation has also been campaigning for additional staff and arguing the allocation granted to it, since it achieved official minor party status, does not reflect the six seats that it holds. Payman and Pauline Hanson recently joined forces to campaign for a more equitable allocation of staff across the parliament. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Justice Department charges former FBI boss James Comey for third time
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Washington: The US Department of Justice has charged former FBI director James Comey with leaking national defence information, marking the third time the political enemy of President Donald Trump has been indicted in the past 13 months.

The charges, unsealed on Monday (US time), accuse Comey with directing an individual, “through one and more co-conspirators”, to disclose national defence information to a reporter for a national news publication in 2016, while he was FBI director.

Donald Trump and James Comey. AP

Comey already faces charges over an Instagram photograph he posted showing seashells on a beach arranged to spell “86 47”. This was alleged to be a death threat against Trump because “86” in restaurant parlance means to get rid of something. It has also sometimes been appropriated as a mob term.

Last year, Comey was indicted on charges of making false statements to a 2020 Senate hearing and obstructing a congressional investigation. But that case was thrown out by a judge who found that the prosecutor bringing the case, Trump’s former personal lawyer Lindsey Halligan, was illegally appointed.

World.title: Former ABC News chief’s payout revealed
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Former ABC News director Justin Stevens was given a $353,000 payout when he abruptly exited the public broadcaster in May.

Stevens, who spent 19 years at the ABC, exited earlier this year after managing director Hugh Marks had already lined up his replacement, Simon Robinson.

Justin Stevens (left) and ABC managing director Hugh Marks at a Senate estimates hearing in December. Alex Ellinghausen

The figure, which could include leave and other entitlements, was revealed in the ABC’s annual report, released on Monday evening as executives from the broadcaster prepare to appear in front of a Senate estimates committee on Tuesday.

The ABC has experienced significant turnover in its senior ranks since the arrival of Marks. Almost his entire management team has been replaced during this period, including the recent exit of chief operating officer Melanie Kleyn, who has been replaced by Trent Dickeson from Seven West Media. Kleyn was paid a full package of $869,771 in 2026 and is expected to have landed a severance package as well.

World.title: ASX set to dip, Wall Street climbs; Anthropic files for IPO; Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 workers
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to dip, Wall Street climbs; Anthropic files for IPO; Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 workers Stan Choe Updated October 27, 2026 — 8:15am ,first published 5:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
