US stocks climbed as investors digest Anthropic’s filing for its initial public offering and look ahead to key big tech earnings this week. The S&P 500 rose 0.7 per cent and more than recovered its losses from last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 146 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite closed 0.8 per cent higher. Anthropic’s IPO filing gave tech stocks a boost on Monday. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to dip, with futures pointing to a loss of 6 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.2 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.25¢. Anthropic PBC filed for its long-awaited IPO, a landmark moment in the artificial-intelligence industry that is growing ever-hungrier for cash to power ahead.



The company behind Claude expects to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT, a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission showed. Anthropic filed confidentially in June for a listing. Investors are telling bankers on the deal that their estimate of a fair valuation has shifted down to around $US1.4 trillion to $US1.5 trillion ($2-$2.1 trillion) following the company’s investor day, according to people familiar with the matter. A valuation of closer to $US1.75 trillion is potentially achievable, some of the people said, asking not to be identified as the information isn’t public. Microsoft closed 1.5 per cent higher after it announced it will offer buyouts to about 60,000 workers, part of the company’s efforts to trim costs and retool its workforce for the artificial intelligence era. Some personnel in the US, Canada, India and the UK at a vice president level and below will be eligible, said a Microsoft spokesperson. Related Article Opinion

World markets The ‘death spiral’ that could destroy this Wall Street boom The strongest lift for the market came from Nvidia, which rose 2.4 per cent. That helped the chip company recover some of its drop from three straight losing weeks, its longest such streak since June, and maintain its position as the largest stock on Wall Street above Apple.



But stocks elsewhere in the artificial-intelligence industry remained unsettled. They’ve been swerving on worries about whether their industry’s boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips. Stocks are recovering their losses from last week ahead of a number of earnings reports this week from big companies, including Amazon and Intel. The company behind Claude expects to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT AP Meta Platforms bounced up and down after outlining plans to raise $US35 billion by selling stock to help pay for its AI investments. It also said it could raise another $US60 billion by selling shares of a new class of its stock once it begins trading. Meta’s stock initially dropped more than 2 per cent, but it quickly flipped to a gain and then pulled back to a loss of 1.9 per cent. Meta said Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom have already indicated they may buy a total of $US5 billion of stock in its offering. That’s a signal of strong interest from big chip companies that stand to benefit from additional AI investments. But it also gives fuel to critics of “circular financing” who say it raises the risk if AI isn’t as successful as expected.



SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket company that also runs the xAI business, had similar swings. It opened with a loss and then flipped to a gain of 0.4 per cent after it agreed to a roughly $US40 billion deal with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management to lease AI computing power. Musk warned over the weekend that hundreds of companies that rent out AI computing power are under threat because of the difficulty in borrowing money, saying on his social-media platform, X, that they could face “guppy-level death and consolidation.” CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed money to buy AI computing power that it rents to customers, has been at the centre of investors’ worries in recent weeks. On Monday, it dropped 5.5 per cent quickly after trading began, only to flip to a gain of 1.8 per cent by the close. Such minute-to-minute swings have become commonplace for it in recent days. Profit reports from huge tech companies this upcoming week could offer more details about how spending on AI is going, and whether it’s producing the profits and productivity that proponents promised. Alphabet and Microsoft will report their latest quarterly results on Wednesday, with Amazon to follow on Thursday.



Companies across all industries are under pressure to report strong growth in their profits. Expectations for big growth are what allowed their stock prices to run to records recently despite worries about high inflation, high interest rates and other concerns. Verizon Communications fell 3.5 per cent even though it reported a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, as its revenue fell short of forecasts. Roughly one out of every three stocks in the S&P 500 is scheduled to report its latest quarterly results this week. In stock markets abroad, Brazilian stocks fell sharply after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection in a result that surprised investors. Other governments around the world are also feeling pressure because of their high debt loads and worries about strained budgets. France has been at the centre of the worries recently following violent protests in the country.



But yields on French government bonds eased Monday, and its CAC 40 stock index rose 0.8 per cent for one of the world’s better moves. Indexes also rose in other European markets following a mixed finish in Asia. The European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan will be meeting to vote on interest rates later this week. Related Article AI AI darling NextDC announces board and pay purge after Melbourne power disaster In the US bond market, yields fell for longer-term Treasurys. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.98 per cent from 5.00 per cent late Friday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month. The two-year Treasury yield edged up to 4.71 per cent from 4.69 per cent late Friday. It more closely tracks expectations for what the Federal Reserve will do with overnight interest rates, and the widespread expectation is that it will say on Wednesday that it is leaving the federal funds rate alone following its latest meeting.



The Fed last month hiked the fed funds rate for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing inflation, which has remained much higher than anyone would like. The price for a barrel of Brent crude fell toward $US109 in the morning, but it later erased the losses and returned to $US111.40. It remains near the high end of its range since the war with Iran began. The highest price for the most actively traded contract in the market for Brent crude since then is nearly $US120, reached in March. World.title: Australian musician G Flip and reality star partner Chrishell Stause break up
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCelebrity relationships Australian musician G Flip and reality star partner Chrishell Stause break up Chris Hook October 27, 2026 — 7:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Australian musician G Flip has broken up with their American reality TV star partner Chrishell Stause after a four-year relationship. Stause, 45, who appears on the Netflix real estate show Selling Sunset, announced the break-up with her 33-year-old partner in an emotional Instagram video on Tuesday morning (AEDT). “I have a pretty humbling update to share with you guys, G and I are no longer together,” she said. “We have agreed to treat this public separation with love and respect for each other. It’s not hard for me because I am in love with this person and I don’t have all the information and the reasons … I’m sure, like always, with time you get the lessons you’re meant to get and I know that will happen.



“ I’m going to heal and everything’s going to be fine and I’m definitely never doing this again,” Stause finished. Chrishell Stause and G Flip attend the 2022 ARIA Awards in Sydney. Hanna Lassen G Flip confirmed the split via a post on her Instagram account. “After 4+ years Chrishell and I are no longer together. I will always love her. We will always share a special connection and I will cherish our memories together deeply,” she wrote. “My head & heart are feeling very heavy right now, and I’m not able to talk but I want to thank you all for your support and appreciate you respecting our privacy at this difficult time.”



Melbourne-born performer G Flip, whose real name is Georgia Claire Flipo, met Stause at a Halloween party, hosted by fellow Australian star Tones and I in 2021, according to Vulture. They married in Las Vegas in 2023 and just last year G Flip told this masthead’s Sunday Life magazine they were trying to start a family. Loading “We’ve been going through a rough time with the IVF process,” G Flip said. “We’ve been struggling with it, and though we don’t like talking too much about it because it ends up ruining our day, we acknowledge it. Queer couples are couples like anyone else.



“To anyone going through IVF or finding themselves on a rough road with bringing life into the world, we feel for you and we understand and we see you.” G Flip first broke through after featuring on Triple J’s Unearthed segment in 2018, then released a debut album About Us in 2019, which garnered three ARIA nominations. Their second album Drummer debuted at No.1 on the ARIA charts in 2023 and G Flip went on to win their first ARIA that year for Best Australian Live Act, followed by the 2024 Song of the Year for The Worst Person Alive. They came out as non-binary in 2021, and discussed their identity with Sunday Life last year. “A non-binary person is who I am – I don’t know how to be anything else. I use they/them pronouns and am very proud of that. I am in a queer relationship and have a beautiful wife. I write from experience and from the perspective of a non-binary queer person.



“When I was growing up, I didn’t have that representation. The backbone of my G Flip project is to be the person I never saw when I was younger. I want to make sure I am making art so that a queer kid somewhere in the world can see me online and feel they are like me.” After meeting Stause, their relationship was kept largely under wraps, before Stause spoke about G Flip on a Selling Sunset reunion before video emerged of the pair kissing just a few weeks later in May 2022. Although Stause had been dating real estate agent Jason Oppenheim at the time they met, they reportedly broke up in late 2021 over Stause’s desire to have children. In June last year, amid G Flip and Stause’s attempts to get pregnant they renewed their wedding vows, hiring a castle in the Hollywood Hills for the event. Next month G Flip heads to Australia for a series of shows across the country, both solo and as the support act for Robbie Williams’ stadium shows in Sydney and Melbourne. Opposition spokesman for foreign affairs Ted O’Brien says Labor’s trade deal with the EU is not in the best interests of Australia and is calling on Albanese to drop the agreement’s climate clauses.

“The main concern I have is the inclusion of legally binding obligations with respect to climate change,” he told News24 this morning.

The EU mandates legally binding climate change rules in its free trade agreements, including enforcing commitments to the Paris Agreement.

Opposition spokesman for foreign affairs Ted O’Brien. James Brickwood

But O’Brien said he had written to Foreign Minister Penny Wong with a “constructive proposal” to remove the climate clauses from the trade deal.

“What we’re not prepared to do is basically give away the right of future governments to set policy in this country … That is what Labor is proposing through these climate clauses, and so they’re saying nothing to worry about,” he said.

“My answer is: Okay. Put that in writing. That that’s what you do in the real world, and I don’t think it’s too much to ask. They need to cooperate.”

World.title: This brother and sister co-founded Anthropic five years ago. Now they are worth $19 billion each
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesWall Street This brother and sister co-founded Anthropic five years ago. Now they are worth $19 billion each Tom Maloney , Rebecca Torrence and Dylan Sloan October 27, 2026 — 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Anthropic’s seven co-founders each hold roughly 1.4 per cent of the company, its IPO filing revealed, giving them individual fortunes of more than $US13 billion ($18.5 billion). That vaults all of them, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, among the top 300 people on the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, and makes them richer than well-known finance billionaires like Bill Ackman and Stan Druckenmiller. Siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei co-founded Anthropic five years ago. Bloomberg The fortunes, which are based on Anthropic’s $US965 billion valuation in its last funding round, jumped from Bloomberg’s previous calculation of $US8 billion each. If Anthropic succeeds in reaching a $US2 trillion valuation in its initial public offering — a number that was previously floated by investors — they would rise to more than $US27 billion each before accounting for dilution from newly issued shares, according to Bloomberg’s wealth index. The founders’ net worth underscores the utter dominance of tech, and particularly artificial intelligence, in driving both the US stock market and wealth creation this year. Tech fortunes among the world’s 500 richest people gained a combined $US845 billion through the first nine months of 2026, while billionaires outside tech saw their average net worth shrink.



Related Article Opinion

World markets The ‘death spiral’ that could destroy this Wall Street boom In a letter to potential shareholders, Anthropic’s co-founders said that AI and Anthropic “represents one of the greatest economic opportunities in history.” Along with the Amodeis, the other Anthropic co-founders are Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and Christopher Olah. All seven have pledged to dedicate 80 per cent of their personal equity in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, according to the filing. The size of the founders’ stakes belies their control over the company. Under Anthropic’s proposed governance structure, each founder remains a member of the Founder LLC — which controls a Class F share carrying 50.1 per cent of shareholder voting power — as long as they retain at least 2 per cent of the number of Class A shares they held when the company goes public. That means a founder could dispose of 98 per cent of their existing stake and still retain an equal say with the other founders over how that controlling share is voted.



The founders’ majority voting control is somewhat offset by Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, however, which has the power to elect and remove four members of the company’s seven-person board. The trust is designed to continue indefinitely, while the founders’ special voting share will eventually expire once fewer than three qualifying founders remain, whether because of death, incapacity, resignation or because they have sold or given away more than roughly 98 per cent of the Class A shares they held at the IPO. Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark. Bloomberg The trust is governed by five trustees, who largely select their own replacements. San Francisco-based Anthropic was started in 2021 by a group of former OpenAI employees who left following disagreements over the company’s future direction. Anthropic had an $US80.7 billion net loss on revenue of $US16.3 billion in the first six months of 2026, versus a $US13 billion net loss on revenue of $US1.2 billion in the same period last year, the filing shows. Anthropic confirmed that chief executive officer Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei sold some of their shares in the company’s tender offers in 2025 and 2026. Last year, Anthropic kicked off a $US157 million tender that saw both siblings unload some of their stock. This year, Anthropic did a $US4.7 billion tender; the Amodeis, chief financial officer Krishna Rao, and Holden Karnofsky, the spouse of Daniela Amodei, all sold shares in that offering.



Anthropic also paid $US5 million in regulatory filing fees on behalf of the Amodeis this year related to their acquisition and ownership of Anthropic securities. In a letter to potential shareholders, Anthropic’s co-founders said that AI and Anthropic “represents one of the greatest economic opportunities in history.” Bloomberg It’s not just the founders who are getting rich: Anthropic’s employees and other option holders were sitting on about $US98 billion in potential gains from their stock options as of June, based on figures in the filing. Those gains reflect how sharply the company’s value has risen since many employees received their stock options. Employees and other holders could buy the shares underlying their outstanding options at an average price of just $US2.89 a share as of June. Altogether, exercising those options would cost about $US5.2 billion — while on paper, the underlying shares are estimated to be worth more than $US103 billion. Anthropic also operates a donation-matching program that lets employees pledge a portion of their equity awards to eligible charities, with the company matching those donations in shares of its non-voting Class N stock. In August, it recognised a $US2 billion expense tied to employee donations in that month that resulted in it issuing 28 million shares for matching purposes. The co-founders’ pledge to donate 80 per cent of their equity isn’t eligible for the matching program.

World.title: Legal shootout as rival soccer comps feud over fees, safety concerns
World.content:
SportSoccerFootball Australia Legal shootout as rival soccer comps feud over fees, safety concerns Jon Pierik October 27, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A local soccer association is fighting Football Victoria over changes it claims will lead to higher fees for families if they are forced to play under the governing body’s banner. The Greater Melbourne Soccer Association – which has about 2500 registered players across 60 senior teams and 46 under-six to under-eight teams, and runs the biggest over-35s competition in the state – has taken its concerns to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. A feud is simmering between the Greater Melbourne Soccer Association and Football Victoria. Under rules to be introduced next year, clubs affiliated with Football Victoria will require written approval to join external competitions where FV offers a corresponding competition. The Greater Melbourne Soccer Association fears clubs could be deregistered if they do not join FV-sanctioned competitions, and says the proposed changes will affect thousands of players.



The association, which has engaged law firm Lander and Rogers to challenge the new restrictions, wrote the ACCC to raise concerns about possible breaches of the competition and consumer act, relating to misuse of market power and exclusive dealing. Related Article Analysis

Australia Cup Let them in: South Melbourne just showed the A-League what it has been missing Andrew Ellis, the president of the association, said the impending restrictions could impact the affordability, diversity and independence of community soccer in Melbourne. “Football Victoria runs its own competitions. It shouldn’t also get to decide whether clubs can participate in ours,” he said. “Clubs should be able to enter teams in both FV and GMSA competitions without putting their affiliation at risk. They deserve the freedom to choose competitions that best suit their players, families and communities.”



Ellis said the restrictions could force clubs to enter the more expensive FV leagues. A detailed report by his association, based on 2026 figures, said registration for a senior team of 25 players was $2200, while a Football Victoria metropolitan fee for the same team would be $6800. For junior players in under-seven and under-eight competitions, there was a $38 discrepancy in fees according to the Greater Melbourne Soccer Association’s analysis. Soccer is typically one of the more expensive sports to play at junior and pathway level because of the cost of registration fees, compared with other sports. FV did not comment specifically on the figures provided by the association but said in a statement it was not seeking to stymie competitions or clubs.



“Football Victoria is not seeking to prevent alternative football leagues from operating, nor to stop clubs, players or administrators from participating in other organisations. Rather, clubs that wish to retain the benefits and protections of affiliation to Football Victoria and the Football Australia pathway must meet minimum standards when participating in external competitions,” the statement said. Related Article Analysis

A-League Men The A-League can’t afford to play more games. It also can’t afford not to FV said the three core areas of proposed changes were child safety safeguards, insurance and dealing with disciplinary and integrity standards. “Ultimately, this is about ensuring that all activities involving FV-affiliated clubs meet appropriate standards of safety, accountability and governance, regardless of where football is being played,” the statement said. FV has engaged legal firm Carrington Legal to fight their case.



Ellis said FV’s initial response to his claims was that rival leagues providing the equivalent competitions would not be approved. He said in subsequent legal correspondence, FV said change was needed to ensure the appropriate insurance, consistent child safety standards, event scheduling, governance and integrity mechanisms were all met. Lander and Rogers competition law partner Philip Aitken, who has written to the ACCC on behalf of the GMSA, said: “Firms with a substantial degree of market power must not engage in conduct that has the purpose, effect or likely effect of substantially lessening competition”. Ellis said the GMSA supported the highest standard of administration.



“We fully support appropriate child safety, insurance, integrity and governance standards across community football,” he said. Related Article Premier League ‘He wants to be put out of his misery’. Carrick on brink of Manchester United sacking “FV is not a government regulator, but it is acting like one. We both provide football competitions to clubs and players. FV should not be both a competitor and the referee deciding whether rival competitions can operate. “Football Victoria says it isn’t trying to prevent alternative football competitions from operating. “Its own words tell a very different story. In a briefing pack provided to clubs on 11 September 2026, FV explicitly stated: ‘In summary, if FV provides a competition that an external provider is also offering, that external competition will not be on the approved list’.



“That isn’t a child safety standard. That’s a policy designed to exclude competing competitions. FV is now attempting to justify its restrictions by raising child safety, insurance and disciplinary standards. These are important matters, but none requires clubs to be prevented from participating in alternative competitions.” Ellis said, “GMSA has supported grassroots football for almost 50 years, and we’re not about to walk away from the clubs and communities that have supported us”. World.title: ‘Outrageous’: Payman asks if PM is waiting for attack on her in bitter staff feud
World.content:
PoliticsFederalWorkplace culture ‘Outrageous’: Payman asks if PM is waiting for attack on her in bitter staff feud James Massola October 27, 2026 — 9:13am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Independent WA senator Fatima Payman has stunned a parliamentary committee hearing by asking if Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was waiting for a Helen Haines-style attack on her before finally granting the senator additional staff. Payman refused to withdraw the comment, stating she would only do so if she were granted the additional political staffers. One Nation senator Pauline Hanson and senator Fatima Payman at a press conference in September. Alex Ellinghausen On the same day when MPs lined up to deliver tributes to Haines, who last week had both her legs amputated after she was rammed by a four-wheel-drive outside her office, many politicians called for the temperature to be turned down on political debate. Payman, who has been targeted more than most MPs with abuse and extremist threats, has been asking for nearly two years for Albanese to allocate her two additional “adviser” level staff – who are paid better than electorate staff that all MPs have – to cope with the demands of being an independent representative.



Last Thursday, a Queensland Bunnings worker pleaded guilty to six counts of using a carriage service to menace or harass Payman, including a phone call in March where he hoped the senator would be run over by a truck. Last November, a Ballarat man pleaded guilty to threatening the senator by email, writing that there was a bullet with her name on it. Payman’s office estimates it has referred over 100 incidents to Australian Federal Police. In a Senate estimates hearing late on Monday evening, Payman asked Special Minister of State Don Farrell why senators including Lidia Thorpe and Tammy Tyrrell received extra personal staffing allocations after leaving their original political parties. Loading “Has the prime minister refused to make a decision on my request because, unlike all the other defectors, I defected from the Labor Party? Am I being made an example of?” Payman asked.



Farrell said he would raise the matter with Albanese again, prompting a furious response from the WA senator. “I’ve been raising it for two years ... my staff are expected to do the job of an office that has seven full-timers, so I don’t know how the ‘same job, same pay’ thing that Labor keeps bragging about applies to my team? “They can’t take this any longer. And is the prime minister waiting for something like what happened to Dr Helen Haines to occur to my office, to me, for him to take our request seriously?” The comment drew an immediate rebuke from Farrell and Labor committee chair senator Karen Grogan.



“I personally think that’s an outrageous suggestion, Senator Payman,” Farrell said. Related Article One Nation Hanson demands PM play fair and double her staffing allocation Payman shot back: “I can’t believe that I’m saying that, or making that suggestion, because it’s been two years.” Grogan then interrupted and suggested that Payman take a moment “to think about those kind of accusations” and said the senator had made an outrageous statement. Farrell suggested Payman “go further and withdraw that suggestion about the prime minister’s motivation. Because it’s absolutely not the case”.



But Payman refused to withdraw her comment and said: “With all due respect, I haven’t made any accusation.” Grogan replied: “I think you just did.” Payman said: “I mean, you can take it as an accusation, minister. But once you’ve discussed it [staffing allocations] with the prime minister, and if he thinks that’s an accusation, then I’ll withdraw it.” The visibly upset WA senator then added: “I’ve been waiting two years, chair, and I am tired of looking in my staff’s eyes and saying you’ll just have to deal with this because the prime minister is petty and is taking it out on me.” Grogan said the comments were unparliamentary and that she would be “delighted” to raise it with Senate president Sue Lines. “We should be better than that, and particularly on a day like today, we should all be better than that, but you’re not going to be,” Grogan replied.



Albanese has sole discretion over the amount of staff allocated to independent and opposition parties, and most independents have either one or two additional adviser-level staff. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership Albanese granted Greens 15 staff just before party blocked inquiry into PM’s powers Earlier in the hearing, Payman asked Farrell a series of questions about the allocation of extra staff to independent MPs, including why independent MP Nicolette Boele and Greens leaders Larissa Waters – and then David Shoebridge – all had their requests for extra staff met while she did not. The new Greens leader had his request to maintain the additional advisers allocated to Waters within two weeks, compared to the 23 months Payman has been waiting. Days later, the Greens voted with Labor to block One Nation’s motion calling for a staffing inquiry. Farrell replied: “I’m sure the prime minister, as he always does, gives it due consideration and at this point has not made a decision to allocate additional staff to yourself.”



One Nation has also been campaigning for additional staff and arguing the allocation granted to it, since it achieved official minor party status, does not reflect the six seats that it holds. Payman and Pauline Hanson recently joined forces to campaign for a more equitable allocation of staff across the parliament. World.title: Justice Department charges former FBI boss James Comey for third time
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Washington: The US Department of Justice has charged former FBI director James Comey with leaking national defence information, marking the third time the political enemy of President Donald Trump has been indicted in the past 13 months.

The charges, unsealed on Monday (US time), accuse Comey with directing an individual, “through one and more co-conspirators”, to disclose national defence information to a reporter for a national news publication in 2016, while he was FBI director.

Donald Trump and James Comey. AP

Comey already faces charges over an Instagram photograph he posted showing seashells on a beach arranged to spell “86 47”. This was alleged to be a death threat against Trump because “86” in restaurant parlance means to get rid of something. It has also sometimes been appropriated as a mob term.

Last year, Comey was indicted on charges of making false statements to a 2020 Senate hearing and obstructing a congressional investigation. But that case was thrown out by a judge who found that the prosecutor bringing the case, Trump’s former personal lawyer Lindsey Halligan, was illegally appointed.

World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Former ABC News director Justin Stevens was given a $353,000 payout when he abruptly exited the public broadcaster in May.

Stevens, who spent 19 years at the ABC, exited earlier this year after managing director Hugh Marks had already lined up his replacement, Simon Robinson.

Justin Stevens (left) and ABC managing director Hugh Marks at a Senate estimates hearing in December. Alex Ellinghausen

The figure, which could include leave and other entitlements, was revealed in the ABC’s annual report, released on Monday evening as executives from the broadcaster prepare to appear in front of a Senate estimates committee on Tuesday.

The ABC has experienced significant turnover in its senior ranks since the arrival of Marks. Almost his entire management team has been replaced during this period, including the recent exit of chief operating officer Melanie Kleyn, who has been replaced by Trent Dickeson from Seven West Media. Kleyn was paid a full package of $869,771 in 2026 and is expected to have landed a severance package as well.

World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to dip, Wall Street climbs; Anthropic files for IPO; Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 workers Stan Choe Updated October 27, 2026 — 8:15am ,first published 5:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. US stocks climbed as investors digest Anthropic’s filing for its initial public offering and look ahead to key big tech earnings this week. The S&P 500 rose 0.7 per cent and more than recovered its losses from last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 146 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite closed 0.8 per cent higher. Anthropic’s IPO filing gave tech stocks a boost on Monday. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to dip, with futures pointing to a loss of 6 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.2 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.25¢. Anthropic PBC filed for its long-awaited IPO, a landmark moment in the artificial-intelligence industry that is growing ever-hungrier for cash to power ahead.



The company behind Claude expects to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT, a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission showed. Anthropic filed confidentially in June for a listing. Investors are telling bankers on the deal that their estimate of a fair valuation has shifted down to around $US1.4 trillion to $US1.5 trillion ($2-$2.1 trillion) following the company’s investor day, according to people familiar with the matter. A valuation of closer to $US1.75 trillion is potentially achievable, some of the people said, asking not to be identified as the information isn’t public. Microsoft closed 1.5 per cent higher after it announced it will offer buyouts to about 60,000 workers, part of the company’s efforts to trim costs and retool its workforce for the artificial intelligence era. Some personnel in the US, Canada, India and the UK at a vice president level and below will be eligible, said a Microsoft spokesperson. Related Article Opinion

World markets The ‘death spiral’ that could destroy this Wall Street boom The strongest lift for the market came from Nvidia, which rose 2.4 per cent. That helped the chip company recover some of its drop from three straight losing weeks, its longest such streak since June, and maintain its position as the largest stock on Wall Street above Apple.



But stocks elsewhere in the artificial-intelligence industry remained unsettled. They’ve been swerving on worries about whether their industry’s boom is under threat because of how expensive it’s become for companies to borrow money to build data centres and buy more AI chips. Stocks are recovering their losses from last week ahead of a number of earnings reports this week from big companies, including Amazon and Intel. The company behind Claude expects to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT AP Meta Platforms bounced up and down after outlining plans to raise $US35 billion by selling stock to help pay for its AI investments. It also said it could raise another $US60 billion by selling shares of a new class of its stock once it begins trading. Meta’s stock initially dropped more than 2 per cent, but it quickly flipped to a gain and then pulled back to a loss of 1.9 per cent. Meta said Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom have already indicated they may buy a total of $US5 billion of stock in its offering. That’s a signal of strong interest from big chip companies that stand to benefit from additional AI investments. But it also gives fuel to critics of “circular financing” who say it raises the risk if AI isn’t as successful as expected.



SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket company that also runs the xAI business, had similar swings. It opened with a loss and then flipped to a gain of 0.4 per cent after it agreed to a roughly $US40 billion deal with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management to lease AI computing power. Musk warned over the weekend that hundreds of companies that rent out AI computing power are under threat because of the difficulty in borrowing money, saying on his social-media platform, X, that they could face “guppy-level death and consolidation.” CoreWeave, a company that’s borrowed money to buy AI computing power that it rents to customers, has been at the centre of investors’ worries in recent weeks. On Monday, it dropped 5.5 per cent quickly after trading began, only to flip to a gain of 1.8 per cent by the close. Such minute-to-minute swings have become commonplace for it in recent days. Profit reports from huge tech companies this upcoming week could offer more details about how spending on AI is going, and whether it’s producing the profits and productivity that proponents promised. Alphabet and Microsoft will report their latest quarterly results on Wednesday, with Amazon to follow on Thursday.



Companies across all industries are under pressure to report strong growth in their profits. Expectations for big growth are what allowed their stock prices to run to records recently despite worries about high inflation, high interest rates and other concerns. Verizon Communications fell 3.5 per cent even though it reported a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, as its revenue fell short of forecasts. Roughly one out of every three stocks in the S&P 500 is scheduled to report its latest quarterly results this week. In stock markets abroad, Brazilian stocks fell sharply after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection in a result that surprised investors. Other governments around the world are also feeling pressure because of their high debt loads and worries about strained budgets. France has been at the centre of the worries recently following violent protests in the country.



But yields on French government bonds eased Monday, and its CAC 40 stock index rose 0.8 per cent for one of the world’s better moves. Indexes also rose in other European markets following a mixed finish in Asia. The European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan will be meeting to vote on interest rates later this week. Related Article AI AI darling NextDC announces board and pay purge after Melbourne power disaster In the US bond market, yields fell for longer-term Treasurys. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.98 per cent from 5.00 per cent late Friday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier this month. The two-year Treasury yield edged up to 4.71 per cent from 4.69 per cent late Friday. It more closely tracks expectations for what the Federal Reserve will do with overnight interest rates, and the widespread expectation is that it will say on Wednesday that it is leaving the federal funds rate alone following its latest meeting.



The Fed last month hiked the fed funds rate for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing inflation, which has remained much higher than anyone would like. The price for a barrel of Brent crude fell toward $US109 in the morning, but it later erased the losses and returned to $US111.40. It remains near the high end of its range since the war with Iran began. The highest price for the most actively traded contract in the market for Brent crude since then is nearly $US120, reached in March. World.content:
CultureCelebrityCelebrity relationships Australian musician G Flip and reality star partner Chrishell Stause break up Chris Hook October 27, 2026 — 7:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Australian musician G Flip has broken up with their American reality TV star partner Chrishell Stause after a four-year relationship. Stause, 45, who appears on the Netflix real estate show Selling Sunset, announced the break-up with her 33-year-old partner in an emotional Instagram video on Tuesday morning (AEDT). “I have a pretty humbling update to share with you guys, G and I are no longer together,” she said. “We have agreed to treat this public separation with love and respect for each other. It’s not hard for me because I am in love with this person and I don’t have all the information and the reasons … I’m sure, like always, with time you get the lessons you’re meant to get and I know that will happen.



“ I’m going to heal and everything’s going to be fine and I’m definitely never doing this again,” Stause finished. Chrishell Stause and G Flip attend the 2022 ARIA Awards in Sydney. Hanna Lassen G Flip confirmed the split via a post on her Instagram account. “After 4+ years Chrishell and I are no longer together. I will always love her. We will always share a special connection and I will cherish our memories together deeply,” she wrote. “My head & heart are feeling very heavy right now, and I’m not able to talk but I want to thank you all for your support and appreciate you respecting our privacy at this difficult time.”



Melbourne-born performer G Flip, whose real name is Georgia Claire Flipo, met Stause at a Halloween party, hosted by fellow Australian star Tones and I in 2021, according to Vulture. They married in Las Vegas in 2023 and just last year G Flip told this masthead’s Sunday Life magazine they were trying to start a family. Loading “We’ve been going through a rough time with the IVF process,” G Flip said. “We’ve been struggling with it, and though we don’t like talking too much about it because it ends up ruining our day, we acknowledge it. Queer couples are couples like anyone else.



“To anyone going through IVF or finding themselves on a rough road with bringing life into the world, we feel for you and we understand and we see you.” G Flip first broke through after featuring on Triple J’s Unearthed segment in 2018, then released a debut album About Us in 2019, which garnered three ARIA nominations. Their second album Drummer debuted at No.1 on the ARIA charts in 2023 and G Flip went on to win their first ARIA that year for Best Australian Live Act, followed by the 2024 Song of the Year for The Worst Person Alive. They came out as non-binary in 2021, and discussed their identity with Sunday Life last year. “A non-binary person is who I am – I don’t know how to be anything else. I use they/them pronouns and am very proud of that. I am in a queer relationship and have a beautiful wife. I write from experience and from the perspective of a non-binary queer person.



“When I was growing up, I didn’t have that representation. The backbone of my G Flip project is to be the person I never saw when I was younger. I want to make sure I am making art so that a queer kid somewhere in the world can see me online and feel they are like me.” After meeting Stause, their relationship was kept largely under wraps, before Stause spoke about G Flip on a Selling Sunset reunion before video emerged of the pair kissing just a few weeks later in May 2022. Although Stause had been dating real estate agent Jason Oppenheim at the time they met, they reportedly broke up in late 2021 over Stause’s desire to have children. In June last year, amid G Flip and Stause’s attempts to get pregnant they renewed their wedding vows, hiring a castle in the Hollywood Hills for the event. Next month G Flip heads to Australia for a series of shows across the country, both solo and as the support act for Robbie Williams’ stadium shows in Sydney and Melbourne. World.title: Australia news LIVE: US names first submarine to deploy to WA under AUKUS; Plibersek asked to reassure young women public life is still safe after Haines attack
World.content:
Opposition spokesman for foreign affairs Ted O’Brien says Labor’s trade deal with the EU is not in the best interests of Australia and is calling on Albanese to drop the agreement’s climate clauses.

“The main concern I have is the inclusion of legally binding obligations with respect to climate change,” he told News24 this morning.

The EU mandates legally binding climate change rules in its free trade agreements, including enforcing commitments to the Paris Agreement.

Opposition spokesman for foreign affairs Ted O’Brien. James Brickwood

But O’Brien said he had written to Foreign Minister Penny Wong with a “constructive proposal” to remove the climate clauses from the trade deal.

“What we’re not prepared to do is basically give away the right of future governments to set policy in this country … That is what Labor is proposing through these climate clauses, and so they’re saying nothing to worry about,” he said.

“My answer is: Okay. Put that in writing. That that’s what you do in the real world, and I don’t think it’s too much to ask. They need to cooperate.”

World.title: This brother and sister co-founded Anthropic five years ago. Now they are worth $19 billion each
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesWall Street This brother and sister co-founded Anthropic five years ago. Now they are worth $19 billion each Tom Maloney , Rebecca Torrence and Dylan Sloan October 27, 2026 — 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Anthropic’s seven co-founders each hold roughly 1.4 per cent of the company, its IPO filing revealed, giving them individual fortunes of more than $US13 billion ($18.5 billion). That vaults all of them, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, among the top 300 people on the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, and makes them richer than well-known finance billionaires like Bill Ackman and Stan Druckenmiller. Siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei co-founded Anthropic five years ago. Bloomberg The fortunes, which are based on Anthropic’s $US965 billion valuation in its last funding round, jumped from Bloomberg’s previous calculation of $US8 billion each. If Anthropic succeeds in reaching a $US2 trillion valuation in its initial public offering — a number that was previously floated by investors — they would rise to more than $US27 billion each before accounting for dilution from newly issued shares, according to Bloomberg’s wealth index. The founders’ net worth underscores the utter dominance of tech, and particularly artificial intelligence, in driving both the US stock market and wealth creation this year. Tech fortunes among the world’s 500 richest people gained a combined $US845 billion through the first nine months of 2026, while billionaires outside tech saw their average net worth shrink.



Related Article Opinion

World markets The ‘death spiral’ that could destroy this Wall Street boom In a letter to potential shareholders, Anthropic’s co-founders said that AI and Anthropic “represents one of the greatest economic opportunities in history.” Along with the Amodeis, the other Anthropic co-founders are Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and Christopher Olah. All seven have pledged to dedicate 80 per cent of their personal equity in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, according to the filing. The size of the founders’ stakes belies their control over the company. Under Anthropic’s proposed governance structure, each founder remains a member of the Founder LLC — which controls a Class F share carrying 50.1 per cent of shareholder voting power — as long as they retain at least 2 per cent of the number of Class A shares they held when the company goes public. That means a founder could dispose of 98 per cent of their existing stake and still retain an equal say with the other founders over how that controlling share is voted.



The founders’ majority voting control is somewhat offset by Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, however, which has the power to elect and remove four members of the company’s seven-person board. The trust is designed to continue indefinitely, while the founders’ special voting share will eventually expire once fewer than three qualifying founders remain, whether because of death, incapacity, resignation or because they have sold or given away more than roughly 98 per cent of the Class A shares they held at the IPO. Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark. Bloomberg The trust is governed by five trustees, who largely select their own replacements. San Francisco-based Anthropic was started in 2021 by a group of former OpenAI employees who left following disagreements over the company’s future direction. Anthropic had an $US80.7 billion net loss on revenue of $US16.3 billion in the first six months of 2026, versus a $US13 billion net loss on revenue of $US1.2 billion in the same period last year, the filing shows. Anthropic confirmed that chief executive officer Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei sold some of their shares in the company’s tender offers in 2025 and 2026. Last year, Anthropic kicked off a $US157 million tender that saw both siblings unload some of their stock. This year, Anthropic did a $US4.7 billion tender; the Amodeis, chief financial officer Krishna Rao, and Holden Karnofsky, the spouse of Daniela Amodei, all sold shares in that offering.



Anthropic also paid $US5 million in regulatory filing fees on behalf of the Amodeis this year related to their acquisition and ownership of Anthropic securities. In a letter to potential shareholders, Anthropic’s co-founders said that AI and Anthropic “represents one of the greatest economic opportunities in history.” Bloomberg It’s not just the founders who are getting rich: Anthropic’s employees and other option holders were sitting on about $US98 billion in potential gains from their stock options as of June, based on figures in the filing. Those gains reflect how sharply the company’s value has risen since many employees received their stock options. Employees and other holders could buy the shares underlying their outstanding options at an average price of just $US2.89 a share as of June. Altogether, exercising those options would cost about $US5.2 billion — while on paper, the underlying shares are estimated to be worth more than $US103 billion. Anthropic also operates a donation-matching program that lets employees pledge a portion of their equity awards to eligible charities, with the company matching those donations in shares of its non-voting Class N stock. In August, it recognised a $US2 billion expense tied to employee donations in that month that resulted in it issuing 28 million shares for matching purposes. The co-founders’ pledge to donate 80 per cent of their equity isn’t eligible for the matching program.

World.title: Legal shootout as rival soccer comps feud over fees, safety concerns
World.content:
SportSoccerFootball Australia Legal shootout as rival soccer comps feud over fees, safety concerns Jon Pierik October 27, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A local soccer association is fighting Football Victoria over changes it claims will lead to higher fees for families if they are forced to play under the governing body’s banner. The Greater Melbourne Soccer Association – which has about 2500 registered players across 60 senior teams and 46 under-six to under-eight teams, and runs the biggest over-35s competition in the state – has taken its concerns to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. A feud is simmering between the Greater Melbourne Soccer Association and Football Victoria. Under rules to be introduced next year, clubs affiliated with Football Victoria will require written approval to join external competitions where FV offers a corresponding competition. The Greater Melbourne Soccer Association fears clubs could be deregistered if they do not join FV-sanctioned competitions, and says the proposed changes will affect thousands of players.



The association, which has engaged law firm Lander and Rogers to challenge the new restrictions, wrote the ACCC to raise concerns about possible breaches of the competition and consumer act, relating to misuse of market power and exclusive dealing. Related Article Analysis

Australia Cup Let them in: South Melbourne just showed the A-League what it has been missing Andrew Ellis, the president of the association, said the impending restrictions could impact the affordability, diversity and independence of community soccer in Melbourne. “Football Victoria runs its own competitions. It shouldn’t also get to decide whether clubs can participate in ours,” he said. “Clubs should be able to enter teams in both FV and GMSA competitions without putting their affiliation at risk. They deserve the freedom to choose competitions that best suit their players, families and communities.”



Ellis said the restrictions could force clubs to enter the more expensive FV leagues. A detailed report by his association, based on 2026 figures, said registration for a senior team of 25 players was $2200, while a Football Victoria metropolitan fee for the same team would be $6800. For junior players in under-seven and under-eight competitions, there was a $38 discrepancy in fees according to the Greater Melbourne Soccer Association’s analysis. Soccer is typically one of the more expensive sports to play at junior and pathway level because of the cost of registration fees, compared with other sports. FV did not comment specifically on the figures provided by the association but said in a statement it was not seeking to stymie competitions or clubs.



“Football Victoria is not seeking to prevent alternative football leagues from operating, nor to stop clubs, players or administrators from participating in other organisations. Rather, clubs that wish to retain the benefits and protections of affiliation to Football Victoria and the Football Australia pathway must meet minimum standards when participating in external competitions,” the statement said. Related Article Analysis

A-League Men The A-League can’t afford to play more games. It also can’t afford not to FV said the three core areas of proposed changes were child safety safeguards, insurance and dealing with disciplinary and integrity standards. “Ultimately, this is about ensuring that all activities involving FV-affiliated clubs meet appropriate standards of safety, accountability and governance, regardless of where football is being played,” the statement said. FV has engaged legal firm Carrington Legal to fight their case.



Ellis said FV’s initial response to his claims was that rival leagues providing the equivalent competitions would not be approved. He said in subsequent legal correspondence, FV said change was needed to ensure the appropriate insurance, consistent child safety standards, event scheduling, governance and integrity mechanisms were all met. Lander and Rogers competition law partner Philip Aitken, who has written to the ACCC on behalf of the GMSA, said: “Firms with a substantial degree of market power must not engage in conduct that has the purpose, effect or likely effect of substantially lessening competition”. Ellis said the GMSA supported the highest standard of administration.



“We fully support appropriate child safety, insurance, integrity and governance standards across community football,” he said. Related Article Premier League ‘He wants to be put out of his misery’. Carrick on brink of Manchester United sacking “FV is not a government regulator, but it is acting like one. We both provide football competitions to clubs and players. FV should not be both a competitor and the referee deciding whether rival competitions can operate. “Football Victoria says it isn’t trying to prevent alternative football competitions from operating. “Its own words tell a very different story. In a briefing pack provided to clubs on 11 September 2026, FV explicitly stated: ‘In summary, if FV provides a competition that an external provider is also offering, that external competition will not be on the approved list’.



“That isn’t a child safety standard. That’s a policy designed to exclude competing competitions. FV is now attempting to justify its restrictions by raising child safety, insurance and disciplinary standards. These are important matters, but none requires clubs to be prevented from participating in alternative competitions.” Ellis said, “GMSA has supported grassroots football for almost 50 years, and we’re not about to walk away from the clubs and communities that have supported us”.
