World.title: 'Strengthening ties' or 'Shameful'?: Why Israel's new Pacific status is splitting the region
World.content:
Israel's inclusion into the Pacific region's main political body has drawn sharply contrasting reactions across the region.

While the official diplomatic tone from Pacific leaders, including New Zealand, has been welcoming and focused on consensus, civil society groups have described the move as wrong and demanded a review.

Others, such as Kiwi media academic Professor David Robie, have called it "shameful", while veteran Solomon Islands diplomat Collin Beck said it puts into question the "credibility" of the Pacific Islands Forum's (PIF) partnership mechanism.

Israel announced its acceptance into the Forum via a news release last Wednesday, which swiftly attracted a range of reactions - both for and against the move.

The announcement coincided with Israel's Agency for International Development Cooperation (MASHAV) head Eynat Shlein's visit to the region.

PIF secretary-general Baron Waqa welcomed Israel’s Ambassador to Fiji and Pacific Island Countries Maya Yaron and Head of MASHAV Ambassador Eynat Shlein, who travelled from Israel to the Pacific for engagements across the region this week. Pacific Islands Forum

Fijian Deputy Prime Minister Viliame Gavoka offered a biblical justification for Israel's inclusion, speaking for the "entire Pacific Islands", while the Pacific Conference of Churches demanded the PIF review its decision.

The 18-member PIF has just over two dozen dialogue and development partners, which include countries such as the United States, China, the United Kingdom, France, Japan and Indonesia, that support the development priorities of the region.

Israel has been added to the list as a sectoral partner and will offer support in the areas of water management, desalination, agriculture and climate change adaptation.

"Strengthening ties with the Pacific Island nations is one of my objectives. Earlier this year, I opened Israel's Embassy in Fiji, which also serves nine other Pacific Island nations, all friendly to Israel," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said.

"Under the current government, three of these countries, Papua New Guinea, Fiji and Nauru, have opened embassies in Jerusalem."

The PIF Secretariat, which is headed by former Nauru President Baron Waqa, has not publicly confirmed Israel's status yet. However, the New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters said the decision by PIF leaders should be respected and described criticism of Israel's inclusion as an "insult" to Pacific Island nations.

"Pacific support a rules-based international system, respect for international law," Beck, who is a Solomon Islands career diplomat and senior government official, said in a comment on a Facebook post on RNZ.

"We must engage with all peaceful countries," he wrote.

However, he added that the PIF's "mechanism on partnership now lacks credibility".

He said the review of how the PIF works with its partners "must come with criteria that [have] humanity at its centre, international law, respect for lives will surely place the Pacific on the right side of history".

He also noted that there should be respect for the Pacific Ocean of Peace Declaration adopted by Pacific leaders in September 2025.



Professor Robie, who has decades of experience researching and writing on the region, said the move undermines the Forum's founding commitment in 1971 to regional decolonisation.

"In what is probably one of its most shameful acts ever, the Pacific Islands Forum has betrayed one of its founding principles in admitting Israel - already a global rogue pariah state - as a development partner in the middle of the genocide of an Indigenous people, the Palestinians," he wrote for the Asia Pacific Media Network.

"As decisions of this nature are made by consensus, it means that all 18 member states of the region's main political body - including Australia and New Zealand - have given their blessing."

He pointed out that Israel, alongside the United States, had also voted against decolonisation at the UN Decolonisation Committee (C-24) meeting earlier this month.

"Six Pacific countries and territories - American Samoa, French Polynesia (Mā'ohi Nui), Guam (Guåhan), New Caledonia (Kanaky), Pitcairn and Tokelau - are still on the UN Decolonisation list," he wrote.

World.title: Council votes to restore protections for Waikanae urupā after 56 years
World.content:
The Kāpiti Coast District Council has voted to restore protections to a Māori burial ground after more than fifty years of challenges by iwi.

Local iwi Ātiawa ki Whakarongotai welcomed the decision which adds Kārewarewa urupā in the Waikanae Beach area to the District Plan as a site of significance to Māori.

Kārewarewa urupā is associated with the 1839 Battle of Kūititanga, many of those who died in the battle were buried at the urupā, and the site has been used as an urupā since the mid-19th century.

Audio player for " Why was The Battle of Kūititanga important? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/te-ao-maori/2182444%2Fcouncil-votes-to-restore-protections-for-waikanae-urupa-after-56-years

Why was The Battle of Kūititanga important? Afternoons Download MP3 6m

In 2020 the Waitangi Tribunal found there were a series of failings by the Crown which led to the iwi's loss of ownership and control of the Kārewarewa urupā and the removal of its 'Māori Cemetery' designation in 1970.

Following the loss of the cemetery designation, roughly half of the area was developed into housing.

Although further development mostly stalled after the remains of 11 people were uncovered at the site in the early 2000s.

Ātiawa ki Whakarongotai resource management expert Dr. Mahina-a-rangi Baker, who prepared the iwi case, said the decision by Kāpiti Coast District Council demonstrates that communities are capable of reckoning with very challenging histories.

"This has been an intergenerational fight to respect the basic human decency of our people, and recognise our long-standing presence in this land."

Dr Mahina-a-rangi Baker lead the submissions for Ātiawa ki Whakarongotai in the proposed plan change for Kārewarewa Urupā. RNZ/Pokere Paewai

At the Independent Hearing Panel in June, Kahu Ropata told RNZ that Kārewarewa was significant not only to Ngāti Toa, Te Āti Awa and Ngāti Raukawa, but to the entire nation as the site of the Battle of Kūititanga is nearby.

"Kārewarewa is definitely part of our early connections to the Kapiti Coast. It's one of the first settlements that Ngāti Toa arrived at, and then later on Te Āti Awa and Taranaki. So in terms of the dispersion of the iwi here, it has huge significance to the families of Waikanae," he said.

"There's definitely a difference between a cemetery and a urupā. And a cemetery is an allocated piece of land where you can inter people. An urupā has slightly different connotations, and with that comes different sort of engagement rules, i.e. karakia appropriateness in terms of wāhī tapu and things sacred."

Moving Kārewarewa Urupā to Schedule 9 of the District Plan recognises it as a site and area of significance to Māori - and limits the activities and development that could be undertaken in the future.

Under the proposal the site would be split into two areas or wāhanga, wāhanga tahi covers the undeveloped land and would have a high level of protection.

Wāhanga rua is the area that has already been developed, it would have a moderate level of protection.

Residents will continue to live in their homes and the change allows for a "reasonable level of development" to occur provided land disturbance volumes are reasonably low and discovery protocols are followed.

Map of the area affected by Proposed Plan Change 3 - Kārewarewa Urupā. The red highlighted area is the undeveloped part of the urupā, while the grey area has already been developed. Supplied/Kāpiti Coast District Council

Following the Waitangi Tribunal's 2020 report the Council proceeded with an attempt to restore protections, however that was quashed by the High Court after a challenge taken by Waikanae Land Company, the landowner.

The Council subsequently initiated the current process in 2024.

World.title: Work visas under India FTA worse deal than options already available, lawyer says
World.content:
New work visas under the India trade deal are "cosmetic at best" and completely undermine Winston Peters' warnings of "open slather immigration", an immigration lawyer says.

The two new pathways secured under the agreement opened last Tuesday, allowing up to 5000 skilled Indian professionals to work in New Zealand at any one time for up to three years.

Alastair McClymont told RNZ the newly published conditions showed the visas offered a worse deal than other options already available and would attract "very few, if any" extra migrants.

Listen to Caucus: Top political commentators unpick and make sense of New Zealand's election campaigns with frank and forthright discussion.

For example, workers had no right to bring their partners or children with them, and their work here would not count towards the experience needed to qualify to live in New Zealand permanently.

Alastair McClymont is an immigration lawyer. Supplied

McClymont said other work visas - which Indian citizens could still apply for - remain "significantly more attractive", offering both family rights and a route to settling here.

He accused New Zealand First of employing "incredibly dangerous" populism, and fuelling racism and abuse towards Indians through false warnings of mass migration and a "butter chicken tsunami".

"There's really nothing in here."

'Confusing' - NZ First leader Winston Peters

Asked for his response, Peters said the new work visa requirements actually proved him right on a different complaint - Indian workers would be treated worse than people coming here under similar trade deals.

"That was precisely my allegation," he told RNZ. "How can we justify that?"

In June, Peters dropped a bombshell in Parliament, accusing National of "covertly" changing course to adopt more "discriminatory" migration settings for Indians.

He also claimed officials wanted to keep the changes quiet for fear of India's reaction.

Peters told RNZ the whole situation had been "very, very confusing", with National Party ministers claiming one thing and Indian Prime Minister Narenda Modi claiming another.

"The only way to remove that misunderstanding is to release the documents," he said.

VNP / Phil Smith

RNZ's initial request for documentation under the Official Information Act was refused on the basis the decision-making process was "ongoing". RNZ has lodged a fresh request now that the deal is in force.

Immigration Minister Erica Stanford told RNZ she had always been clear the new entry visas were extra options on top of all the other work visas Indian citizens could apply for.

"All work visas are designed for different purposes, and have different requirements and settings."

Asked why the rules differed from those in the China and South Korea trade deals, she said: "Each agreement is negotiated individually."

She said the immigration settings met New Zealand's commitments under the India trade deal.

'Storm in a teacup'

McClymont told RNZ his main concern was the number of people who believed claims the deal was opening the door to mass migration, and the racism and abuse toward the Indian community as a result.

He said the actual rules published on Tuesday showed claims otherwise were wrong, calling it a "storm in a teacup".

He said Indians applying under the Accredited Employer Work Visa, which had been around for a while, were able to use their work experience in New Zealand for a pathway to residency and bring their family into New Zealand while they worked.

"None of these things are being offered to the Indian citizens under these new visa categories announced as part of the Indian Free Trade Agreement and therefore are very unlikely to be attractive to many Indian citizens."

McClymont said he couldn't see the point of any of the provisions: "It's cosmetic at best."

World.title: 'Outrageous absurdity': Couple fears waterfront ferris wheel will spoil apartment views
World.content:
A couple living opposite the site of a proposed ferris wheel on Auckland's waterfront is concerned about how it would affect the view from their apartment, as well as noise, pollution, and potential seismic risk.

The attraction was one of the options that the city's cultural, events, and destination agency, Tātaki Auckland Unlimited, said it was exploring for activities along Quay Street Promenade this summer, as part of a wider plan to open the Central Wharves to the public for the first time.

Skyline Attractions has applied to operate the ferris wheel on the Queens Wharf Breastworks, the waterfront promenade near the Downtown Ferry Terminal.

Nearby residents, the Mummerys, say this is a scaled drawing of the Quay Street North facade, with the black circle showing depicting the 32m ferris wheel. Supplied / Maryanne Mummery

From 10am to 10pm, the ferris wheel would carry up to 144 passengers at a time across 24 gondolas.

The proposal also included a cultural centre in co-ordination with Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei, ticket booths, and an ice cream cart.

In a statement, director of destination Annie Dundas said it could be up and running before Christmas, with a potential December 2026 opening date.

"However, the wheel remains subject to the necessary consents and approvals before plans can be confirmed," she said.

Dundas said the trial opening of Quay Street Promenade later this year would help to inform the longer-term planning for the wider waterfront, which was being led by the council's Auckland Urban Development Office in partnership with mana whenua.

The chief executive for business association Heart of the City, Viv Beck, welcomed the proposal, and said it would be a big drawcard for visitors and locals alike.

"It would be an absolute winner. Really would be exciting if this could be pulled off, particularly before Christmas.

"We're seeing a real opportunity for, basically, attractions, sort of, complementing the great food and other offering we have.

"We can see a growing appeal of the city centre as a leisure and entertainment destination.

"So, we'd love to see it. Absolutely love to."

Beck said the location, overlooking the Waitematā Harbour, would offer a "spectacular" view during the day and at night.

"If it was able to happen before Christmas, we've got the giant Christmas tree, Te Manaaki, that's attracting thousands of people. So, imagine having another sort of attraction very close by. Imagine New Year's Eve, being up and seeing the beautiful view."

However, the proposal has caused sleepless nights for Maryanne and Alan Mummery.

The couple has lived at 148 Quay Street for more than 33 years.

They said the 32-metre-tall ferris wheel would not be much more than 32 metres from their apartment.

"What a 30-plus years it has been. We've watched a complete reshaping of our waterfront and our much-loved port. The Hilton Hotel was built, the Cloud was built, all the wharf sheds, apart from Shed 10, were pulled down. Covid arrived. And now, in 2026, the most bizarre suggestion of all: a giant ferris wheel right opposite the living spaces of hundreds of people," Maryanne said.

"Not only did we not know about this outrageous absurdity, it simply is an untenable suggestion for a small piece of port-gifted recreational land."

The couple has called for Auckland Council to reject the proposal.

World.title: New Zealand election: Where political parties stand on Pasifika issues
World.content:
In short:

Nearly every major party agrees that costs of living and economic pressure are hurting Pacific families the most - but they disagree on how to fix it.

Major differences exist on immigration, criminal justice approaches and whether foreign aid should be redirected to domestic services.

RNZ Pacific put six key questions to the main political parties so Pasifika voters can compare policies before casting their ballot.

Early voting has opened for the general election in Aotearoa New Zealand.

New Zealand uses MMP, mixed member proportional representation. Enrolled voters can have their say on the party vote - the party they want to win the election and run the next government - and their local electorate vote, for the candidate they want to represent their constituency in parliament.

However, new enrolments have closed - same-day enrolment on voting day is no longer permitted.

RNZ Pacific asked all the main political parties where they stand on Pasifika issues, with a 100-word limit on their responses to each of the six questions. Here's what they said.

How does your party plan to respond to cost-of-living pressures in Aotearoa?

d3sign

ACT: ACT will cut wasteful government spending, balance the books without new taxes, and reduce unnecessary costs on households and businesses.

We will enable competition in both the supermarket industry and electricity by removing red-tape and regulation that prevents businesses competing, enabling lower prices.

We will lower the carbon tax and return net ETS auction revenue to New Zealanders through a Carbon Tax Refund.

Green Party: Aotearoa has enough for all of us to live a good life.

The Green Party is focussed on ensuring everyone can have good jobs, afford their groceries, live in warm homes, and have more time with the people they love.

We will cut household costs by lowering power bills, making public transport free for many people and capping adult fares at $2, and taking action to make nutritious food more affordable. We will fund this by ensuring the wealthiest individuals and largest corporations contribute their fair share, while giving tax cuts to 96 percent of New Zealanders.

Labour: Labour's number one focus at this election is the cost of living - it is what is hurting our Pacific families the most.

We will take action to get the cost of living under control.

Labour will: reinstate pay equity in the first 100 days and give an immediate pay rise to care and support workers, which will back the many hard-working Pacific women in the job to get ahead; introduce three free doctor's visits to ensure Pacific families are getting the care they need, when they need it; cap public transport fares to $20 a week in Auckland, Wellington and [cut-off as per 100-word limit]

National: National is committed to fixing the basics and building the future, and in many instances, Pacific people have the most to gain.

National will not impose new taxes, continue investing in health, schools, law and order, roads, defence capability and other frontline services New Zealanders rely on, reprioritise spending and show ongoing restraint so that overall government expenditure comes down towards 30 per cent of GDP, return to surplus in 2028/29 and stay there, keep government debt on a downward trajectory towards 40 per cent of GDP, and maintain debt below 40 per cent of GDP over time.

New Zealand First: Did not respond to RNZ Pacific.

However, the party has previously said it would increase the minimum wage by at least inflation levels every year for the next three years, restrict Superannuation to citizens only from 2029, and give a permanent boost to the Working For Families in-work tax credit.

It also wants to split up the energy gentailers (generators and retailers), saying this policy would ensure energy gentailers could "no longer control both the power and the price". Read RNZ's full policy guide here.

Opportunity: Bringing down the cost of living is a bottom line for us in any coalition or confidence-and-supply negotiations.

We would empower the Commerce Commission to intervene in sectors such as supermarkets, electricity and banking to ensure greater competition and fairer prices.

We would also accelerate the transition to clean, renewable energy to reduce our reliance on imported fossil fuels and ease pressure on household budgets at the petrol pump. In the longer term, we support a universal Citizen's Income to provide greater financial security as Aotearoa navigates the disruptions of artificial intelligence and climate change.

Te Pāti Māori: Te Pāti Māori will transform and rebalance the tax system to ensure that those in our whānau who work the hardest, often in multiple jobs, keep more of what they earn in their own pockets.

Our tax proposals target wealth rather than work in order to ensure that Aotearoa remains a place where our young people can actually live and not be forced to leave our shores in search of futures elsewhere.

What is your position on visa-free access to Aotearoa for Pacific Island nationals?

123RF

ACT: ACT is open to trialling easier access while maintaining effective border controls. ACT has publicly been open to a one-year visa-free trial for Samoa, with continuation conditional on visitors respecting the rules.

We have not committed to unrestricted visa-free access across the Pacific, however, if this proves to be beneficial this could be expanded.

Green Party: The Greens have long supported visa-free access to Aotearoa for people from Pacific Islands. In early 2025, we launched a petition calling on the Government to extend visa-free travel to Pacific Island nationals.

Pacific whānau should not face higher costs, longer delays or greater bureaucratic barriers than travellers from many wealthier countries. Aotearoa is part of the Pacific family, with deep whakapapa, cultural and community connections across Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa. A Pacific visa waiver would strengthen those relationships and make it easier for families to connect.

Labour: Labour will make travel to New Zealand easier and cheaper for Pacific citizens by expanding visa-waiver access to them.

National: National has no current plans regarding visa-free access for Pacific Island nationals.

However, in June this year visitor visa fees for Pacific nationals were reduced by $55 to $120 for 12 months. This brings the total cost, including the standard immigration levy, from $216 down to $161 for eligible Pacific visitor visa applicants.

New Zealand recognises the importance of its relationships with Pacific countries and Pacific peoples, including strong family, cultural, economic and regional connections.

New Zealand continues to support Pacific-specific pathways and settings, including the Pacific Access Category, the Samoan Quota and the Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme.

New Zealand First: Did not respond to RNZ Pacific.

However, in February, Winston Peters accepted a petition by Samoan activist Arthur Anae calling for people from six Pacific nations - Fiji, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu - to be issued a short-term visa on arrival in New Zealand. Peters said last month that it "possibly could happen in the future".

Opportunity: Opportunity does not have a formal position on visa-free access for Pacific Island nationals.

However, we recognise the significant challenges faced by Pacific families in Aotearoa when loved ones need to travel urgently to attend a funeral or visit a terminally ill family member.

We are committed to listening to New Zealand's Pasifika communities and Pacific governments, and working constructively with other political parties to explore solutions that address these concerns with compassion and fairness.

Te Pāti Māori: Te Pāti Māori stands in solidarity with our sibling islands across the Pacific family. We support amnesty and justice for our Pacific cousins whose elders came to Aotearoa and were mistreated upon arrival.

The legacy of the Dawn Raids must not be forgotten. As ocean relatives, Te Pāti Māori believes that justice lies in greater unity across the Pacific through free and open access between our peoples and islands.

Te Pāti Māori supports visa-free access to Aotearoa for Pacific Island nationals.

Aotearoa is a Pacific country. We share whakapapa and it makes no sense to deny other Pacific peoples the right to remain connected with their ocean kin.

What is your position on aid to the Pacific Islands?

A NZ Airforce Hercules drops aid in Tonga after Cyclone Gita RNZ Pacific / Koro Vaka'uta

ACT: ACT recognises the importance of a stable, prosperous Pacific and helping our neighbours when disaster strikes. However, aid must demonstrate results and value for taxpayers.

However, aid must demonstrate results and value for taxpayers. ACT would reduce overall foreign aid to 2017 levels, while protecting aid to the Pacific and support for Ukraine.

Green Party: The Green Party supports increasing aid to the Pacific, shaped by Pacific priorities. Funding aid to the Pacific is critical for New Zealand's regional security, economic stability, and shared prosperity.

Our Pacific Peoples spokesperson, Teanau Tuiono, has been part of Pacific delegations throughout this term and seen firsthand the instability caused by the withdrawal of aid by the US.

The Greens are clear that development assistance must serve communities and the public good, not militarisation or extractive commercial interests. Climate finance should recognise that Pacific peoples have contributed little to the climate crisis while facing some of its worst effects.

Labour: Unlike other parties, Labour will not cut our foreign aid budget - instead Labour will progressively increase overseas development assistance towards 0.7 percent of GDP as fiscal conditions allow.

Our foreign aid is a small but important contribution we make as a good global citizen and a good neighbour to our Pacific Island brothers and sisters.

National: The aid provided to the Pacific Islands is carefully considered by Cabinet, and often under very specific contexts.

New Zealand recognises the importance of its relationships with Pacific countries and Pacific peoples, including strong family, cultural, economic and regional connections.

National has announced it deliver a further NZ$604 million uplift in Pharmac's medicines budget. We will largely pay for it by reducing foreign aid and associated administration costs by 10 per cent, while fully protecting aid to the Pacific.

NZ First: Did not respond to RNZ Pacific.

However, leader Winston Peters said National's foreign aid cut campaign promise "will take us back decades in foreign affairs".

"We need to double the size of the economy and we cannot do that if we neglect the very markets we need to be in."

He said the coalition had just restored New Zealand's influence and relationships around the world.

Peters also travelled to all member countries of the Pacific Islands Forum as foreign minister.

Opportunity: The Pacific is our family, and supporting its wellbeing is both a moral responsibility and in Aotearoa New Zealand's national interest.

Opportunity will maintain New Zealand's strong focus on Pacific development assistance, supporting our neighbours to build stable, resilient and prosperous communities.

We believe this support is increasingly important as Pacific nations face the escalating impacts of climate change, transnational drug trafficking and geopolitical competition.

We want to work in partnership with Pacific nations to address these challenges and support their long-term self-determination.

Te Pāti Māori: Te Pāti Māori is a staunch supporter of unity across the Pacific family, including on the matter of military neutrality and the Blue Pacific Ocean of Peace Declaration.

Te Pāti Māori also acknowledges concerns by our kin that climate change presents an existential threat to all Pacific peoples.

Te Pāti Māori wholeheartedly supports aid for the Pacific. We must continue to work together in the spirit of shared kinship to realise our shared aspirations and to solve the strategic risks and challenges of our time.

Do you have a plan on dealing with overstayers from the Pacific, and if so, what is it?

A public meeting that included government ministers and community leaders was called on 6 May 2023 following an incident the previous week that was reminiscent of the Dawn Raids of the 1970s. RNZ Pacific / Lydia Lewis

ACT: ACT's approach applies to overstayers from every country.

We will establish a dedicated enforcement unit within Immigration New Zealand, require platform employers to verify and report work rights, and remove accreditation from employers who facilitate overstaying.

Green Party: All migrants should be treated with dignity. Our plan is a fair, broad and accessible amnesty providing pathways to residency for overstayers who have made their lives in Aotearoa.

People without valid visas are often part of our families, churches, workplaces and communities, yet their status can leave them vulnerable to exploitation and family separation.

We would end discriminatory enforcement practices, ensure people can obtain independent advice, and reform temporary visas so fewer people fall out of status.

Labour: There are already systems in place to manage visa overstayers, and we expect those systems to continue to be applied fairly and appropriately.

National: National has no specific plans regarding overstayers from the Pacific, but we expect all visitors to follow the law and abide by the conditions set with their visit.

As previously mentioned, in June this year visitor visa fees for Pacific nationals were reduced by $55 to $120 for 12 months. This brings the total cost, including the standard immigration levy, from $216 down to $161 for eligible Pacific visitor visa applicants.

A dedicated escalation process also now enables Pacific applicants to request expedited processing for any visa type, such as in urgent situations like attending a funeral.

NZ First: Did not respond to RNZ Pacific.

However, New Zealand First has previously said it will offer a two-year clemency period for Pacific Islanders who overstay their visas.

The 24-month period would be "to facilitate any Pacific overstayer to apply to remain in the country legally on a valid visa", and those who failed to do so would be deported after the period lapsed, "permanently ineligible to apply for any visa in the future, due to their heightened risk of reoffending".

Opportunity: Opportunity does not have a formal policy on Pacific overstayers, but we recognise the complexity and human impact of this issue.

We support a considered, cross-party approach involving Immigration New Zealand, Health New Zealand and the Ministry of Education to understand the wider implications.

Crucially, we would listen to Pasifika communities to better understand why people overstay including family circumstances, safety concerns, economic hardship and access to essential services. Through broader community consultation, including models such as Citizens' Voice, we believe Aotearoa can work towards a fair, compassionate and evidence-based response.

Te Pāti Māori: Te Pāti Māori rejects the targeting of our Pacific whanaunga and migrant communities from beyond the Pacific.

Based on our own Māori experience of colonisation, we reject Western political attitudes that seek to decide who belongs in Aotearoa, a Pacific country, and who does not.

We have supported recent efforts by Teanau Tuiono, and by the late Efeso Collins before them, to provide justice to Pacific Island communities through amnesty.

What are your plans for the Ministry of Pacific Peoples?

Ministry of Pacific Peoples

ACT: ACT would abolish the Ministry for Pacific Peoples as part of creating a smaller, more accountable government. Agencies delivering health, education, housing and other services should be responsible for meeting Pacific peoples' needs and delivering measurable results.

Green Party: The Green Party supports a strong, properly resourced Ministry for Pacific Peoples.

Decades of underinvestment have weakened the public institutions and collective capability we need to deliver for our communities.

Decisions affecting Pasifika people should be made with communities. The Ministry has an essential role in ensuring Pacific communities shape government decisions and in improving outcomes across housing, health, education, employment and culture.

The Greens are uninterested in treating it as a political football or cutting programmes that directly support Pasifika wellbeing because we are committed to working across government and partnering genuinely with diverse Pacific communities.

Labour: Labour will protect and retain the Ministry of Pacific Peoples given its important contribution to Pacific communities across New Zealand.

National: There will always be the need and the requirement and the opportunity for some specialist focus within the government service for Pacifica people. However, there are no immediate plans to change the current arrangements.

New Zealand First: Did not respond to RNZ Pacific.

Opportunity: Opportunity will continue to support the Ministry for Pacific Peoples and its role in advocating for Pacific communities, strengthening outcomes for Pacific peoples, and ensuring their voices are heard in government decision-making.

We believe the Ministry has an important role in supporting the wellbeing, aspirations and prosperity of Pacific peoples in Aotearoa.

Te Pati Māori: Te Pāti Māori would retain the Ministry of Pacific Peoples and wish to acknowledge the contributions already made by the wider Pacific Island community to the Aotearoa we all call home.

Do you have any policies targeted at addressing the high incarceration rates of Pasifika?

123rf

ACT: ACT's focus is on reducing crime and reoffending, rather than setting arbitrary targets to reduce prisoner numbers. Safer communities require accountability for offending alongside effective rehabilitation.

ACT supports requiring prisoners to complete skills and rehabilitation programmes before being considered for parole, helping them overcome barriers to employment, reintegrate into society and reduce further offending.

Green Party: Too many Pasifika people end up in prison because the system treats them unfairly and help often comes too late.

We want to stop problems before they escalate-by backing Pasifika-led services, making sure people can get a good lawyer, and helping those leaving prison find a home, a job and support from their community.

Where it is safe, people should be held accountable without being sent to prison. Pasifika communities know what works, and they should lead the solutions.

Labour: The focus must be on addressing the root causes of crime like poverty, addiction, mental health, homelessness - and preventing the harm before it happens.

National: We want to see fewer people in prison, but only as a result of fewer victims of serious violent crime, which are disproportionately more likely to be Māori and Pacific.

The good news is we're making progress, with 37,000 fewer victims of serious violent crime than when we came into Government.

We want to continue to drive these numbers down and restore law and order. That's why we've already committed to reforming Zealand's consent laws, abolishing good character assessments at sentencing for all convicted sex offenders, and removing the right to silence when a child is murdered

New Zealand First: Did not respond to RNZ Pacific. However, the party will bring in tougher sentences for serious crime - including 'life means life' provisions - as part of its law-and-order policy package.

The policy package also contained a commitment to strengthen the 'coward punch' law, requiring judges to impose a minimum non-parole period of eight years' imprisonment for coward punches causing death.

Opportunity: Opportunity's Smart on Crime policy focuses on evidence-based solutions to reduce offending and address the overrepresentation of Pasifika in our justice system.

We support investment in expert-designed, rigorously evaluated initiatives, including culturally responsive programmes and vocational training. We see value in expanding specialist courts, such as the Pacific Youth Court, and restorative justice approaches that support meaningful outcomes for victims, offenders and communities.

We would also strengthen post-release support through specialist case management, helping people access stable housing, employment and practical assistance to reduce reoffending and support successful reintegration into their communities.

Te Pāti Māori: Our Justice policy will benefit both Māori and Pasifika communities.

We will overhaul discriminatory legislation (such as three strikes, move on orders, and the Misuse of Drugs Act), we will invest in mental health and addiction services, and we will transform the justice system from a punitive approach to a rehabilitative, community-based approach.

We know that the criminal justice system is broken and we commit to working alongside Pasifika leaders and communities to tackle this challenge.

Does your party have plans to expand or reduce the number of RSE workers coming in from the Pacific?

Mike, a ni-Van RSE worker, has been coming to Clyde Orchards from Vanuatu for almost 20 years. Gianina Schwanecke / Country Life

ACT: ACT supports the RSE scheme and secured a coalition commitment to increase its cap, which rose from 19,500 to 20,750 in 2024. We support more flexible arrangements, clearer deductions and safeguards against exploitation.

Green Party: The Green Party would not set RSE numbers in isolation from workers' rights or the effects on Pacific communities.

Aotearoa cannot build a resilient economy on cheap labour and insecure employment.

Before any expansion, the scheme must be redesigned to prevent exploitation, provide safe accommodation and fair pay, allow workers to leave abusive employers, strengthen union voice and worker representation, and create pathways to residency.

These are decisions that must be made with Pacific governments, unions, workers and affected communities, including consideration of skills lost from island economies.

Labour: Labour is committed to working with Pacific countries to expand regional labour mobility, improve worker protections and training, and manage workforce pressures.

National: There are no current plans to change the number of RSE workers arriving from the Pacific.

However, we know that Pacific businesses are more likely to employ Pacific workers, which is why our government has continued to invest in initiatives such as the Pacific Business Trust.

In 2024/25, the programme delivered over 11,300 business engagements, 200 business assessments and 33 targeted business development workshops.

New Zealand First: Did not respond to RNZ Pacific.

However, the party's immigration policy includes making all visa holders ineligible from claiming jobseeker, accommodation supplement, or any other benefits during their first 10 years; and Student Visa holders would not have automatic work rights after completion of their studies, and would be required to leave the country before being able to apply for another visa.

Opportunity: Opportunity supports Pacific labour mobility as part of Aotearoa New Zealand's commitment to helping Pacific nations build economic resilience and prosperity.

The Recognised Seasonal Employer (RSE) scheme also provides essential seasonal workers for our horticulture and viticulture industries.

Rather than committing to a fixed increase or reduction, we would assess labour demand alongside the priorities of Pacific governments to ensure an appropriate balance.

Our approach would aim to deliver mutual benefits for New Zealand industries and Pacific communities, while supporting sustainable economic opportunities across the region.

Te Pāti Māori: Te Pāti Māori will ensure that there continues to be opportunities for RSE workers coming from the Pacific, but we need to make changes to visa conditions to protect our seasonal workers.

Every person who lives and works in Aotearoa deserves the freedom to be treated with dignity, to be free from exploitation, and to build a better life for themselves and their whānau. Visas that tie people to a single employer undermine these freedoms and create conditions that can lead to exploitation.

Under the Recognised Seasonal Employer Limited Visa, and the Accredited Employer Work Visa, a worker is unable [cut off due to 100-word limit].

If you could tell Pasifika voters one thing, what would it be?

Tofiga Maletino performing a Samoan dance group from Alfriston College. Nick Monro / RNZ

ACT: Your hard work should mean a better future for your family.

ACT stands for lower living costs, more choice in your children's education, safer communities and the freedom to get ahead through work and business.

We want a government that respects your contribution, treats everyone equally and delivers results for your family. We want to invigorate New Zealand with the aspiration and ambition the country was once known and world famous for.

Green Party: Aotearoa would not be the country it is without the generations of care, work, culture and leadership Pacific communities have contributed.

We want an economy that works for all of us - where everyone can access the essentials of a good life, young people can put down roots, and aspirations dreamt up in South Auckland garages have the support to become reality.

Our record - from restoring citizenship rights for Sāmoan elders to campaigning for a Pacific visa waiver - shows what community organising and political courage can achieve together.

Labour: This election is about the cost of living.

Only Labour has a plan to make everyday life more affordable and only a vote for Labour will ensure a change of government. Make sure your voice is heard by getting enrolled to vote before 25 October.

National: Three years ago, National was elected to fix the basics.

Kiwis have done the hard yards over the past three years and our plan is working, with the economy growing faster than Australia and the UK, inflation and interest rates down, kids back in school, and safer streets with fewer victims of crime.

Pacific childhood immunisation rates have increased from 73.5 per cent to 81.76 per cent, and regular attendance among Pacific learners has nearly doubled.

The choice is clear. National has a positive plan to grow the economy, with less debt, more jobs, higher wages and no new taxes.

New Zealand First: Did not respond to RNZ Pacific.

Opportunity: Everything about Opportunity's approach from politics to the economy will be familiar to Pasifika peoples such as decision-making that is grounded on consensus building with an economic view that values intergenerational thinking and collective prosperity.

Māori and Pasifika communities have always known how to build unity, enduring community survival and valuing conservation of natural resources.

These have now become recognised as our way forward as Aotearoa New Zealand and Opportunity Party will be guided and led by these values to build a sustainable and inclusive future for all peoples to thrive together.

Te Pāti Māori: The future of an Aotearoa we can all share in must be grounded in our shared-kinship and collective obligations to one another. While Te Pāti Māori acknowledges the cultural diversity of the Pacific family, we believe that our collective future across this great ocean lays in whakapapa inherited from our ancestors.

Whakapapa must be the foundation for the collective overcoming of the challenges of the 21st century, such climate change, military escalation and social cohesion.

We owe this responsibility of belonging to future generations as their birthright inheritance.

World.title: Strong winds forecast to ease, cold weather and 'yo-yo temperatures' on way
World.content:
Audio player for " Heather Keats on what to expect from the strong winds " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/regions_otago/2173538%2Fstrong-winds-forecast-to-ease-cold-weather-and-yo-yo-temperatures-on-way

Heather Keats on what to expect from the strong winds Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Strong winds that have been battering the country and fanning scrub fires are easing - but cold weather is in store.

MetService head of weather news Heather Keats told Morning Report the wind was making it difficult to fight the wildfires, but rain was expected to help.

Keats said another front was expected to arrive over the South Island on Wednesday bringing a further change in wind direction and strength, but was not expected to be as severe.

The country was in for "yo-yo temperatures" as the strong north-west wind turned to a southerly before easing, she said. Dunedin reached 28C on Monday, but would have a high of 13C on Tuesday, then 20C on Wednesday, and Thursday it would be 13C maximum again.

Over the weekend, Wellington's Mt Kaukau recorded a maximum 148km/h and Mt Somers in Canterbury had gusts of 222 km/h.

Wellington airport had 113 km/hr winds at 4am on Tuesday and Dunedin had 87 km/h.

Keats said strong winds and rising temperatures could make for a challenging wildfire season as the country headed into summer.

Heavy rain warnings for the Grey and Buller districts and Tararua Ranges were lifted on Tuesday morning, as were strong wind warnings for Marlborough, Wellington and Wairarapa.

Strong winds fan flames

A large smoke plume could be seen rising over the tussocky Central Plateau landscape near Waiouru, on 26 October, 2026. Supplied/ Sarah Moodie

The strong winds had fanned the flames of multiple bushfires in separate parts of the country on Monday.

The Defence Force warned a blaze in the Waiouru military zone could still take hours to be fully extinguished, and may not be out until Tuesday evening.

The large scrub fire was sparked during live fire training on Sunday and has burnt through more than 230 hectares.

It said the blaze, which took hold again on Monday, drew in nine firefighting crews and five helicopters alongside military personnel.

Fire and Emergency said crews were withdrawn from the fire ground overnight, but are expected back on site Tuesday morning.

Footage from motorists travelling on the Desert Road SH1 on Monday showed large plumes of smoke just north of the Waiouru township.

Smoke warning issued after Roxburgh fire

Firefighters helped by rain put out a blaze in the central Otago town of Roxburgh.

Homes were evacuated on Ladysmith Road, east of Roxburgh township. Screenshot / Google Maps

However Fire and Emergency on Tuesday advised locals to stay inside and close windows and doors as a significant amount of smoke was expected in the area.

Crews were back at the site to dampen remaining hotspots and heavy machinery was being used to fell damaged trees.

At least seven fire crews worked on the blaze - which was thought to have started in trees about 2.45pm Monday - with FENZ saying strong winds added to the problem.

Six households east of Roxburgh township had been evacuated and hundreds were left without power. By Tuesday morning all but 35 properties had the power supply back.

Central Otago Mayor Tamah Alley told RNZ on Tuesday the last evacuees were on their way home. She said sustained rain overnight had helped put the blaze out.

Alley said the community had rallied together."It was really heartening to see the community come together yesterday and offers of assistance and places to stay and food and kennels for animals and the like were put out very quickly."

In Southland, crews were brought back on Monday to work on a scrub fire that burned through about 80 hectares. The fire started on Sunday afternoon on high-country land in the Centre Hill area.

Fire restriction

The Bay of Plenty issued fire restrictions from Tuesday following a spate of fires in the region.

Outdoor fires will need permission from Fire and Emergency New Zealand until further notice in Whakatāne, Waihau Bay, Ōpōtiki, Coastal Strip, Urewera, Galatea, Plateau North, and Plateau Central.

FENZ Bay of Plenty Community Risk Manager Luke Burgess said restrictions were coming in earlier because of forecast El Niño conditions that made fires easier to start.

He said more than 70 fires had started in the past month, many starting from unattended beach fires or burn piles.

"The Bay of Plenty has a lot of valuable conservation land, beaches, agriculture, and forestry, and we need the community to help us keep them safe from fire this summer."
