Tech.title: The Anthropic S-1 Filing Is Also an AI Doomsday Primer
Tech.content:
Anthropic has officially filed the prospectus for its initial public offering, which means the AI lab has put all kinds of formerly private information on display. While the prospectus contains the eye-popping revenue—and even larger expenditures—you might expect, the biggest section of the filing by far is given over to “risk factors,” which are all the things that could squash Anthropic’s big plans. Or, in this case, humanity itself.

While much has been made about the extent to which AI represents an existential threat to humankind, the specific mechanisms by which it could bring about that destruction are largely opaque. If nothing else, the 94 pages that Anthropic’s prospectus devotes to risk factors make clear both where it sees the danger coming from, and the ways in which its researchers are running toward it in order to win the AI arms race.

“Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the prospectus reads, citing concerns both from critics and regulators and from inside Anthropic itself. (It’s the first of three times the phrase “existential risks” pops up.)

Anthropic is careful to tie that outcome, though, to a specific process: recursive self-improvement.

The idea behind RSI is strikingly simple. It describes a state in which humans hand over the research and development of AI models to other AI models. AI already plays a big role here—and at least one lab has used something close to RSI to speed up development on a model that punches above its weights—but the scenario that sparks doomsday talk is one in which humans are no longer in the loop at all.

Tech.title: Anthropic’s IPO Prospectus Reveals What’s Under the Hood
Tech.content:
Anthropic filed key paperwork on Monday ahead of a highly anticipated initial public offering, providing new details about its finances and the risks facing its business.

According to the filing, the artificial intelligence company plans to go public on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. The IPO could come later in November, The Wall Street Journal reported. The S-1 prospectus does not include details on how much the company plans to raise or its targeted valuation; The New York Times reported in August that it was looking to raise more than $100 billion with a valuation around $2 trillion.

“The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history,” Anthropic wrote in the filing. “We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater.”

The paperwork offers a window into the company’s finances through the first half of 2026. Its revenue grew to more than $16 billion, up from about $4.5 billion in 2025. The Claude maker emphasized its growing enterprise business, noting that more than 11,900 customers spent at least $100,000 in the past twelve months; more than 1,900 spent $1 million or more; and roughly 250 customers spent $10 million or more.

Despite its growing revenue, Anthropic has yet to turn a profit. It posted a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, compared to a net loss of $13 billion in the same period last year.

While it’s expected that a company accurately reports its risk factors, the prospectus also features a particularly thorough list of potential business quagmires, noting that investing in the stock carries “a high degree of risk.”

Those risks range from the ability to secure adequate compute to intense competition from rival labs to advanced AI systems’ potential to “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

The filing warns about the possibility that sophisticated AI could be abused by threat actors to launch cyberattacks and develop novel biological weapons, or by authoritarian governments to surveil their citizens. Anthropic also pointed to the risk that it could lose control of the AI models it develops.

It also highlighted the volatility of government action, specifically noting the Trump administration’s decision to designate the company as a supply chain risk.

Tech.title: The US Government Is Hiding a Secret Court Ruling About How It Spies on Americans
Tech.content:
Two Democratic senators who have long overseen US intelligence say the Trump administration is illegally withholding a secret court’s findings from Congress until lawmakers renew a program that lets federal agents read Americans’ communications without a warrant.

Seven months ago, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to search filters that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires. The court approved another year of surveillance anyway. The ruling has never been made public, and Senators Ron Wyden of Oregon and Adam Schiff of California say the administration’s own deadline for releasing it passed in September.

The program, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), lapsed in June after Congress failed to renew it, though collection continues under the court’s March approval. The administration’s own public documentation says rulings like this one are reviewed for public release “within 180 days of issuance.” That window closed September 13, even as intelligence officials press lawmakers to reauthorize the program by the end of the year.

Wyden, the longest-serving member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Schiff, the former chair of its House counterpart, say the administration owes Congress an explanation for the delay, and the names of the officials responsible, by November 6.

“If this administration won’t follow this simple statutory directive,” the senators told Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Attorney General Todd Blanche in a demand letter obtained exclusively by WIRED, “it is unclear why Congress or the American people should trust this administration to follow any of the other legal limits to Section 702.”

Outside Congress, Demand Progress and 22 other civil liberties and government accountability groups on Monday urged congressional leaders to refuse to reauthorize Section 702 “while the administration actively withholds legally mandated information about how the surveillance program operates.” Signatories range from the American Civil Liberties Union to the conservative-backed Project for Privacy and Surveillance Accountability.

The Trump administration has already been pressed, and has promised, to release the ruling. In April, senators Tom Cotton and Mark Warner, the Intelligence Committee’s Republican chair and Democratic vice chair, pressed the administration to release it within 15 days so it could inform the Senate’s debate. In July, asked in writing whether he would commit to declassifying it by the 180-day deadline, Blanche replied, “Yes.”

Warner “has been clear that he supports transparency with regard to Section 702,” his communications director, Rachel Cohen, tells WIRED. Neither former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard nor Bill Pulte, who briefly replaced her as acting director, “were responsive,” Cohen says, “but Senator Warner expects that DNI Clayton will declassify the opinion, consistent with the bipartisan letter and as required by law.”

Tech.title: Download iOS 27.2 Now to Bring These Features and More to Your iPhone
Tech.content:
More than a month after Apple released iOS 27 to the general public, the tech giant released iOS 27.2 on Monday. While iOS 27 brought Siri AI and more to your device, iOS 27.2 expands Siri AI to other languages, and the update brings a few upgrades in other apps, such as FaceTime and Apple Music.

If you’re wondering what happened to iOS 27.1, the foldable iPhone Duo launched on 27.1 on Friday. That is the only device that will run iOS 27.1, and all devices can update to 27.2 now.

CNET/Apple

Here are some of the features you can try in iOS 27.2. Don’t forget, Apple Intelligence features are only available on Apple Intelligence-compatible devices, like the iPhone 18 Pro.

More from CNET

Siri AI in more languages

Siri AI is available on iOS 27 now. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

In iOS 27.2, Siri AI comes to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish in beta. Siri AI was initially only available in English.

Apple previously said Siri AI would expand to these additional languages, so this shows the company moving quickly on that promise.

Use front and rear cameras simultaneously in FaceTime

In iOS 27.2, you can use your front and rear-facing cameras at the same time in FaceTime calls. This allows you to FaceTime with a larger group of people — you don’t have to squeeze everyone into a single frame to see the person on the other end of the call. However, everyone on the call needs to be on iOS 27 or later for this feature to work.

Apple Music gets a new color scheme

The old Apple Music logo (left) next to the logo introduced in iOS 27.2. Screenshot by CNET

The iOS 27.2 update also brings a new look to the Apple Music app. The app icon is now black and white, as opposed to the reddish hue it had in previous iOS versions. Tapping into the app also reveals new blue menu items throughout, rather than the same reddish tone as the older app logo.

Refreshed Podcasts options

The Podcasts app also gets an update in iOS 27.2. The update introduces two rows to the top of the Home tab within the app: New Episodes and Continue Playing. This can help you keep track of which podcasts are new and which you still have to finish.

It’s a small, pleasant addition to the interface, and I appreciate how it helps keep my podcasts organized.

Apple TV profile expansion

In iOS 27.2, you can create TV Profiles in your Apple TV app. You can assign a profile to your child or someone else and ensure your preferences aren’t messed with.

So if you’re tired of being recommended kids’ shows after letting your child watch the series Shape Island, you can create a profile for your child and let them watch those quirky little shapes all they want. (But also, it’s possible that I like Shape Island more than my son does, so you should check it out.)

Apple TV multiview on iOS

Another Apple TV update in iOS 27.2 is Multiview. If you subscribe to Apple TV you can watch up to four live sports streams, including streams from Major League Soccer and Formula 1, at once. That way, you don’t miss an important game, or you can look at a map of the racetrack while watching feeds from driver-view cameras.

The updated Health app is gone

The refreshed Health app isn’t available in iOS 27.2. Apple

Apple removed the redesigned Health app before releasing iOS 27.2 to the general public. Developers and beta testers could explore the refreshed app in early iOS 27.2 betas and see things like a new Longevity tab and your Health Age.

The redesign was always expected to launch sometime later this year. So it’s not surprising this feature isn’t included in the general release of iOS 27.2. It’s also not unusual for Apple to include features in early beta versions of software, then remove or change them in later betas or upon the release of an iOS update.

Here are the full release notes for iOS 27.2.

Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max)

Siri Al can recall your past conversations, so you can ask Siri about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week.

Siri Al can draw from more sources to give you a great answer, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, your voicemails, and better results from Safari history and Reading List.

Excluded Apps lets you choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access, all from one setting.

Granular text selection lets you select and copy just the part of a Siri response you need.

Siri Al is available in more languages, with support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. Siri Al is not available in the EU or mainland China.

Other

Suggestions in Messages help you take action based on the context of your conversations, such as adding a Calendar invite for dinner.

Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, avoid adding duplicate photos and display a reminder before albums expire, so participants can save important photos and videos.

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground.

The Home tab in the Podcasts app offers two separate sections for New Episodes and Continue Playing, letting you find the latest updates from your shows and then pick up where you left off.

The Friends tab in the Games app provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages.

Simple Profiles in the Apple TV app lets everyone in your household have their own profile, with recommendations that fit what they like to watch.

FaceTime supports adding a third-party sign language interpreter or live captioner to a call.

For more, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and why your battery might be draining faster after updating. You can also check out why the iPhone Duo will launch with iOS 27.1 and our iOS 27 cheat sheet.

Tech.title: Are We All Maxxed Out? Dictionary.com Names ‘Maxxing’ Its 2026 Word of the Year
Tech.content:
Are you focusmaxxing today? Knowledgemaxxing? Maybe fibermaxxing? Dictionary.com has chosen “maxxing,” which can seemingly be attached as a suffix to any other English word, as its Word of the Year for 2026.

Dictionary.com defines maxxing as “the practice of pursuing an activity to the fullest or optimizing a certain aspect of your life.” It’s not a lot different from older expressions such as taking it to the max, maxing out a credit card or feeling maxed out. Words like max, maximum and maximize have their roots in the Latin maximus — meaning “greatest” or “largest.”

But maxxing takes it to another level. The word has an additional x and can be tacked onto the back of seemingly any word. Dictionary.com said that two of the most common of these in 2026 have been looksmaxxing and tokenmaxxing.

More from CNET

Looksmaxxing — maximizing one’s physical appearance — was the most popular internet search term in 2026 for derivations of maxxing, according to Dictionary.com. Certain internet content creators popularized the term and have gained large followings with their sometimes extreme approaches to improving their looks.

Tokenmaxxing is another frequently searched term. In the world of AI, token refers to a small bit of written text that AI language models process to formulate responses. The term tokenmaxxing generally refers to using AI as much as possible at work, as companies integrate AI more and more into workflows. It’s no joke: Some companies are tracking and evaluating their workers on how much and how effectively they use AI in their jobs.

Maxxing can also be used on its own, such as, “Have you been maxxing on anything lately?”

Dictionary.com said the popularity of “maxxing” in all its various uses indicates how much we value optimization, as does the rising use of prefixes super- and ultra- in 2025.

“Whatever we’re doing, we want to push it further,” Dictionary.com reports. “But its expanding uses also reveal how people are responding to that impulse. Some embrace it. Some exaggerate it for laughs. Others flip it on its head to describe stepping away from the relentless pursuit of more. The open question is whether this need for optimization has peaked or if we’ll push even harder next year.”

If you let your imagination fly, you can maxx on anything — dietmaxxing to lose weight, bookmaxxing to read more, bingemaxxing for all that streaming.

Data center among the top 5

Dictionary.com’s shortlist of top words this year included affordability, data center (spelled as two words), odyssey and unc. Affordability has been one of the most common words in politics in the lead-up to the midterms — can people pay for what they need? Data centers are sprouting up all over the US and are either gateways to economic prosperity or harbingers of doom, depending on whom you talk to.

Unc, short for uncle, refers to someone who’s out of touch with Gen Z and Gen Alpha culture; and odyssey cracked the top five thanks to the popularity of The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan’s 2026 film adapted from Homer’s Greek epic about Odysseus’ journey home after the Trojan War.

Tech.title: OpenAI Has a Surprising Defense Against Election Deepfakes
Tech.content:
One of the biggest problems of the AI age is that AI deepfakes are now so realistic that they’re practically indistinguishable from real photos. That matters a lot during election season, when voters are looking for reliable, truthful information on their candidates and polling sites. OpenAI is implementing a new safeguard to prevent people from making political deepfakes.

The US midterm election is only a week away on Nov. 3. Tech issues are taking center stage in many races, especially as AI and data center concerns rise for folks across the country. (Check out CNET’s guide to spotting political scams.)

If you were to go into ChatGPT today and ask it to generate an image “depicting election interference or that may discourage voting,” as OpenAI put it in an Oct. 20 update, the chatbot would create the image, given it doesn’t violate any other content guidelines. But it will be in an illustrated or cartoon style — all requests to have the image appear photorealistic should be ignored.

More from CNET

For example, CNET asked ChatGPT to create an image of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers standing outside a polling location. Every such prompt generated an image in a cartoon style. A photorealistic version of this kind of image would likely spark anxiety, if not outright panic, for voters.

Every edit request for ChatGPT to make an image of ICE officers outside a polling location generated a picture in a cartoon style to avoid confusion for people who see it. Screenshot by Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

The idea is to make it harder for bad actors to create realistic political deepfakes that could interfere with or question the integrity of an election without stymying people’s ability to create political content in general. In another example, CNET Managing Editor Jon Reed couldn’t trick ChatGPT into creating a photojournalist-style image that showed a voting machine recording the wrong choice.

Voting machines recording results other than a voter’s selection is a common election myth. Screenshot by Jon Reed/CNET

“The problem with deepfakes isn’t social commentary, it’s deception. So our aim is to degrade the evidentiary value of an image, while preserving room for illustrations and social commentary,” Josh Lawson, OpenAI’s head of elections, told CNET. The goal is to “make our platform less useful to bad actors by adding another layer of friction,” he said.

This cartoonification of AI images is a practical way to make political deepfakes a little harder to create. Improving AI image models, like ChatGPT Images 2.5, is a double-edged sword. Newer models make fewer errors or hallucinations, making better content for creators. But removing those flubs makes it even harder for everyone else to identify AI-created content with the naked eye. Verification or AI labeling methods have tried to help, but those methods aren’t industry-wide nor foolproof.

When I asked Gemini maker Google about any precautions it is taking specifically for AI images, a spokesperson pointed me to its midterm election policy, which says the company is “rolling out additional protections to limit the creation of misleading election-related images” but doesn’t include any details on how.

Anthropic doesn’t have a traditional image or video generator, and a spokesperson told CNET that any attempts to use Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections violate its policies. The company also posted this general election guidance earlier this month.

Claude refused to make a photorealistic image with potentially “sensitive election-related” content. Screenshot by Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

There’s no guarantee that OpenAI will keep this system in place once the election cycle is over. But it’s a solid sign from one of the biggest AI labs that it is taking its role in safeguarding American elections’ integrity at least somewhat seriously.

For more, check out what to do when you’ve been deepfaked and everything to know about the Take It Down Act.

Tech.title: Microsoft’s Massive Employee Buyout Shows How AI Is Reshaping the Economy
Tech.content:
Following billions in AI investments last fiscal year, Microsoft announced Monday that it is offering buyouts to roughly 60,000 employees, about a quarter of its workforce, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The voluntary exit offer applies to staff at experience level 70 or below across the US, Canada, India and the UK.

According to Microsoft, the move is tailored to give “eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support.” Microsoft didn’t say how many employee buyouts it will accept, though it’s likely fewer than those offered the deal. The company didn’t immediately respond to CNET’s request for comment.

The move comes a few months after Microsoft reported it invested about $116 billion in property and equipment — largely for cloud and AI data-center capacity — in the 2026 fiscal year, about $50 billion more compared with the 2025 fiscal year. Microsoft’s operating income increased by about $30 billion between the 2026 and 2025 fiscal years.

More from CNET

In September, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft is planning on tripling its computing power in the coming years, which could result in the company using more energy than all of New York City at peak hours.

The buyout affects teams including Xbox, Windows, Copilot and finance, but excludes certain data-center, sales and marketing staff, according to Bloomberg. Xbox already cut 1,600 employees in July in one round of layoffs, and another round is expected before June 2027. The voluntary exit offers show that Microsoft is prioritizing infrastructure buildout, automation and capital efficiency over hiring.

Employment in AI-exposed roles such as software development and customer experience has fallen by more than 4% this year, while roles that rely on AI automation are showing slower job growth, according to Stanford HAI’s Digital Economy Lab. Though AI might not yet be eliminating jobs at scale, companies are spending billions on compute while becoming far more selective about adding personnel.

Tech.title: My iPhone Duo In-Store Experience Almost Has Me Convinced I Need One
Tech.content:
Using an iPhone Duo with my own hands turned out to be a remarkably different experience than I imagined.

After watching (too many of) the first YouTube videos and reading reviews last week, I feel like I have a pretty good handle on what the iPhone Duo is: a small iPad Mini, a squat iPhone that transforms into a big iPhone. I appreciated the translucent window animation when you unfold it. I smiled at the interior glow when the alarm went off in tent mode.

Those are all features. I was looking for experience. You can’t get that from watching videos.

More from CNET

To be up front, I’d already decided that the iPhone Duo isn’t the new iPhone for me. As a photographer (and author of a book about iPhone photography/?pt=CNET), the camera features of the iPhone 18 Pro are objectively superior to what the iPhone Duo offers. And the $2,000 price is a big ask. I’d written off the iPhone Duo as someone else’s luxury.

Now, though, my hands-on time has me wondering if there’s room in my pockets for a Duo.

I spent about 20 minutes with a model at the Apple University Village store in Seattle, so these are first impressions. I defer to my colleague, senior technology reporter Abrar Al-Heeti, who has the most hands-on experience with the iPhone Duo out of anyone at CNET, for her review. “If anything, the Duo’s high cost and limited availability only reinforce that Apple’s foldable isn’t for everyone,” wrote Al-Heeti. “Personally, I have no plans of switching back to a slab phone anytime soon.”

Yes, the opening animation is wonderful

I would go so far as to say that the Duo’s opening effect is everything. It doesn’t need to exist. No one is fooled into thinking the front glass is actually translucent, and if you want to get pedantic, what appears on the inner screen isn’t exactly what you saw on the front screen.

That doesn’t matter.

The iPhone Duo’s opening effect is magical. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET/Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

The transition is polished in a way that is quintessentially Apple. There’s a bit of whimsy, the welcome surprise of something you haven’t seen a phone do before and didn’t expect it to do.

The iPhone Duo itself is not necessary. You can buy perfectly capable, affordable phones that do what you already need a phone to do. But that’s not the point. It shows us and other companies that a foldable phone doesn’t have to just be the same phone experience with a bigger screen.

Multitasking is a new gesture to learn

I had to ask an eagerly helpful Apple employee how to do this. With the Duo’s 7.6-inch main screen open, you can set a separate app on each half of the screen.

I expected that a half-swipe from the bottom would trigger it, but it brought up the app switcher interface instead. Instead, you start with the half-swipe and then drag your finger toward the left or right half of the screen. It’s a novel iOS control specifically for the Duo, but it has iPadOS SplitView vibes – just bypassing needing to use the dock or app window traffic light buttons.

I’m sure people will learn it quickly, but it’s still a new gesture in iOS and iPadOS land.

Browsing apps is a subtle improvement

With the iPhone Duo closed, the home screen is like every other iPhone: swiping left lets you view other app screens until you get to the App Library, which puts apps into categories.

On the inner screen, home screen apps hang out on the right side (keeping that translucent glass effect of the opening animation, above), leaving the left side app-free. (Apple’s demo model had a full-screen-size Photos widget in that space.) Swipe left, however, and the apps slide over to make room for the next “screen” of apps, and so on until the App Library drifts in.

Navigating the home screen on the iPhone Duo.

The easy design solution would be for the very large screen to just show all the apps when you open the phone. Why waste all the pixels on the left side? Big screen means more stuff!

But that would be disorienting. The object permanence of the apps you were just looking at breaks – do they shift to the left so now you’re looking at different apps? Do other apps take up the space at left, even though they’re not “first-page” apps?

No. Because Apple has set expectations for the experience based on the opening animation.

Activating cameras on the screens can require an extra swipe

One thing, in practice, I didn’t catch in videos was how the iPhone Duo handles which screen is used for the camera’s viewfinder. It has four cameras: a selfie camera on the front screen, the main and ultrawide cameras on the back and an under-display selfie camera on the interior.

One great advantage of foldables is being able to open the phone so the front screen shows what the back cameras are seeing – when taking selfies, this means you can use the higher-quality cameras while still seeing how you’re framed. It can also be used as a preview for the subject; you’re taking the photo and looking at the expansive inner screen, while they get to see how you’re framing them in case they have suggestions.

As a photographer, that’s slightly horrifying, because although I’m fine with showing the person some in-progress shots, I don’t want them art-directing me. But I can see how it would be helpful when you’ve asked another person to take your picture; so often I get well-meaning images with acres of space around the edges, and my friends and I as small figures in the middle.

You can activate the outer screen as a camera viewfinder by sliding the unlock control. Jeff Carlson/CNET

On the iPhone Duo, the front screen displays a Slide to Open control to unlock it for use with the Camera app. It’s reminiscent of the very first iPhone’s unlock mechanism. That way, you’re not accidentally activating the screen.

Another way to choose what the outer display shows is by using the Outer Display control on the inner screen. Jeff Carlson/CNET

There’s also a mode control in the top-left corner of the Camera app to specify the role the outer display will play: Duo Preview (described above), Kid Cue (a random Snoopy animation to draw the attention of youngsters who otherwise wouldn’t aim their faces toward the camera long enough for a good shot). There’s also an option to turn the screen off.

So, so swirly

My last hands-on impression also centers on experience, but not in the way I’m sure Apple would like. Unlike prior iPhones, the Duo has many different states, which Apple calls “poses.” The accelerometer tracks not only whether the phone is held vertically or horizontally, but also the angle at which the device is folded and positioned.

The phone can be opened and viewed vertically, for example, and then you bend the screen into a 90-degree angle like a laptop – it changes the content, such as playing a movie on the “top” screen and its playback controls on the “bottom” screen.

Netflix on the iPhone Duo Kerry Wan/CNET

Perhaps the settings need more tuning, but in the several minutes I had with the phone, it seemed to spend a lot more time spinning its interface from horizontal to vertical to upside down. It wasn’t glitching; it was trying to keep up as I turned, folded, unfolded and used the phone.

The canonical definition of “up” on a phone slips away on a device so adaptable. Even more, you need to use the feel of the hardware buttons (which are in unusual locations compared with current iPhones).

Are customers stricken by iPhone Duo vertigo going to return their devices? Not likely. Because, like the multitasking gesture and the translucent opening effect, they’ll adapt to the new experiences the Duo is delivering.

I’ve been here before

After 20 minutes of being an iPhone Duo detective, I am genuinely considering getting one. This isn’t without precedent: When the original iPhone arrived, I fawned over the design and features in the same way as I’m doing here, but I didn’t need one, especially since my Palm Treo was a perfectly good smartphone.

Within a few months, the Treo found its new home in a desk drawer, and I’ve owned iPhones ever since. I’m not saying I’m going to place an iPhone Duo order, but I can’t not say that, either.

If you’re wondering about the iPhone Duo’s durability, something I couldn’t really test in 20 minutes, CNET has designed and constructed a custom machine called the Fold-a-Phone that is currently hard at work testing how many times Apple’s foldable can be opened and closed.

Tech.title: This New Simulation of the Early Universe Is Massive, Detailed and Gorgeous
Tech.content:
The origin of the universe is one of the greatest scientific mysteries of all time. Scientists have developed numerous theories and testable predictions about how the universe began, including the Big Bang model, cosmic inflation and quantum-cosmology proposals.

To test those theories, researchers from the Center for Astrophysics, a collaboration between Harvard and the Smithsonian, assembled the Lumina Project, a simulation of the early universe far larger than any prior one.

The details of the simulation, published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (PDF), describe how regular matter, dark matter and radiation likely interacted during the first 2 billion years of the universe, covering a region equivalent to a cube roughly 1.5 billion light-years on each side.

More from CNET

For reference, the prior champion for the largest early-universe simulation was the Thesan simulation in 2022, which simulated about a billion years of the early universe across a region roughly equivalent to a 300-million-light-year cube.

It does all of this in incredible detail, largely due to observations made by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope and other telescopes that spend considerable time observing the oldest celestial objects. By looking at those ancient space objects, scientists have been able to piece together at least some ideas of what the early universe may have looked like.

There’s a lot of science at work here

The simulation was made on the Frontier supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee. Frontier has around 37,000 GPUs across its system, and the Lumina Project used about 15,000 of them.

That’s what helped the simulation become the largest and most detailed simulation ever made, giving researchers plenty of unique features to work with.

One example is helium reionization, a process that scientists believe took place in the early universe. Back then, the universe was so hot that virtually all matter was ionized, meaning it consisted of charged particles. When the universe cooled about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, atoms started combining together to make regular hydrogen and helium. Then, a short time later (comparatively speaking), the first generation of stars emerged and emitted enough ultraviolet light to reionize nearby hydrogen and helium atoms.

“Lumina follows both hydrogen and helium reionization,” Zier told CNET in an email. “This allows us to study these processes together in one self-consistent simulation, meaning it captures reionization as it occurred while allowing its effects to immediately influence the evolving universe within the model.”

Aaron Smith, an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas and an author on the paper, said the team is incredibly fortunate to be building simulations like Lumina. “For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation,” Smith said in a statement.

The main function of Lumina is to help scientists test and confirm theories about the early universe and gauge whether their understanding of physics aligns with the simulation’s results.

The team has already used the simulation to make some interesting predictions, including that there were “fewer massive galaxies” in the early universe than James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest. The simulation also houses the mysterious little red dots spotted by JWST, which some scientists now believe are black hole stars.

Stunning imagery of the early universe

A side benefit is that the simulation has some truly gorgeous imagery, showing off a lot of interactions of the early universe, including gases at various temperatures mixing together, chemical reactions and the locations of early galaxies and stars. Since the simulation also fills in where dark matter and dark energy would be, the entire thing is a gorgeous litany of colorful clouds, threads and filaments.

Take the above video, for instance. It starts with a wide shot of the entire Lumina simulation volume, then zooms into a single galaxy in virtually empty space, showing how vast this simulation really is. Try pausing the video at almost any point to capture a really cool screenshot.

This next video flies the viewer through a massive halo within the simulation. It starts by adding in various layers, such as dark matter density, gas temperature, gas metallicity (how much heavier elements there are in the cosmic gas, and stellar light. At the end of the video, the layers are turned off, and what you’re left with is a cluster of galaxies.

The Lumina Project has 15 spectacular videos, showcasing everything from gas densities to hydrogen and helium reionization.

Tech.title: MapQuest Has a Feature Google Maps Doesn’t: A License Plate Reader Map
Tech.content:
MapQuest’s app now has a map layer for something most navigation apps leave out: the cameras watching the road. The Surveillance layer, which MapQuest announced Oct. 15, uses small eyeball icons to mark the reported locations of automated license plate readers from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions, Axon and several other companies.

Tap one, and the app shows the camera type, its coordinates and which way it’s pointed. MapQuest’s general manager said drivers asked for the feature, and it arrives as license plate readers face mounting pushback from privacy advocates and lawmakers.

In a post on Bluesky, MapQuest said its app shows locations of license plate readers from Flock and many other companies — Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, Verkada and more.

More from CNET

To activate the feature, open the MapQuest app, tap the Layers icon and turn on the Surveillance option. You will then see tiny eyeballs on the map that indicate where license plate readers are located. If you click on an eyeball, it will show what type of license plate reader it is — dome or fixed, for example — and the exact coordinates.

MapQuest has been riding a wave of relevance, years after being relegated to lower-tier status by the likes of Google, Apple and Waze. In August, MapQuest refused to change Lake Ontario to Lake America in its maps despite President Donald Trump’s executive order. It then muscled into Android Auto to give drivers an alternative to Google Maps on their dashboards.

But MapQuest isn’t the first app to reveal locations of license plate readers. The others include DeFlock, FlockHopper, Pelican and LPR Maps. Some of them rely on crowdsourcing — drivers notify the app when they believe they have spotted a license plate reader and where it is.



Displaying surveillance camera locations was among the top three requests among MapQuest users, general manager Doug Bergen told CNET.



“In the last month, we’ve been inundated with direct requests from our users,” Bergen said. “They want to know where cameras are and what kind they are. Adding that information gives them a clearer picture of the road ahead and more choice in what their map shows.”



Bergen said that camera location data comes from OpenStreetMap, a global map of the world built by volunteers.

The Roads Have Eyes! 👁️Turn on the Surveillance Layer in Map Options to see known license plate readers from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, Verkada, and other outdoor surveillance cameras. — MapQuest (@mapquest.com) 2026-10-15T22:48:59.486Z

Although license plate readers have been around for decades and there are more than 140,000 all over the US, the technology has become highly unpopular. Flock cameras can collect a huge trove of data from a car: its license plate, make, model and color, and its location. Civil liberties groups and others say that all this information — input into law enforcement databases across the country — helps to create a mass surveillance network that can track everyone, not just suspected criminals.

There have been instances of Flock data being misused, such as police officers stalking ex-spouses and girlfriends and people being wrongly pulled over and accused of stealing their cars.

License plate readers are also used for more mundane operations, such as electronic toll collection on roads and bridges, traffic violations, parking enforcement, vehicle repossessions and parking gate activation for access to restricted areas.

I’m surrounded by license plate readers

I tried the new MapQuest feature. Being more of a Google Maps person, I didn’t have the MapQuest app, so I installed it on my phone.

I opened the app, found the Surveillance layer and turned it on. I was greeted by a bunch of eyeballs on the map in my city and county. I clicked on several of them and saw their coordinates and what type they were — dome, fixed, pan/tilt and so on — but I didn’t see the names of the companies that own them.

But at least now I know which streets have eyes on me.

Tech.title: Watch Us Fold the iPhone Duo Thousands of Times on Our Weeks-Long Livestream
Tech.content:
The iPhone Duo wowed us as Apple’s first foldable phone, but it’s time to test out how its first-gen hinge holds up. We’re now testing the $1,999 iPhone Duo using our custom-made folding machine, the Fold-a-Phone, which has been diligently opening and closing the phone since we bought the Duo on Friday.

Learn more: The iPhone Duo Just Passed 55,000 in Our Fold-a-Phone Testing Machine. Can It Beat the Galaxy Z Fold 8?

CNET is livestreaming our iPhone Duo long-term folding test on our YouTube channel, which you can watch embedded here. Our robust in-house machine will open and close the foldable around 20,000 times per day to simulate years of wear and tear on the hinge. You’ll be able to watch this testing on a livestream from our CNET Labs location in Louisville, Kentucky.

More from CNET

Our iPhone Duo folding test is ongoing, with our Fold-A-Phone machine running since Friday. Faith Chihil/CNET

The livestream won’t just be for watching a phone open and close — you’ll also be able to chat with CNET editors who will be available to answer your iPhone Duo questions live in the chat. Will Apple’s first foldable live up to the likes of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold? Will its neat opening animation remain slick over thousands of folds? Join us and find out.

This long-term test will join our iPhone Duo review, which provides a snapshot of what it’s like to be among the first to use Apple’s first foldable phone. If you’re sold on it, check out the best iPhone Duo deals. And if you want to compare even further, you can check out our roundup of the best foldable phones currently available if you want help deciding between the Duo and other folding and flip-style phones from Samsung, Motorola and Google.
